<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication of Fra Giocondo’s edition of Vitruvius to Giuliano de' Medici, following the title page. The author establishes a connection between the Medici family's virtues and the perfection of the arts.</meta>

# To GIULIANO de' Medici, Brother Giovanni Giocondo <note>Giovanni Giocondo (c. 1433–1515), known as Fra Giocondo, was a Franciscan friar, architect, and renowned classical scholar who produced one of the most important early editions of Vitruvius.</note> sends heartiest greetings.

Both the liberal and mechanical arts <note>original: *virtutes tam liberales quam mechanicae*. In the Renaissance, "liberal arts" included subjects like grammar and logic, while "mechanical arts" included architecture and engineering.</note> thrive and are perfected all the more when they are practiced by those who are captivated by their delights and pursue them with tireless and skillful study. This is what I hear of you, Giuliano de' Medici <note>Giuliano de' Medici (1479–1516) was the son of Lorenzo the Magnificent and the brother of Pope Leo X.</note>—an excellent man most devoted to these pursuits—whose reputation is spread abroad: that you do not fall short of your father and ancestors, who were endowed with excellent talent and the greatest virtues.

Indeed, to whom is the most famous Medici family unknown? Through every age, it has been most illustrious with so many and such distinguished leading men. Through you and your brother—though both of you were tossed about by various adverse fortunes in your younger years—the family’s splendor has not diminished; rather, by the wondrous grace of God, it has increased to such an extent that it has even given to our Christian religion a Supreme Pontiff <note>This refers to Giovanni de' Medici, who was elected as Pope Leo X in 1513, just before this edition was published.</note> in your elder brother. He had not yet reached the fortieth year of his age, yet he has surpassed the rank and dignity of kings and empires. To this height he was raised not by the wickedness of simony <note>Simony is the act of buying or selling church offices. Fra Giocondo is praising the Pope by contrasting him with others who might have "bought" their way into the papacy.</note> (as it has done for many others), nor by frauds, nor by immoderate ambition, but by the integrity of his life, the holiness of his character, and the sincere reputation of his virtues. 

For these qualities so bind the affection of souls that we are compelled to love and venerate even those we do not know and whose faces we have never seen. This has recently happened to me; for when I had heard many things worthy of a man about you, as I have said, spread with the highest praise, I did not hesitate to dedicate to you these monuments of my labors concerning the studies and writings of Vitruvius. Since I understood these were to be submitted for a second printing <note>The first edition of Fra Giocondo's Vitruvius was printed in Venice in 1511. This 1513 edition includes revisions and was produced in a smaller, more portable format.</note> under my name, I did not think I should pass them over negligently. Instead, I revised them to make them somewhat better and added them to the treasures of your studies, especially since the person to whom the dedication of the first printing was to be entrusted—which now seems preserved for you by the will of God—passed from this life before he could see the work itself completed.

Receive, therefore, [these tokens] of my spirit's love and veneration, and /

<summary>A formal dedication by Fra Giocondo to Giuliano de' Medici, praising the Medici family's ascent—specifically the election of Pope Leo X—and offering this revised second edition of Vitruvius as a tribute to Giuliano's personal interest in the arts.</summary>
<keywords>Giuliano de' Medici, Fra Giocondo, Vitruvius, Pope Leo X, Medici family, Renaissance architecture, patronage, simony</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page concludes Fra Giocondo’s dedication to Giuliano de' Medici. It transitions from praising the Medici family to explaining the specific value of the book (Vitruvius's *De architectura*) and offering final moral counsel to Giuliano as he takes on a leadership role in Florence.</meta>

...long-standing <note>The transcription begins with the end of the word *longa* (long-standing) from the previous page.</note> evidence concerning you. And since I have not been known to you until now, may it not displease your Excellency <note>original: *claritatem tuam*</note> to know me through these first efforts. For since, through my care, you will have an accurate, useful, and even delightful reading of this author <note>The Roman author Vitruvius, whose work on architecture Giocondo had painstakingly edited for this edition.</note>—whose like you will find very rarely elsewhere—you will find no small harvest of Latin and Greek terms pertaining to architecture, which have even been adopted by our own people. You will also find knowledge of ancient buildings, which includes gnomonics <term>gnomonics: the science of designing and constructing sundials</term> and mechanics <term>machination: in this context, the engineering and construction of machines</term>. In these matters, you will find a wealth of information unparalleled by any other source.

If you examine this work more diligently, you will not only learn the rules of architecture, but you will also emerge thoroughly learned in several other disciplines as well. This will allow you to understand the skill of every craftsman in their own profession, and to see how much the liberal studies <note>The "liberal arts" (grammar, rhetoric, logic, etc.) were seen as the intellectual foundation for the "mechanical" or practical arts.</note> contribute to the mechanical arts, which are to the body like a living spirit.

Therefore, my Giuliano, as an old and somewhat bold man, I ask your pardon for what I have said and for what I might say even more freely. I am fully persuaded that you are a man of great virtue and even greater spirit; however, because the strength of virtues usually grows through praise, and they are more ardently embraced by those whom the virtues themselves embrace, I respectfully advise you of this: as the brother of such a great Pope and easily the leading citizen of the Florentine Republic, conduct yourself with everyone so that you are considered the "delight of our age," just as it is read that the famous Titus <note>A reference to the Roman Emperor Titus, whom the historian Suetonius called "the delight and darling of the human race" (*amor ac deliciae generis humani*).</note> was in his own time. Emulate the justice and piety of the Antonines—both the Pious and the Philosopher <note>The Roman Emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, the latter often called "the Philosopher."</note>.

Although you have, as I said, your father, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers as examples to imitate—all famous for every kind of virtue—I do not think it inappropriate to take examples from those ancient figures as well, especially since they have been praised for such a vast span of time. In this way, from many various and fragrant flowers, you may place a woven and perpetual crown upon your head. You now seem to be born not for yourself alone, but for many others; by favoring their progress, show yourself to them as you would wish each of them to show themselves to you, if fortune or virtue had placed them in the rank you now hold.

Be happy, and fare well, mindful of old Giovanni Giocondo.

<summary>Fra Giocondo concludes his dedication by presenting his edition of Vitruvius as an essential tool for both architectural mastery and general education. He encourages Giuliano de' Medici to emulate the virtues of both his ancestors and the great Roman emperors in his leadership of Florence.</summary>
<keywords>Fra Giocondo, Vitruvius, Giuliano de' Medici, architecture, gnomonics, mechanics, liberal arts, Roman Emperors, Florentine Republic, Renaissance humanism</keywords>

**On the divisions of architecture, regarding the distribution of private and public buildings, and of gnomonics and mechanics.** <term>gnomonics: the science of designing and constructing sundials</term> <term>mechanics: referred to here as "machinationis," the engineering of construction and military machines</term> Chapter III.

**On bricks.** Chapter III.

**On lime.** Chapter V.

## CHAPTERS OF THE TENTH BOOK.

<margin>d</margin>**What a machine is, and its difference from a tool; its origin and necessity.** <note>The marginal "d" is a guide letter for the rubricator to paint a decorative initial "D" for "De" (Concerning). Vitruvius distinguishes between a "machine" (machina), which requires many workers, and a "tool" (organum), which is handled by a single person.</note> Chapter I.
**On hoisting machines for sacred buildings and public works.** <term>hoisting machines: "machinationibus tractoriis," engines used for lifting heavy materials during construction</term> Chapter II.
**On the various names of machines and the method by which they are erected.** Chapter III.
**A machine similar to the one above, to which larger loads can be more safely entrusted, having changed only the windlass into a drum.** <note>original: "colossicotera," a Latinized Greek term referring to machines designed for moving colossal weights or statues.</note> Chapter IIII.
**Another kind of hoisting machine.** Chapter V.
**Ctesiphon’s ingenious method for hauling heavy loads.** <note>Ctesiphon was a Greek architect famous for his work on the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus; he devised a rolling frame to transport massive columns.</note> Chapter VI.
**On the discovery of the quarry from which the temple of Diana at Ephesus was constructed.** Chapter VII.
**On the extension and rotation of machines for lifting weights.** Chapter VIII.
**On the types of devices for drawing water, and first, the drum.** <term>drum: "tympano," a large, hollow water-wheel powered by treading</term> Chapter IX.
**On wheels and drums for grinding flour.** <note>This chapter describes one of the earliest known water-powered mills.</note> Chapter X.
**On the screw which lifts a great quantity of water, but not as high.** <note>original: "coclea," better known today as the Archimedean screw, used for irrigation and drainage.</note> Chapter XI.
**On the Ctesibian machine which lifts water very high.** <note>A double-action force pump invented by Ctesibius of Alexandria.</note> Chapter XII.
**On hydraulic machines by which [musical] organs are made.** <note>The "hydraulis," a water-powered pipe organ.</note> Chapter XIII.
**By what means we may measure the distance traveled when carried by carriage or ship.** <note>Vitruvius describes an early odometer using a gear system to drop small stones into a box at set intervals.</note> Chapter XIIII.
**On the principles of catapults and scorpions.** <term>scorpions: "scorpionum," a type of engine for shooting bolts or arrows</term> Chapter XV.
**On the principles of ballistae.** <term>ballistae: heavy artillery machines used for hurling large stones</term> Chapter XVI.
**On the proportion of stones to be thrown to the size of the ballista’s hole.** Chapter XVII.
**On the tensioning and tuning of catapults and ballistae.** <note>Engineers tuned these weapons by striking the tensioned hair-ropes to achieve a specific musical pitch, ensuring equal power on both sides.</note> Chapter XVIII.
**On offensive and defensive matters, and first, the invention of the battering ram and its engine.** <term>battering ram: "arietis," a heavy timber used to break down walls</term> Chapter XIX.
**On the tortoise for the filling of ditches.** <note>original: "testudine," a wheeled shed or mobile shield that protected soldiers as they approached fortifications.</note> Chapter XX.
**On other types of tortoises.** Chapter XXI.
**The conclusion of the entire work.** Chapter XXII.

-># MARCUS VITRUVIUS ON ARCHITECTURE, BOOK ONE.<-

<insert>To Caesar Augustus</insert>

While your divine mind and power, Emperor Caesar, were gaining possession of the empire of the world—and with all enemies laid low by your unconquered valor, while the citizens were glorying in your triumph and victory, and all conquered nations looked to your command, and while the Roman people and senate, freed from fear, were being governed by your most noble thoughts and counsels—I did not dare to publish my writings on architecture, which I had developed with great thought, fearing that by interrupting at an unsuitable time, I might incur your displeasure. 

When, however, I observed that you have care not only for the common life of all and the establishment of the state, but also for the suitability of public buildings—so that through you, the city was not only increased by the addition of provinces, but the very majesty of the empire might possess distinguished prestige through its public buildings—I did not think I should delay in publishing these works for you at the earliest opportunity. This is because I was first made known to your father <note>original: "parenti tuo." This refers to Julius Caesar, who was the adoptive father of Augustus.</note> through my work, and was a devoted admirer of his character. When the council of the heavens had dedicated him to the dwellings of immortality <note>A reference to the deification of Julius Caesar after his assassination.</note> and had transferred your father’s empire into your power, that same devotion of mine, remaining faithful to his memory, transferred its loyalty to you. Therefore, along with Marcus Aurelius, Publius Minidius, and Gnaeus Cornelius, I was appointed to the preparation of <term>ballistae</term> and <term>scorpions</term> <note>ballistae and scorpions: "balistarum & scorpionum." These were types of ancient Roman artillery; the ballista launched heavy stones or bolts, while the scorpion was a smaller, high-precision catapult for bolts.</note>...

### What Architecture Is and the Education of Architects.
### Chapter 1.

<margin>a</margin>Architecture is a science <term>scientia: here meaning a systematic body of knowledge</term> adorned with many disciplines and various kinds of learning; by its judgment, all works completed by other arts are tested. It is born from practice <term>fabrica: the manual labor and technical execution of a craft</term> and theory <term>ratiocinatione: the intellectual or systematic reasoning behind a design</term>. Practice is the continuous and habitual exercise of experience, which is carried out by hand using whatever material is necessary for a specific design. Theory, however, is that which can demonstrate and explain things crafted with skill through the principles of proportion. Therefore, architects who have strived to be skilled with their hands without formal learning <note>original: "sine litteris," literally "without letters," referring to a lack of a liberal arts education or theoretical study</note> have not been able to achieve an authority corresponding to their labors. On the other hand, those who relied only on theories and learning...

...ecialized design. Those who relied on practice alone were unable to provide a reason for the forms they adopted; they seem to have chased a shadow, not the reality. But those who have mastered both, like men fully armed, have more quickly and with authority attained their goal.

For in all matters, but especially in architecture, these two things are present: that which is signified <note>original: "significatur." This refers to the actual building or the subject at hand.</note> and that which signifies <note>original: "significat." This refers to the theoretical explanation or the drawings that represent the work.</note>. The thing signified is the subject being discussed. That which signifies is the demonstration explained by scientific principles. Therefore, it appears that anyone professing to be an architect ought to be practiced in both areas. Consequently, he must be both naturally gifted and teachable through instruction. For neither talent without instruction, nor instruction without talent, can produce a perfect craftsman.

He should be literate, skilled in drawing <term>graphidos: the art of drafting, sketching, or technical illustration</term>, learned in geometry, and not ignorant of optics; he should be instructed in arithmetic, know many histories, have listened diligently to the philosophers, understand music, not be ignorant of medicine, know the opinions of legal experts, and have knowledge of astrology and the laws of the heavens.

The reasons why this should be so are as follows: An architect must know letters so that he can make his memory more reliable through written notes <term>commentariis: journals or notebooks used for recording professional observations</term>. Next, he must have knowledge of drawing, so that he can more easily delineate <term>deformare: in this context, to sketch out or give form to a concept</term> the appearance of the work he intends through painted illustrations. 

Geometry, moreover, provides many aids to architecture; first, it teaches the use of the straightedge and compasses, from which the layouts of buildings on their sites are most easily managed, along with the alignment of squares, levels, and straight lines. Likewise, through optics <term>opticen: the science of light and vision</term>, light from the heavens is correctly directed into buildings from specific quarters. Through arithmetic, the costs of buildings are calculated, and the principles of measurements...

# THE BOOK

...explained, and difficult questions regarding symmetry <term>symmetriarum: the balanced proportions of parts in relation to the whole</term> are solved through geometric reasoning and methods.

Furthermore, an architect ought to be acquainted with many histories, because they often design many ornaments for their works, and they must be able to provide an account of why they created them to those who ask for the reasoning behind the subjects. 

For example, if someone should place marble statues of women in long robes—which are called <term>caryatids: columns carved in the shape of female figures</term>—in place of columns in a work, and furthermore should position <term>mutules: projecting decorative blocks under a cornice</term> and cornices above them, he will provide this explanation to those who inquire: 

The city of Caryae in the Peloponnese <note>a large peninsula in southern Greece</note> conspired with the Persian enemies against Greece. Afterward, the Greeks, having been gloriously liberated from the war through victory, by common consent declared war on the people of Caryae. Thus, once the town was captured, the men killed, and the city destroyed, they led the matrons <note>original: "matronas"; high-ranking married women</note> away into slavery. 

Nor did they allow these women to set aside their long robes or their matronly ornaments, so that they would not only be led in a single triumphal procession, but would appear to pay the penalty for their city as an eternal example of slavery, weighed down by a heavy insult. For this reason, the architects of that time designed images of these women for public buildings, positioned to carry a heavy burden, so that the punishment for the sin of the people of Caryae <note>original: "caryatium"</note> might be made known to future generations and passed down in memory.

In the same way, the Spartans <note>original: "Lacones"</note>—under the leadership of Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus—defeated an almost infinite number of the Persian army with only a small force at the Battle of Plataea <note>a decisive 479 BCE battle during the Greco-Persian Wars</note>. After celebrating a glorious triumph, they used the spoils and booty of war to construct the Persian Portico <note>original: "porticum Persicam"; a roofed colonnade or porch</note> as a sign of victory for posterity and a trophy dedicated to the praise and courage of the citizens. 

In that place, they positioned statues of the captives dressed in foreign attire <note>original: "barbarico uestis ornatu"</note>, forced to support the roof as a punishment for their pride and as a mark of well-deserved insult. They did this so that enemies would be struck with dread at the sight of such fortitude, and so that citizens, looking upon this example of valor, would be inspired by glory and remain ready to defend their liberty. 

Consequently, since that time, many architects have placed statues of Persians to support <term>entablatures: the horizontal layers of a building (architrave, frieze, and cornice) that rest upon columns</term> and their ornaments. Through this historical motif <note>original: "argumento"</note>, they have greatly increased the magnificent variety and richness of their architectural works.

...also in the conduction of water. For in the water's courses and circuits, and on level plains, and in the force of pressure, natural pockets of air <note>original: "spiritus naturales"</note> are formed in various ways. No one will be able to remedy the problems caused by these unless they have learned the principles of the nature of things from philosophy. Likewise, whoever reads the books of Ctesibius <note>an Alexandrian inventor and the father of hydraulics</note> or Archimedes <note>the famous Greek mathematician and engineer</note>, and others who wrote instructions of this kind, will not be able to understand them unless they have been instructed in these matters by philosophers. 

Furthermore, the architect must understand music so that he has a grasp of the theory of scales <note>original: "canonicam rationem"</note> and mathematical notation. Moreover, he must be able to properly tune <note>original: "temperaturas"</note> ballistae, catapults, and scorpions <note>various types of ancient siege engines and artillery</note>. For in the frames <note>original: "capitulis"</note> on the right and left, there are equal-toned <note>tuned to the same pitch</note> holes through which ropes made of twisted sinew are stretched by means of windlasses and levers. These are not secured or tied off until they produce certain and equal ringing sounds to the ears of the craftsman. For the arms which are enclosed in those tensioned ropes, when they are stretched back, must release the strike equally and simultaneously. If they are not equal-toned <note>in harmonic balance</note>, they will hinder the straight flight of the projectiles. 

Likewise, in theaters, there are bronze vessels placed in chambers under the seats according to mathematical calculations. These, which the Greeks call <term>echeia</term> <note>original: "ἠχεῖα"; sounding vessels or "echoers" used for acoustic amplification</note>, are arranged to create musical harmonies or chords, divided into the intervals of the fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>, the fifth <note>original: "diapente"</note>, and the octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>. This is done so that when the voice of the actor on stage sounds in harmony with these arrangements, it strikes the vessels and is amplified, reaching the ears of the spectators clearer and more pleasingly. No one can build water organs <note>original: "hydraulicas machinas"</note> or other similar instruments without the principles of music. 

Indeed, the architect must also know the discipline of medicine because of the variations of the sky—which the Greeks call <term>climates</term> <note>original: "κλίματα"; referring here to latitudinal zones and their specific weather patterns</note>—and the air...

Since this profession <note>original: "disciplina"</note> is so distinguished and rich in various and numerous fields of study, I do not think anyone can rightly claim to be an architect suddenly, unless they have climbed through these levels of disciplines from childhood, nourished by the knowledge of many letters and arts, and thus reached the very summit <note>original: "summum templum" - literally "the highest temple"</note> of architecture. 

But perhaps it will seem marvelous to unlearned men that a human nature can master such a great number of subjects and hold them in memory. However, when they notice that all disciplines have a connection and communication <term>communicationem</term> <note>original: "cōicationem" - an abbreviated form used in the Latin text</note> with one another, they will easily believe it can be done. For the "circle of learning" <note>original: "Encyclios disciplina" - the root of our word "encyclopedia," referring to a well-rounded education</note> is composed of these parts like a single body. ...marks, and the common connection between all disciplines, and for that reason they learn all things more easily. Therefore, regarding the ancient architects, **Pythius**—who nobly designed the <term>Temple of Minerva at Priene</term><note>A famous 4th-century BCE Greek temple in modern-day Turkey, considered a masterpiece of the Ionic order</note>—says in his commentaries that an architect ought to be able to do more in all arts and sciences than those who, through their own industry and practice, have brought individual subjects to the highest peak of fame.

However, this is not actually achievable in practice. For an architect does not need to be, nor can he be, a grammarian <note>original: "grammaticus"</note> in the way that **Aristarchus** was, though he should not be unlettered <note>original: "agrammatos"</note>; nor a musician like **Aristoxenus**, though he should not be unmusical <note>original: "amusos"</note>; nor a painter like **Apelles**, but he should not be unskilled in drawing; nor a sculptor like **Myron** or **Polyclitus**, but he should not be ignorant of the principles of sculpture; nor, finally, a physician like **Hippocrates**, but he should not be ignorant of medicine <note>original: "aniatrologicus"</note>. He should not be singularly excellent in the other sciences, but rather, not unskilled in them.

For in such a great variety of things, no one can achieve individual perfection, since it is barely within a person's power to even know and perceive their underlying theories. It is not just that architects cannot reach the highest level of execution in all things; even those who focus exclusively on the specific properties of a single art do not all achieve the highest rank of praise. Therefore, if in individual sciences, individual craftsmen—and not even all of them, but only a few in a lifetime—have barely attained nobility, how can an architect (who must be skilled in many arts) do something so miraculous and great as to not only lack for nothing in these fields, but even to surpass all the craftsmen who have applied themselves to single subjects with the greatest industry? Thus, in this matter, **Pythius** appears to have erred, because he did not notice that an art consists of two things...

<meta>This page continues Vitruvius's argument that an architect does not need to be a master of every single discipline, but rather possess a theoretical understanding of many. He is distinguishing between the specialist (who masters the manual "work") and the polymath or architect (who understands the "reasoning").</meta>

->### BOOK<-

...not achieve perfection in all things. For each individual art is composed of two parts: the actual work <note>original: "opus"</note> and its theoretical reasoning <note>original: "ratiocinatio"</note>. Of these, the first—the physical execution of the work—belongs specifically to those who are trained in individual crafts. The second—the theory—is shared by all learned people. 

For instance, both physicians and musicians discuss the rhythm of the pulse and the movement of feet in poetic meter. Yet, if a wound needs healing or a patient must be rescued from danger, the musician will not step in; that task is the specific duty of the physician. Likewise, it is the musician, not the physician, who will play the musical instrument <note>original: "organo"</note> so that the ears may find pleasure in the songs.

Similarly, there is a common ground for discussion between astronomers and musicians regarding the <term>sympathy of the stars</term> <note>The ancient belief that the movements of celestial bodies and musical intervals followed the same mathematical laws of harmony</note> and the harmonies found in squares and triangles, as well as the <term>fourth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron"</note> and the <term>fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente"</note> intervals. With geometers, they share discussions on vision—which is called **optical theory** <note>original: "logos optikos"</note> in Greek. In all other branches of learning, many things—or even all of them—are common property, at least when it comes to theoretical debate. 

However, the actual execution of works, which are brought to a state of elegance through manual labor and practical handling, belongs to those who have been specifically trained in a single art to create them. Therefore, an architect appears to have done more than enough if he possesses a moderate knowledge of the principles and theories of those individual sciences necessary for architecture. This ensures that he does not fail if he is required to judge or approve matters within those arts. 

But those to whom nature has granted such great ingenuity, sharpness, and memory that they can deeply master geometry, astronomy, music, and the other disciplines, go beyond the duties of architects and become **mathematicians** <note>In this context, "mathematici" refers to high-level theoretical scientists whose expertise spans all mathematical and physical sciences</note>. Because of this, they can easily debate any of those disciplines, as they are armed with the many "weapons" of those sciences. Such individuals, however, are rarely found; examples from the past include **Aristarchus of Samos**...

## Chapter II: Of what things Architecture consists.

<margin>a</margin>
Architecture consists of **Order** <note>original: "ordinatio"</note>, which in Greek is called *taxis* <note>original: "τάξις"</note>; **Arrangement** <note>original: "dispositio"</note>, which the Greeks call *diathesis* <note>original: "διάθεσιν"</note>; **Eurythmy** <note>Graceful proportion and beauty in the adjustment of parts</note>; **Symmetry**; **Propriety** <note>original: "decore"</note>; and **Economy** <note>original: "distributio"</note>, which in Greek is called *oikonomia* <note>original: "οἰκοnomía"</note>. 

**Order** is the balanced adjustment of the individual parts of a work, and the comparison of the proportions of the whole arrangement to its symmetry. This is composed of **Quantity**, which in Greek is called *posotes* <note>original: "ποσότης"</note>. Now, Quantity is the module...

...of the members <note>The text begins mid-sentence, concluding the definition of Eurythmy: the beauty and fitness of the proportions</note> from the very nature of the work, and a harmonious result produced by the individual parts in relation to the whole work. 

**Arrangement** <note>original: "dispositio"</note>, however, is the proper placement of things and an elegant effect in the composition of the work, matched with quality. The types of arrangement, which in Greek are called *ideas* <note>original: "ἰδέαι"</note>, are these: **ground plan**, **elevation**, and **perspective**. 

A **ground plan** <note>original: "ichnographia"</note> involves the continuous use of the compass and the ruler, through which the outlines of the building's forms are laid out upon the ground of the sites.

Likewise, **perspective** <note>original: "sciographia"</note> is a sketching of the front and the receding sides, with all lines corresponding to the center of a circle <note>This describes the use of a vanishing point to create the illusion of depth in a drawing.</note>.

->[A woodcut illustration within a rectangular border showing the same building from a perspective view (sciography). The front facade and the receding right side are visible, demonstrating depth and perspective lines.]<-

These types of drawing arise from **thought** and **invention**. **Thought** <note>original: "cogitatio"</note> is care full of study and industry, the result of a purpose achieved through vigilance and pleasure. **Invention** <note>original: "inventio"</note>, however, is the explanation of obscure problems and the method of a new thing discovered with a lively vigor. These are the definitions of arrangement...

of arrangements. **Eurhythmy** <note>original: "Eurythmia"</note> is a graceful appearance and a fitting aspect in the compositions of the members. This is achieved when the members of the work are suitable: the height to the width, the width to the length, and when all parts correspond to the total **symmetry** <note>original: "symmetria"</note> of the whole. Likewise, **symmetry** is the proper agreement between the members of the work itself, and the correspondence between the separate parts and the appearance of the entire figure, based on a fixed module. Just as in the human body there is a symmetrical ratio from the forearm, the foot, the palm, the finger, and the other parts, so it is in the perfection of finished works. And first in sacred buildings, the calculation of symmetries is found either from the thickness of the columns, or from a **triglyph** <note>A tablet with three vertical grooves in a Doric frieze</note>, or from the **module** <note>original: "embate"</note> in a **ballista** <note>A large ancient missile launcher</note> through the hole—which the Greeks call the **peritreton** <note>original: "περίτρητον"</note>—or in ships by the space between the oarlocks, which is called the **two-cubit measure** <note>original: "διπηχαϊκή"</note>; likewise, the logic of symmetries is found from the members of other works.

**Propriety** <note>original: "Decor"</note>, however, is the faultless appearance of a work, approved by things composed with authority. This is achieved by **ritual placement** <note>original: "statione," which the author notes the Greeks call "θεματισμὸς" (thematismos)</note>, or by custom, or by nature. By ritual placement, when temples are built under the open sky <note>original: "sub diuo"</note> and **open to the air** <note>original: "hypetra"</note> for Jupiter the Light-Bringer, and for the Sky, the Sun, and the Moon. For we see the appearances and effects of these gods present in the open and shining world. For Minerva, Mars, and Hercules, **Doric** temples shall be made. For it is fitting that buildings be established for these gods without luxuries, on account of their virtue. For Venus, Flora, Proserpina, and the nymphs of the springs, the **Corinthian** style <note>original: "corinthio genere"</note> will seem to have the appropriate characteristics, because for these goddesses, works that are more slender, flowery, and adorned with leaves and **volutes** <note>Spiral, scroll-like ornaments</note> will seem to increase the rightful propriety due to their delicacy. For Juno, Diana, Father Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, and the other gods who are of the same...

For when sick bodies are moved from a pestilent location to a healthy one, and the use of water from healthy springs is provided, they will recover more quickly. Thus it will happen that, due to the nature of the place, the divinity will receive greater and increased respect with dignity. 

Likewise, there will be natural propriety if **bedrooms** <note>original: "cubiculis"</note> and **libraries** <note>original: "biblyothecis"</note> receive light from the east; if **baths** and **winter apartments** receive light from the winter sunset <note>the southwest</note>; and if **picture galleries** <note>original: "pinacothecys"</note> and those parts which require a constant light receive it from the north, because that region of the sky is neither brightened nor darkened by the course of the sun, but remains certain and unchangeable throughout the whole day. **Distribution** <note>original: "Distributio," often called 'Economy'</note>, however, is the convenient management of resources and the site...

Furthermore, for those powerful individuals by whose counsel the Republic is governed, buildings should be arranged for their specific needs; and overall, the distributions of buildings must be made appropriate for all types of persons.

### On the choice of healthy sites, those which are harmful to health, and from where light is captured. Chapter IV.

*For the city walls themselves, these shall be the principles. First, the selection of the healthiest site. # BOOK I

...[facing the] south <note>original: "meridientem"; the beginning of this word appeared on the previous page</note>, they will not be healthy, because throughout the summer the southern sky grows warm as the sun rises, and at midday it burns.
Likewise, that which faces the west grows lukewarm after sunrise, heats up at noon, and glows hot in the evening. Therefore, by these shifts of heat and cooling, the bodies of those who are in these places are impaired. This can be observed even in things that are not living creatures. For in covered wine cellars, no one takes light from the south, nor from the west, but from the north, because that region never undergoes changes but is perpetually steady and unchanging.
For this reason, granaries that face the course of the sun quickly lose their quality; and provisions <term>provisions: "obsonia," referring to prepared foods or side dishes</term> and fruits that are not placed in that part of the sky which is turned away from the sun’s path are not preserved for long. For heat, when it cooks things through, always strips the air of its stability, and by sucking out natural virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the inherent properties or life-force of a substance</note> with glowing vapors, it dissolves them, and making them soft through fervor, renders them weak.
We observe this even in iron; although it is hard by nature, it becomes so soft when heated by the vapor of fire in furnaces that it is easily worked into every kind of shape. Yet, when that same iron is soft and glowing, if it is cooled by being dipped in cold water, it hardens again and is restored to its original quality.
One may also consider this to be true from the fact that in summer—not only in plague-ridden places but even in healthy ones—all bodies become weak from the heat; whereas through the winter, even those regions that are most pestilential are made healthy, because they are solidified by the cooling temperatures. No less significant is the fact that bodies moved from cold regions into hot ones cannot endure but are dissolved. However, those from hot places...

# BOOK I

### THE FIRST. <note>Refers to the header "PRIMVS," indicating the First Book of the treatise.</note>

...toward the cold regions of the north, bodies not only do not suffer from the change of location in their health, but are even strengthened. For this reason, one must be careful in the placement of city walls to avoid those regions which can scatter heat and drafts toward human bodies. For because all bodies are composed of principles which the Greeks call elements <note>original: "στοιχεῖα"</note>—that is, heat, moisture, the earthy, and air—and by these mixtures in a natural temperament <term>temperament: "temperatura," referring to the specific balance or proportion of the four elements within a body</term>, the qualities of all living creatures in the world are shaped according to their kind.

Therefore, in those bodies where heat exceeds its principles, it kills and dissolves the others with its fervor. These defects are produced by a burning sky from certain directions, when it settles into open veins more than the body can endure from its natural temperament of mixtures. Likewise, if moisture has occupied the veins of bodies and made them unequal, the other principles, as if corrupted by liquid, are diluted, and the virtues of the composition are dissolved. 

Likewise, from the cooling of moisture, winds, and breezes, defects are poured into bodies. No less does the natural composition of air, and even the earthy in the body, weaken the other principles by increasing or decreasing them—the earthy by a fullness of food, the air by the heaviness of the sky.

But if anyone wishes to perceive these things more diligently through the senses, let him observe and attend to the natures of birds, fish, and land animals, and thus he will consider the differences of temperament. For the race of birds has one mixture, fish another, and the nature of land animals has one far different. Birds have less of the earthy, less moisture, a moderate amount of heat, and much air. Therefore, being composed of lighter principles, they more easily [fly] into the force of the air...

...they struggle. But the aquatic nature of fish, which are tempered by heat and composed mostly of air and earthy elements, yet have very little moisture—the less they have of the principles of moisture in their bodies, the more easily they endure in the water. Therefore, when they are brought to land, they leave their life along with the water. Likewise, terrestrial creatures, which are tempered from the principles of air and heat, and have less of the earthy but a great deal of moisture—because their moist parts are abundant—they cannot preserve their life in water for long.

Therefore, if these things appear as we have proposed, and we perceive through our senses that the bodies of animals are composed of these principles, and we have indicated that they suffer and dissolve through excesses or deficiencies, we do not doubt that a more diligent search is necessary so that we may choose the most temperate regions of the sky when <term>salubritas: the quality of being healthy or health-giving; a core requirement for Roman urban planning</term> healthfulness must be sought in the placement of city walls.

Thus, I believe the reasoning of the ancients should be recalled again and again. For our ancestors, from the livestock sacrificed that grazed in those places where either towns or permanent camps <note>original: "castra statiua," referring to long-term military encampments rather than temporary marching camps</note> were being established, would inspect the <term>iocinora: the livers of sacrificed animals, traditionally used in divination (haruspicy) but here used by Vitruvius for biological site-surveying</term> livers; and if they were first found to be livid and defective, they would sacrifice others, doubting whether they were damaged by disease or by a fault in the fodder. When they had tested many and proved the sound and solid nature of the livers resulting from the water and fodder, they would establish the fortifications there. 

If, however, they found them defective, they concluded by evidence that the supply of water and food arising in those places would likewise be pestilential in human bodies; and so they would migrate and change regions, seeking healthfulness in all things. That these things happen, so that the healthy properties of the earth are seen in the fodder and food, it is possible

# BOOK I

### THE FIRST.

One may observe and understand this from the lands of the Cretans, which are located around the Potherenus river, situated in Crete between two cities, Knossos and Gortyna. For livestock graze on both the right and left sides of this river; however, those that graze closest to Knossos are <term>splenetica: suffering from an enlarged or diseased spleen</term>, while those on the other side, near Gortyna, do not have a visible spleen. Consequently, physicians investigating this matter found a herb in those places which the cattle, by chewing on it, had used to shrink their spleens. Thus, by gathering that herb, they now treat those suffering from spleen ailments with this medicine, which the Cretans call <term>asplenon: literally "without a spleen" from the Greek ἄσπληνον; commonly identified as the plant spleenwort</term>. From this, it is possible to know that the properties of locations are naturally pestilential or healthy based on the food and water.

Likewise, if city walls are established in marshes, they will be reasonably situated provided that those marshes are along the sea and face the north, or between the north and the east, and if these marshes are higher than the sea coast. For by digging ditches, an outlet for the water to the coast is created; and when the sea rises during a storm, the overflow into the marshes is stirred up by the movement and, by mixing with the salt water, prevents the various kinds of marsh creatures <note>This likely refers to mosquitoes and larvae, which Vitruvius identifies as the source of "pestilential" air</note> from being born there. Furthermore, those creatures that swim down from higher ground to the coast are killed by the unaccustomed saltiness. 

An example of this can be found in the <term>Gallic marshes: specifically those of Cisalpine Gaul in Northern Italy</term> around Altinum, Ravenna, and Aquileia, as well as other municipal towns in such places nearest to the marshes, which for these reasons possess an incredible healthfulness. However, those marshes that are stagnant and have no flowing outlets, neither through rivers nor ditches—such as the <term>Pontine Marshes: a large wetland in Central Italy notorious in antiquity for malaria</term>—rot as they stand, emitting heavy and pestilential vapors.

Having completed this, he opened a channel from the lake to the sea and thus created a harbor for the town out of the lake. As a result, the people of Salepia now live four miles away from their old town in a healthy location.

Great care should be taken to ensure that the approach for attacking the wall is not easy; instead, the layout should follow the steep edges of the terrain and be designed so that the paths leading to the gates are not straight but angled. When built this way, the right side of those approaching—which is not protected by a shield—will be closest to the wall. <note>Ancient soldiers carried their shields in their left hands, leaving their right sides vulnerable to defenders shooting from the walls above.</note> Furthermore, towns should be laid out not in a rectangular shape, nor with sharp projecting corners, but in a curved fashion, so that the enemy can be seen from many vantage points. In places where corners project, defense becomes difficult, as a corner offers more protection to the attacker than to the defender. I believe the thickness of the wall should be constructed so that armed men passing each other on top can do so without hindrance. Additionally, within the thickness, charred olive-wood ties <note>original: "taleæ oleagineæ ustilatæ"</note> should be inserted as frequently as possible, so that both faces of the wall are bound together (as if by clasps) by these ties, ensuring everlasting stability.

->### BOOK ONE.<-

->B<-

For if the enemy should occupy any part of the wall, those who are fighting back will cut them off, and if they act quickly, they will not allow the enemy to penetrate the remaining parts of the towers and the wall, unless the enemy chooses to throw themselves headlong. Therefore, towers should be made round or **polygonal** <note>original: "πολυγώνιαι" (polygōniai)</note>; for siege engines shatter square towers more quickly, because battering rams <term>battering rams: heavy logs, often tipped with iron, used to smash through masonry</term> break the corners by constant pounding. In rounded structures, however, because the stones are driven toward the center—much like the stones in a wedge or arch—the rams cannot cause damage.

Furthermore, fortifications where the wall and towers are joined with ramparts <term>rampart: a defensive embankment made of earth, providing both height and thickness</term> are significantly safer, as neither rams, nor mining <note>original: "suffossiones" — the practice of digging tunnels under walls to make them collapse</note>, nor other engines are able to harm them. However, the method of the rampart should not be used in all places, but only where there is a flat approach to the walls from high ground outside the city for the purpose of an assault.

Therefore, in such places, ditches <note>original: "fossæ"</note> must first be made with the greatest possible widths and depths; then the foundation of the wall must be sunk into the bottom of the ditch, and it must be built with such thickness that the weight of the earthwork can be easily supported.

Likewise, on the inner side of the substructure, a second foundation must be established at a wide distance from the outer one, so that cohorts <note>A 'cohort' was a standard tactical unit of the Roman army, consisting of about 480 men.</note> can stand upon the wide surface of the rampart to defend it, just as if they were drawn up in a battle line. When these foundations have been set at such a distance from each other, other transverse walls should be placed between them, connected to both the outer and inner foundations and arranged like a comb, in the same way that the teeth of a saw are shaped.

<margin>a The teeth of the saw <note>original: "Serræ dentes" — referring to the zig-zag or serrated pattern of the internal buttressing walls used to hold the earth in place.</note></margin>

For when it is constructed in this manner, the massive weight of the earth is distributed into small sections, and the whole weight, pressing down together, cannot by any means push out the **substructures** <term>substructures: the supporting parts or foundations of a wall built underground or at the base</term> of the wall. Regarding the wall itself, and the material from which it should be built or finished, no fixed rule can be laid down, because we cannot obtain the same resources we might desire in every location. 

Instead, where **squared stones** <note>original: "saxa quadrata" — also known as ashlar masonry, where stones are cut into precise rectangular blocks</note> are available, or flint, or **rubble masonry** <term>rubble masonry: a building technique using rough, unhewn stones (caementum) bound together with mortar</term>, or fired brick, or even sun-dried brick, these should be used. For not every region or local site can have such great advantages of the same kind—as in Babylon, where they abound in liquid **bitumen** <note>bitumen: a naturally occurring tar-like petroleum product used as a powerful adhesive mortar</note> and have walls made of fired brick instead of lime and sand—so that by using these materials, a wall might be brought to completion without flaw for all eternity.

## On the division of works that are within the walls, and their arrangement, so that the harmful blasts of the winds may be avoided.

### Chapter VI.

<margin>The arrangement of streets.</margin>Once the city walls have been completed, there follows the division of the areas within the wall, and the directions of the **broad streets** <term>broad streets: "plateae," the main thoroughfares of a Roman city</term> and the **narrow alleys** <term>narrow alleys: "angiportus," the smaller side streets or lanes</term>, oriented according to the regions of the sky. These will be directed correctly if the winds are prudently shut out from the alleys; for if the winds are cold, they cause discomfort; if hot, they spoil the air; if humid, they do harm. Therefore, this defect must be avoided, and care must be taken so that what occurs in many cities does not happen here—just as in the town of Mytilene on the island of Lesbos, which is magnificently and elegantly built, but not prudently situated. In that city, when **Auster** <note>original: "Auster" — the South Wind</note> blows, the people fall ill; when **Corus** <note>original: "Corus" — the North-West Wind</note> blows, they cough; and when **Septentrio** <note>original: "Septentrio" — the North Wind</note> blows, they are restored to health, but they cannot stand in the alleys and streets because of the severity of the cold. 

Wind is a flowing wave of air, with an uncertain overflow of motion. It is born when heat strikes moisture, and the force of the heat squeezes out the power of the blowing spirit. That this is true can be seen from **bronze aeolipiles** <term>aeolipiles: hollow metal vessels with a tiny opening, used as a scientific toy or demonstration to show how heat turns water into a pressurized "wind" or steam</term>, and we can express the truth of the divine, hidden laws of the heavens through these artistic inventions of things. For bronze aeolipiles are made hollow, having a very narrow point through which water is poured; they are then placed near a fire, and before they grow hot, they have no spirit, but as soon as they begin to boil, they produce a powerful blast toward the fire.

In this way, one may understand and judge the great and immense principles of the nature of the heavens and the winds from a small and very brief demonstration. For if the winds are shut out, they will not only create a healthy environment for strong bodies, but even if any diseases should happen to arise from other causes—diseases which, in other healthy places, require treatment by contrary medicines—they will be cured more quickly in these locations because of the temperate climate resulting from the exclusion of the winds. 

The ailments that are difficult to cure in the regions described above <note>The drafty or poorly oriented cities mentioned previously</note> are these: **head colds** <note>original: "gravitudo"</note>, **arthritis** <note>original: "arthretis"</note>, **cough** <note>original: "tussis"</note>, **pleurisy** <note>original: "pleuritis"</note>, **consumption** <note>original: "phthisis" — a wasting disease, usually tuberculosis</note>, **spitting of blood**, and others that are treated not by **depletion** <term>depletion: "detractionibus," medical procedures like bloodletting or purging intended to remove excess humors</term>, but by **restoration** <term>restoration: "adiectionibus," treatments that add nourishment or strength to the body</term>. These are difficult to treat, first because they are contracted from the cold, and secondly because [the body] being exhausted...

...when their strength has been exhausted by disease, the agitated air—stirred by the movements of the winds—thins them out further. It draws the vital moisture <note>original: "succum" — literally "sap" or "juice," referring here to the bodily humors necessary for health</note> out of their sickened bodies and makes them even more emaciated. On the other hand, air that is gentle and thick, which has no harsh drafts or frequent fluctuations, provides a steady stability that adds strength to their limbs; it nourishes and restores those who are afflicted by these diseases.

Some authors have been content to say there are four winds: from the equinoctial east, **Solanus** <note>The East wind</note>; from the south, **Auster**; from the equinoctial west, **Favonius** <note>The West wind</note>; and from the north, **Septentrio**. However, those who have investigated the matter more diligently have handed down that there are eight. This was most notably the work of **Andronicus of Cyrrhus** <note>A Greek astronomer of the 1st century BCE</note>, who even set up a model in Athens: an octagonal marble tower. On each of the eight sides of the tower, he designed carved images of the individual winds, each facing the direction from which it blows. Above that tower, he fashioned a marble cone, and on top of it, he placed a bronze **Triton** <note>A mythological sea-god, often shown with a human torso and a fish tail</note> holding out a rod in his right hand. He engineered the figure so that it would be turned around by the wind and always stand facing the breeze, holding the pointer-rod directly over the image of the wind that was currently blowing.

Therefore, they are arranged as follows: between **Solanus** <note>East</note> and **Auster** <note>South</note>, blowing from the direction of the winter sunrise <note>original: "ab oriente hyberno" — the southeast</note>, is **Eurus**. ### FIRST.

...from where the blasts of the winds certainly blow. Since this has been so thoroughly established, so that their regions and origins may be found, the following method of reasoning should be used. Let a marble leveling-slab <note>original: "amussium," a tool used by masons to ensure a surface is perfectly flat</note> be placed according to a level in the middle of the city walls, or let the location be so polished according to a straightedge and level that a leveling-slab is not needed. Upon the middle center of this spot, let a bronze gnomon <note>the vertical rod of a sundial</note> be placed—a tracker of shadows, which in Greek is called a shadow-tracker <note>original: "σκιωτὴρ" (skiatēr)</note>. Around the fifth hour before noon, the outermost tip of the gnomon’s shadow must be taken and marked with a point. Then, with a compass opened to the point that marks the length of the gnomon’s shadow, a circular line should be drawn from the center. Likewise, the growing afternoon shadow of that same gnomon must be observed; when it touches the line of the circle and creates an afternoon shadow equal to the morning shadow, it must be marked with a point. From these two marks, an intersection should be drawn with a compass, and through this intersection and the middle center, a line should be extended to the edge so that the southern and northern regions may be established.

# BOOK ONE

## FIRST.

The layouts of the districts, streets, and alleys should be directed according to these principles. By these methods and this division, the annoying force of the winds will be shut out from dwellings and neighborhoods. For when streets are aligned directly against the paths of the winds, the constant rush and blasts from the open sky, channeled into the narrow throats of the alleys <note>original: "angiportorum," referring to narrow, secondary lanes</note>, will sweep through with even more violent force. For these reasons, the directions of the neighborhoods must be turned away from the regions of the winds, so that as the winds arrive at the corners of the city blocks <note>original: "insularum," literally "islands," the Roman term for a block of buildings surrounded by streets</note>, they may be broken and, being repelled, dissipated.

There are, however, many other names and blasts of winds derived from specific locations, rivers, or mountain storms. Furthermore, there are the morning breezes <note>original: "aurae matutinae"</note>: as the sun emerges from the part of the earth below us, its movement strikes the moisture of the air; as it climbs with force, it pushes and squeezes out the breath of these early morning breezes. Those that persist after the sun has risen are classified as **East Winds** <note>original: "euri venti"</note>. It is for this reason—because it is generated from the breezes <note>original: "auris"</note>—that the Greeks appear to have named that wind *Eurus* <note>original: "εὖρος"</note>. Likewise, the Greek word for 'tomorrow' <note>original: "αὔριον", aurion</note> is said to be named after these morning breezes.

There are, nonetheless, some who deny that **Eratosthenes** <note>The scholar mentioned on the previous page who calculated the Earth's size</note> was able to calculate the true measurement of the world's circumference. Yet, whether that measurement is perfectly accurate or not, it cannot prevent our writing from establishing true boundaries for the [wind] regions...

# BOOK ONE

...regions from which the spirits of the winds arise. Therefore, if this is the case, it will only mean that the individual winds do not have a fixed ratio of measurement, but rather possess either greater or lesser forces. Since these matters have been briefly explained by us, in order that they may be more easily understood, I have decided to set out two diagrams—or as the Greeks call them, **figures** <note>original: "σχήματα", *schemata*</note>—at the end of the volume. One is designed so that it appears from where the specific spirits of the winds arise; the other shows how the harmful blasts may be avoided by directing the alleys and streets <note>original: "uicorum & platearum"</note> in directions opposite to the winds' force.

There shall be a center point on a leveled surface, where the letter **a** is placed. The morning shadow of the **gnomon** <term>gnomon: the vertical rod of a sundial that casts a shadow to indicate time or direction</term> shall be marked at point **b**. Then, from the center at point **a**, with the **compasses** <note>original: "circino"</note> opened to that shadow mark at **b**, a circular line <note>original: "linea rotundationis"</note> is drawn around. The gnomon is then replaced where it was before, and one must wait while the shadow decreases and then, by growing again, becomes equal to the morning shadow in the afternoon. Where it touches the circular line, there shall be the letter **c**. 

Then, from the mark at **b** and the mark at **c**, let an intersection be described with the compasses at point **d**. Next, through the intersection at **d** and the center, let a line be drawn to the edge, on which will be the letters **e** and **f**. This line will be the indicator of the **southern** <note>original: "meridianae"</note> and **northern** <note>original: "septentrionalis"</note> regions. 

Then, a sixteenth part of the entire circumference must be taken with the compasses, and the center of the compasses must be placed on the southern line where it touches the circle at letter **e**, marking points to the right and left, where the letters **g** and **h** will be. Likewise, in the northern part, the center of the compasses must be placed on the circle and the northern line, where the letter **f** is, marking to the right and left, where the letters **i** and **k** are. And from **g** to **k**, and from **h**...

-># BOOK I #<-

## On the selection of sites for the common use of the city.

### Chapter VII.

Once the alleys have been divided and the broad streets established, we must explain the selection of sites for the convenience and common use of the city, regarding sacred buildings, the **forum** <term>forum: the central public square used for judicial and civic business</term>, and other shared spaces. If the city walls are situated along the sea, the area where the forum is to be established should be chosen nearest to the harbor. If, however, the city is inland, the forum should be placed in the very center of the town.

For the sacred buildings of those gods under whose protection the city is chiefly seen to reside—namely **Jupiter**, **Juno**, and **Minerva**—sites should be assigned on the highest ground, from which the greatest part of the city walls can be seen. **Mercury**, however, should be placed in the forum, or, as is the case for **Isis** and **Serapis**, in the marketplace <term>emporio: a commercial district or trading center</term>. **Apollo** and **Father Liber** <note>original: "Libero"; an ancient Italian deity of fertility and wine, often identified with the Greek Dionysus or Roman Bacchus</note> should be placed near the theater.

For **Hercules**, in those cities that do not possess gymnasia or amphitheaters, his site should be at the circus. For **Mars**, the site should be outside the city but near the training field <note>original: "campum"; referring to an open area for military exercise like the Campus Martius in Rome</note>. Likewise, **Venus** should be located near the harbor.

This arrangement is also prescribed in the traditional writings of the **Etruscan diviners** <term>haruspices: priests who interpreted the will of the gods, often by inspecting the entrails of sacrificial animals</term>. They held that temples for **Venus**, **Vulcan**, and **Mars** should be placed outside the walls so that lustful desires do not become customary among the youth or the mothers of families within the city. Furthermore, by drawing the power of **Vulcan** away from the residential buildings through religious rites and sacrifices, the city's structures may be seen as liberated from the fear of fire. As for the divinity of **Mars**, when he is honored outside the walls, there will be no armed conflict among the citizens; instead, he will preserve the city from the dangers of war by defending it against external enemies.

Likewise, **Ceres** should have her place outside the city in a location that people do not need to visit frequently, except for the purpose of sacrifice. This site must be protected with strict religious purity and holy conduct. For the other gods, sites should be chosen that are suitable to the specific requirements of their 

<meta>catchword: temples</meta>

**Dinocrates** the architect, relying on his creative thoughts and skill, set out from Macedonia to join the army when Alexander was coming into power, desiring a royal recommendation. From his homeland, he brought letters from relatives and friends to the high-ranking officers and the **courtiers** <term>purpuratos: literally "those dressed in purple," referring to the elite officials of the royal inner circle</term>, so that he might have easier access. Although they received him kindly, and he requested to be brought before Alexander as soon as possible, they were slow to act, waiting for what they deemed a "fitting time." 

Consequently, Dinocrates, feeling that they were mocking him, sought help from his own resources. He was of very tall stature, with a pleasing face, and possessed the greatest beauty and dignity of form. Trusting, therefore, in these natural gifts, he set aside his clothing at his lodging, anointed his body with oil, crowned his head with a wreath of **poplar leaves** <note>original: "populea fronde"; the poplar was sacred to Hercules, whose appearance Dinocrates was attempting to mimic to grab Alexander's attention</note>, and over his left shoulder...

**covered himself with a lion skin**, and holding a club in his right hand, he marched toward the tribunal where the King was administering justice. <note>Dinocrates dressed as the hero Hercules—who was traditionally depicted with a lion skin and club—knowing that Alexander claimed descent from him.</note> When the novelty of his appearance had distracted the people, Alexander noticed him. Marveling at the sight, the King ordered that a path be cleared for him to approach and asked who he might be.

"I am Dinocrates," he replied, "a Macedonian architect, who brings to you ideas and designs worthy of your renown. For I have shaped **Mount Athos** into the figure of a man. In his left hand, I have designed the walls of a vast city; in his right, a **ritual bowl** <term>pateram: a shallow ceremonial dish used for pouring offerings to the gods</term> to catch the water of all the rivers on that mountain, so that it might flow from there into the sea."

Alexander was delighted by the logic of the design, but immediately asked if there were fields nearby that could support the city with a **grain supply** <term>frumentaria ratione: the logistical system for providing bread and wheat to a population</term>. When he discovered this was not possible except by transport from overseas, he said: "Dinocrates, I notice the excellence of this composition and am delighted by it; but I observe that if anyone were to establish a colony in such a place, his judgment would be condemned. For just as a newborn infant cannot be nourished without the nurse’s milk, nor be led through the stages of growing life, so a city cannot grow without agricultural lands and their harvests flowing within its walls. It cannot maintain a large population without an abundance of food, or sustain its people without plenty. Therefore, just as I think your design is to be praised, I judge the location to be unsuitable. However, I want you to stay with me, for I intend to make use of your services."

From then on, Dinocrates did not leave the King's side and followed him into **Egypt**. There, when Alexander had noticed a naturally safe harbor, an excellent site for a **trading center** <term>emporium: a major hub for international commerce</term>, grain fields throughout all of Egypt, and the great benefits of the massive Nile River, he ordered Dinocrates to build a city in his own name: **Alexandria**. And so...

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

**Dinocrates, recommended by his appearance and the dignity of his physique**, reached such renown. But for me, Emperor <note>Augustus Caesar, to whom Vitruvius dedicated his work.</note>, nature did not grant height; age has lined my face, and ill health has sapped my strength. Therefore, since I have been abandoned by these physical advantages, I shall strive to reach recognition through the help of my scientific knowledge and my writings, as I hope to do.

In the first volume, I wrote about the duties of architecture and the boundaries of the art, as well as the city walls and the division of building sites within those walls. The proper order would now follow with sacred temples, public buildings, and then private houses—explaining what their **proportions** <term>symmetriis: the harmonious relationship between the parts of a building and the whole</term> and measurements should be. However, I decided I should not put those topics first. Instead, I must first explain the supply of materials from which buildings are completed once they are brought together, describing the structural methods and the properties they possess in use, as well as the natural principles by which they are tempered. 

But before I begin to explain these natural materials, I will first set forth the principles of buildings—where their beginnings arose and how the invention of such things grew. I shall follow the paths of antiquity regarding the nature of things, and the works of those who dedicated themselves to the beginnings of civilization and the refined inventions found in their writings. Therefore, I shall explain these things just as I was taught by them.

### *On the life of primitive men, and on the beginnings of civilization and of shelters and their improvements. Chapter 1.*

In the ancient way, men were born like wild beasts in woods, caves, and groves, and they lived their lives by eating wild food. Meanwhile, in a certain place, dense trees were agitated by storms and winds; rubbing their branches against one another, they sparked a fire. Terrified by the fierce flame—

# BOOK SECOND

...been granted by nature, above all other animals, the ability to walk not prone but upright, so that they might behold the magnificence of the universe and the stars. Likewise, with their hands and joints, they could easily handle whatever task they wished. In that gathering, some began to construct shelters of foliage, others to dig caves beneath mountains; some, imitating the nests and construction of swallows, made places to take shelter out of mud and twigs. Then, by observing the shelters of others and adding new ideas to their own thoughts, they improved the designs of their huts day by day. 

Since humans were of a nature both imitative and teachable, and as they took pride in their daily inventions, they showed the results of their buildings to one another. By thus exercising their talents in competition, their standards and skills were improved every day. First, they wove walls by erecting forked posts and weaving twigs between them, which they then covered with mud. Others, drying clods of mud into sun-dried bricks, built up walls, binding them together with timber. To avoid the rains and the heat, they covered these with reeds and foliage. Later, when these roofs could not withstand the rains of winter storms, they created gables <term>fastigia: the sloped ends of a roof that form a triangle; a pediment</term> and, by applying a coating of mud and sloping the roofs, they allowed the rainwater to run off.

We can observe that architecture was established from these origins by looking at the fact that, to this day, foreign nations still build using these methods. For instance, in Gaul, Spain, Lusitania <note>modern-day Portugal</note>, and Aquitaine, buildings are constructed with oak shingles or thatch. Among the nation of the Colchians <note>An ancient kingdom on the Black Sea, in modern-day Georgia</note> in the region of Pontus, because of the abundance of forests, they lay whole trees flat on the ground to the right and left, leaving a space between them as wide as the length of the trees allows. At the ends of these, other trees are placed across them, which enclose the mid-

At Athens, the Areopagus <note>The "Hill of Ares," where a famous council met; Vitruvius points to an ancient mud-roofed building there as a relic of the past</note> remains a specimen of antiquity to this day, covered with mud. Likewise, on the Capitoline Hill, the Hut of Romulus <note>A sacred site in Rome where the legendary founder's original thatch hut was supposedly preserved</note> serves as a reminder and a sign of ancient customs, being roofed with sacred straw. By these signs, we can judge the ancient inventions of buildings, reasoning that they were constructed in such a manner.

However, as their hands became more practiced <note>original: "tritiores," meaning "more worn" or "rubbed smooth" through frequent use</note> by building every day, and by exercising their clever talents through practice, they arrived at the arts through habit. Then, the diligence added to their spirits ensured that those who were more studious in these matters proclaimed themselves to be craftsmen <term>fabros: builders, smiths, or skilled artisans</term>. Since these things were first established in this way, and since Nature had not only endowed humans with senses like the other animals, but had also armed their minds with thoughts and deliberations, and had placed the other animals under their power, they then progressed step by step from the construction of buildings to other arts and disciplines. Thus, they led themselves from a wild and rustic life to a gentle civilization <term>humanitatem: humanity, culture, or civil refinement</term>. Then, building up their spirits and looking forward with greater thoughts...

->### BOOK II<-

...inventions born from a variety of arts, they began to complete not just huts, but even houses built upon foundations with walls of brick <term>lateritijs parietibus: walls made of sun-dried or fired bricks</term>, or constructed from stone, and covered with timber <note>original: "materia," which Vitruvius typically uses to refer specifically to building timber</note> and tiles. Then, as their judgment wandered through the observations of their studies, they led their craft from uncertain methods to the certain principles of symmetry <term>symmetriarum rationes: the mathematical relationships and proportions between the various parts of a building</term>. After they noticed that nature’s offspring of materials were profuse, and that an abundant supply for building had been provided by her, they nurtured this supply by working with it; having increased it through the arts, they adorned it with pleasures for the elegance of life. Therefore, I will speak—as well as I can—about those things which are suitable for use in buildings, what qualities they possess, and what virtues they have. 

But if anyone wishes to argue about the order of this book, and thinks it ought to have been established first, let him not think I have erred. I will give my reason thus: when I was writing the "body of architecture" <note>The complete treatise or systematic collection of architectural knowledge</note> in the first volume, I thought I should explain with what learnings and disciplines it is adorned, define its types with boundaries, and describe the things from which it was born. Therefore, I declared there what an architect ought to be. Consequently, in the first book I spoke of the duty of the art; in this one, I will discuss the natural properties of materials and what use they have. For this book does not profess to explain the birth of architecture as a concept, but rather where the origins of buildings were established, and by what methods they were nurtured and progressed step-by-step to this current definition. Therefore, the arrangement of this volume is in its proper order and place. 

Now I shall return to my purpose. I will reason about the resources <note>original: "copijs," referring to the abundance of natural building materials</note> suitable for the completion of buildings—how they are seen to be procreated by the nature of things, and by what mixtures the joining of their first principles <note>This refers to the ancient theory that all matter is composed of a mixture of the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note> are tempered—so that these matters are not obscure, but clear to readers. For no types of materials, nor...

...bodies, nor can things be born without a coming together of principles <term>principiorum coetu: the gathering or assembly of the fundamental elements of matter</term>, nor can they be subjected to the intellect; nor otherwise does the nature of things allow the precepts of physicists to have true explanations, unless the causes which are in these things—how and why they are so—have demonstrations through subtle reasoning.

## On the principles of things according to the opinions of philosophers.
### Chapter II.

Thales indeed first thought that water was the principle of all things. Heraclitus of Ephesus—who, on account of the obscurity of his writings, was called by the Greeks *Skoteinos* <note>original: "σκοτινὸς," meaning "The Obscure" or "The Dark One"</note>—thought it was fire. Democritus and his follower, Epicurus, thought it was atoms—which our people have called "un-cuttable bodies" <note>original: "insecabilia corpora"</note> and some have named "indivisibles." The discipline of the Pythagoreans, however, added air and the earthy element to water and fire. Therefore, even if Democritus did not name specific materials but only proposed indivisible bodies, he seems to have meant these very elements; for since they are distinct, they are neither gathered together, nor do they suffer destruction <note>original: "internitionem," referring to complete annihilation or internal decay</note>, nor are they divided by cutting, but through eternal time they perpetually retain an infinite solidity within themselves. 

Since, therefore, all things seem to come together and be born from the meeting of these elements, and since these were distributed by the nature of things into infinite kinds, I thought it necessary to explain the varieties and differences of their use, and what qualities each would have in buildings <note>original: "aedificijs"</note>. Thus, when these things are known, those who intend to build will not make mistakes, but will prepare supplies for their buildings that are perfectly suited for use.
