### On bricks. Chapter III.

Therefore, I will first speak about **bricks** <term>lateribus: sun-dried mud bricks, which were the standard wall-building material before the widespread use of fired bricks</term>, and from what kind of earth they ought to be formed. They should not be made from sandy, gravelly, or gritty mud <term>luto: the raw clay or mud mixture used for brickmaking</term>, because when bricks are made from these types, they first become heavy; then, when they are splashed by rain while in the walls, they crumble and dissolve; and the **straw** <term>paleae: chaff or straw added to the clay to act as a binder and prevent shrinkage cracks</term> placed in them does not hold together because of the roughness of the soil.

Instead, bricks should be made from white chalky earth, or from **red earth** <term>rubrica: a red ochre or clay-rich soil</term>, or even from **coarse sand** <note>original: "masculo sabulone," literally "male sand." In Roman technical writing, "male" often denoted a coarser, stronger, or more robust variety of a material.</note>. These types, because of their lightness, possess strength; they are not heavy to work with and are easily stacked.

They should be formed during the spring and autumn so that they may dry at a uniform pace. Those prepared during the **summer solstice** <term>solstitium: the height of summer</term> are faulty because the sun fiercely bakes the outer skin, making them appear dry on the surface while they remain damp inside. Later, as the interior dries and shrinks, it breaks through the outer dry layer; thus, becoming full of cracks, they are made weak.

Bricks will be most useful if they have been formed two years before use, for they cannot dry thoroughly in less time. When they are built into a wall while fresh and not dry, and the **plaster** <term>tectorio: a protective and decorative coating of lime and sand, often called stucco</term> is applied and hardens into a rigid layer, the bricks settle as they dry and cannot maintain the same height as the plaster. Being moved by this shrinkage, they no longer adhere to the plaster but are separated from the bond. Consequently, the plaster—separated from the structure and being too thin to stand on its own—breaks. The walls themselves, settling haphazardly, are ruined.

For this reason, the people of **Utica** <note>original: "Uticenses," the inhabitants of Utica, an ancient Phoenician and Roman city in modern-day Tunisia, famous for its strict building standards.</note> only use bricks in wall construction if they are dry and have been formed five years prior, and only after they have been approved by the authority of a magistrate.

In Farther Spain <note>original: *Hispania ulteriore*</note> at Calentum, in Gaul at Marseilles <note>original: *Massilia*</note>, and in Asia at Pitanae, there are bricks which, once molded and dried, float when thrown into water. The reason they are able to float seems to be that the earth from which they are molded is like pumice; because it is light and has been solidified by the air, it does not admit nor soak up liquid. Therefore, since the material has a light and porous quality and does not allow the power of moisture to penetrate its body, no matter what its weight may be, it is forced by the nature of things (just like pumice) to be supported by the water. These bricks have great practical advantages, as they are not heavy when used in buildings, and once they are molded, they are not dissolved by the weather.

### On Sand. Chapter 4.

<margin>i</margin>
In masonry structures <term>cementitijs structuris: walls made of rubble stones set in mortar</term>, the first thing to investigate is the sand, to ensure it is suitable for mixing into the material and that it does not have soil mixed into it. The types of quarried sand <term>fossiciae: sand dug from pits rather than taken from water sources</term> are these: black, gray, red, and "carbuncle" <note>original: *carbunculus*; likely referring to a reddish volcanic sand or pozzolana</note>. Of these, the best will be the one that makes a crunching sound when rubbed in the hand; however, sand that is earthy will lack that roughness. Likewise, if it is thrown onto a white garment and then shaken or brushed off, it will be suitable if it does not stain the cloth nor leave any dirt behind. But if there are no sand-pits from which it may be dug, then it must be sifted from rivers or from gravel beds, or even from the seashore. However, sea sand has these flaws when used in structures: it dries with difficulty, and a wall cannot bear being continuously loaded <note>i.e., built higher without pausing</note> unless it is allowed to rest and settle at intervals.

-># SECOND [BOOK]<-

...nor does it support vaulting <term>concamarationes: arched or vaulted ceilings</term>. Sea sand, moreover, has this further drawback: when plastering is applied to walls made with it, the salt it releases dissolves the plaster. Quarried sands <term>fossiciae: sand dug from pits</term>, however, dry quickly in structures, the plaster remains stable, and they support vaulting—but only if they are used fresh from the pits. For if they lie out too long after being dug up, they are broken down by the exposure to the sun, moon, and frost, and turn to earth.

Thus, when they are thrown into a masonry structure, they cannot hold the rubble stones <term>cementa: small stones or broken pieces used in Roman concrete</term> together, but instead crumble and slip away, and the walls cannot support the loads. However, while fresh quarried sands have such great virtues in structures, they are not as useful for plastering; because of their richness <note>In this context, "richness" refers to a high concentration of minerals or clay that makes the mixture too "fat" and prone to shrinking</note>, the lime mixed with chaff <note>original: *palea*; while most editions read *harena* (sand) here, this text specifies chaff, which was sometimes added to plaster to prevent cracking</note> cannot dry out without cracking due to its intensity. River sand, on the other hand, because of its leanness—as is seen in *signinum* <term>signinum: a waterproof material made of lime, sand, and crushed pottery</term>—achieves solidity in plastering through the pounding of beaters <note>Referring to the process of "tamping" or beating the plaster to compact it and remove air</note>.

## On Lime. Chapter V.

<margin>d</margin>
Now that the supply of sand has been explained, care must also be taken regarding lime, to ensure it is burned from white stone or flint. That which is made from dense and harder stone will be more useful in construction <term>structura: the core masonry of the wall</term>, while that made from porous stone is better for plastering. When the lime has been slaked <note>original: *extincta*; the process of adding water to quicklime to make it usable</note>, it should be mixed with the sand in such a way that if it is quarried sand, three parts of sand and one of lime are blended together. If, however, it is river or sea sand, two parts of sand should be added to one of lime. For in this way, there will be a proper ratio for the consistency of the mixture. Also, in the case of river or sea sand, if one adds a third part of crushed and sifted pottery <term>testa: fragments of broken bricks or terracotta</term>, it will make a better consistency of the material for use.

--- Page 66 ---
<meta>This page concludes Chapter 5 of Book 2, explaining the chemical and physical transformation of limestone into lime through heat. It then begins Chapter 6, introducing the unique properties of volcanic ash from the region of Naples.</meta>

->BOOK<-

When lime receives water and sand, it strengthens the masonry; the reason for this seems to be that stones, like all other bodies, are tempered by the four principles <note>Referring to the classical elements: air, water, earth, and fire</note>. Those that have more air are soft; those with more water are made flexible by the moisture; those with more earth are hard; and those with more fire are more brittle. Therefore, if these stones—before they are cooked <note>original: *coquantur*; meaning heated in a kiln to create quicklime</note>—are merely crushed and mixed with sand and thrown into a structure, they will neither solidify nor be able to hold the masonry together. But when they are cast into a furnace and seized by the intense heat of the fire, they lose the strength of their original solidity; then, with their internal forces burnt out and exhausted, they are left with open and empty pores <term>foraminibus: small openings or channels within the material</term>.

Therefore, when the liquid and air within the body of the stone have been exhausted and stripped away, leaving only a residual latent heat, the stone receives a new power once it is dipped in water before that heat can escape. As the moisture penetrates the gaps of the pores, it begins to boil <note>original: *conferuescit*; describing the violent, heat-producing chemical reaction of "slaking" lime</note>. Once cooled in this way, the lime expels the heat from its body. Furthermore, the stones do not return to their original weight after being removed from the furnace; even though they stay the same size, it is found that once the liquid has been boiled away, they have decreased in weight by about a third. Therefore, because their pores and gaps are now open, they greedily pull the mixture of sand into themselves and bond together. As they dry, they unite with the rubble stones <term>cementis: small, rough stones used in Roman concrete</term> and create the solidity of the building.

## SECOND BOOK

...[When mixed] with lime and rubble, it not only provides superior strength to other buildings, but even massive piers which are constructed in the sea solidify under water. This seems to occur for the following reason: beneath these mountains, both the earth is hot and springs are frequent; these would not exist unless there were massive fires of burning **sulfur**, **alum**, or **bitumen** deep in the depths. Therefore, the deep fire and the vapor of the flames, passing through the gaps and burning within, make the earth soft and porous. Consequently, the **tufa** <term>tophus: a light, porous volcanic rock</term> produced there is absorbent and devoid of moisture.

Thus, when these three things <note>Vitruvius refers to the lime, the volcanic ash, and the stone rubble, all of which have been "fired" or processed by intense heat</note>, processed by the intensity of fire in a similar manner, are combined into a single mixture, they suddenly cohere as soon as they receive water. They are quickly hardened by the moisture and solidify so that neither waves nor the force of the water can dissolve them.

The presence of intense heat in these regions can also be demonstrated by the fact that in the mountains near Cumae and Baiae, there are sites excavated for steam baths. In these, a hot vapor rising from the depths by the power of fire pierces through the earth and, by flowing through it, emerges in these locations, thus providing excellent benefits for sweating <note>The Romans used these natural geothermal vents for medicinal saunas and thermal baths</note>. 

It is likewise recounted that in ancient times, fires grew and abounded beneath **Mount Vesuvius**, and from there, flames were vomited onto the surrounding fields. For this reason, what is now called "spongestone" or **Pompeian pumice** <note>original: *pumex Pompeianus*</note> appears to have been scorched from another type of stone and reduced to this particular quality. 

This type of spongestone extracted there is not found in all places, but only around **Mount Etna** and the hills of **Mysia**—which the Greeks call **the Scorched Lands** <note>original: *κατακεκαυμένοι* (katakekaumenoi); a region in Lydia/Mysia known for its volcanic landscape</note>—and in other locations with similar geographical properties. If, therefore, boiling springs of water are found in these places, and hot vapors in the hollows of the mountains, and the locations themselves [were recognized] by the ancients...

## SECOND BOOK

...[fires] are remembered to have spread through the fields. It seems certain that due to the intensity of fire, moisture has been stripped away from the **tufa** <term>tophus: a light, porous volcanic rock</term> and the earth, just as it happens in kilns with the production of lime. Therefore, when these dissimilar and unequal substances are seized and brought into a single force, the dry heat of the materials—being suddenly saturated with water—simmers together with the latent heat in their shared bodies. This causes them to bind together forcefully and quickly acquire the quality of solidity.

A question remains <note>original: "desyderatio"</note>: since there are so many hot springs in **Tuscany** <note>original: "Hetruria"</note>, why is that same dust <note>the volcanic pozzolana</note> not also found there, which would allow structures to solidify underwater in the same way? Thus, it seemed appropriate to explain the nature of these things before the question is asked. 

In all places and regions, the same types of earth and stone are not born; some are earthy, others gravelly <note>original: "sabulosa"</note>, likewise some are pebbly <note>original: "glareosa"</note>, in other places sandy, and in still others different. They are of entirely dissimilar and unequal kinds, just as the qualities of the earth depend on the variety of the regions. 

This can be observed most clearly in the fact that where the **Apennine Mountains** <note>the mountain range running down the length of Italy</note> encircle the regions of Italy and Tuscany, pits for digging sand <term>fossicia arenaria: sand or volcanic ash excavated from pits</term> are not lacking in almost all locations. However, across the Apennines, in the part facing the Adriatic Sea, none are found. Likewise, in **Greece** <note>original: "Achaia"</note>, **Asia Minor** <note>original: "Asia"</note>, and generally across the sea, they are not even mentioned by name. 

Therefore, not in all places where hot waters boil and springs are frequent can the same opportunities arise in the same way. Rather, everything is created as the nature of things <note>original: "natura rerum"</note> has established—not according to human will, but distributed by chance. Thus, in those places where there are no earthy mountains but rather materials arranged with specific qualities, the power of fire emerging through the veins...

### On Stone Quarries. Chapter VII.

<margin>d</margin>
I have spoken about **lime** and **sand**, their varieties, and what virtues they have. It follows in order to explain about **stone quarries**, from which both **squared stones** <term>quadrata saxa: ashlar masonry blocks cut to specific dimensions</term> and supplies of **rubble-stone** <term>cementorum: small, rough stones used as the aggregate in Roman concrete</term> for buildings are extracted and prepared. These are found to have unequal and dissimilar qualities. For some are soft, such as the **red stones** found around the city <note>Rome</note>, as well as those from **Pallia**, **Fidenae**, and the **Alban Hills**. Others are of a moderate hardness, such as the stones from **Tibur** <note>modern Tivoli; this refers to Travertine</note>, **Amiternum**, or **Mount Soracte**, and those of similar types. Some are hard, like **flint** <note>original: "siliceæ", referring to the hard basalt used for paving Roman roads</note>.

There are also many other types: in Campania, red and black tufa; in Umbria, Picenum, and Venice, white tufa, which can even be cut with a toothed saw like wood. But all these soft stones have this advantage: when stones are taken from these quarries, they are very easily handled during construction. If they are used in covered places, they endure the weight and labor of time; but if they are placed in open and exposed areas, they are broken up and dissolved by ice and frost. Likewise, along the sea coasts, they are eaten away by the salt spray and melt away, nor can they endure great heat. **Tiburtine** stone, however, and those of the same kind...

...everything; they suffer damage from both heavy loads and from storms, but they cannot be safe from fire. As soon as they are touched by it, they crack and shatter into pieces. This is because their natural composition contains very little moisture. Similarly, they do not have much earthy matter, but consist mostly of air and fire. Therefore, since moisture and earth are lacking in them, when fire touches them and the force of the vapor drives out the air, the heat follows deep inside, fills the empty spaces between the particles, and begins to boil, making the stones as glowing and hot as the fire itself.

There are also many stone quarries in the territory of the **Tarquinians** <note>original: "Tarquiniensium", referring to the people of the ancient Etruscan city of Tarquinii</note> which are called **Anitian** <note>a high-quality volcanic tufa</note>. In color, they are like those from the **Alban Hills**. The largest workshops for these are around **Lake Bolsena** <note>original: "lacum Vulsiniensem"</note> and also in the district of **Statonia**. These stones possess endless virtues. They are neither harmed by the season of frosts <note>original: "gelicidiorum"</note> nor the touch of fire; rather, they are firm and endure for a great age because their natural mixture contains little air or fire, a moderate amount of moisture, and a great deal of earth. Thus, being solidified by a dense composition, they are damaged neither by storms nor by the violence of fire. 

This can be judged most clearly from the monuments near the town of **Ferentium** <note>an ancient town in Etruria, modern Ferento</note> which are made from these quarries. For they feature large, excellently made statues, as well as smaller figures, and flowers and **acanthus** <term>acanthus: a Mediterranean plant with jagged leaves, used as a primary decorative motif in Greek and Roman architecture</term> elegantly carved. Although these works are ancient, they appear as fresh as if they had just been made.

Furthermore, **bronze-smiths** <term>fabri aerarij: craftsmen who work with copper and its alloys, particularly bronze</term> use stone from these quarries to make molds for casting bronze, and they derive the greatest utility from them for pouring metal. If these quarries were located near the City <note>Rome</note>, it would be worthwhile for all public works to be completed using materials from these workshops. However, since necessity, due to proximity...

...[necessity] forces the use of stones from the **red quarries** <note>the *Rubrae* quarries on the Via Flaminia near Rome</note>, the **Palliensian** quarries <note>likely located near the *Palus* or marshes near the city</note>, and other sources close to the city. Those stones which are damaged by the weather during that two-year period should be cast into the **foundations** <note>original: *fundamenta*</note>. The rest, which remain unblemished, having been tested by the nature of things, can endure being built above the ground. These precautions must be observed not only for **squared stones** <note>original: *quadratis lapidibus*, referring to ashlar masonry where stones are cut to precise rectangles</note>, but also for **rubble-work structures** <note>original: *cementitijs structuris*, masonry made of smaller, irregular stones bonded with mortar</note>.

## Chapter 8. On the types of masonry, their qualities, methods, and locations.

<margin>s</margin>The types of masonry are these: **reticulated** <note>original: *reticulatum*, a decorative style where square stones are set diagonally to resemble a net or lattice</note>, which everyone uses now, and the **ancient** style, which is called **irregular** <note>original: *incertum*, rubble masonry made of stones of varying shapes and sizes</note>. Of these, the reticulated style is more beautiful, but it is prone to developing cracks because its **beds** <note>original: *cubilia*, the horizontal surfaces of the stones</note> and **joints** <note>original: *coagmenta*</note> are loose in all directions. Irregular stones, however, sitting one upon another and **interlocking** <note>original: *imbricata*, literally "tiled" or "overlapping"</note> with each other, provide a structure that is not as handsome but is stronger than the reticulated kind.

-><sig>D ij</sig><-

Both of these styles, however, should be built from very small stones, so that the walls, being thoroughly saturated with mortar made of **lime** <note>original: *calce*</note> and **sand** <note>original: *arena*</note>, may be held together for a longer time. Because the stones are of a soft and porous nature, they dry out the structure by sucking the moisture from the mortar. But when there is an abundant supply of lime and sand, the wall, retaining more moisture, will not quickly become weak, but will be held together by these materials. 

However, as soon as the moisture has been drawn out of the mortar through the porousness of the **rubble** <note>original: *cementorum*, referring to *caementa*, the small, rough stones used in the core of the wall</note>, the lime separates from the sand and dissolves. Consequently, the rubble stones cannot bond with the mortar, which in the long run makes the walls ruinous. This can be observed even in several monuments built around the city from **marble** or **squared stones**, which are packed in the middle with a filling <insert>of rubble</insert>...

...structures, as the material is faded by age; because the moisture has been sucked out of the porous **rubble** <note>original: *cementorum*, referring to the rough stones used in the core of a wall</note>, they tumble down, and as the joints of the **masonry courses** <note>original: *coagmentorum*</note> are dissolved by decay, the walls fall apart. 

If anyone wishes to avoid this defect, they should leave a middle cavity and, alongside the **upright stones** <term>orthostatae: large stone slabs or blocks set vertically to form the outer face of a wall</term>, build inner walls two feet thick made of squared red stone, or of brick, or of regular lava stones. These facings should then be bound together with **iron clamps** <note>original: *ansis ferreis*</note> and lead. 

For in this way, the work—constructed not in a random heap but in an orderly fashion—can last forever without flaw, since the bedding and the joints sit firmly upon one another and are tied together at their connections. This prevents the masonry from being thrust outward and does not allow the upright stones, which are bound to one another, to slip out of place.

Therefore, the construction method of the Greeks <note>original: *graecorum structura*</note> is not to be despised. ...absorb <note>original: *sugere*, likely the end of the word from the previous page</note> moisture, but instead they preserve the stones in their own natural dampness until a great age. Furthermore, the beds <note>the horizontal surfaces where stones meet</note> of these stones are first laid flat and level, which does not allow the material to collapse; rather, they are bound together by the continuous thickness of the walls and remain stable into extreme old age. 

The second method is what they call **emplekton** <term>emplekton: a Greek term meaning "interwoven," describing a wall with finished stone faces and an internal fill</term>, which even our rural builders use. In this style, the outer faces are polished, but the remaining stones are left as they were found <note>original: *uti sunt nata*, referring to rough-hewn or unpolished stone</note>, laid with mortar and bound with alternating joints. 

But our [Roman] builders, in their haste to finish the work, set the courses <note>original: *coria*</note> upright and focus only on the outer faces. In the middle, they stuff the space with broken rubble <note>original: *cementis*</note> mixed separately with mortar. Thus, three distinct layers are created in that structure: two facing skins and one central filling. 

The Greeks, however, do not build this way. Instead, they lay the stones flat and arrange the lengths of the courses with alternating joints that reach into the thickness of the wall. They do not fill the middle with rubble; rather, they consolidate the wall into a single, solid thickness using the facing stones themselves. Furthermore, throughout the construction, they intersperse single stones that span the entire thickness of the wall, showing a finished face on both sides. These they call **diatonoi** <term>diatonoi: Greek for "stretching through," referring to "header" stones that act as anchors by spanning the full width of a wall</term>, which greatly strengthen the solidity of the walls by binding them together.

By a false opinion, this spring is thought to afflict those who drink from it with a "venereal disease" <note>original: *venereo morbo*; in this context, it refers to the legend that the water made men effeminate or "soft"</note>. For it cannot be that the water makes people soft and shameless, as is said; rather, the power of that spring is its crystal clarity and its excellent flavor.

When Melas and Areuanias led a joint colony there from Argos and Troezen, they drove out the barbarian Carians and Leleges. These people, having been driven to the mountains, would gather and range about, committing robberies and cruelly devastating the colonists. Later, one of the colonists, for the sake of profit, set up a tavern at that spring because of the goodness of its water, stocking it with every kind of supply. By operating this business, he began to entice those barbarians. Thus, coming down one by one and gathering for social meetings, they were changed from their hard and fierce ways and were brought back, of their own will, to the customs and refinement of the Greeks. Therefore, that water gained its reputation not from a shameful or corrupting disease, but because the minds of the barbarians were softened by the sweetness of civilization <note>original: *humanitatis dulcedine*</note>.

### FIRST.

...[pa]rietes <note>Original: *rietes*. This is a fragment of *parietes*, meaning walls.</note>, so that the spaces do not become too narrow, are placed with the same thickness. However, sun-dried brick walls <term>sun-dried brick: *lateritij*, bricks made of clay and straw dried in the sun rather than fired in a kiln</term>—unless they are of double <term>double-brick: *diplinthij*</term> or triple <term>triple-brick: *triplinthij*</term> thickness—cannot support more than a single floor <term>floor: *contignationem*, literally a "joining of beams"</term> at a thickness of one and a half feet. In the majesty of this city <note>Referring to Rome</note> and given the infinite density of its citizens, it was necessary to provide countless dwellings. Therefore, since the flat ground area could not accommodate such a great multitude to live in the city, the situation itself forced a move toward the help of height in buildings. And so, by using stone piers, fired-brick structures <term>fired-brick: *testacea*, ceramic masonry that is much stronger than sun-dried clay</term>, and concrete walls <term>concrete: *cementitijs*, a mixture of rubble and mortar</term>, heights were built up, joined by frequent levels of flooring, and they create upper-story apartments <term>upper apartments: *cænaculorum*</term> with excellent views and great utility. Therefore, through balconies <term>balconies: *mænianis*</term> and various levels multiplied in the tall space, the Roman people have excellent dwellings without overcrowding.

Since the reason has been explained why, due to the necessity of narrow spaces, sun-dried brick walls are not permitted in the city, when it is necessary to use them outside the city so they last without defects, this is how it should be done. At the top of the walls, a layer of fired brick should be placed under the roof tiles to a height of about one and a half feet, and it should have projecting cornices <term>cornices: *proiecturas coronarum*, the decorative and functional overhangs of a roof</term>; in this way, the defects that usually occur in these walls can be avoided. For when the roof tiles <term>tiles: *tegulæ*</term> are broken or blown off by winds, allowing rainwater <term>rainwater: *hymbribus*</term> to leak through, the fired-brick protective layer <note>Original: *lorica testacea*. A *lorica* usually refers to a soldier’s breastplate; here it refers to the "armor" protecting the wall.</note> will not allow the sun-dried brick underneath to be damaged; instead, the projection of the cornices will throw the dripping water beyond the vertical line, and in that way, it will keep the structures of the sun-dried brick walls intact. 

As for the fired brick itself, whether it is of the best quality or defective for building, no one can judge immediately, because only when it is placed on a roof during storms and summer heat—if it remains firm then—is it proven...

BOOK

<margin><unclear>...is.</unclear></margin> For if a brick is not made from good clay, or is insufficiently fired, it will reveal its flaws when it is touched by frost and rime. Therefore, a material that cannot endure the strain upon a roof cannot be firm enough to bear the weight in a wall’s structure. For this reason, walls built using tiles taken from old roofs will possess the greatest stability. As for wattle-and-daub <term>wattle-and-daub: *craticii*, a construction method using woven wooden laths plastered with mud or clay</term>, I truly wish they had never been invented. For as much as they are advantageous for their speed of construction and the way they save space, they are an even greater and more general disaster because they are as ready for fire as bundles of kindling. Therefore, it seems better to incur the higher cost of fired bricks <term>fired bricks: *testaceorum*</term> than to be in danger by the cheapness of wattle-and-daub. Furthermore, when used in plasterwork <term>plasterwork: *tectoriis*</term>, they cause cracks because of the arrangement of their uprights and crossbeams. For when they are plastered, they absorb moisture and swell, and then as they dry, they shrink; being thus thinned, they break the solid surface of the plaster. But since speed, a lack of funds, or the partition of a narrow space may force their use, this is how it should be done: the foundation should be built high, so that the walls are kept away from the debris and the pavement. When buried in these, the wood becomes rotten with age, then settles and leans, which destroys the appearance of the plaster. I have now explained, as well as I could, the different kinds of walls and the preparation of their materials, along with their virtues and defects. Next, I shall explain the nature of timber and the methods by which it is obtained, ensuring it is not weak for old age, just as the nature of things demonstrates.

This is much like the bodies of women when they have conceived; they are not judged to be healthy from the time of conception to birth. Even in the slave markets, when women are pregnant, they are not guaranteed to be sound <note>Vitruvius is referring to Roman commercial law, where a seller had to disclose "defects." Pregnancy was considered a temporary state of physical depletion that affected the "soundness" of the body for labor.</note>, because the growing fetus <term>fetus: *præseminatio*, literally the "pre-seeding" or growth within the womb</term> within the body draws nourishment into itself from all the nutritive properties of the food. The stronger the fetus becomes as it approaches the maturity of birth, the less it allows that very body from which it is created to remain solid.

Thus, once the offspring is born, that which was previously diverted for another kind of growth is freed by the separation of the birth. It is then received back into the empty and open veins, and by absorbing the sap, the body hardens and returns to its original natural firmness. By the same reasoning, during the autumn season, as the leaves wither when the fruit ripens, the roots of the trees receive the sap from the earth back into themselves; thus, the trees are recovered and restored to their former solidity. 

Indeed, the power of the winter air compresses and consolidates them during that time (as was written above). Therefore, if a tree is felled for that reason and at the time described above, the timber will be seasoned <term>seasoned: *tempestiua*, meaning harvested at the right time for maximum durability</term>.

The cutting, however, should be done in this way: the trunk of the tree should be sliced to the middle of the pith, and then left standing so that the sap may dry out by dripping through the cut. In this way, the useless liquid inside, flowing out through the sapwood <note>original: *torulum*, referring here to the outer layers or the "cushion" of the wood where the sap flows</note>, will not allow the rot to stagnate within, which would otherwise corrupt the quality of the timber. Only then, when the tree is dry and no longer dripping, should it be felled <term>felled: *deijciatur*, literally "thrown down" or cut down</term>; it will then be at its best for use.

One may observe this same principle in shrubs <term>shrubs: *arbustis*, often referring to trees used in vineyards</term>. For when each of them, at its own season, is cut at the base...

Thus, by drying out, they acquire a long-lasting durability. However, those trees that have no exit for their moisture rot as the fluids thicken inside, which makes them hollow and defective. Therefore, if standing and living trees do not weaken while drying out, there is no doubt that when they are felled for timber and treated by that same method, they will provide great benefits for the longevity of buildings.

These woods, however, differ from one another and possess distinct qualities, such as **oak**, **elm**, **poplar**, **cypress**, **fir**, and others most suitable for construction. For oak cannot perform the same function as fir, nor cypress the same as elm; nor do the others share similar natural characteristics. Rather, each individual genus is composed of its own specific properties of the primary elements <note>Vitruvius follows the ancient scientific theory that all matter is composed of four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water. First, the **fir** contains a great deal of air and fire, but very little moisture and earth. Being composed of the lighter powers of nature, it is not heavy. Thus, relying on its natural stiffness, it does not easily bend under a load but remains straight in a timber floor-frame <term>contignatione: a structure made of joined timbers, such as a floor or ceiling</term>. However, because it contains more heat, it breeds and nourishes the woodworm <term>tarmitem: a wood-boring insect or larva</term>, and is damaged by it. It also catches fire quickly because the porous air within its body is open to receiving flame, and so it emits a powerful fire. 

Furthermore, in that part of the tree closest to the ground before it is cut, the wood is knot-free and "clear" <note>original: *liquida*; here describing a smooth, knot-free texture caused by the high concentration of sap near the roots</note> as it receives moisture through the roots from the surrounding soil. But in the upper part, the intensity of the heat drives branches out into the air through knots. When it is cut at a height of about twenty feet and hewn for...

On the other hand, the **oak** <note>original: *quercus*; specifically the common or English oak</note>, being abundant in the earthly properties of its primary elements but having very little moisture, air, or fire, possesses an infinite longevity when buried in earthworks. This is because when it is touched by moisture, it lacks the openness of pores due to its density; thus, it cannot absorb liquid into its body. Instead, fleeing from the moisture, it resists and twists, causing the structures in which it is used to develop cracks.

The **winter oak** <note>original: *esculus*; likely the *Quercus frainetto* or Italian oak, prized by Romans for its balanced strength</note>, because it is tempered by all the elements, is of great utility in buildings. However, when it is placed in a moist environment, it absorbs liquid deep through its pores; as the air and fire are expelled by the action of the wet power, it becomes tainted and decays.

The **Turkey oak**, **cork oak**, and **beech** <note>original: *cerrus, suber, fagus*</note> similarly possess a mixture of moisture, fire, and earth, but a great deal of air. Because their porous nature allows moisture to penetrate deep within them, they rot quickly.

The **white** and **black poplar**, as well as the **willow**, **linden**, and **chaste tree** <note>original: *uitex*; the *Vitex agnus-castus*, a shrub with flexible branches used for weaving</note>, are saturated with fire and air, tempered with moisture, and contain very little of the earthly element. Because they are composed of a lighter mixture, they are found to have an excellent stiffness in use. Since they are not made hard by a mixture of earth, they are white due to their porousness, and they provide a convenient ease of handling for carvings.

The **alder**, however, which is produced closest to the banks of rivers and seems to be a minimally useful timber, possesses in itself remarkable qualities. For it is tempered by a great deal of air and fire, not much earth, and only a little moisture. Likewise, the **Hornbeam** <note>original: *Carpinus*</note>, because it consists of a minimal mixture of fire and earth but a maximum tempered balance of air and moisture, is not brittle but possesses a most useful workability. Therefore, the Greeks—because they fashion yokes for draft animals out of this wood, and since yokes among them are called *zyga* <note>original: ζύγα</note>—also call this tree *zygeia* <term>zygeia: the Greek name for the hornbeam, derived from its use in making yokes</term>.

No less to be admired are the **Cypress** and **Pine**. Although they possess an abundance of moisture and an equal mixture of the other elements, they tend to sag in construction due to their saturation of liquid; however, they are preserved for a great age without defects. This is because the liquid deep within their bodies has a bitter taste, which, by its acridity, does not allow rot <note>original: *cariem*; wood-decay or "caries"</note> to penetrate, nor does it admit those harmful little insects. Therefore, works constructed from these species remain for an eternal...

In **Ephesus**, the cult statue <note>original: *simulachrum*</note> of **Diana** in her temple is made of this wood, as are the <term>coffered ceilings</term> <note>original: *lacunaria*; the decorative recessed panels of a ceiling</note> both there and in other famous shrines, chosen for their eternal quality. The **Larch** <note>original: *Larix*</note>, however, is known only to those townsfolk who live near the banks of the **Po River** and the shores of the **Adriatic Sea**. Because of the extreme bitterness of its sap, it is not only protected from decay and moths, but it also does not catch fire from a flame. It cannot burn on its own unless it is heated by other wood—much like stone is burned in a furnace to make lime <note>The author compares the larch to limestone, which requires an external heat source to undergo a chemical change but does not "burn" with its own flame</note>. Even then, it does not catch fire or produce charcoal; instead, it is consumed slowly over a long period. 

This is because it contains a very small proportion of the elements of fire and air. Instead, it is a material densely solidified with moisture and earthy matter, lacking the open pores through which fire might penetrate. It rejects the force of fire and does not allow itself to be quickly harmed by it. Because of its great weight, it is not supported by water (it does not float), so when it is transported, it must be placed either in ships or on rafts made of **fir** <note>original: *abiegnas rates*; fir wood was light and buoyant, making it the ideal "vessel" to carry the heavy larch</note>.

It is worth knowing how this material was discovered. ### On Fir from the Upper and Lower Regions, with a Description of the Apennines. Chapter 10.

The first foothills of the **Apennine** mountains rise from the **Tyrrhenian Sea** <note>the "Lower Sea" on the west coast of Italy</note> toward the Alps and the farthest regions of **Etruria** <note>original: *Hetruriæ*; modern-day Tuscany and parts of Umbria and Lazio</note>. Indeed, the ridge of this mountain range curves around, and at its middle bend, it nearly touches the shores of the **Adriatic Sea**, continuing its winding path down toward the strait <note>the Strait of Messina</note>.

Therefore, its closer slope, which faces the regions of **Etruria** and **Campania**, is influenced by sunny conditions, for it receives the constant force of the sun's path. However, the farther slope, which inclines toward the **Upper Sea** <note>the Adriatic</note>, is situated toward the north and is held in perpetual shadow and shade. Consequently, the trees that grow in that part, nourished by the power of moisture, not only grow to immense sizes themselves, but their veins, filled with a great deal of moisture, are swollen and saturated with an abundance of sap.

When, however, they are cut down and hewn, they lose their vital power; as they dry out, the stiffness of their veins changes because of the porous <note>original: *raritatem*; the text breaks off here mid-sentence</note>...

However, those trees produced in places facing the course of the sun—having no gaps between their veins because they have been dried out and solidified by the heat—are much stronger. This occurs because the sun not only "licks" the moisture from the earth but also draws out the **humors** <term>humores: in ancient science, these were the vital fluids (like sap) whose balance determined the health and density of a living thing</term> from the trees themselves.

Lacking the porousness caused by excess moisture, they provide great utility and longevity when they are hewn into timber. For this reason, the "Lower Sea" <note>original: *infernates*; referring to the timber from the western, Tyrrhenian side of Italy</note> timbers brought from sunny places are better than those brought from the shaded regions of the "Upper Sea" <note>original: *supernatibus*; referring to the eastern, Adriatic side</note>.

Therefore, those who are able to follow the prescriptions of these teachings will be wiser and will be able to choose the proper use of each kind of material for their works.

Thus, since the preparations have been explained, the remaining volumes will deal with the buildings themselves. First, in the following book, I shall write about the **sacred temples** of the immortal gods, and their **symmetries** and **proportions**, as the proper order of the subject requires.

### BOOK THREE.

Delphic Apollo <note>The god Apollo’s oracle at Delphi was considered the highest authority on wisdom in the ancient world.</note> declared Socrates the wisest of all men through the responses of the **Pythia** <term>Pythia: the high priestess of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracular prophecies</term>. Socrates, however, is remembered for having said—both wisely and with great learning—that the breasts of men ought to have been provided with windows and kept open, so that they would not have hidden feelings, but rather ones laid open for consideration. If only the nature of things <note>original: *rerum natura*; a phrase referring to the natural order of the universe</note> had followed his opinion and made our thoughts explicit and visible! 

For if this had been the case, not only would the virtues or vices of the mind be seen at a glance, but the mastery of scientific disciplines, being placed directly under the observation of the eyes, would be proven not by uncertain judgments; instead, an outstanding and stable authority would be granted to those who are truly learned and knowledgeable. 

Therefore, since these things were not established in this way, but rather as the nature of things willed, it follows that men—with their talents obscured within their breasts—cannot easily judge the true depth of the knowledge hidden within an artist's craft. Even the artists themselves, though they may promise their own expertise, cannot achieve an authority matching the diligence of their studies unless they are wealthy, or possess a reputation through the long-standing fame of their workshops, or are skilled in social influence and public eloquence. Without these advantages, they are not believed to truly know that which they profess. 

We can observe this most clearly among ancient sculptors and painters; for among those who [possessed] the marks of status and the favor of recommendation...

### BOOK THREE.

...works have remained in eternal memory for posterity, such as **Myron**, **Polycletus**, **Phidias**, **Lysippus**, <note>These were the most famous sculptors of the Greek Golden Age, whose names were synonymous with perfection in the Roman era.</note> and others who achieved renown through their art. For because they created works for great cities, kings, or noble citizens, they attained this status. But those who possessed no less zeal, talent, and skill, yet produced excellent and perfectly finished works for citizens of humble fortune, have achieved no lasting memory. They were abandoned not by their own industry or artistic skill, but by luck—men such as **Hellas of Athens**, **Chion of Corinth**, **Myagrus of Phocaea**, **Pharax of Ephesus**, **Bedas of Byzantium**, and many others besides. 

In the same way, there were painters such as **Aristomenes of Thasos**, **Polycles**, and **Atramitenus**, **Nicomachus**, and others who did not lack industry, nor the study of art, nor skill; rather, the smallness of their family inheritance, the weakness of their luck, or the victory of their rivals in the competition for status stood in the way of their recognition. It is not surprising if artistic virtues are hidden due to a general ignorance of the craft; but it is truly shameful when the social influence of dinner parties <note>original: *gratia conviviorum*; Vitruvius is complaining that architectural commissions are often handed out based on social networking and favors swapped at banquets rather than objective merit.</note> often sways people from true judgment toward false approval.

Therefore (as **Socrates** believed), if our senses, opinions, and the knowledge gained through scientific disciplines <term>scientiae: here meaning specialized technical knowledge or "know-how"</term> had been clear and transparent, then social favor and ambition would have no power. Instead, if someone had reached the highest level of knowledge through genuine and certain labors of study, commissions would be granted to them automatically. However, since these qualities are not illustrious nor visible to the eye as we think they should be, and I notice that the uneducated often surpass the learned through social favor, I have decided not to compete with the uneducated through social climbing. Instead, by publishing these instructions, I will demonstrate the true value of our science. 

And so, Emperor, in the first volume...

### BOOK THREE

...In this light, I have explained the art to you: what virtues it possesses, which disciplines an architect ought to be equipped with, and I have set forth the reasons why he should be skilled in these areas. I have also distributed the theories of the highest forms of architecture into specific categories and defined them with clear boundaries. 

Then, dealing with what was first and most necessary, I explained through reasoning how healthy locations for city walls should be chosen. I showed the nature of the winds and the directions from which each one blows using geometric diagrams <note>original: *formationibus grammicis*; referring to linear or mathematical drawings used to map the compass of winds.</note>, and I taught how to distribute streets and alleys within the walls so they are correctly aligned. Thus, I established the definitions of the first volume. 

Likewise, in the second volume, I treated the utility of various materials in construction and the virtues they possess according to their natural properties. Now, in the third volume, I shall speak of the sacred temples of the immortal gods and explain how they ought to be designed.

### Chapter 1: On the Composition of Sacred Temples, Symmetries, and the Measure of the Human Body.

The composition of temples depends on symmetry, the rules of which architects must observe with the greatest diligence. Symmetry is derived from proportion, which in Greek is called *analogy* <note>original: ἀναλογία; meaning a correspondence or relationship between parts.</note>. Proportion is the balanced agreement of the parts in any work and of the whole, from which the ratio of symmetry is calculated. 

For no temple can have a coherent system of composition without symmetry and proportion—that is, unless it possesses an exact relationship of parts, just like those of a well-formed human being. For nature has so composed the human body that the face, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair...

...to the lowest roots of the hair, it is a tenth part of the whole height. Likewise, the palm of the hand from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger is the same amount. The head, from the chin to the highest point of the crown, is an eighth part. 

From the base of the neck, measured from the top of the chest to the lowest roots of the hair, is a sixth part; to the highest point of the crown, a fourth part. As for the height of the face itself, the first third is from the bottom of the chin to the underside of the nostrils; the nose, from the underside of the nostrils to the middle point between the eyebrows, is the same; and from that point to the lowest roots of the hair, where the forehead begins, is likewise a third part <note>original: "tertiae patris"; likely a printer's error for "partis" (part).</note>. 

The foot is one-sixth of the body's height; the cubit <note>term: "cubit" (Latin: *cubitus*); an ancient unit of measure based on the length of the forearm from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> is one-fourth; the chest is also one-fourth. The other limbs also have their own proportional measurements, which the famous painters and sculptors of antiquity used to achieve great and infinite renown. 

In a similar way, the components of sacred temples ought to have a most suitable proportional correspondence in relation to the total magnitude of the whole. Furthermore, the natural center of the body is the navel. For if a man is placed on his back with his hands and feet spread out, and the center of a compass is placed on his navel, the circle described by the compass will touch the fingers of both hands and the toes of the feet.

Therefore, if nature has so composed the **human body** <note>original: "corpus hominis"</note> that its **limbs** <note>original: "membra"</note> correspond in their proportions to its total configuration, the ancients seem to have had good reason to establish that, even in the completion of their works, the individual parts should have an exactness of measurement relative to the appearance of the entire figure. Consequently, while they handed down these rules for all works, they did so especially for the **temples of the gods** <note>original: "ædibus deorum," literally "houses of the gods"</note>, buildings in which the merits and flaws of the craftsmanship are destined to remain forever.

No less did they gather the **systems of measurement** <note>original: "mensurarum rationes"</note>, which are seen to be necessary in all works, from the members of the body—such as the **finger** <note>original: "digitum"</note>, the **palm** <note>original: "palmum"</note>, the **foot** <note>original: "pedem"</note>, and the **cubit** <note>original: "cubitum"</note>—and they organized these into the **perfect number**, which the Greeks call **perfect** <note>original: "τέλειον" (teleion)</note>. ### THIRD BOOK

<header>THIRD</header>

...they established the number called **ten** <note>original: "decem"</note>; for the ten-fold number of fingers is found from the hands. From the fingers, the **palm** <note>original: "palmus"</note> was derived, and from the palm, the **foot** <note>original: "pes"</note> was found. Just as in both palms there are ten joints perfected by nature, it also pleased Plato that this number be considered perfect because it is completed from individual units—which the Greeks call **monads** <note>original: "μοναδες"</note>—into a **decussis** <note>original: "decussis," the Latin term for the number ten, named for the cross-shaped X mark</note>. As soon as these units become eleven or twelve, whatever they exceed cannot be perfect until they reach another *decussis*. These individual units are the small components of that number.

Mathematicians, however, arguing the contrary, stated that the number called **six** <note>original: "sex"</note> is perfect. They reasoned that this number has divisions that correspond to the number six in their ratios: thus, one-sixth is one; one-third is two; one-half is three; two-thirds—which they call **dimoiron** <note>original: "δίμοιρον"</note>—is four; five-sixths—which they call **pentamoiron** <note>original: "πεντάμοιρον"</note>—is five; and the perfect whole is six.

When the calculation grows beyond six, by adding a single unit it becomes **one-sixth more** <note>original: "ἔφεκτον" (ephekton), meaning a ratio of 7:6</note>. When eight is reached, which is the addition of a third, it is the **one-and-a-third** <note>original: "ἐπίτριτος" (epitritos), a 4:3 ratio</note>. When nine is reached by adding a half, it is the **one-and-a-half** <note>original: "ἡμιόλιος" (hemiolios), a 3:2 ratio</note>. When two parts are added and ten is reached, it is the **one-and-two-thirds** <note>original: "ἐπιδίμοιρον" (epidimoiron), a 5:3 ratio</note>. In the number eleven, because five units are added, it is the **one-and-five-sixths** <note>original: "ἐπιπεντάμοιρον" (epipentamoiron)</note>. Twelve, however, because it is produced from two simple numbers, is called **double** <note>original: "διπλασίωνα" (diplasiona)</note>.

No less significant is the fact that a person's foot is the sixth part of their height; thus, based on the number of feet that complete a body, they established that the body is defined by these six units of height. They also observed that the **cubit** <note>original: "cubitum," a measurement from the elbow to the fingertip</note> consists of six palms...

<header>BOOK</header>

...and twenty-four fingers. From this, the Greek cities also seem to have established that, just as the **cubit** <note>original: "cubitus," a unit of measure roughly the length of a forearm</note> consists of six **palms** <note>original: "palmi"</note>, they would use that same number in the **drachma** <note>original: "drachma," a silver coin</note>. For they established in the drachma six minted bronze pieces—similar to our *asses*—which they call **obols** <note>original: "obolos"</note>, and quarters of obols—which some call **dichalca** and others **trichalca**—to represent the twenty-four fingers in the drachma.

Our ancestors, however, first chose **ten** <note>original: "decem"</note> as the ancient number, and established ten bronze **asses** <note>the *as* was the basic Roman bronze coin</note> in a **denarius** <note>original: "denarius," from the word for "ten"</note>; for that reason, the coin's composition retains the name *denarius* to this day. They also called its fourth part—which was made of two *asses* and a third half-*as*—a **sestertius** <note>original: "sestertium," literally "two and a half"</note>.

Afterward, when they realized that both numbers, six and ten, were perfect, they combined both into one and made the most perfect number, **sixteen** <note>original: "decussissexis," a combination of ten (decussis) and six (sexis)</note>. They found the authority for this in the **foot** <note>original: "pes"</note>. For when two palms are removed from a cubit, a foot of four palms remains; since a palm has four fingers, it follows that a foot has sixteen fingers, and the bronze *denarius* has the same number of *asses*.

Therefore, if it is agreed that the number system was discovered from the human joints, and that the proportional relationship of the individual members was found to correspond to the overall appearance of the body, it remains for us to accept the methods of those who, when building the temples of the immortal gods, ordered the parts of the works so that their distributions were made fitting in both their separate and universal proportions and **symmetries** <note>original: "symmetrys," referring to the harmonious relationship between parts of a building</note>.

The primary forms of temples, from which the appearance of their figures is determined, are: first, **in antis** <note>original: "in antis," a temple where the side walls extend to the front to enclose two columns</note>, which in Greek is called **temple in parastades** <note>original: "ναώς ἐν παράστασι" (naos en parastasi)</note>; then **prostyle**, **amphiprostyle**, **peripteral**, **pseudodipteral**, **dipteral**, and **hypethral**.

<summary>Vitruvius explains how Greek and Roman coinage and measurements were derived from human proportions, eventually combining the 'perfect' numbers 6 and 10 into 16. He concludes by beginning a classification of temple types based on these mathematical symmetries.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

The configurations of these buildings are determined by the following rules. A temple **in antis** <note>original: "in antis," an architectural term for a temple where the side walls extend to the front to frame the columns</note> is one that has piers at the front of the walls which enclose the **cella** <note>original: "cella," the inner chamber of a temple housing the cult statue</note>. Between these piers, in the center, two columns are placed, and above them a **pediment** <note>original: "fastigium"</note> is positioned according to the system of proportions that will be described in this book. An example of this style is the temple of the **Three Fortunes** <note>original: "Tres fortunas," a triple temple complex on the Quirinal Hill</note>, specifically the one of the three which is closest to the **Colline Gate** <note>original: "portam collinam," one of the primary gates in the Servian Wall of ancient Rome</note>.

<image-desc>A woodcut architectural floor plan of a temple "in antis." It shows a rectangular cella with side walls (antae) extending forward. Two circular columns are positioned in the space between the ends of these projecting walls.</image-desc>

The **Prostyle** <note>original: "prostylos," from the Greek for "columns in front"</note> temple has all the same features as the *in antis* style, but it features two columns positioned directly opposite the corner piers to support the **architraves** <note>original: "epistylia," the horizontal beams that rest on the columns</note>, just as in the *in antis* style; it also has single columns on the right and left at the returns. An example of this is located on the **Tiber Island** <note>original: "insula tiberina"</note> in the temple of **Jupiter and Faunus**.

## On the five varieties of temples. Chapter II.

There are five varieties of temples, which are named as follows: *pychnostyle*, meaning with crowded columns; *systyle*, with columns slightly further apart; *diastyle*, with columns spread wider; *araeostyle*, where they are separated more than is proper; and *eustyle*, which has a proper distribution of intervals. 

Therefore, the *pychnostyle* <term>pychnostyle: from the Greek "pyknos" (dense) and "stylos" (column)</term> is that in which the thickness of one and a half columns can be placed in the **intercolumniation** <note>the clear space between two adjacent columns</note>. Examples of this style include the temple of the **Divine Julius** <note>the temple built by Augustus to honor the deified Julius Caesar</note>, the temple of **Venus in Caesar's Forum** <note>the Temple of Venus Genetrix, the ancestral deity of the Julian clan</note>, and any others designed in this manner.

# BOOK III

<image-desc>A woodcut architectural diagram enclosed in a double-line rectangular frame. It depicts four classical columns with bases and capitals supporting a flat entablature. The vertical spaces between the columns are labeled with the letter 'b'.</image-desc>

<margin>
b. Intercolumniations <note>original: "intercolumnia"</note>, in which a thickness of two columns is interposed.
</margin>

Both of these types <note>referring to the pycnostyle and systyle arrangements discussed previously</note> have a faulty usage. For when **mothers of families** <note>original: "matres familiarum"; the Roman matrons who participated in public religious rites</note> ascend the steps for a **public prayer** <note>original: "supplicationem"; a solemn period of prayer or thanksgiving</note>, they cannot walk through the intercolumniations arm-in-arm to approach the temple, unless they form single files. Likewise, the view of the doors is obstructed by the density of the columns, and the **statues** <note>original: "signa"; referring to the cult statues of the gods within the temple</note> themselves are obscured. Also, the walkways around the temple are hindered because of the narrowness.

The arrangement of the **diastyle** <term>diastyle: from the Greek *diastylos*, meaning "columns set far apart"</term>, however, will be this: when we can place the thickness of three columns in the **intercolumniation** <note>original: "intercolumnio"; the clear space between the shafts of two adjacent columns</note>, such as in the temple of **Apollo** and the temple of **Diana**. This layout has this difficulty: that the **architraves** <term>architraves: the horizontal beams (original: "epistylia") that rest directly on the column capitals</term> often break because of the great width of the intervals.

<summary>This page critiques the practical inconveniences of closely spaced columns, such as crowding during religious processions, and introduces the diastyle arrangement, noting that its wide spacing risks structural failure in the stone beams.</summary>
<keywords>diastyle, intercolumniation, architraves, temple of Apollo, temple of Diana, Roman matrons, architectural proportions</keywords>

In the **araeostyle** <term>araeostyle: from the Greek *araiostylos*, meaning "thinly set columns"; an arrangement where the columns are spaced very far apart</term> arrangement, however, it is not possible to use **architraves** <term>architraves: the horizontal beams (original: "epistyliis") that rest directly on the column capitals</term> made of stone or marble. Instead, continuous beams made of **timber** must be placed upon them. The appearance of these temples is **heavy-set** <note>original: "barycæ"</note>, **top-heavy** <note>original: "barycephalæ"; literally "heavy-headed," referring to the massive roof structure necessitated by the wide spacing</note>, low, and wide. Furthermore, they decorate their **pediments** <note>original: "fastigia"; the triangular gable end of a temple roof</note> in the **Tuscan fashion** <term>Tuscan fashion: an architectural style originating with the Etruscans, known for its simplicity and frequent use of wood and terracotta rather than stone</term> with **statues** <note>original: "signis"</note> made of clay or gilded bronze. Examples of this style include the temple of **Ceres** and the temple of **Hercules** at the **Circus Maximus**, as well as the **Capitolium** in **Pompeii**.

We must now provide the account of the <term>eustyle</term> <note>from the Greek for "well-styled" or "beautifully proportioned"</note>, which possesses the most commendable principles for practical use, appearance, and structural strength. For the spaces in the intervals should be made the width of two columns and one-quarter of a column's thickness. However, the central <term>intercolumniation</term> <note>the space between two adjacent columns</note>—one which shall be at the front and the other at the rear—should be the width of three columns. For in this way, the design will have a charming appearance, the entrance will be used without hindrance, and the walkway around the <term>cella</term> <note>the inner chamber of a temple housing the statue of a deity</note> will possess a sense of authority.

*...ness. We have no example of this* <note>the eustyle arrangement described on the previous page</note> *in Rome, but in Asia, there is the octastyle* <note>having eight columns across the front</note> *temple of Father Liber* <note>original: "liberi patris"; the Roman god of wine and fertility, identified with the Greek Dionysus</note> *at Teos. For from the symmetry of the **dipteral*** <note>having a double row of columns on all sides</note> *temple, he removed the interior rows of columns (thirty-eight in number), and by that method, he made savings in both expense and labor. He created an excellent spaciousness for walking in the middle around the **cella*** <term>the inner chamber of a classical temple where the cult statue was kept</term>*, and he diminished nothing of the appearance, but without the need for superfluous parts, he preserved the dignity of the entire work through its distribution. For the principle of the **pteroma*** <term>the side-colonnade or "wing" of a temple</term> *and the arrangement of columns around the temple was invented so that the appearance might have dignity because of the visual density of the intercolumniations* <note>the spaces between the columns</note>*. Furthermore, if a heavy downpour of rain should occur and trap a multitude of people, they might have a free space to wait in the temple and around the cella with plenty of room. These things are thus explained in the arrangements of **pseudodipteral** temples; wherefore it seems that Hermogenes achieved the effects of his works with sharp and great skill, leaving behind sources from which posterity might draw the principles of the disciplines. In **areostyle** temples* <note>where columns are spaced very far apart, four or more diameters</note>*, the columns are to be made so that their thickness is one-eighth part of their height. Likewise, in the **diastyle*** <note>where columns are spaced three diameters apart</note>*, the height of the column is to be measured into eight and a half parts, and the thickness of one part shall be the column's thickness. In the **systyle*** <note>where columns are spaced two diameters apart</note>*, the height should be divided into nine and a half parts, and one of these parts should be given to the thickness of the column. Likewise, in the **pycnostyle*** <note>where columns are very close together, only one and a half diameters apart</note>*, the height is to be divided into ten parts, and one of those parts is to be made the column's thickness. # BOOK THREE

...and one part of it <note>referring to the "module" or standard unit of measurement established in the previous section</note> should be established as the thickness of the lower **shaft**, and in this way, the ratio of the **intercolumniations** <term>the clear spaces between adjacent columns</term> will be maintained according to its proper proportion.

For as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the shafts must be increased in relative proportions. Indeed, if in an **araeostyle** <term>a temple layout with very wide spacing between columns, typically three or more column diameters apart</term> the thickness were only a ninth or tenth part <note>of the column's height</note>, the column would appear thin and meager. This is because the surrounding air, through the wide span of the intercolumniations, "consumes" the shaft and diminishes its visual thickness. Conversely, in **pycnostyle** <term>a temple layout with very narrow spacing, where columns are set only one and a half diameters apart</term> arrangements, if the thickness were an eighth part, the density and narrowness of the spacing would create a swollen and ungraceful appearance.

Therefore, it is necessary to follow the symmetries specific to each type of work. Furthermore, the corner columns should be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their diameter, because they are "cut around" <note>original: "circunciduntur"; meaning they are surrounded by bright open sky rather than the shaded interior of the colonnade</note> by the open air and thus appear more slender to those looking at them. Therefore, what deceives the eye must be corrected by mathematical reasoning.

The **tapering** <term>original: "contractura"; the slight narrowing of the column towards the top to make it look straight and sturdy</term> at the tops of the column **necks** <term>original: "hypotrachelijs"; the section of the shaft immediately below the capital</term> should be made in this manner: if a column is from the smallest size up to fifteen feet high, the lower thickness should be divided into six parts, and five of those parts should constitute the thickness at the top.

Likewise, for a column from fifteen to twenty feet high, the lower shaft should be divided into six and a half parts, and five and a half of those parts should form the thickness of the upper part of the column.

Likewise, for those from twenty to thirty feet, the lower shaft should be divided into seven parts, and the top tapering should be finished at six of those parts.

For a column from thirty to forty feet high, the lower thickness should be divided into seven and a half parts; of these, let the top have a ratio of six and a half parts for its tapering.

These proportions are necessary because, due to the distance of the height, the "climbing eye" is easily deceived. Therefore, adjustments must be added to the thicknesses. The sense of sight constantly pursues beauty; if we do not flatter its pleasure by adjusting the proportions and adding to the modules <note>the standard units of measurement</note>—so that what the eye would otherwise perceive as a flaw is corrected by these adjustments—the structure will appear clumsy and ungraceful to those looking upon it. # BOOK THREE

The foundations <term>original: *substructionis*; the underlying masonry supporting a building</term> of these works should be excavated, if solid ground can be found, from the solid and into the solid, as deep as seems appropriate for the size and proportion of the work. This structure should be built as solidly as possible across the entire floor. Above the ground, walls should be constructed under where the columns will stand, half again as thick as the columns are intended to be, so that the lower parts are stronger than the upper parts. These foundations are called **stereobates** <term>original: *stereobatæ*; the solid platform or pedestal that supports a suite of columns</term>, for they take up the heavy loads. Furthermore, the projections of the **bases** <term>original: *spirarum*; the circular moldings at the bottom of a column shaft</term> must not extend beyond the solid foundation. Likewise, the same thickness of the wall must be maintained above, and the intervening spaces should be either **vaulted** <note>built with arches to distribute weight</note> or filled in solid.

# BOOK THREE

<note>original: *da fistucationibus*; regarding the process of driving piles into the earth with a rammer</note> regarding the use of ramming, so that the foundations may be firmly fixed. If, however, solid ground is not found, but the site consists of loose earth or is a marshy <note>original: *paluster*; a wetland or swampy area often requiring specialized engineering in antiquity</note> place, then the site must be excavated, cleared out, and driven through with piles of alder, olive, or charred oak. These piles should be driven as closely together as possible using machines, and the intervals between the piles should be filled with charcoal. Then, the foundations should be filled in with the most solid masonry.

Once the foundations have been built up, the **stylobates** <term>original: *stylobatæ*; the top course of the platform upon which the columns rest</term> must be placed at a level. Above the **stylobates**, the columns are to be arranged as has been written above: whether in the **pycnostyle** <term>original: *pycnostylo*; a style with very closely spaced columns</term> fashion, or the **systyle**, **diastyle**, or **eustyle** <term>original: *eustylo*; the "ideal" spacing considered most beautiful and functional</term>, according to the rules previously established.

In the **araeostyle** <term>original: *Areostylis*; a style with very wide spacing between columns, often requiring wooden beams instead of stone</term>, there is freedom to set the spacing however one wishes. However, in **peripteral** <term>original: *peripteris*; a temple surrounded by a single row of columns on all sides</term> temples, the columns should be placed so that there are twice as many **intercolumniations** <term>original: *intercolumnia*; the clear space between two column shafts</term> on the sides as there are on the front. In this way, the length of the work will be double its width. For those who have simply doubled the number of columns <note>rather than the spaces between them</note> seem to have erred, because the length appears to run on one intercolumniation further than it ought.

The steps at the front are to be arranged so that they are always an odd number. For, since the first step is ascended with the right foot, the first step onto the level of the temple itself should also be taken with the right foot. I believe the height of these steps should be set so that they are neither thicker than a **ten-inch** <term>original: *dextante*; ten-twelfths of a Roman foot</term> measure, nor thinner than a **nine-inch** <term>original: *dodrante*; nine-twelfths of a Roman foot</term> measure; for in this way, the ascent will not be difficult. Likewise, if there are to be steps around the whole temple, they should be made in the same manner. Its height, if it is to be an **Attic style** <term>original: *atticurges*; a popular base design consisting of two rounded moldings separated by a hollow curve</term> base, should be divided so that the upper part is one-third the thickness of the column, and the remainder is left for the **plinth** <term>original: *plinthus*; the flat, square block at the very bottom of a column base</term>. After removing the plinth, the remaining height is divided into four parts: let the **upper torus** <term>original: *torus*; a large, convex, ring-shaped molding</term> be one-fourth. The remaining three parts are to be divided equally, with one part forming the **lower torus**, and the other part consisting of the **scotia** <term>original: *scotia*; a concave molding that creates a deep shadow</term>—which the Greeks call a *trochilos* <note>original: *trochilus*; literally "a pulley," describing the shape of the concave molding</note>—along with its **fillets** <term>original: *quadrae*; the small, flat, square-edged moldings that border the scotia</term>.

# BOOK THREE

<page-num>38</page-num>

...should have their perpendicular side positioned [toward the temple walls]. The exterior parts, however, should follow their own **tapering** <term>original: *contractura*; the gradual narrowing of a column shaft as it rises</term>. In this way, the forms of the building's composition and the tapering will be precisely executed according to a correct system. Once the **shafts** <term>original: *scapi*; the main vertical body of the columns</term> of the columns are set, the proportions of the **capitals** <term>original: *capitula*; the decorative tops of the columns</term>—if they are to be **cushion-shaped** <term>original: *pulvinata*; the standard form of an Ionic capital, resembling a soft cushion or bolster pressed down by the weight above</term>—shall be established by these symmetries: 

The **abacus** <term>the flat, square plate at the very top of a capital</term> should have a length and width equal to the thickness of the bottom of the shaft plus one-eighteenth of that thickness. Its total thickness, including the **volutes** <term>original: *uolutis*; the distinctive spiral, scroll-like ornaments of the Ionic order</term>, should be half of that width. 

One must recede from the outer edge of the abacus toward the interior for the faces of the volutes by one-eighteenth and a half part. Along the abacus, in the four parts of the volutes, lines should be dropped according to the square of the edge of the abacus; these are called **vertical lines** <term>original: *catheti*; plumb lines used as geometric references for drawing the spiral</term>. 

Then, the total thickness is to be divided into nine and a half parts. One and a half parts are assigned to the thickness of the abacus, and the remaining eight parts are for the construction of the volute. Next, from the line that was dropped along the outer edge of the abacus, another line should be drawn further inward by a width of one and a half parts. 

These lines are then divided so that four and a half parts remain under the abacus. At the point that divides the four-and-a-half and the three-and-a-half parts, the center of the **eye** <term>original: *oculus*; the small circle at the very center of the spiral volute</term> shall be marked. From that center, a circle is drawn with a compass, with a diameter equal to one of the eight parts mentioned before; this will be the size of the eye. A diameter corresponding to the vertical plumb line is drawn within it. 

Then, beginning from the top just under the abacus, in each movement of the **quadrants** <term>original: *tetrantorum*; the four quarters of a circle</term>, the radius is reduced by half the space of the eye until the spiral returns to the same quadrant that is under the abacus. 

The thickness of the capital is to be made such that, out of the nine and a half parts, three parts hang down below [the **bead molding** <note>original catchword: *astragalum*</note>...]
