### BOOK THREE

->THIRD<-

<page-num>58</page-num>

When the **capitals** are finished, they are then to be placed on the tops of the column **shafts** <term>original: *scapis*; the main vertical part of the column</term>, not perfectly level, but according to the same **module** <term>original: *modulus*; a standard unit of measurement in classical architecture</term> so that whatever addition was made to the **stylobates** <term>the top step of the temple platform on which the columns stand</term> corresponds to the symmetry of the **architraves** <term>original: *epistylium*; the horizontal beam that rests directly on the column capitals</term> in the upper members.

The rule for the architraves is to be maintained thus: if the columns are from a minimum of 12 feet to 15 feet in height, the height of the architrave should be half the thickness of the bottom of the column. Likewise, from 15 feet to 20 feet, let the column height be measured into 13 parts, and let the height of one part become the height of the architrave. Likewise, if from 20 to 25 feet, let the height be divided into twelve and a half parts, and one of those parts shall become the height of the architrave. Likewise, if from 25 to 30 feet, let it be divided into twelve parts, and one part of that becomes the height. 

In the same manner, the heights of the architraves are to be determined according to these proportional parts based on the height of the columns. For the higher the line of sight climbs, the less easily it pierces the thickness of the air; therefore, as the distance of the height increases and the visual strength is worn away, it reports an uncertain quantity of the modules to the senses <note>Vitruvius describes an ancient theory of optics where the "density" of the air between the eye and a tall object causes the object to appear smaller or distorted, requiring architects to make parts larger as they get higher up</note>. For this reason, a proportional supplement must always be added to the symmetry of the members so that when the works are in higher places, or even when they are **colossi** <term>exceptionally large statues or structures</term>, they may maintain the correct appearance of their magnitude. 

The width of the architrave at the bottom, which will be above the capital, should be as great as the thickness of the top of the column just below the capital; the very top of the architrave should be as wide as the bottom of the column shaft. The **cymatium** <term>a decorative S-shaped molding</term> of the architrave is to be made one-seventh of its height, and its projection should be the same. The remaining part, excluding the cymatium, is to be divided into 12 parts; of these, the first **fascia** <term>original: *fascia*; one of the three flat, horizontal bands that make up an Ionic architrave</term> should be three parts, the second four, and the uppermost five. Likewise, the **frieze**... <note>original: *Zo...* for *Zophorus*; the text cuts off as it begins to describe the frieze layer above the architrave</note>

# BOOK

The **frieze** <note>original: *zophorus*</note> above the **architrave** <note>original: *epistylium*</note> is to be a quarter part smaller in height than the architrave itself. 
But if **sculpted figures** <note>original: *sigilla*</note> are to be included, the frieze should be a quarter part higher than the architrave, so that the carvings may have proper presence and authority. 
The **molding** <note>original: *cymatium*</note> is to be one-seventh of its height, and its projection should be equal to its thickness. 
Above the frieze, the **dentils** <note>original: *denticulus*; tooth-like rectangular blocks</note> are to be made as high as the middle **band** <note>original: *fascia*</note> of the architrave, and their projection should be equal to their height. 

The spacing between them, which in Greek is called the **metoche** <term>original: *μετοχὴ*; the "sharing" or gap between decorative elements</term>, is to be divided so that the face of each dentil is half its height in width. The hollow of this spacing should be two-thirds of the width of the dentil face. The molding of this section should be one-sixth of its height. 

The **cornice** <note>original: *corona*</note> with its molding—excluding the **gutter** <note>original: *sima*</note>—should be as high as the middle band of the architrave. The projection of the cornice, including the dentils, should be equal to the total height from the frieze to the top of the cornice's molding. Indeed, all **projections** <note>original: *ecphorae*</note> generally have a more graceful appearance when their projection is equal to their height. 

As for the **tympanum** <term>original: *tympanum*; the triangular face of the pediment</term> which is in the **pediment** <note>original: *fastigium*; the peaked roof end</term>, its height is to be determined thus: the front of the cornice from its outermost moldings is to be measured and divided into nine parts; one of these parts shall be set as the height in the center of the tympanum. 

Meanwhile, the architraves and the **necks of the columns** <term>original: *hypotrachelia*; the part of the column shaft just below the capital</term> must correspond exactly to a vertical plumb line. The cornices which are placed above the tympanum are to be made equal to the lower ones, excluding the gutters. Furthermore, the **gutters**—which the Greeks call **epitithedes** <term>original: *ἐπιτιθίδas*; literally "things placed upon," the crown moldings or rain gutters</term>—are to be made one-eighth higher than the height of the cornices. 

The **corner ornaments** <term>original: *acroteria*; decorative pedestals often supporting statues at the points of the roof</term> are to be as high as the center of the tympanum, while the middle ornament is to be one-eighth higher than those at the corners.

# BOOK

All the members that are to be placed above the capitals of the columns—that is, the <term>architraves</term> <note>original: "epistylia"; the main horizontal beams resting on the columns</note>, the <term>friezes</term> <note>original: "Zophori"; the decorative band above the architrave</note>, the <term>cornices</term> <note>original: "coronæ"</note>, the <term>pediments</term> <note>original: "tympana"</note>, the <term>gables</term> <note>original: "fastigia"</note>, and the <term>pedestals</term> <note>original: "acroteria"; the bases for statues at the corners or apex of a roof</note>—must be tilted forward by a twelfth part of their own height. The reason for this is that when we stand opposite the facade, if two lines are extended from the eye, and one touches the lowest part of the work while the other touches the highest, the line touching the highest part will be longer. Thus, as the line of sight proceeds further toward the upper part, it makes the object appear to be leaning backward. However, when the members are tilted forward (as written above), they will then appear to the eye to be perfectly vertical and level. The <term>flutes</term> <note>original: "striges"</note> of the columns are to be twenty-four in number. They should be hollowed out in such a way that if a <term>square</term> <note>original: "norma"; a tool for measuring right angles</note> is placed in the hollow of the flute and turned, it touches the corners of the flute's edges on the right and left, so that the point of the square can travel through the entire curve by being rotated.

->d<-

The thickness of the <term>flutes</term> <note>the vertical grooves on a column</note> must be made according to the measurement found in the middle of the column, following the proportions established in the drawing. On the <term>simas</term> <note>the upturned edge of a roof or gutter</note> which are located above the <term>corona</term> <note>the projecting part of the cornice</note> on the sides of the temple, lion heads are to be carved. These should be positioned so that they are first marked out directly above each individual column; the remaining heads are then arranged at equal intervals so that each one corresponds to the middle of a roof tile. Those heads placed directly over the columns should be bored through to the channel that catches the rainwater from the tiles. However, the heads in between should be solid, so that the force of the water falling through the tiles into the channel is not thrown down through the <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>the open spaces between columns</note>, which would drench those passing by. Instead, only the heads over the columns will appear to vomit forth streams of water from their mouths. I have described the arrangements of Ionic temples as clearly as I could in this—

# MARCUS VITRUVIUS ON ARCHITECTURE

## BOOK FOUR

<margin>d</margin>
<margin>13</margin>
When I noticed, Emperor <note>Referring to Augustus Caesar</note>, that many people had left behind instructions and volumes of commentaries on architecture that were not organized, but merely scattered fragments of beginnings, I thought it a worthy and most useful task to first bring the body of this discipline to a complete order, and to explain the qualities of each individual type in prescribed volumes. Therefore, Caesar, in the first volume I set forth for you the duties of the architect and the subjects in which he ought to be educated; in the second, I discussed the supply of materials from which buildings are constructed; in the third, moreover, I dealt with the arrangements of sacred temples and the variety of their types—what and how many species they have—and the distributions of those features found in each type. From the three styles, I taught the characteristics of the Ionic order, which possesses the most subtle qualities in the proportions of its modules <note>term: module; a standard unit of measurement used to determine the proportions of a building</note>. Now, in this volume, I shall speak about the Doric and Corinthian institutions and all their details, and I shall explain <note>original: "expicabo," likely a typo for "explicabo"</note> their differences and properties.

### On the origins and inventions of the three types of columns.
### Chapter 1.

However, the height of their capitals makes them proportionally taller and more slender than the Ionic. The height of a Corinthian capital is equal to the entire thickness of the column shaft. # BOOK 4

<note>original: "LIBER 4" - The OCR reads "LIBER 0", but the context of the orders and the Roman numeral IV (4) in Vitruvius's *De Architectura* confirms this is Book 4.</note>

The height of these columns makes them appear more slender. The other members placed above the columns are arranged on Corinthian columns either according to **Doric** proportions or **Ionic** customs. This is because the Corinthian style itself never had its own specific system for cornices and other ornaments; instead, mutules <note>rectangular blocks under the soffit of the cornice</note> are placed in the cornices and drops <note>original: "guttæ" - small cone-shaped ornaments</note> are arranged on the architraves in the Doric fashion. Alternatively, following Ionic institutions, the friezes <note>original: "Zophori"</note> are decorated with sculptures and distributed alongside dentils <note>small tooth-like blocks</note> and cornices. Thus, by interposing a new capital between these two styles, a third order was created for architectural works.

From the different formations of columns, three names have arisen: **Doric**, **Ionic**, and **Corinthian**. Of these, the Doric was the first to be born in ancient times. For in Achaia and the whole Peloponnese, Dorus—the son of Hellen and the nymph Orseis <note>OCR: "opticos", likely a corruption of "Orseidos"</note>—reigned as king. He built a temple to Juno in the ancient city of Argos, and the form of this shrine happened to be of that style. Later, this same style was used in the other cities of Achaia, even though the system of proportions <note>term: "symmetriarum ratio" - the mathematical relationship between parts</note> had not yet been born.

Afterward, the Athenians, following the oracles of the Delphic Apollo and by the common counsel of all Greece <note>original: "hellados"</note>, led thirteen colonies into Asia at one time. They appointed leaders for each colony and gave the supreme command to Ion, the son of Xuthus and Creusa (whom Apollo at Delphi had even declared to be his own son in his oracles). He led these colonies into Asia, occupied the borders of Caria, and there established very great cities: Ephesus, Miletus, Myus (which was long ago swallowed by the water, and whose sacred rites and voting rights the Ionians assigned to the Milesians), Priene, Samos, Teos,

# BOOK FOUR

...Colophon, Chios, Erythrae, Phocaea, Clazomenae, Lebedos, and Melite. This Melite, on account of the arrogance of its citizens, was destroyed in a war declared by the common counsel of these other cities. In its place, later through the kindness of King Attalus and Arsinoe, the city of the Smyrneans was received among the Ionians. When these cities had driven out the Carians and Leleges <note>ancient indigenous peoples of the Aegean region</note>, they called that region of the land Ionia, after their leader Ion. 

Establishing temples to the immortal gods there, they began to build shrines. First, they established a temple to **Panionian Apollo** <note>original: "Apollini pannionio" - Apollo as the patron of the Panionium, the religious confederacy of Ionian cities</note> just as they had seen in Achaia, and they called it **Doric**, because they had first seen it built in that style in the cities of the Dorians. 

In that temple, when they wished to place columns but did not yet have their system of proportions <term>symmetrias: the proportional relationship between the parts and the whole</term>, and were seeking by what methods they could make them so that they would be suitable for bearing weight and possess an approved beauty <term>uenustatem: aesthetic grace or charm</term> in appearance, they measured the footprint of a man. Having found that a foot is the sixth part of a man’s height, they applied this proportion to the column. Whatever thickness they gave to the base of the shaft, they extended it six times in height, including the capital. Thus the Doric column began to provide the proportion, strength, and beauty of a man’s body in buildings.

# BOOK TWO

In the same way, later on, when they intended to establish a temple for **Diana** and were searching for a new kind of appearance, they used these same principles to translate the design into a **feminine slenderness**. First, they made the thickness of the column an eighth part of its height, so that it would possess a taller appearance. Beneath it, they placed a base <term>spira: the molded foot of a column</term> <note>original: "spirā"</note> to serve as a shoe. 

Upon the capital <note>the top-most part of the column</note>, they placed **volutes** <term>volutas: spiral, scroll-like ornaments</term> <note>original: "uolutas"</note>, arranged like curled locks of hair hanging down on the right and left. They decorated the front of the column with moldings <term>cymatiis: decorative wave-like strips</term> and festoons <term>encarpis: carved garlands of fruit or flowers</term> <note>original: "cymatiis & encarpis"</note> to represent braided hair. Down the entire shaft, they let down flutes <term>strias: vertical grooves</term> <note>original: "strias"</note>, resembling the folds of a matronly robe <note>original: "stolarum rugas"</note>. 

Thus, through two distinct styles, they achieved the invention of columns: one being the **masculine** style, characterized by a bare appearance without ornament; the other being the **feminine** style, which they imitated through its delicacy, decoration, and symmetry <term>symmetria: the proportional harmony of parts</term>. 

Later generations, however, advancing in their elegance and the refinement of their judgment, and finding delight in even more slender modules, [established] seven diameters for the thickness...

This style, which the **Ionians** created, was first named **Ionic**. *The first invention of that capital* <note>the ornate top of the column</note> *is recorded to have occurred in this way:*

*A maiden, a citizen of **Corinth**, who was already of marriageable age* <note>original: "matura nuptijs"</note>, *was seized by a disease and passed away. # BOOK FOUR

...covered it with a roof tile <note>original: "tegula texit"</note>. This basket <term>calathus: a wicker basket, often associated with women's work or religious offerings</term> <note>original: "Is calathus"</note> happened to have been placed directly over the root of an **acanthus** plant. In the meantime, the acanthus root, pressed down by the weight, sent forth leaves from its center and little stalks around the springtime <note>original: "circa uernum tempus"</note>; these stalks, growing along the sides of the basket and forced by the weight of the corners of the tile, were compelled to form curves at the edges, creating **volutes** <term>volutes: spiral, scroll-like ornaments that characterize the tops of columns</term> <note>original: "uolutarum"</note>. 

Then **Callimachus**, who was nicknamed *Catatechnos* <term>Catatechnos: a Greek term meaning 'refined craftsman' or 'master of the craft'</term> <note>original: "catatechnos"</note> by the Athenians for the elegance and refinement of his marble-work, noticed this monument while passing by. He observed the basket and the tenderness of the leaves growing around it; delighted by the style and the novelty of the form, he created columns for the **Corinthians** based on this model. He established their **symmetries** <term>symmetries: the proportional relationships between the various parts of a structure</term> and, from that point, determined the principles for the finished works of the Corinthian order. 

The symmetry of this capital <note>the decorative top of the column</note> is to be fashioned so that the height of the capital, including the **abacus** <term>abacus: the flat, square slab forming the very top of a column's capital</term> <note>original: "abaco"</note>, is equal to the thickness of the column at its base. The width of the abacus should be proportioned so that its diagonal measurement from corner to corner is twice its height; in this way, the faces will have the correct proportions in every direction.

The faces of the width should be curved inward from the outer corners of the abacus by an amount equal to one-ninth of the width of that face <note>original: "suæ frontis latitudinis nona"</note>. At the base of the capital, they should have a thickness equal to that of the very top of the column shaft, excluding the **fillet** <term>apothesis: the curved molding where the shaft meets the capital</term> <note>original: "apothesim"</note> and the **bead molding** <term>astragalus: a small, rounded convex molding</term> <note>original: "astragalum"</note>. The thickness of the **abacus** should be one-seventh of the total height of the capital. Once the thickness of the abacus is subtracted, the remaining part is to be divided into three sections. Of these, one part is given to the lower leaf; a second leaf should occupy the middle height; and the **stalks** <term>cauliculi: the stems from which the decorative foliage and spirals emerge</term> <note>original: "cauliculi"</note> should be of the same height. From these stalks, the projected leaves grow out so as to support the abacus; these leaves, which spring from the stalks, run out to the furthest corners as **volutes** <term>volutes: the large spiral scrolls at the corners</term>, while smaller **spirals** <term>helices: the smaller internal scrolls of the capital</term> <note>original: "helices"</note> should be carved within the middle space of the abacus, positioned beneath the flowers. ### BOOK IV
## On the ornaments of columns. Chapter II.

*Since the origins and inventions of the different types of columns*
<margin>9</margin> *have been described above, it seems appropriate for me*
*to discuss their ornaments using the same logic—how*
*they came to be, and the principles and origins from*
*which they were discovered. In all buildings, timber-work* <term>materiatio: the structural woodwork or framing of a building</term> <note>original: "materiatio"</note> *is*
*placed on top, known by various names. Just as these terms*
*vary, the timber-work itself serves various practical purposes.*
*For example, beams* <term>trabes: the main horizontal beams, often called architraves in stone</term> <note>original: "trabes"</note> *are placed above columns, pilasters* <note>original: "parastatas"</note>, *and wall-ends* <term>antae: decorative or structural posts at the ends of walls</term> <note>original: "antas"</note>. *In floor framings* <term>contignationibus: the timber framework of a floor or ceiling</term> <note>original: "contignationibus"</note>, *there are joists* <note>original: "tigna"</note> *and planks. Under the roof, if the spans are large, a ridge-piece* <note>original: "columen"</note> *is placed at the very peak of the roof—from which the word "columns"* <note>original: "columnae"</note> *is derived—as well as cross-beams* <note>original: "transtra"</note> *and struts* <note>original: "capreoli"</note>. *If the span is moderate, there is a ridge-piece and rafters* <term>cantherii: the principal rafters supporting the roof's slope</term> <note>original: "canterij"</note> *which project out to the edge of the eaves* <term>subgrudationem: the overhanging part of a roof designed to shed water</term> <note>original: "subgrudationem"</note>.

...imitated these forms and believed those inventions should be pursued. Thus, when ancient craftsmen were building in a certain place, they had placed beams protruding from the inner walls to the outermost parts. They built up the spaces between the beams and then adorned the cornices and gables with more beautiful craftsmanship. Then, they trimmed the projections of the beams—as far as they stood out—to the line and plumb-level of the walls. Because this appearance seemed unattractive to them, they fixed tablets shaped like the <term>triglyphs</term> <note>three-grooved panels in a Doric frieze</note> we see today against the cut ends of the beams on the front, and painted them with blue wax so that the concealed beam-cuts would not offend the eye. Thus, the covered divisions of the beams, arranged as triglyphs, began to occupy the spaces between the beams and the <term>metopes</term> <note>original: "opam"; the gaps between triglyphs</note> in Doric works.

Later, others in different projects extended the <term>rafters</term> <note>original: "canterios"</note> so they projected over the vertical line of the triglyphs, and they rounded off those projections. Just as the system of triglyphs arose from the arrangement of the beams, so the logic of <term>mutules</term> <note>original: "mutilorum"</note> beneath the cornices was derived from the projections of the rafters. For this reason, in stone and marble works, the mutules are carved with a downward slant, which is an imitation of the rafters; indeed, they are necessarily placed with an incline to allow for the dripping of rainwater. Therefore, the logic of both triglyphs and mutules in Doric works was discovered through this imitation.

It cannot be as some have mistakenly said—that triglyphs are representations of windows—because triglyphs are placed at the corners and over the centers of columns, locations where the structural reality does not allow for windows at all. For the joints at the corners of buildings are weakened if window openings are placed within them.

<i>i</i> <note>Printer's signature mark</note>

# BOOK FOUR

#### H iij
<meta>catchword: ori</meta>

...having been left behind, and even where triglyphs are now placed; if those areas are judged to have once been spaces for windows <note>original: "luminum spatia"</note>, then by the same logic, it will seem that <term>dentils</term> <note>small, block-like carvings used in Ionic cornices</note> in the Ionic order have occupied the places of windows. For the intervals found both between dentils and between triglyphs are called <term>metopes</term>. Indeed, the Greeks call the sockets for the main beams and the smaller rafters <term>opas</term> <note>original: "όπαϛ"; meaning holes or openings</note>, just as our builders call those hollows "dove-holes" <note>original: "columbaria"; referring to the holes in a dovecote</note>. Thus, the space between two sockets is called a "between-socket" <note>original: "intertignium"</note>, which they named a metope. Just as the logic of triglyphs and <term>mutules</term> <note>sloping decorative blocks</note> was established earlier for the Doric order, the arrangement of dentils in Ionic works has its own specific logic. And just as mutules represent the projection of the primary <term>rafters</term> <note>original: "canteriorum"</note>, so the dentils in Ionic architecture are an imitation of the projections of the smaller <term>laths</term> <note>original: "asserum"; the smaller wooden strips in a roof frame</note>.

Therefore, in Greek works, no one ever places dentils beneath a mutule, because laths cannot be located underneath the primary rafters. If something that in reality must be placed above the rafters and <term>purlins</term> <note>original: "templa"; horizontal roof beams</note> were placed below them in these stone representations, the logic of the work would be fundamentally flawed. Furthermore, the ancients did not approve of, nor did they establish, the use of dentils in <term>pediments</term> <note>original: "fastigijs"; the triangular gables of a temple</note>, but used plain cornices instead. This is because neither primary rafters nor laths are distributed across the front of a gable, nor can they project forward there; instead, they are positioned sloping down toward the eaves <note>original: "stillicidia"</note> to shed water. Thus, they believed that something which cannot happen in reality could not have a sound logic when depicted in an imitation.

For they translated everything into the perfection of their finished works with a certain propriety and according to the true principles derived from nature. They approved only of those features whose explanations, when discussed, can maintain the logic of truth. And so, from these origins...

<summary>Vitruvius explains that architectural ornaments like dentils and triglyphs are not arbitrary decorations but stone imitations of functional wooden roof components (rafters and laths). He emphasizes that these features must follow the "logic of truth," meaning they should only be placed where their wooden ancestors would have naturally functioned.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR

...origins, they left behind established symmetries and proportions for every style. Having followed in their footsteps, I have spoken above about the Ionic and Corinthian systems; now, however, I shall briefly explain the Doric rule and its complete appearance.

### On the Doric Rule. Chapter III.

<margin>n</margin>Some ancient architects asserted that sacred temples should not be built in the Doric style, because the symmetries produced in them were flawed and awkward. Thus Tarthesius denied it, as did Pytheus, and no less Hermogenes. For Hermogenes, when he had a ready supply of marble for the completion of a Doric temple, changed his plan and, using that same supply, built an Ionic temple to Father Liber <note>original: "Libero patri"; another name for Bacchus or Dionysus</note>. This was not because the appearance, style, or dignity of the form is unlovely, but because the arrangement is hindered and inconvenient regarding the placement of the <term>triglyphs</term> <note>tablet-like blocks with three vertical grooves</note> and the <term>lacunaria</term> <note>sunken panels in a ceiling, also called coffers</note>.

For it is necessary that triglyphs be placed over the centers of the columns <note>original: "contra medios tetrantes"; literally "opposite the middle quarters"</note>, and that the <term>metopes</term> <note>the square spaces between triglyphs</note> created between the triglyphs be as long as they are high. Conversely, at the corner columns, the triglyphs are placed at the very ends rather than over the column centers. Consequently, the metopes flanking these corner triglyphs do not end up square, but are longer than the others by half the width of a triglyph. Yet, if they wish to make the metopes equal, they must narrow the outermost <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>the spaces between columns</note> by half the width of a triglyph. Whether this is resolved by altering the length of the metopes or by narrowing the spacing between columns, the result is considered a defect. For this reason, the ancients appear to have avoided the system of Doric symmetry in sacred temples. We, however, shall explain it as the sequence of our work requires, just as I have received it from my teachers.

<summary>Vitruvius introduces the Doric order, noting that famous ancient architects avoided it due to the 'Doric problem'—the geometric difficulty of aligning triglyphs and metopes at the corners of a building.</summary>
<keywords>Doric order, triglyphs, metopes, intercolumniation, Hermogenes, Tarthesius, Pytheus, architectural symmetry, temple design</keywords>

# BOOK FOUR

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

...we may, so that if anyone wishes to proceed by attending to these principles, they may have the proportions explained, by which they can produce sacred buildings in the Doric style that are perfected, corrected, and without flaws. The front of a Doric temple, at the level where the columns are set, should be divided into twenty-seven parts if it is to be <term>tetrastyle</term> <note>a temple with four columns across the front</note>, or forty-four parts if it is <term>hexastyle</term> <note>a temple with six columns across the front</note>. Of these, one part will be the <term>module</term> <note>original: "modulus"; the basic unit of measurement for the entire building</note>, which is called *embatēs* <note>original: "εμβάτης"</note> in Greek. From the establishment of this module, all the distributions of the entire work are calculated through these proportions. 

The thickness of the columns shall be two modules, and the height, including the capital, shall be fourteen. The thickness of the capital is to be one module, and its width is to be two modules and one-sixth of a module. The thickness of the capital is to be divided into three parts, of which one shall be the <term>plinth</term> <note>the flat, square slab at the top of a capital</note> with its <term>cymatium</term> <note>a wave-like decorative molding</note>; the second shall be the <term>echinus</term> <note>the rounded, cushion-like molding</note> with its rings; and the third shall be the <term>hypotrachelion</term> <note>the "necking" or the part of the column shaft just below the capital moldings</note>. The column is to be tapered, just as was written in the third book concerning the Ionic order.

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

The height of the <term>architrave</term> <note>original: "epistylium"; the main stone beam that rests directly on the column capitals</note> is to be one module, including the <term>fillet</term> <note>original: "tenia"; a small, flat projecting band</note> and the <term>drops</term> <note>original: "guttae"; small, decorative peg-like shapes</note>. The fillet should be one-seventh of a module. The length of the drops under the fillet, positioned opposite the triglyphs, should hang down to a height of one-sixth of a module, including their listel. Furthermore, the width of the bottom of the architrave should match the <term>necking</term> <note>original: "hypotrachelium"; the top of the column shaft just below the capital</note> at the very top of the column. Above the architrave, the <term>triglyphs</term> <note>rectangular blocks with vertical grooves</note> and their <term>metopes</term> <note>original: "methopae"; the square panels between the triglyphs</note> are to be placed; these are to be one and a half modules high and one module wide across the front. They are to be arranged so that they are placed over the corner columns and over the centers of the middle columns in alignment with the center of the column quadrants. Two triglyphs are to be placed over the remaining <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>the spaces between columns</note>, but three are to be placed in the center spaces of the <term>pronaos</term> <note>the front porch of the temple</note> and the <term>posticum</term> <note>the rear porch</note>. By thus widening the central intervals, those approaching the statues of the gods will have an unobstructed entrance.

The width of the triglyph should be divided into six parts. Of these, five parts are in the middle, and two half-parts are designated on the right and left. One listel in the middle shall form a <term>thigh</term> <note>original: "femur"</note>, which is called *meros* <note>original: "μηρὸς"</note> in Greek. Beside this, the <term>channels</term> <note>original: "canaliculi"; the vertical grooves</note> are to be carved to the depth of a mason’s square. In order, other "thighs" are to be established to the right and left of these, and half-channels are to be carved at the outer edges.

# BOOK [IV]

With the triglyphs thus arranged, the **metopes** <note>original: *methopae*; the square spaces between triglyphs</note>, which are located between the triglyphs, should be as high as they are wide. Likewise, at the very corners, **half-metopes** should be inset with a width of half a **module** <note>The "module" is the basic unit of measurement in classical architecture, usually half the diameter of the column base</note>. By doing this, all the errors in the metopes, the spacing of columns, and the **lacunaria** <note>The recessed panels of a coffered ceiling</note> will be corrected, because the divisions will have been made equal.

The **triglyph capitals** <note>The small flat head atop the grooved triglyph block</note> are to be made one-sixth of a module. Above these capitals, the **corona** <note>The projecting "crown" or cornice that sheds water</note> is to be placed with a projection of one-half and one-sixth of a module. It should have a **Doric cymatium** <note>original: *cymatium doricum*; a wave-shaped molding</note> at the bottom and another at the top. Including these moldings, the corona should be half a module thick.

On the underside of the corona, aligned vertically with the triglyphs and the centers of the metopes, the distributions of the **channels** <note>original: *viarum direptiones*; the spaces between the mutule blocks</note> and the **guttae** <note>Small, drop-like ornaments</note> must be marked out. These should be arranged so that there are six guttae in length and three in width. Because the metopes are wider than the triglyphs, the remaining spaces [on the underside] should be left plain or have **lightning bolts** carved into them. Along the very edge—the "chin"—of the corona, a line called a **scotia** <note>A dark, recessed groove or "shadow-line"</note> should be cut. All other remaining parts, such as the **tympana** <note>The triangular face of the pediment</note>, the **sima** <note>The gutter molding</note>, and the rest of the corona, should be finished exactly as was described for the Ionic order. This system of proportions is established for **diastyle** <note>original: *diastylis*; a style of building where columns are spaced widely apart, specifically three diameters wide</note> works.

-> [Image: A woodcut illustration of a classical temple facade. Four fluted columns stand on a tiered base, supporting a horizontal beam (entablature) decorated with alternating triglyphs and metopes. The structure is crowned by a triangular roof section known as a pediment.] <-

The columns themselves should be **fluted** <note>original: *striari*; the process of carving vertical grooves into a column shaft</note> with twenty grooves. If these grooves are to be flat-faced, they should have twenty distinct angles. However, if they are to be hollowed out, the shape must be formed in this way: a square with equal sides should be drawn, as large as the width of the intended groove. Then, the point of a compass is placed in the center of that square, and a curved line is drawn that touches the corners of the square. The depth of the flute will be the amount of curvature between that circular line <note>The text here provides a geometric formula for masonry, ensuring each flute is perfectly proportional to the column's circumference.</note>

# BOOK [IV]

<header>FOURTH BOOK</header>

The length of the temple is distributed such that the width is half of the length, and the **inner chamber** <note>original: *cella*; the sacred interior room where the deity's image resided</note> itself is one-fourth longer than its width, including the wall where the folding doors are positioned. The remaining three parts of the length should extend as a **front porch** <note>original: *pronai*; the entrance vestibule or portico</note> towards the **pilasters** <note>original: *antas*; square piers at the end of the side walls</note> of the walls; these pilasters ought to have the same thickness as the columns. If the temple is wider than twenty feet, two columns should be placed between the two pilasters to separate the space of the **side passages** <note>original: *pteromatos*; the side wings or walkways</note> from the porch area. Likewise, the **spaces between the columns** <note>original: *intercolumniatria*</note> that fall between the pilasters and the columns should be closed off with marble **screens** <note>original: *pluteis*; low balustrades or partitions</note> or with screens made of **fine woodwork** <note>original: *ex intestino opere*; detailed joinery or carpentry</note>, arranged so they have doors through which one can enter the porch.

# BOOK IV

<header>FOURTH BOOK</header>

Likewise, if the width is greater than forty feet, columns should be placed inside, aligned with the positions of the columns that stand between the **pilasters** <note>original: *antas*; square piers at the end of temple walls</note>. These internal columns should have the same height as those on the front of the temple, but their **thicknesses** <note>original: *crassitudines*</note> should be thinned according to these proportions: if the front columns are one-eighth [of their height] in thickness, these inner ones should be made one-ninth. But if the front ones are one-ninth or one-tenth, they should be reduced proportionally <note>Vitruvius suggests that columns inside a building should appear more slender than those outside to maintain a sense of space and elegance</note>.

# BOOK IV

<header>FOURTH BOOK</header>

...should be made. For in an enclosed space, if any parts are thinned out, they will not be noticed, but rather they will appear more graceful. When there are twenty-four **flutes** <note>original: *striæ*; the vertical grooves or ridges on a column</note> on the exterior columns, twenty-eight or thirty-two should be made on these interior ones. Thus, what is taken away from the body of the shaft will be restored by the increased number of flutes; the loss of thickness will be less apparent, and so the thickness of the columns will be equalized despite the disparity in their actual measurements. This is achieved because the eye, by touching more numerous and frequent points, wanders through a greater circuit of vision. For if two columns of equal thickness are measured with lines around them—one of which is not fluted and the other fluted—and the line touches the hollows of the grooves and the corners of the flutes, even though the columns are equally thick, the lines that encircle them will not be equal, because the circuit of the flutes and grooves will create a greater length of line. 

If this is seen to be the case, it is not out of place in narrow locations and enclosed spaces to establish more slender **proportions** <note>original: *symmetrias*; the harmonious relationship between parts</note> for columns in the work, since we have the adjustment of the fluting as an aid. Furthermore, the thickness of the walls of the **shrine** <note>original: *cellæ*; the inner chamber of the temple where the cult statue stood</note> itself ought to be made in proportion to its size, provided that their **pilasters** <note>original: *antæ*; square piers at the end of the walls</note> are equal in thickness to the columns. If the walls are to be built of masonry, they should be properly constructed with the smallest possible **rubble stones** <note>original: *cementis*; small unhewn stones used in core masonry</note>. 

But if they are made of **squared stone** <note>original: *quadrato saxo*; precisely cut ashlar blocks</note> or marble, it seems best to use moderately sized and equal blocks, because the middle stones, by overlapping the central joints, will make the completion of the whole work firmer. Likewise, the raised edges around the joints and the beds of the stones will create a more **visually pleasing** <note>original: *graphicoteram*; a Latinized Greek term meaning "more graphic" or "more picturesque"</note> delight in their appearance.

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

### On the orientation of temples according to the regions of the world.
### Chapter V.

The **temples** <note>original: *ædes*; literally "dwellings," here referring to the sacred houses of the gods</note> of the immortal gods must be arranged according to the cardinal directions in this way: if nothing prevents it and the choice is free, the temple and the statue placed in the **inner chamber** <note>original: *cella*; the central room where the cult statue resided</note> should face the western region of the sky. In this way, those who approach the altar to make offerings or perform sacrifices will face the eastern part of the heavens, as will the cult image itself within the temple. Thus, those undertaking vows will look upon the temple and the eastern sky at once, and the statues themselves will seem to look upon the supplicants and sacrificers as they rise from the east. It appears necessary that all altars of the gods should face the east.

However, if the nature of the site interferes with this, the orientation of these buildings must be altered so that as much of the city walls as possible can be seen from the temples of the gods. Likewise, if temples are built along rivers, as they are seen to do in Egypt near the Nile, they ought to face the riverbanks. Similarly, if the buildings of the gods are situated along public roads, they should be positioned so that passersby can look toward them and offer greetings while in their sight.

### On the proportions of doors and door-frames for sacred temples.
### Chapter VI.

For the doors and their **frames** <note>original: *antepagmentorum*; the decorative door-jambs or moldings around an opening</note> in temples, these are the principles: first, determine the style in which they are to be built. For the types of **doorways** <note>original: *thyromaton*; a term derived from Greek referring to large ornamental doors or gates</note> are these: Doric, Ionic, and Attic-style. The **proportions** <note>original: *symmetriæ*; the harmonious relationship of measurements</note> of the Doric style are determined by these rules: the top **cornice** <note>original: *corona*; the uppermost projecting part of the frame</note>, which is placed above the upper frame, must be perfectly level with the tops of the capitals...

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

...columns which are in the porch. The opening of the **doorway** <note>original: *hyperthyri*; the space above the door or the doorway itself</note> should be established so that the total height of the temple, from the floor to the **coffered ceilings** <note>original: *lacunaria*; the recessed decorative panels in a ceiling</note>, is divided into three and a half parts. Of these, two parts are to be assigned to the height of the door opening. This height should then be divided into twelve parts; five and a half of these shall be the width of the opening at the bottom.

The opening should narrow toward the top. If the opening is between the floor and sixteen feet high, it should narrow by one-third of the width of the **jamb** <note>original: *antepagmenti*; the decorative frame or molding around the door</note>. From sixteen to twenty-five feet, the upper part of the opening should narrow by one-fourth the width of the jamb. If from twenty-five to thirty feet, the top part should narrow by one-eighth of the jamb. Any doors higher than this should be placed perpendicularly <note>meaning the sides should be perfectly vertical rather than tapering</note>.

The **jambs** <note>original: *antepagmenta*</note> themselves should be made with a face thickness equal to one-twelfth of the opening’s height, and they should narrow at the top by one-fourteenth of their own thickness. The height of the **lintel** <note>original: *supercilij*; the horizontal beam at the top of the door frame</note> should be the same as the thickness of the jambs at their top. A **molding** <note>original: *cymatium*; a decorative "wave-like" molding</note> must be made, one-sixth the size of the jamb. Its **projection** <note>original: *proiectura*; the distance the molding extends out from the wall</note> should be equal to its thickness. A **Lesbian molding** <note>original: *cymatium lesbium*; a specific double-curved molding</note> with a **bead-and-reel** <note>original: *astragalo*; a small, rounded molding resembling beads</note> should be carved.

Above the molding on the lintel, a **frieze** <note>original: *hyperthyrum*</note> is to be placed, equal in thickness to the lintel, and on it should be carved a **Doric molding** <note>original: *cymatium doricum*</note>, a **Lesbian bead-and-reel**, and a **crowning molding** <note>original: *sima*</note>. Then, a flat **cornice** <note>original: *corona*</note> should be made with its own molding; its projection will be equal to the height of the lintel placed above the jambs. On the right and left, the projections should be made so that the **edges** <note>original: *crepidines*</note> extend out and the moldings are joined together **perfectly at the corner** <note>original: *in ungue*; literally "to the fingernail," a technical term for a precise miter joint</note>.

*If, however, the doorways are to be of the **Ionic order** <note>original: *ionico genere*</note>, the height of the **opening** <note>original: *lumen*</note> is to be determined in the same manner as is seen to be done for the **Doric order** <note>referring to the proportions on the previous page</note>. Let the width be established by dividing the height into two and a half parts; of these, one and a half parts shall constitute the width of the bottom of the opening. The narrowing of the width toward the top <note>original: *contractura*</note> should be done just as in the Doric order. The thickness of the **jambs** <note>original: *antepagmentorum*</note> on their front face should be one-fourteenth part of the height of the opening. The **molding** <note>original: *cymatium*; a wave-shaped decorative trim</note> should be one-sixth of this thickness. Let the remaining part, excluding the molding, be divided into twelve parts. Of these, the first **fascia** <note>original: *corsa*; a flat, stepped band</note> with its **bead-molding** <note>original: *astragalus*; a small rounded molding like a string of beads</note> shall be three parts; the second fascia four parts; and the third fascia five parts. These fascias, together with their bead-moldings, should run all the way around the frame.*

*The **over-door members** <note>original: *hyperthyra*; the architectural elements above the lintel</note> should be composed in the same manner as in the Doric **portal-heads** <note>original: *hypothyridibus*</note>. Let the **brackets** <note>original: *ancones*, also called *prothyrides*</note> be carved and hang down on the right and left to the level of the bottom of the **lintel** <note>original: *supercilium*</note>, excluding the leaf-decoration. These brackets should have a thickness on their face equal to one-third of the thickness of the jambs, and at the bottom, they should be one-fourth part more slender than at the top.*

<vocab>
**Ionic order** (*ionico genere*): One of the three classical Greek orders, characterized by more slender proportions and scroll-like ornaments.
**Opening** (*lumen*): The clear space of the doorway.
**Jambs** (*antepagmenta*): The decorative moldings or casings that frame the door.
**Molding** (*cymatium*): A decorative curve, often S-shaped.
**Bead-molding** (*astragalus*): A small convex molding, often decorated with bead-and-reel patterns.
**Fascia** (*corsa*): A horizontal or vertical band that is part of a larger molding.
**Over-door** (*hyperthyra*): The structure above the door lintel.
**Brackets** (*ancones*): Scroll-like supports (also called consoles) flanking the lintel.
**Lintel** (*supercilium*): The horizontal beam at the top of the door frame.
**Cornice** (*corona*): The topmost projecting part of the door's entablature.
</vocab>

Let the **doors** <note>original: *fores*</note> be constructed so that the **hinge-stiles** <note>original: *scapi cardinales*; the main vertical members of the door frame that contain the pivots or hinges</note> are one-twelfth the total height of the opening. Between the two stiles, the **panels** <note>original: *tympana*</note> should occupy three parts out of twelve in width. The arrangement of the **cross-rails** <note>original: *impages*; the horizontal members of the door frame</note> shall be handled such that, if the total height is divided into five parts, two parts are designated for the upper section and three for the lower. 

Above the center, the middle rails are to be placed; of the rest, let some be fastened at the very top and others at the bottom. The width of a rail should be one-third the width of a panel, and the **molding** <note>original: *cymatium*</note> should be one-sixth the width of the rail. The widths of the stiles should be half the width of a rail. Likewise, the **cover-strip** <note>original: *replum*; a decorative molding used to cover the vertical joint where the two leaves of a double door meet</note> should be one-half plus one-sixth of the width of a rail. The stiles which are positioned in front of the **inner framework** <note>original: *secundum pagmentum*</note> should be set at half the width of a rail.

### BOOK FOUR

If, however, the doors are of the **folding type** <note>original: *valvatae*; door leaves that swing or fold back</note>, the heights shall remain as previously established, but the width should be increased by the width of an additional door leaf. If the entrance is to be a **four-leaf door** <note>original: *quadriforis*</note>, the height should also be increased accordingly.

**Attic-style doors** <note>original: *Atticurges*</note> are completed using the same proportions as the **Doric style** <note>original: *dorica*</note>. Furthermore, **fasciae** <note>original: *corsae*; flat decorative bands</note> are placed beneath the **moldings** <note>original: *cymatia*</note> on the **door-frames** <note>original: *antepagmenta*; the decorative wood or stone frames around the opening</note>. These should be distributed in such a way that they surround the frames, in addition to the molding.

...out of seven parts, they should have two. Furthermore, the door ornaments are not made in the **inlaid style** <note>original: *cerostrata*; likely referring to doors decorated with wax-painting or elaborate horn-like inlays</note> nor as **double-leaf doors** <note>original: *bifora*</note>, but as **folding doors** <note>original: *valvata*</note>, and they should have openings that swing toward the outside. I have explained the proportions of sacred buildings as they ought to be created in the **Doric** <note>original: *doricis*</note>, **Ionic** <note>original: *ionicis*</note>, and **Corinthian** <note>original: *corinthijsq;*</note> styles, following established custom as far as I could reach. Now, I shall describe the **Tuscan arrangements** <note>original: *tuscanicis dispositionibus*</note> and how they ought to be constructed.

### On the Tuscan proportions of sacred buildings.
## Chapter VII.

The site on which the temple is to be established should be measured so that when its length is divided into six parts, one part is subtracted, and the remainder is given to the width <note>This creates a 6:5 ratio of length to width</note>. The length is then divided into two equal halves. The inner half is designated for the space of the **chambers** <note>original: *cellarum*; the enclosed inner rooms of the temple</note>, while the half closest to the front is left for the arrangement of the columns.

Likewise, the width is divided into ten parts. Of these, three parts each to the right and left are given to the smaller chambers, or where the **wings** <note>original: *alae*; side aisles or recessed spaces</note> are to be located; the remaining four parts are assigned to the middle of the temple. The space in front of the chambers, in the **porch** <note>original: *pronao*</note>, shall be designed with columns so that the corner columns are placed directly opposite the **piers** <note>original: *antas*; the thickened ends of the walls</note> of the outermost walls. 

The two middle columns are to be distributed in line with the walls that stand between the piers and the middle of the temple. Another row of columns is to be arranged in the middle, between the piers and the front columns, in those same alignments. At their base, these columns should have a thickness equal to one-seventh of their height. The height of the columns should be one-third of the temple's width. The top of the column should be **tapered** <note>original: *contrahatur*; reduced in diameter</note> so that it is one-fourth thinner than its thickness at the bottom.

And the thickness of the capital <note>original: "capituli"</note> should be divided into three parts, of which one is given to the plinth <note>The square block that makes up the top part of the abacus.</note> which is in the abacus, the second to the echinus <note>A rounded, cushion-like molding found below the abacus; the name is derived from the Greek word for a sea urchin.</note>, and the third to the neck <term>hypotrachelium|The small decorative section or 'necking' that sits between the main shaft and the capital.</term> with the collar <note>original: "apophigi"; the slight curve or 'fillet' where the column shaft transitions into the necking.</note>.

Upon the columns, composite beams <note>original: "trabes compactiles"; horizontal beams made of joined pieces of timber, also known as an architrave.</note> are to be placed, so that they follow the height proportions required by the scale of the work. These composite beams should be positioned so that their thickness matches the width of the necking <note>original: "hypotrachelium"</note> at the top of the column. They should be joined together with dowels <note>original: "subscudibus"</note> and dovetail joints <note>original: "securiclis"</note> in such a way that the joint has a gap of two fingers' width. For when the beams touch each other closely and lack an air vent or the passage of wind, they become trapped with heat and rot quickly. Above the beams and the walls, the projections of the mutules <note>original: "mutilorum"; these are sloping brackets or blocks that support the roof's edge.</note> should extend outwards by a measure equal to one-fourth of the column's height. Likewise, onto the front of these, facings <term>antepagmenta|Ornamental coverings or moldings applied to the ends of beams.</term> are to be fixed. Above these, the triangular face of the pediment <term>tympanum|The recessed decorative wall of the gable, often filled with sculpture.</term> is to be constructed, whether of masonry or wood, and above that, the pediment—

->FOURTH<-

The ridge-beam, rafters, and cross-beams <note>original: "columen, cantherij, templa"; these are the primary structural components of a timber roof frame.</note> are to be positioned so that the drainage slope of the completed roof corresponds to a third <note>original: "tertiario"; likely referring to a roof pitch where the height is one-third of the span.</note>. Round temples are also constructed, some of which are built as **monopteral** <note>A circular building with a roof supported by a single row of columns but having no inner walls.</note>, consisting of a colonnade without an inner chamber <term>cella|The enclosed central room of a temple where the cult statue was typically housed.</term>. Others are called **peripteral**, which are also made without an inner chamber <note>While peripteral usually implies a central room surrounded by columns, the author here describes a specific variation without a cella.</note>; these have a raised platform <term>tribunal|A raised area or dais.</term> and an approach consisting of one-third of their diameter. Furthermore, the column bases <term>stylobata|The continuous level of masonry forming the platform on which the columns rest.</term> should be established as high as the diameter measured between the outer walls of the bases. The columns themselves should be one-tenth as thick as their height, including the capitals and bases. The architrave <term>epistylium|The horizontal beam that rests directly upon the columns.</term> should be half as high as the thickness of a column. The frieze <term>zophorus|The decorative band above the architrave.</term> and the other elements placed above it are to be fashioned according to the proportions <note>original: "symmetriis"</note> I wrote about in the third book.

# BOOK FOUR

If, however, the temple is to be constructed in the **peripteral** <term>peripteros|A circular building surrounded by a single row of columns.</term> style, let two steps and the platform <term>stylobata|The level masonry base upon which columns are placed.</term> be established from the ground up. Then, the wall of the inner chamber <term>cella|The enclosed central room of a temple.</term> is to be positioned, set back from the platform by about one-fifth of the total width, and in the middle, space should be left for the folding doors to provide access. This inner chamber should have a diameter—excluding the walls and the surrounding walkway—equal to the height of the columns above the platform. The columns around the chamber are to be arranged according to the same proportions and symmetries <note>Vitruvius refers back to the standard ratios for column height and thickness established in previous chapters.</note> as described before. 

Regarding the center of the roof, the design should be such that the height of the dome <term>tholus|A rounded, vaulted roof crowning a circular building.</term>, excluding the floral ornament <note>original: "florem"; a decorative finial or carved flower at the very peak of the roof.</note>, is equal to half the diameter of the entire structure. The floral ornament itself should be as large as the column capital <note>The decorated top of a column.</note> at the summit, excluding its pointed section <note>original: "piramidem"; likely referring to the upper block or abacus of the capital.</note>. The remaining elements, it seems, should be fashioned according to the proportions and symmetries as they were written above.

Likewise, temples are established in other styles, arranged according to the same symmetries but having a different kind of layout. Such is the Temple of Castor in the Flaminian Circus, and the Temple of Vejovis <note>An early Roman god, often associated with the underworld or a "little Jupiter."</note> between the two sacred groves. Similarly, but more subtly executed, is the Temple of Diana in the woods, where columns have been added to the right and left at the shoulders of the portico. This specific type of design was first used in the Temple of Castor in the Circus, the Temple of Minerva on the Acropolis in Athens, and the Temple of Pallas at Sunium in Attica. Their proportions are not different, but identical. For the lengths of the inner chambers <note>term: "cellæ" - the enclosed inner rooms of a temple where the cult statue was kept</note> are double their widths, and all the features that are usually found on the front facades are here transferred to the sides.

<image-desc>A floor plan diagram of a temple layout enclosed in a double-line rectangular frame. The plan shows an outer perimeter filled with a grid of 18 column bases (indicated by dots). A central portico area contains the labels 'a' (center) and 'd' (upper left column). To the right is the cella structure, featuring a large central room labeled 'b' and four smaller side rooms labeled 'c'.</image-desc>

Some builders even take the arrangements of columns from the Tuscan styles and transfer them into the Corinthian <note>The most ornate of the three main Greek architectural orders, characterized by slender columns and capitals decorated with acanthus leaves.</note> styles.

BOOK FOUR

...and the arrangements of Ionic works. For in those places where the columns project forward in the portico <note>original: "pronao"</note>, by placing two columns in that same area in line with the walls of the inner chamber <note>term: "cella" - the central room of a temple housing the cult statue</note>, they create a shared logic between Tuscan and Greek works. Others, however, remove the walls of the temple and, by attaching them to the spaces between the columns <note>original: "intercolumnia"</note> of the colonnade <note>term: "pteroma" - the side colonnade of a temple</note>, they create a large extension of the inner chamber where the wall was removed. While keeping the remaining features in the same proportions and symmetries, they seem to have created another kind of shape and name: the **false-peripteral** <note>original: "pseudoperipterum"; a design where the side columns are embedded in the walls rather than standing free</note>. These types are adapted according to the needs of the sacrifices. For temples should not be built with the same logic for all gods, since each deity produces different results through various sacred rites. I have explained all the principles of sacred buildings as they were handed down to me, and I have distinguished their orders and symmetries by their divisions; and where their shapes are different, and by what distinctions they are separated from one another, I have set forth in writing as far as I was able. Now I shall speak about the altars of the immortal gods, so that they may have a design suitable for the logic of sacrifices.

### On the Arrangement of Altars for the Gods. Chapter 8.

Altars should face the east and always be placed lower than the cult statues that are in the temple, so that those who pray and sacrifice may look up toward the divinity. They should be constructed at different heights to suit the dignity of each specific god. Their heights are to be explained thus: for Jupiter and all the celestial gods, they should be built as high as possible. For Vesta <note>Goddess of the hearth</note>, Earth, and Sea, they should be placed low; in this way, the designs of the altars will be properly explained through these arrangements within the middle of the temples. Having explained the compositions of sacred buildings in this book, in the following book we will provide explanations of the layouts of public works.

MARCUS VITRUVIUS ON ARCHITECTURE

## BOOK FIVE.

Those who have set forth the thoughts and instructions of their genius in more extensive volumes, Emperor <note>Vitruvius addresses his patron, the Emperor Augustus, to whom the entire work is dedicated.</note>, have added great and distinguished authority to their writings. This is a practice that our own studies might also allow, so that through such expansions, the authority and weight of these instructions could be increased. However, this is not as straightforward as one might think. For architecture is not written about in the same way as history or poetry.

Histories, by their own nature, hold their readers' attention because they offer a variety of expectations regarding new events. In poetry, the meters and rhythms of the verses, the elegant arrangement of words, the dialogue between characters, and the clear delivery of the lines entice the senses of the readers. This leads them without boredom to the very end of the work.

This, however, cannot be achieved in architectural writings. The vocabulary, born from the specific needs of the craft <note>original: "artis propria necessitate"</note>, presents an obscurity to the senses because the language is unfamiliar. Since these terms are not clear on their own, and their names are not used in everyday speech, the reader's thoughts will become confused if the wide-ranging instructions are not condensed and explained in a few clear sentences. The sheer volume and frequency of the words would otherwise become an obstacle to understanding.

Therefore, I shall briefly set forth the obscure names and the **proportions** <term>commensus: the underlying system of measurement and symmetry used to relate the parts of a building to the whole</term> derived from the individual parts of the works so that they may be committed to memory. In this way, minds will be able to receive them more readily...

<summary>Vitruvius opens Book Five by contrasting the technical nature of architectural writing with the more engaging styles of history and poetry. He argues that architectural prose must be brief and clear to overcome the obscurity of its specialized vocabulary.</summary>
<keywords>Book Five, architectural theory, technical language, literary style, Augustus, proportions, brevity, clarity</keywords>

--- Page 164 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface to Book Five. Vitruvius justifies his concise writing style by citing the Pythagorean tradition of using "cubes" to aid memory and notes the transition from the sacred architecture of Books Three and Four to the public spaces he will discuss here, starting with the Roman Forum.</meta>

-> BOOK <-

...contributing. No less have I observed that since the city is distracted and occupied with both public and private business, I judged that I should write in few words, so that those reading might be able to perceive these matters briefly in their narrow space of leisure. It also pleased Pythagoras and those who followed his school <note>original: "haeresim," referring to a philosophical sect or school of thought</note> to write their teachings in their volumes according to **cubic** proportions. They established a "cube" of 216 verses, and they thought that there should be no more than three such cubes in any one work. 

A cube is a body with six sides, perfectly square with equal width across its flat surfaces. When it is thrown, onto whichever part it falls, so long as it is untouched it possesses an immovable stability, just like the dice that players throw upon a gaming board. He seems to have taken this comparison from the fact that this number of verses, like a cube, into whichever of the senses it settles, effects there an immovable stability of memory. 

The Greek comic poets also, by interposing a song from the chorus, divided the sections of their plays; by thus making parts according to a cubic ratio, they relieve the delivery of the actors through these intervals. Since, therefore, these practices were observed by our ancestors in a natural way, and I notice that I must write about things that are unusual and obscure to many, I decided to write in short volumes so that they might more easily reach the senses of my readers. For in this way, they will be ready for understanding. I have arranged their organization so that those searching for information do not have to collect it from separate places, but may find the explanations of various types within a single body of work and in individual volumes.

Therefore, Caesar <note>A reference to the Emperor Augustus, whom Vitruvius addresses as Caesar throughout the work.</note>, as I set forth the principles of sacred buildings in the third and fourth volumes, in this book I shall explain the arrangements of public places. First, I shall describe how the **forum** <term>forum: the central public square of a Roman city used for judicial, commercial, and social activities</term> ought to be established, because in it...

...the affairs of both public and private matters are governed by magistrates.

## On the forum. Chapter 1.

<margin>g</margin>
The Greeks establish their forums in a square shape with very wide, double **porticoes** <note>covered walkways supported by columns</note>; they adorn them with closely spaced columns and <term>architraves</term> <note>original: "epistyliis," the horizontal beams resting on column capitals</note> made of stone or marble, and they build walkways on the floorings above. In the cities of Italy, however, the same method must not be followed, because a custom has been handed down from our ancestors that **gladiatorial shows** are given in the forum. Therefore, the spaces between the columns should be distributed more widely around the spectacle area. Around the forum, in the porticoes, **bankers' shops** should be placed, and <term>balconies</term> <note>original: "moeniana," named after the official Maenius who first built them for spectators</note> should be situated on the upper floors; these will be correctly arranged for both public use and for the collection of public taxes.

The dimensions of the forum should be made according to the size of the population, so that the space is not too small for use, nor does the forum seem empty because of a lack of people. The width should be determined so that if the length is divided into three parts, two of those parts are given to the width. In this way, its shape will be oblong and its arrangement useful for the requirements of the spectacles. The upper columns should be made one-fourth smaller than the lower ones. This is because the lower parts, which bear the weight, ought to be stronger than the upper ones. 

No less should we imitate the nature of growing things, as seen in smooth trees like the fir, cypress, and pine—every one of which is thicker at the roots, and then, as it grows, proceeds upward with a natural, even <term>tapering</term> <note>original: "contractura," the narrowing of a column as it rises</note> until it reaches the top. Therefore, if the nature of growing things requires this, it is correctly established that upper elements should be made narrower than lower ones in both height and thickness.

The length should be divided into two parts, unless the nature of the site prevents this and forces the <term>symmetry</term> <note>In Roman architecture, "symmetria" refers to the proportional relationship between parts of a building rather than mirror-image balance.</note> to be changed. However, if the site is longer than usual, <term>chalcidica</term> <note>Annexes or halls at the ends of a basilica, often used for judicial or commercial purposes.</note> should be placed at the ends, as they are in the Julia Aquiliana. The columns of the basilica should be made as high as the side aisles are wide. The side aisle should be one-third the width of the central space. The upper columns should be smaller than the lower ones, as described previously. The <term>pluteum</term> <note>A low wall or parapet between columns.</note> placed between the upper and lower columns should be one-fourth smaller than the upper columns, so that those walking on the upper floor of the basilica are not seen by the merchants below. # BOOK <note>original: LIBER; likely Book V of Vitruvius's On Architecture</note>

->**THE BASILICA AT FANO**<-

The arrangements of basilicas <note>a large public hall used for legal and business transactions</note> can possess no less great dignity and beauty than the type which I myself laid out and oversaw the construction of in the Julian Colony at Fano <note>original: "coloniae iuliae fanestri"; modern Fano, Italy</note>. Its proportions and symmetries are established as follows:

The central vaulted ceiling <note>original: "testudo," literally "tortoise shell," referring here to the high central roof</note> between the columns is one hundred and twenty feet long and sixty feet wide. Its portico <note>the covered walkway</note> around the central vault, between the walls and the columns, is twenty feet wide. The columns, reaching a continuous height including their capitals of fifty feet, and having a thickness of five feet, have behind them pilasters <note>original: "parastatas"; square pillars attached to a wall</note> twenty feet high, two and a half feet wide, and one and a half feet thick. These support the beams upon which the floor joists of the porticos are carried.

Above these are other pilasters, eighteen feet high, two feet wide, and one foot thick, which likewise receive the beams supporting the rafters and the roofs of the porticos, which are positioned lower than the central vault. The remaining spaces between the beams of the pilasters and the columns are left open as windows between the intercolumniations <note>the spaces between columns</note>.

In the width of the central vault, there are four columns on each side, including the corner ones on the right and left. Along the length on the side nearest the forum, there are eight columns including the same corner ones; on the other side, there are six including the corner ones. The two middle columns on that side are omitted so as not to obstruct the view of the pronaos <note>the porch or entrance hall</note> of the Temple of Augustus, which is located in the middle of the side wall of the basilica, facing the center of the forum and the Temple of Jupiter.

Furthermore, the tribunal <note>the raised platform for magistrates</note> in that temple is shaped in the form of a hemicycle <note>a semi-circle</note>, but formed with a shallower curve. The width of the front of this hemicycle is forty-six feet, and its depth at the curve is fifteen feet, so that those standing before the magistrates do not interfere with the businessmen in the basilica.

Thus, the double arrangement of the gables—the exterior of the roof and the high interior vaulted ceiling—presents a graceful appearance. Likewise, the removal of the ornaments on the architraves and the distribution of the parapets and upper columns eliminates laborious trouble and significantly reduces the total expense. The columns themselves, however, being carried up in a continuous height to the beam of the vaulted ceiling, seem to increase both the magnificence of the investment and the authority of the work.

### On the Arrangement of the Treasury, Prison, and Senate House. Chapter II.

<margin>a</margin>
The treasury <term>ærarium; a public repository for funds</term>, the prison, and the senate house <term>curia; the meeting place for the local council</term> are to be joined to the forum, but in such a way that their scale and symmetry correspond to the forum itself. Above all, the senate house in particular must be built to suit the dignity of the municipality or city. If it is square, its height should be set by adding half to its width. If, however, it is oblong, the length and width should be added together, and half of that sum should be given to the height up to the coffered ceiling. Furthermore, the walls should be encircled at mid-height with cornices made of woodwork or plaster. If these are not present, the voices of those debating, being carried up to the height of the ceiling, will not be intelligible to the listeners. But when the walls are encircled by cornices, the voice, being delayed by them before it is dissipated into the air above, will be understood by the ears.

### On the Theater. Chapter III.

<margin>e</margin>
Once the forum has been <gloss>established</gloss>, then for the <gloss>viewings</gloss> <gloss>of the games</gloss> on the feast days of the <gloss>immortal</gloss> gods, a site for the theater must be chosen, <gloss>as</gloss> healthy as possible, just as was written in the first book regarding the healthiness in the placement of city walls. <gloss>For</gloss> during the games, people are held by these delights <gloss>throughout</gloss> the day, sitting with their spouses and children; <gloss>because of</gloss> the pleasure, their bodies remain motionless and their pores <note>original: "venas", literally 'veins', but Vitruvius refers to the skin's pores through which air is absorbed</note> are kept open. The blasts <gloss>of the breezes</gloss> settle into these openings, and if they come from marshy regions or other unhealthy areas, they will pour harmful <gloss>vapors</gloss> <note>original: "spiritus", meaning air or breath</note> into the bodies. Therefore, <gloss>if</gloss> the site for the theater is chosen with greater care, these defects will be avoided. Care must also be taken that it does not face the full force of the Sun from the south; <gloss>for</gloss> when the sun fills the curve of the theater, the enclosed air [becomes hot...]

Regarding the **foundations**, if they are on mountains, the process will be easier; but if necessity forces them to be built in a flat or marshy place, the reinforcements and <gloss>substructures</gloss> must be made in the way written about the foundations of sacred buildings in the third book. Above the foundations, the tiered seating <note>original: "gradationes"</note> should be built from the substructure using supplies of stone and marble.

The <term>precincts; horizontal walkways separating levels of seating</term> <note>original: "praecinctiones"</note> should be made in proportion to the height of the theaters, and no higher than the width of the walkway itself. And in short, it must be so managed that when a line is stretched from the bottom step to the top, it touches all the edges and angles of the steps; in this way, the voice will not be obstructed.

Many spacious <gloss>entrances</gloss> should be arranged, with the upper ones not joined to the lower ones, but made continuous and direct from all places without twists, so that when the people are dismissed from the shows, they are not squeezed, but have separate exits from all places without hindrance.

Also, careful attention must be paid so that the place is not "dead" <note>original: "surdus", literally 'deaf'; in acoustics, a space that absorbs sound rather than reflecting it</note>, but that the voice can travel as clearly as possible within it. This can be achieved if a site is chosen where resonance is not hindered. Now, the voice is a <term>flowing breath; spiritus fluens</term>, made perceptible to the hearing by the striking of the air. It moves in infinite circular rounds, just as if a stone were thrown into standing water...
