However, if they are hindered by narrow spaces or other necessities, then it will be necessary to use ingenuity and sharpness of mind to make subtractions from or additions to the symmetries, so that an aesthetic beauty <note>original: "venustates"</note> not unlike true symmetry may be completed.

## To which regions of the heavens each type of building should face, so that they are suitable for use and health.

->Chapter VII.<-

Now we shall explain by what properties the types of buildings should be aptly oriented toward their use and the regions of the heavens. Winter dining rooms <term>triclinia: rooms containing three couches for dining in a U-shape</term> and baths <term>balnearia: bathing suites in a private house</term> should face the winter sunset <note>the southwest</note>. Therefore, it is necessary to use evening light; furthermore, because the setting sun, having its brilliance directly ahead, gives off heat and makes that region warmer in the evening time. Bedrooms <term>cubicula: private chambers or sleeping quarters</term> and libraries should face the east; for their use requires the morning light. Likewise, in libraries, the books will not decay <note>original: "putrescent"; Vitruvius suggests that dampness from other winds causes mold</note>; for in those which face the south and west...

<summary>Vitruvius explains how architects must adapt ideal proportions to restricted sites and begins detailing the ideal solar orientation for rooms, such as eastward-facing libraries and westward-facing winter dining rooms.</summary>
<keywords>architectural symmetry, site constraints, orientation, triclinia, libraries, solar heat, Vitruvius</keywords>

--- Page 222 ---
<meta>This page continues Vitruvius’s practical advice on the orientation of specialized rooms. Having previously discussed libraries, the text now addresses the preservation of books and the specific placement of seasonal dining rooms and art galleries to ensure comfort and consistent lighting. It then transitions into Chapter 8, which distinguishes between private and public areas of a Roman home.</meta>

<header>BOOK SIX</header>

[libraries] face [the east], they are damaged by moths and dampness, because the incoming humid winds create and nourish them, and by infusing damp breezes, they ruin the scrolls <note>original: "uolumina"</note> with mold <note>original: "pallore", referring to the pale discoloration caused by decay</note>. Spring and autumn dining rooms <term>triclinia: dining rooms named for the three couches arranged around a central table</term> should face the east; for when they are shielded from the direct glare, as the sun moves toward the west, they become temperate at the time they are typically used. Summer rooms should face the north, because that region—unlike the others, which become sweltering during the summer solstice because of the heat—is always cooled since it is turned away from the sun’s path, providing both healthfulness and pleasure in its use. The same applies to picture galleries <term>pinacothecæ</term>, the weaving rooms of embroiderers <term>plumariorum textrinæ</term>, and the workshops of painters, so that the colors used in their work may remain unchanged in quality due to the consistency of the light.

### On the proper places for private and common buildings, and the styles suitable to various social ranks. Chapter VIII.

When these matters have been arranged according to the regions of the sky, one must also consider the principles by which private spaces are reserved for the heads of the family <note>original: "patribus familiarum"</note> and how the common areas shared with outsiders should be constructed. ## On the logic of rural buildings, and the descriptions and uses of their many parts.

### Chapter IX.

Now I will speak of rural arrangements, so that they may be convenient for use, and by what logic one ought to situate them. First, concerning healthfulness—as was written in the first volume regarding the placement of city walls—the climate regions should be inspected, and villas situated accordingly. Their sizes should be prepared in proportion to the measure of the land and the abundance of produce. The <term>courtyards</term> <note>original: "chortes"</note> and their dimensions should be defined according to the number of livestock and how many yokes of oxen are needed to work there. In the courtyard, the kitchen should be designated in the warmest possible place. It should have the ox-stalls <note>original: "bubilia"</note> connected to it, whose stalls should face the hearth and the eastern region of the sky; this is because oxen do not become rough-coated <note>Vitruvius refers to the belief that warmth and light kept the animals' coats sleek and healthy</note> by looking at the light and the fire. Also, farmers unskilled in climates do not think it right for oxen to face any other region of the sky except the sunrise. The widths of the stalls ought to be neither less than ten feet nor greater than fifteen; the length should be such that each individual yoke occupies no less than seven feet. The baths <note>original: "balnearia"</note> should likewise be joined to the kitchen; for in this way, the service of rural bathing...

### BOOK SIX

In the same way, **mangers** <note>original: "praesepia"</note> placed outside the kitchen in the open air, facing towards the east, are not without their uses. For when oxen are brought out to them during clear winter weather, they become sleeker and healthier by taking their morning fodder in the sunlight. **Granaries** <note>original: "horrea"</note>, haylofts, grain-stores, and **bakeries** <note>original: "pistrina"</note> should be built outside the main villa, so that the residence is safer from the danger of fire. 

If any more elegant parts are to be built within the villas, they should be constructed according to the **proportions** <term>symmetry: the balanced relationship between the parts of a building</term> established for urban houses in the previous chapters, provided they are built without hindering the practical needs of the farm. 

Care must be taken that all buildings are well-lit; this is seen to be much easier for villas, because there is no neighbor’s wall to stand in the way and block the light. In the city, however, either the height of shared walls or the narrowness of the site creates shadows and darkness. Therefore, one should test the situation in the following way: 

From the direction where light is needed, stretch a line from the top of the wall that appears to be obstructing to the specific spot where the light should enter. If, when looking upward along that line, a wide expanse of clear sky is visible, then the light in that location will be unobstructed. But if beams, lintels, or **upper floorings** <note>original: "contignationes"</note> get in the way, the opening should be made from a higher part, and the light let in that way. 

In short, the rule to follow is this: wherever the sky can be seen, window spaces should be left in those positions. In this way, the buildings will be filled with light. While light is most necessary in **dining rooms** <note>original: "tricliniis"</note> and other chambers, it is also essential for passages, slopes, and staircases, because in these places people carrying heavy loads often run into one another when coming from opposite directions.

## On the arrangement of Greek buildings and their parts, and their different names, which differ significantly from Italian customs and uses. Chapter 10.

Because the Greeks do not use **atriums** <note>original: "atrijs"</note>, they do not build according to our customs. Instead, for those entering from the front door, they create passages that are not very wide, with stables on one side and rooms for doorkeepers on the other, and the inner doors are immediately closed off. This place between the two doors is called the **gatehouse** <note>original: "θυρωρεῖον" (thyroreion)</note> in Greek. 

Then there is the entrance into the **peristyle** <term>peristyle: a courtyard surrounded by a colonnade or covered walkway</term>. This peristyle has porticoes on three sides. On the side that faces south, it has two **antae** <note>square pilasters or pillars</note> set a wide distance apart, upon which beams are placed. Two-thirds of the distance between these antae is given to the depth of the space within. This place is called the **vestibule** <note>original: "προστάς" (prostas) or "παραστάς" (parastas)</note> by some. Within these areas, large halls called **oeci** are established, where the mothers of the families sit with their wool-working. 

To the right and left of the vestibule, bedrooms are placed, one of which is called the **thalamus** <note>the principal or master bedroom</note> and the other the **amphithalamus** <note>a secondary bedroom or side-chamber</note>. Around the porticoes, daily dining rooms, bedrooms, and rooms for the servants are arranged. This part of the building is called the **women's quarters** <note>original: "gineconitis"</note>. 

Larger houses are joined to these, having wider peristyles in which the four porticoes are of equal height, or one side that faces south is constructed with taller columns. This type of...

...peristyle, which has one portico higher than the others, is called **Rhodian**. These houses have magnificent vestibules and their own dignified doorways. The porticoes of the peristyles are decorated with white plaster, stucco-work, and paneled ceilings made of fine joinery. In the porticoes facing north, they place **Cyzicene** dining rooms <term>Cyzicene: a large, luxurious dining hall named after the city of Cyzicus, usually designed to open onto gardens</term> and picture galleries. To the east, they place libraries; to the west, **exedrae** <note>recessed areas with seating for conversation</note>; and facing south, they place square halls <note>original: "oecos"</note> of such great size that they can easily accommodate four sets of dining couches with ample space for servants and performances.

Men's banquets are held in these halls. For it was not the custom, according to their social habits, for the mothers of the family to recline at dinner. These peristyles of the house are called **andronitides** <term>andronitides: the men's quarters</term>, because in these areas, the men go about their business without interference from the women.

Furthermore, to the right and left, small suites are established having their own doors, dining rooms, and comfortable bedrooms, so that arriving guests are received not into the main peristyles, but into these guest quarters. For when the Greeks became more refined and wealthy through good fortune, they would prepare dining rooms, bedrooms, and storerooms for arriving guests. On the first day, they would invite them to dinner; on the next, they would send chickens, eggs, vegetables, fruit, and other rustic produce. 

Therefore, painters, imitating these gifts sent to guests in their artwork, called such pictures **xenia** <term>xenia: hospitality gifts, also referring to still-life paintings of food and produce</term>. In this way, the guests did not seem to be away from home while staying in these quarters, as they enjoyed private freedom in these lodgings. Between these peristyles and the guest quarters are passages called **mesaulae** <term>mesaulae: middle halls or passages</term>, because they are placed in the middle between two courts. Our people <note>the Romans</note>, however, call these **androns** <note>original: "andronas"</note>.

For in history, Atlas is depicted supporting the world because he was the first to use the vigor and skill of his mind to provide humans with the principles of the sun’s course, the moon, the rising and setting of all the stars, and the movements of the heavens. For this benefit, he is depicted by painters and sculptors as supporting the world; and his daughters, the Atlantides (whom we call the <term>Vergiliae</term>, but the Greeks call the <term>Pleiades</term> <note>original: πλειάδας</note>), are dedicated among the stars in the heavens.

## *On the Stability and Foundations of Buildings.* Ch. XI.

<margin>4</margin>Buildings that are established on level ground will undoubtedly remain firm into old age if their foundations are constructed as we have explained in the previous books regarding city walls and theaters. However, if underground chambers <note>original: hypogea; subterranean rooms or cellars</note> and vaulted spaces <note>original: concamerationes</note> are to be built, their foundations must be made thicker than the structures that will be in the upper parts of the buildings. Furthermore, their walls, piers, and columns should be placed directly in the center of the lower structures, aligned perpendicularly so that they correspond to the solid parts below. For if the loads of walls or columns are placed over "hanging" spans <note>meaning unsupported or hollow areas</note>, they cannot maintain permanent stability. Additionally, it will be effective if posts are placed under the thresholds between the piers and <term>antae</term> <note>pilasters flanking a doorway</note>. For when thresholds and beams are burdened with masonry, they sag <note>original: pandantes</note> in the middle, which eventually breaks the masonry beneath them. But when posts are placed underneath and wedged tight, they do not allow the beams to settle or be damaged. Likewise, care must be taken that arches <note>original: fornicationes</note> relieve the weight of the walls, with their joints divided like wedges <note>original: cuneorum; referring to voussoirs</note> and their closures meeting at a center point. For when arches are finished with wedge-shaped stones outside the ends of the beams or thresholds, the wood, relieved of the weight, will first of all not sag; secondly, if any defect arises from age, it can be easily replaced without the labor of installing temporary supports <note>original: fulturarum</note>. Likewise, in buildings constructed with piers where arches are closed by wedge-shaped divisions with joints aligned to the center: the end piers in these cases must be made wider in space so that they have the strength to resist when the wedges, pressed by the weight of the walls and pushing toward the center, try to thrust out the <term>abutments</term> <note>original: incumbas; the parts of the pier that support the arch's weight</note>. Therefore, if the...

<summary>Vitruvius provides technical instructions on ensuring structural stability, emphasizing that foundations for buildings with basements must be thicker and that arches should be used to divert weight away from wooden beams to prevent sagging.</summary>
<keywords>foundations, structural stability, underground chambers, vaults, arches, wedge-shaped stones, piers, abutments</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of structural stability from Chapter 11. The previous page concluded with the necessity of using wedge-shaped stones in arches to distribute weight. This page details how to handle the pressure of the earth against foundations and the use of buttresses for reinforcement.</meta>

<header>SIXTH [BOOK]</header>
<sig>O iii</sig>

corner piers of spacious dimensions will hold the wedge-like stones <note>original: cuneos; refers to the voussoirs or wedge-shaped blocks of an arch</note> in place and provide stability to the works. **When** these matters have been carefully addressed and such diligence applied, it is equally important to ensure that all parts of the structure are perfectly vertical <note>original: perpendiculo respondeant; literally, 'respond to the plumb line'</note> and do not lean in any direction. However, the greatest care must be given to the foundations <note>original: substructionum</note>, because the pressure of the earth behind them <note>original: terræ congestio</note> often causes countless defects. This earth does not always maintain the same weight it has in summer; during winter, it absorbs a great deal of rainwater, increasing in both weight and volume. This expansion often bursts or pushes out the retaining walls of the structure. Therefore, to remedy this flaw, the following method should be used: first, determine the thickness of the wall based on the volume of the earth it must hold back. Then, build <term>buttresses</term> <note>original: anterides or erismae; external supports providing lateral stability to a wall</note> along the front at the same time as the wall. These should be spaced apart at a distance equal to the planned height of the foundation and should be as thick as the foundation itself. They should project at the base by the full thickness established for the foundation, and then gradually taper upward so that at the very top, their projection equals the thickness of the main wall.

**Moreover**, on the inside, against the earth, <term>toothed structures</term> <note>original: dentes; these are internal spur walls that extend into the soil to anchor the main wall</note> should be built into the wall in a saw-like fashion, so that each "tooth" extends from the wall by a distance equal to the intended height of the foundation. These toothed structures should have the same thickness as the walls themselves. **Likewise**, at the outer corners, once you have moved back from the interior angle, a space equal to the height of the foundation should be marked out in both directions; from these marks, a **diagonal** structure <note>original: diagonios; a cross-brace or angled wall</note> should be placed, and from its midpoint, another structure should be joined to the corner of the wall. **In this way**, the teeth and diagonal structures will not allow the wall to be pressed by the full force of the earth, but will instead dissipate the pressure by holding back the weight of the fill <note>original: impetum congestionis; the "attack" or force of the piled-up earth</note>. 

I have now explained how works ought to be established without defects and how those beginning a project should take precautions. For there is not the same level of concern regarding the replacement of roof tiles, beams, or planks; these things, however faulty they may be, are easily changed. Therefore, they are not even considered to be among the "solid" or permanent parts of a building. By what methods these [foundations] can be made firm, and how they should be established from...

He emphasizes that foundations require more care than surface elements like roofs because they cannot be easily replaced if they fail.</summary>

# BOOK SIX

...I have set forth. However, regarding what types of **building materials** <note>original: "copiarum"; referring here to the supply of resources like stone, wood, or sand</note> ought to be used, this is not within the power of the architect. This is because not all kinds of materials are produced in all locations, as was explained in the previous volume. Furthermore, it is within the power of the owner to decide whether he wishes to build with **brickwork** <note>original: "lateritio"</note>, **rubble masonry** <note>original: "cementicio"</note>, or **squared stone** <note>original: "saxo quadrato"; also known as ashlar masonry</note>.

Therefore, the evaluations of all finished works are considered in three parts: by the **craftsmanship's precision** <note>original: "fabrili subtilitate"</note>, by their **magnificence**, and by their **arrangement** <note>original: "dispositione"</note>. When a finished work is viewed and found to be magnificent, the expenditures will be praised by every authority. When it is viewed and found to be crafted with precision, the <term>master-builder's</term> <note>original: "officinatoris"; the person supervising the physical construction or the contractor</note> exacting standards will be approved. But when a work possesses authority through its beauty, **proportions**, and <term>symmetries</term> <note>original: "symmetrijs"; the harmonious relationship between the parts of a building</note>, then the glory shall belong to the architect.

These qualities are correctly established when the architect allows himself to accept advice from both craftsmen and **laypeople** <note>original: "idiotis"; in this context, the term refers to non-experts or those without formal training in architecture, rather than its modern derogatory meaning</note>. For all people, not just architects, are able to recognize what is good; but between laypeople and architects, there is this difference: the layperson cannot know what the result will be until he has seen it finished, whereas the architect, once he has conceived it in his mind, has already defined what it will be in terms of beauty, utility, and **propriety** <note>original: "decore"; the sense of what is appropriate or fitting for the building's purpose</note> before he has even begun.

I have written down, as clearly as I could, those things I thought useful for private buildings and how they should be constructed. Regarding their **finishes** <note>original: "expolitionibus"; the final decorative layers such as plaster, paint, or polish</note>, however—so that they may be elegant and remain without defects into their old age—I shall explain in the following volume.

O iiij

# BOOK SEVEN.

Our ancestors wisely and usefully established the practice of handing down their thoughts to posterity through **written records** <note>original: "commentariorum relationes"; refers to written accounts or reports intended for public or future use</note>, so that these ideas might not perish but, growing in volume through each successive age, might reach the highest level of **scholarly refinement** <note>original: "doctrinarum subtilitatem"</note> over time as they were published. Therefore, we owe them not just modest, but infinite thanks, because they did not selfishly remain silent but took care to entrust the ideas of all kinds of subjects to memory through their writings.

For if they had not done so, we would not have been able to know what deeds were performed at **Troy**, nor what **Thales**, **Democritus**, **Anaxagoras**, **Xenophanes**, and the rest of the **natural philosophers** <note>original: "physici"; referring to thinkers who studied the physical world and the nature of reality</note> thought about the nature of things. Nor would the **ethical boundaries** <note>original: "agendae uitae terminationes"; the goals or limits defined for how a person should live a good life</note> defined for mankind by **Socrates**, **Plato**, **Aristotle**, **Zeno**, **Epicurus**, and other philosophers be known to us. Neither would the deeds of **Croesus**, **Alexander**, **Darius**, and other kings, or the principles by which they acted, have been known, unless our ancestors had carried them forth for the memory of all posterity through the compiled records of their teachings.

And so, just as we must give thanks to these authors, conversely, those who steal their writings and pass them off as their own are to be condemned. Furthermore, those who do not rely on their own thoughts as writers, but through envious character boast while violating the work of others, are not only to be rebuked but even...

He lists famous Greek philosophers and kings as examples of those whose legacies only survive because earlier writers took the time to record them.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN

Because they lived in an impious manner, they are to be condemned to punishment; nevertheless, these matters have not gone unrecorded, having been recounted with great care by the ancients. It is not out of place for us to explain the outcomes of those judgments as they have been handed down to us. The Attalid Kings <note>The dynasty that ruled Pergamon in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE.</note>, led by the great delights of philology <note>original: "philologiae"; here meaning a love of literature and learning</note>, established a magnificent library at Pergamon for the common enjoyment of all. Then, likewise, Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, ruler of Egypt.</note>, incited by an infinite zeal and a desire for study, strove with no less industry to establish a similar institution in the same manner at Alexandria. 

When he had completed this with the greatest diligence, he did not think it sufficient unless he also took care to increase its growth by "sowing seeds" for future generations. Therefore, he dedicated games to the Muses and Apollo, and just as is done for athletes, he established prizes and honors for the victors among competing writers. 

When these arrangements were made and the games were approaching, it was necessary to choose learned judges to evaluate the entries. When the King had already selected six from the city but could not quickly find a suitable seventh, he turned to those who were in charge of the library and asked if they knew anyone ready for the task. Then they told him there was a certain Aristophanes <note>Aristophanes of Byzantium, a famous grammarian and critic.</note>, who with the greatest zeal and diligence read through all the books in the library, in order, every single day. 

Accordingly, at the assembly for the games, when secret seats had been assigned to the judges, Aristophanes was summoned with the others and sat in the place designated for him. When the first group of poets was brought in for the competition and their writings were recited, the entire populace, by signaling, tried to advise the judges on what they should approve. Thus, when the opinions were asked from each judge, the six spoke as one, awarding the prize to the one they noticed had most pleased the multitude.

# BOOK VII

...they awarded the first prize, and the second to the next in line. However, when Aristophanes <note>Aristophanes of Byzantium, a famous scholar and grammarian who became the head of the Library of Alexandria</note> was asked for his opinion, he ordered that the one who had pleased the public the least should be declared the winner. When the King and the entire assembly became violently indignant, he stood up and, by asking, obtained permission to speak. 

Once silence was established, he showed that only one of them was truly a poet, while the others had recited the work of others. He argued that judges ought to approve original writings, not thefts. While the people marveled and the King remained doubtful, Aristophanes, relying on his memory, brought out an infinite number of volumes from certain bookcases. By comparing these with the recited poems, he forced the competitors to confess that they were thieves. Therefore, the King ordered them to be tried for theft, and once condemned, he dismissed them with ignominy. However, he honored Aristophanes with the most ample gifts and appointed him over the library.

In the following years, Zoilus came to Alexandria from Macedonia. He had adopted a surname so that he was called "Homeromastix" <note>original: "Homeromastix," meaning "The Scourge of Homer"</note>. He recited to the King his own writings which he had composed in opposition to the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*. But when Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, King of Egypt</note> noticed that the father of poets and the leader of all philology <note>term: philology (philologiae), here meaning the love of learning and literature</note> was being harassed in his absence, and that a man whose writings were admired by all nations was being slandered by this newcomer, he was indignant and gave him no answer. 

When Zoilus had remained in the kingdom for a longer time, pressed by poverty, he submitted himself to the King, requesting that something be granted to him. The King, however, is said to have replied that if Homer, who had died a thousand years before, could feed many thousands of men for all eternity, then surely a man who claimed to possess a better genius ought to be able to support not only himself, but many others as well. In short, his death—as if he were condemned for parricide—is recorded in various ways: some wrote that he was [crucified] by Philadelphus...

# BOOK VII

...[some say he] was fixed to a cross; others that he was pelted with stones; still others that he was thrown alive onto a funeral pyre at Smyrna. Whichever of these fates befell him, he earned a punishment worthy of his crimes. For no less seems to be deserved by one who prosecutes those who cannot be present to explain the intent behind their writings. 

But I, Caesar <note>Referring to Emperor Augustus, to whom Vitruvius dedicated his work</note>, do not bring forth this body of work by changing the titles of others and inserting my own name, nor have I set out to win approval by disparaging the ideas of anyone else. Instead, I give boundless thanks to all those writers who, through the outstanding skill of their genius gathered from ancient times, have prepared such abundant resources of every kind for those who follow. From these sources, as if drawing water from springs and <term>conveying</term> <note>original: "traducentes"</note> it to our own purposes, we possess more <term>fruitful</term> <note>original: "foecundiores"</note> and ready abilities for writing; and relying on such authors, we dare to compile new systems of instruction. Therefore, taking such beginnings from those whom I noticed had prepared the way for the logic of my own purpose, I began to move forward from that point. 

For first, <term>Agatharcus</term> <note>An Athenian painter of the 5th century BCE</note> created a stage set at Athens when <term>Aeschylus</term> <note>The "Father of Tragedy"</note> was presenting a play, and he left a commentary about it. This ensures that, although the reality is uncertain, certain images of buildings in stage paintings might provide a realistic appearance; thus, things drawn on flat, vertical fronts appear to some to recede and others to project <note>This is the first known historical reference to the mathematical principles of linear perspective</note>.

# BOOK SEVEN

*Pytheos* <note>original: "tagenes" - likely a transcription error for Pytheos</note> *wrote on the Temple of Minerva <note>Athena</note> at Priene in the Ionic style; Phileos wrote on the Temple of Minerva in the Doric style, which is on the Acropolis at Athens; Ictinus and Carpion on the Parthenon; Theodorus of Phocis on the Round Building <note>the Tholos</note> at Delphi; Philo on the proportions of sacred buildings and on the naval arsenal which was in the port of Piraeus; Hermogenes on the Ionic Temple of Diana <note>Artemis</note> at Magnesia, which is a "false-double-colonnade" <term>pseudodipteros: a building designed to look like it has a double row of columns to save cost and space</term>, and on the Temple of Father Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note> at Teos, which is a "single-winged" <term>monopteros: a circular building with a single ring of columns supporting a roof</term>. On the Mausoleum <note>The Great Tomb of Mausolus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>, Satyrus and Phiteus wrote.* To these men, indeed, fortune granted the highest and greatest gift. For their arts are judged to possess the most noble praise through perpetual ages, flourishing in everlasting bloom because they produced outstanding works through their intellects. For on each of the four sides of the Mausoleum, individual artists took up their parts in competition to decorate and prove their skill: *Leochares, Bryaxis, Scopas, and Praxiteles*; some also believe *Timotheus* was involved. The eminent excellence of their art forced the fame of that work to be included among the Seven Wonders of the World. Furthermore, many less famous men wrote down rules of proportions, such as *Nexaris, Theocydes, Demophilus, Pollis, Leonidas, Silanion, Melampus, Sarnacus, and Euphranor*. No fewer wrote concerning machines, such as *Cliades, Archytas, Archimedes, Ctesibius, Nymphodorus, Philo of Byzantium, Diphilus, Charidas, Polyidus, Phyros, and Agesistratus*. From their commentaries, I have gathered what I observed to be useful for these matters and have compressed them into a single body of work; I did this especially because I noticed that while many volumes on this subject have been published by the Greeks, very few have been produced by our own people <note>referring to Romans</note>. *Fuffitius*, indeed, was the first who undertook to publish a volume on these matters.

# SEVENTH BOOK

Likewise, Terentius Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note>, in his work on the *Nine Disciplines*, included one book on architecture; Publius Septimius wrote two. Beyond these, however, no one else seems to have devoted themselves to this kind of writing until now, even though there were great architects among our own ancient citizens who could have produced equally elegant writings.

For at Athens, the architects Antistates, Calleschros, Antimachides, and Porinos laid the foundations for the temple of Olympian Jupiter <note>original: "Ioui olympio"; the Greek god Zeus</note> when Pisistratus <note>a 6th-century BC ruler of Athens</note> was building it. After his death, however, they left the project unfinished due to the interruptions of the State. Therefore, about two hundred years later, King Antiochus promised to fund the work. The Roman citizen Cossutius then masterfully designed the grand scale of the inner chamber <term>cella: the inner room of a temple housing the cult statue</term>, the placement of the columns in the double-colonnade <term>dipteros: a building surrounded by a double row of columns</term>, and the arrangement of the entablatures <term>epistylia: the horizontal beams resting on the columns</term> and other ornaments according to the rules of symmetry, using great cleverness and the highest scientific knowledge.

This work is considered magnificent not only by the common crowd but also by the discerning few. Indeed, there are four locations where sacred buildings are so ornately arranged with marble works that they are celebrated with the most illustrious fame. Because of their excellence and the wise planning of their designs, these structures are held in awe as being worthy of the dwelling-place of the gods.

First is the Temple of Diana <note>Artemis</note> at Ephesus, built in the Ionic style by Chersiphron <note>OCR: Ctesiphonte</note> of Knossos and his son Metagenes. This temple is said to have been completed later by Demetrius, a servant of Diana herself, and Paeonius of Ephesus. At Miletus, the same Paeonius and Daphnis of Miletus established a temple to Apollo, likewise using Ionic proportions. At Eleusis, Ictinus completed the inner chamber of Ceres <note>Demeter</note> and Proserpina <note>Persephone</note> in the Doric style and of massive size. He built it without exterior columns to allow more space for the performance of sacrifices. That building, how...

Instead, I decided to explain each subject in individual volumes. Thus, because in the sixth volume I fully described the principles of private buildings, in this volume, which holds the seventh place, I will explain finishes <term>expolitio: the final surfacing, plastering, and decorating of a building</term>, and the methods by which they can achieve both beauty and durability.

...permanently solid, and thus it should be leveled and prepared alongside the base layer. If the site consists of filled-in ground <note>original: "congestitius locus"; soil that has been moved or piled up rather than being natural, solid earth</note>, whether in whole or in part, it must be solidified with great care by ramming <term>fistucationibus: the process of compacting earth using heavy rammers or "fistucae"</term>.

In the case of timber floor frames <term>contignationibus: the structural framework of joists and beams that support a floor</term>, one must be very careful that no wall which does not reach the very top is built up directly under the pavement. Instead, a gap should be left so that the boarding <term>coaxationem: the layer of wooden planks laid over the joists</term> remains suspended above the wall. For when a wall is built solid to the top, as the timber framing dries out or sags under weight, the masonry wall remains rigid; this inevitably causes cracks to form in the pavements to the left and right of the wall line.

Care must also be taken not to mix boards of winter oak <note>original: "esculini"; likely *Quercus frainetto*, known for its stability</note> with common oak <note>original: "querni"; likely *Quercus robur*</note>. This is because as soon as common oak absorbs moisture, it warps and causes cracks to open in the pavements. However, if winter oak is not available and necessity forces the use of common oak due to a shortage, it should be managed as follows: the boards should be cut quite thin. The less strength they have, the more easily they can be held in place when fixed with nails. Furthermore, two nails should be driven into the ends of every single board on the joists, so that no part of the corners can warp or lift up. As for Turkey oak <note>original: "cerro"</note>, beech, or ash, none of these can last to a great age.

Once the boarding <note>original: "coassationibus"</note> is finished, if there is fern <note>original: "filex"</note> available, it should be spread over it; if not, use straw. This is done so that the timber may be protected from the defects caused by contact with lime <note>Lime is alkaline and can chemically "burn" or degrade certain woods</note>. Then, a foundation layer of stones <term>statuminetur: from 'statuminatio', the first layer of a floor consisting of large, hand-sized stones</term> is to be laid, using stones no smaller than what a hand can hold.

After the foundation stones are laid, the rubble layer <term>ruderetur: from 'rudus', a layer of broken stone or brick mixed with lime</term> is applied. If the rubble is new, one part of lime should be mixed with three parts of stone; if it is recycled rubble <note>original: "rediuiuum"; literally "brought back to life", referring to salvaged building materials</note>, the mixture should be five parts to two. Then, the rubble is applied and solidified by frequent pounding with wooden beaters <note>original: "uectibus ligneis"</note> by teams of ten men. ...the thickness becomes nine inches <note>original: "dodrantis"; a measurement of three-quarters of a foot</note>. On top of this, a <term>nucleus: a finer bedding layer composed of crushed pottery and lime</term> should be applied, having a mixture of three parts of crushed pottery to one of lime, so that the pavement is no less than six fingers <note>approx. 4.5 inches</note> in thickness. Upon this nucleus, the pavements are to be constructed to the precision of a straightedge and level, whether they are made of <term>sectilibus: cut slabs of stone or marble in geometric shapes</term> or <term>tesseris: small cubes used for mosaics</term>. When these have been constructed and the proper slopes have been established, they should be rubbed down <note>original: "fricentur"; the process of grinding and polishing the floor surface</note> so that, if they are cut slabs, no edges protrude in the rhombs, or triangles, or squares, or hexagons; rather, the arrangement of the joints should be level and uniform with one another. If it is built with mosaic tiles, all their corners must be equally level and nowhere protruding from the polishing. For if the corners are not all equally flat, the polishing will not be as precise as it ought to be. Likewise, Tiburtine herringbone brickwork <note>original: "testacea spicata tiburtina"; bricks from Tivoli laid in a pattern resembling an ear of grain</note> must be carefully finished so that there are no pits or protruding humps, but rather they are laid flat and rubbed down to the straightedge. Upon the polishing—when it has been perfected by smoothing and finishing—marble dust is sifted over it, and protective layers of lime and sand are applied on top.

For pavements in the open air, however, they must be made with the greatest care, because timber floor frames, expanding with moisture or shrinking with dryness, or sagging from settling, cause defects in the pavements by their movement. Furthermore, frost and ice do not allow them to remain intact. Therefore, if necessity forces their use, they must be made as follows to be as least defective as possible: once the first layer of boarding is laid, another layer of boarding should be laid across it transversely and fixed with nails, so that it provides a double layer of protection to the framing. Then, one-third part of crushed pottery is mixed with new <term>ruderi: a layer of rubble or broken stone</term>, and a mixture of two parts lime to five of mortar should provide the proper consistency. After the <term>statuminatione: a foundation layer of large, hand-sized stones</term> is laid, the rubble layer is applied, and once it is thoroughly pounded, it should be no less than one foot thick. ...However, once the <term>nucleus: the fine finishing bedding layer for a floor</term> has been laid (as described above), a pavement made of large <term>tesserae: small square cubes of stone or tile</term>, cut to about two fingers <note>approx. 1.5 inches</note> in size, should be built. It should have a slope of two fingers for every ten feet of length. If this is well-tempered and properly rubbed down, it will be protected from all defects. To ensure that the mortar between the joints does not suffer from the effects of frost, it should be saturated with <term>amurca: the watery dregs of pressed olives</term> every year before winter; in this way, it will not allow the icy frost to penetrate it. 

If, however, even greater care seems necessary, two-foot tiles <note>original: "tegulæ bipedales"; standard Roman bricks measuring approx. 18x18 inches</note> should be laid over the <term>rudus: a thick foundation layer of rubble and lime</term>, joined together over a sub-layer of mortar. These tiles should have small channels a finger wide cut into the edges of their joints; when these are joined, they should be filled with lime mixed with oil, and the joints should be rubbed and pressed together. In this way, the lime remaining in the channels will harden and prevent water or anything else from passing through the joints. Once this layer is complete, the nucleus is to be spread over it and worked by beating it with rods. On top of this, either large tesserae or herringbone brickwork <note>original: "spica testacea"; bricks laid in a pattern resembling an ear of grain</note> should be built with the slopes described above. When constructed in this manner, they will not easily fall into decay.

# On the slaking of lime for finishing white plaster and stucco-work.
## Chapter 2.

When we have finished with the care of pavements, we must then explain white plaster-work <note>original: "albarijs operibus"; decorative white stucco or plastering</note>. This will be done correctly if the lumps of the best lime are <term>slaked: the process of soaking quicklime in water to prepare it for mortar</term> a long time before they are needed. This ensures that if any lump was not sufficiently burned in the kiln, its strength is broken down by the long soaking in the water, and it is forced to cook through thoroughly. These pebbles, when they are thoroughly soaked during the work, dissolve and ruin the smooth finish of the plaster. However, when proper care has been taken in the soaking, and the material has been more carefully prepared for the task, a hoe <note>original: "ascia," a tool used for mixing and testing mortar</note> should be taken, and just as timber is hewn, so should the lime be chopped in the soaking pit. ...as it is drying, the leveling of the **sand-mortar** <note>original: "arenati," a mixture of lime and sand</note> should be shaped, so that the lengths are measured against a straightedge and line, the heights against a plumb-line, and the angles are forced to correspond to the square. For in this way, the appearance of the **plasterwork** <note>original: "tectoriorum"</note> intended for paintings will be flawless. As it dries again, a second and then a third layer should be applied. Thus, the better grounded the leveling is from the sand-mortar, the firmer the solidity of the plasterwork will be against the passage of time.

When, in addition to the <term>rough rendering</term> <note>original: "trullissatio," the first coarse coat of mortar applied to a wall</note>, no fewer than three coats <note>original: "corijs," literally "skins" or layers</note> of sand have been shaped, then the leveling layers of **marble grain** <note>original: "marmoreo grano," crushed marble used instead of sand for a finer finish</note> must be worked in, while the material is tempered in such a way that when it is worked, it does not stick to the trowel <note>original: "rutrum"</note>, but the bare iron is released cleanly from the mortar. Once the grain has been applied and is drying, a second coat of medium grain should be leveled. When that has been worked and well-rubbed, a third, finer layer should be applied.

So, when the walls have been made solid with three coats of sand and likewise three of marble, they will be unable to receive cracks or any other flaw. But also, when the solid foundations are worked with beating-rods <note>original: "baculorum," used to compact the mortar</note> and smoothed with the firm whiteness of marble, and when colors are applied with polishing, they will express brilliant luster.

Moreover, when colors are carefully applied to <term>wet plaster</term> <note>original: "udo tectorio," the defining characteristic of the "fresco" technique, from the Italian for "fresh"</note>, they do not fade, but are permanently enduring. This is because the **lime** <note>original: "calx"</note>, having had its moisture cooked out in the kilns and made porous by a parched emptiness, draws into itself whatever materials happen to touch it. By mixing various properties and bringing together their elements or principles, it solidifies as one in whatever form it has been shaped; once dry, it is restored so that it seems to possess the unique qualities of its own kind. Therefore, plasterwork that has been correctly made neither becomes rough with age nor loses its color when wiped, unless it was applied without sufficient care or on a dry surface. When, therefore, plastering on the walls is done in this way...

...have been carried out (as written above), they will be able to possess both **firmness** and **splendor**, as well as a lasting quality against the effects of age. However, when only one coat <note>original: "corium," literally a skin or layer</note> of sand and one of fine marble is applied, its thinness—being less strong—is easily broken; nor will it obtain the proper brilliance from polishing because of the weakness of its thickness. For just as a **silver mirror** made of a thin leaf gives blurred images and has a faint, weak reflection, but one that has been made from a solid composition—receiving the polishing with firm strength—returns brilliant and clear images to the viewers, so **plasterwork** <note>original: "tectoria"</note> made of thin material not only becomes cracked but also quickly fades away.

But those works founded on the solidity of sand-mortar and marble, which are thick in substance, when they have been worked over with frequent polishings, not only become shining but even reflect clear images to those looking at the work.

Greek plasterers, however, not only use these methods to make firm works, but also, once the mortar is placed—with lime and sand mixed there—a group of ten men is brought in to pound the material with wooden poles, and they only use it once it has been worked into a uniform, well-beaten mass. Therefore, some people cut out slabs <note>original: "crustas"</note> from old walls to use as <term>panels</term> <note>original: "abacis," decorative wall panels or slabs</note>. And the plaster of these panels and mirrors, through their divisions, have prominent projections around them.

But if plasterwork is to be done on <term>wattle-and-daub walls</term> <note>original: "cratitijs," walls made of wooden frames and woven branches plastered with mud</note>, in which cracks must necessarily occur at the uprights and crossbeams (this is because when they are smeared with mud, they necessarily absorb moisture; then, as they dry and shrink, they cause cracks in the plasterwork)...

...to prevent this <note>the cracking of plaster mentioned at the end of the previous page</note> from happening, this shall be the method. When the entire wall has been coated with mud, then long reeds are to be fastened to that work with wide-headed nails <note>original: "clauis muscarijs," literally 'fly-headed nails,' used like modern washers to hold reeds or laths in place</note>. Next, after another layer of mud is applied, if the first reeds were fixed crosswise, the second set should be fixed vertically. Thus (as written above), the sand-mortar, the marble-dust, and the entire plaster finish should be applied. In this way, the double layer of reeds fixed in transverse rows to the walls will provide a continuous, secure foundation that will not allow any segments to shift or any cracks to form.

## On finishes in damp places.
### Chapter IV.

<margin>q</margin>
I have already explained the methods by which plasterwork should be made in dry places; now I shall set forth how <term>finishes</term> <note>original: "politiones," the final smooth, polished layers of stucco or plaster</note> are prepared in damp places, so that they may remain without defects. First, in rooms located on the ground floor, a rough coat of <term>pounded brick</term> <note>original: "testa," crushed pottery or brick mixed with lime, known for its hydraulic and moisture-resistant properties</note> should be applied and leveled from the bottom floor up to a height of about three feet, instead of using sand-mortar, so that these parts of the plaster are not damaged by moisture.

However, if any wall suffers from constant moisture, one should move back slightly from it and build another thin wall, separated from the first as far as the situation allows. Between these two walls, a channel should be led lower than the level of the room's floor, having vents <note>original: "nares," literally 'nostrils'</note> leading to an open area. Likewise, when the wall has been built to its full height, air-holes <note>original: "spiramenta"</note> should be left. For if the moisture does not have exits through these vents at both the bottom and the top, it will nonetheless spread through the new masonry. When these things are completed, the wall should be rough-coated with pounded brick, leveled, and then finished with the final plaster coating.

Thus, at their banquets, whatever is spilled from cups or from <term>spitting</term> <note>original: "sputismatis"</note> dries as soon as it falls; and the servants who move about there, even if they are barefoot, do not feel the cold from this specific type of pavement.

### *On the Method of Painting in Buildings. Chapter V.*

In other rooms—that is, those used in spring, autumn, and summer, as well as in <term>atriums</term> <note>the central reception halls of a Roman house</note> and <term>peristyles</term> <note>open courtyards surrounded by columns</note>—certain methods of painting were established by the ancients based on specific principles. For a painting is an image of something that exists, or can exist, such as a person, a building, a ship, or other things, from whose fixed forms and defined bodily limits a likeness is taken through modeled representation. From this, the ancients, who first established the methods of <term>finishing</term> <note>original: "expolitionibus," referring to the final plastering and decorative coats</note>, began by imitating the varieties and arrangements of <term>marble veneers</term> <note>original: "crustarum marmorearum"</note>; then they moved to the various distributions of moldings, and yellow and red <term>panels</term> <note>original: "cuneorum," literally wedges or sections</note> among themselves. Afterward, they advanced so far as to imitate the forms of buildings and the prominent projections of columns and <term>pediments</term> <note>original: "fastigiorum"</note>...

...ting. However, in open spaces, such as <term>exedrae</term> <note>recessed areas or rooms designed for conversation, often opening onto a courtyard</note>, because of the great expanse of the walls, they would design the fronts of stages in the tragic, comic, or satyric style. In <term>walkways</term> <note>original: "ambulationibus"</note>, because of the long distances, they would decorate the walls with various <term>landscapes</term> <note>original: "topiorum," from the Greek word for "place"</note>, expressing images from the specific qualities of certain locations. For they paint harbors, promontories, shores, rivers, springs, <term>canals</term> <note>original: "eurypi"</note>, shrines, sacred groves, mountains, livestock, and shepherds. In some places, they also feature <term>grand-scale paintings</term> <note>original: "megalographiam"</note> containing images of the gods or arranged depictions of myths—no less than the Trojan battles or the wanderings of Ulysses through various landscapes, and other subjects produced from the nature of things by similar logic.

But these subjects, which were taken from real things as examples by the ancients, are now rejected due to perverted tastes. For monsters are now painted upon the plaster rather than clear images of definite things. In place of columns, reeds are set up; in place of <term>pediments</term> <note>the triangular gable found above a portico or window</note>, there are fluted <term>tendrils</term> <note>original: "arpaginetuli"</note> with curled and winding leaves. Likewise, there are <term>candelabra</term> supporting the figures of small shrines, and rising above their pediments are many tender stalks growing from roots with curls, which have little figures sitting within them without any logic. No less common are stalks with flowers from which half-formed figures emerge, some with human heads and others with the heads of beasts.

These things, however, neither exist, nor can they be made, nor have they ever been. Therefore, new fashions have forced matters to such a point that, through ignorance, bad judges have turned a blind eye to the virtues of the arts. For how can a reed truly support a roof, or a candelabrum support small shrines and the ornaments of a pediment? Or how can a stalk so thin and soft support a sitting figure? Or how can flowers and half-formed figures procre...

...any reason? Yet people, seeing these false things, do not find fault; instead, they are delighted, and they do not notice whether such things are actually possible or not. Indeed, at Tralles <note>a Greek city in modern-day Turkey</note>, when Apaturius of Alabanda had fashioned a stage set with an elegant hand in the small theater—which they call an <term>ekklesiasterion</term> <note>original: "ἐκκλησιαστήριον"; a building used for the assembly of citizens</note>—he created statues in place of columns and centaurs to support the <term>architraves</term> <note>original: "epistylia"; the main beam resting across the tops of columns</note>. Furthermore, above this, he nonetheless built an <term>upper stage</term> <note>original: "episcenium"</note> in which <term>tholi</term>, <term>porticoes</term> <note>original: "pronai"</note>, half-pediments, and all the various parts of a roof were decorated with paintings. Therefore, when the appearance of this stage set began to charm the eyes of everyone because of its elaborate detail, and they were already prepared to approve the work, Licinius the mathematician stepped forward. 

He said that while the people of Alabanda were considered clever enough in all civic matters, they were judged to be foolish because of a minor fault of impropriety. In their <term>gymnasium</term> <note>a place for both exercise and education</note>, all the statues are of lawyers <note>original: "causas agentes"</note>, while in the <term>forum</term> <note>the public square and marketplace</note>, the statues are of people holding throwing-disks, or running, or playing ball. Thus, the unseemly placement of the statues, which ignored the specific nature of the locations, brought a public stain on the city's reputation. 

"Let us see to it now," Licinius continued, "lest Apaturius’s stage set makes <term>Alabandians</term> or <term>Abderites</term> <note>residents of Abdera were proverbially known in the ancient world for being slow-witted or foolish</note> of us as well. For which of you [would have in your] houses...

I have sufficiently explained what I could to remind people to depart from error in plaster-work. Now I shall speak of preparations, so that they may be of use; and first, since lime was discussed at the beginning, it now remains to speak of marble.

# BOOK SEVEN

<margin>Marble preparation</margin>
Marble is not produced of the same kind in all regions. In certain places, clods are born containing shining flakes—much like salt—which, when crushed and ground, are highly useful for plastering and decorative cornice work. However, in places where these natural deposits are not available, the "marble chips" or "shards" <note>Latin: *assulae*</note> which stonemasons discard from their work are crushed with iron pestles and separated by sieves. Once sifted, they are set aside in three grades: the coarsest part is applied first with lime as a sandy base (as described above), followed by the second grade, and finally the finest grade. When these layers have been applied and smoothed by diligent rubbing of the plaster, consideration must be given to the colors, so that they may express a translucent brilliance. The distinction and preparation of these colors shall be as follows.

### On Colors, and First Concerning Ochre
### Chapter 7

<margin>Natural vs. artificial colors</margin>
Some colors are produced naturally in specific places and are dug from the earth, while others are perfected by processing different substances or through the tempered mixing of ingredients, so that they provide the same utility in finished works. First, we shall explain those which are dug up as they occur naturally, such as what is called *ochra* <note>original: "$\tilde{\omega}\chi\rho\alpha$"; yellow earth pigment</note> in Greek. This is found in many places, including Italy, but the best was formerly the Attic variety. This is no longer available because in the era when the silver mines at Athens employed great gangs of laborers, they would dig tunnels deep underground to find silver. Whenever a vein of ochre was found there by chance, they would pursue it just as they did the silver. Therefore, the ancients had an excellent supply of it for their polished finishes...

Likewise, abundant supplies of red ochre <note>original: "rubricæ"</note> are extracted in many places, but the best is found in only a few, such as Sinope in the Pontus region, Egypt, and the Balearic Islands of Spain; no less also in Lemnos, the revenues of which island the Roman Senate and People granted to the Athenians to enjoy. 

Paretonian white, however, takes its name from the very places where it is dug up. By the same logic, Melian white is so named because that mineral resource is said to exist on Melos, an island of the Cyclades. Green earth <note>original: "Creta uiridis"</note> is likewise produced in several places, but the best is from Smyrna. The Greeks, however, call this <term>theodotium</term> <note>original: "θεοδότιον"</note> because there was a man named Theodotus on whose estate that kind of earth was first discovered. Orpiment, which is called <term>arsenikon</term> <note>original: "αρσένικον"</note> in Greek, is mined in Pontus. Realgar <note>a bright red-orange arsenic sulfide</note> is also found in several places, but the best mine is in Pontus, very close to the river Hypanis. In other places, such as the territories of Magnesia and Ephesus, there are locations where it is dug up ready for use, requiring neither grinding nor sifting, but is as fine as if it had been crushed by hand and sifted.

## On the Properties of Cinnabar. Chapter VIII.

<margin>1</margin> I shall now enter into an explanation of the properties of cinnabar <note>original: "minium," referring here to the ore of mercury</note>. It is recorded that this was first discovered in the Ephesian fields of Cilbianus, the nature and logic of which are quite admirable. For a clod is mined which is called <term>anthrax</term> <note>meaning "coal" or "carbuncle"</note> before it reaches the state of cinnabar through processing; it is a vein like iron, rather reddish in color, having a red dust around it. When it is being dug, it emits frequent drops of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui," or mercury</note> from the blows of the iron tools, which are immediately collected by the miners. When these clods have been collected into the workshop, on account of their abundance of moisture...

# BOOK SEVEN

<page-num>126</page-num>

The lumps are cast into the furnace so that they may dry out, and the smoke that is raised from them by the heat of the fire, when it settles on the floor of the furnace, is found to be quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; literally "living silver," known today as mercury</note>. When the lumps are removed, the drops that remain are too small to be collected, but they are swept into vessels of water, and there they join together and are fused into one. When this substance fills a measure of four sextarii <note>a Roman dry and liquid measure, roughly equivalent to a pint or half a liter</note>, it is found to weigh one hundred pounds when put on the scale. When it is poured into a vessel, if a stone weighing one hundred pounds is placed upon it, the stone floats on the surface; the liquid cannot be pressed down by such a weight, nor can it be squeezed out or dispersed. Yet, if the hundred-pound stone is removed and a single scruple <note>a "scrupulum" was a small Roman unit of weight, about 1.14 grams</note> of gold is placed there, it will not float, but will sink to the bottom by its own nature. Thus, it cannot be denied that the gravity of things depends not on the magnitude of their weight, but on their specific kind.

This substance is prepared for use in many ways. For neither silver nor copper can be properly gilded <note>original: "inaurari"; the process of fire-gilding using a mercury-gold amalgam</note> without it. Furthermore, when gold is woven into a garment, and that garment is worn out with age and no longer fit for honorable use, the rags are placed in earthen vessels and burned over a fire. The resulting ash is thrown into water, and quicksilver is added to it. This mercury seizes all the tiny grains of gold and forces them to unite with itself. After the water is poured off, the mixture is poured into a cloth and squeezed by hand; the quicksilver, being liquid, slips out through the gaps in the cloth, while the gold, compressed by the squeezing, is found inside in a pure state.

# BOOK

Through frequent boilings, the colors are brought to their proper state. When these processes are completed, the cinnabar <note>original: "minium"; here referring to natural mercuric sulfide or vermilion</note> loses the natural virtues it possessed due to the loss of the quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and it becomes tender in nature and weak in its strength. Therefore, when it is applied in the polished plasterwork of indoor rooms, it remains without defects in its own color. However, in open places—that is, in peristyles <note>open courtyards surrounded by columns</note>, or exedrae <note>semi-circular recessed seating areas</note>, or other places of that kind where the sun and moon can cast their brightness and rays—when the area is touched by them, the pigment is spoiled; losing the virtue of its color, it turns black. 

Thus, among many others, the scribe Faberius, when he wished to have his house on the Aventine Hill elegantly finished, had all the walls of the peristyles coated with cinnabar; after thirty days, they turned to an unlovely and mottled color. Consequently, he contracted to have other colors applied instead. But if anyone should be more discerning and wish a cinnabar finish to retain its color, once the wall is polished and dry, let him apply Punic wax <note>a refined beeswax bleached in seawater and treated with nitre</note> liquefied by fire and tempered with a little oil, using a brush of bristles. Then, afterwards, by placing charcoal in an iron vessel and heating the wall closely, he should force that wax to sweat and become evenly distributed. Finally, he should rub it down with a candle <note>wax taper</note> and clean linen cloths, just as nude marble statues are cared for. This process is called *encaustic* <note>original Greek: καῦσις, meaning "burning in"</note> in Greek. 

In this way, the protective coat of Punic wax prevents the brightness of the moon and the rays of the sun from licking away and snatching the color from these polished surfaces. Furthermore, the workshops that were once at the mines of the Ephesians have now been transferred to Rome, because this type of ore was later discovered in the regions of Spain. From those mines, the clumps of ore are brought and processed in Rome by the tax-farmers <note>publicani; contractors who managed state-owned resources</note>. ### On colors that are made by art. Chapter X.

I shall now proceed to those things which, through the specialized treatment of other types of substances, receive the properties of colors. And first, I shall explain black pigment <note>original: "atramentum"; here referring specifically to lampblack, a carbon-based black</note>, the use of which is of great necessity in construction, so that the methods by which it is prepared according to certain technical rules may be known. For a room is built like a sweating-chamber <note>original: "laconicum"; a circular vaulted room used as a steam bath</note>, and it is finished finely with marble and smoothed. Resin is placed in the furnace. The power of the fire, by burning the resin, forces it to emit soot through the openings into the sweating-chamber. This soot sticks to the walls and the curve of the vaulted ceiling. Collected from there, part of it is mixed with gum and worked for use as scribes' ink; the rest is used by decorators <note>original: "tectores"; skilled plasterers or wall-painters</note> who mix it with glue...

the way it was invented is quite wonderful. For sand is ground with flowers of soda <note>original: "nitri flore"; likely natron or sodium carbonate used as a flux</note> so finely that it becomes like flour. This is mixed with Cyprian copper made into thick filings (like sawdust) and sprinkled with water so that it clumps together. Having been transformed by the heat of the fire, they are reduced to a blue color. Burnt ochre <note>original: "Usta"; a toasted version of yellow earth</note>, however, which is very useful in plastering work, is tempered in this way: a lump of good yellow ochre <note>original: "silis boni"</note> is heated until it is glowing in the fire; it is then extinguished with vinegar, and it turns a purple color.

## How white lead, verdigris, and sandarac are made.
### Chapter XII.

Regarding white lead <note>original: "cerussa"</note> and verdigris <note>original: "aerugine"</note>, which our people call <term>eruca</term> <note>a green pigment formed by the corrosion of copper</note>, it is not out of place to describe how they are prepared. For the Rhodians, arranging vine-cuttings in jars, pour in vinegar and place lead masses <note>original: "plumbeas massas"; "pigs" or ingots of lead</note> on top of the cuttings; then they seal the jars with lids so that, being closed, they release no air. After a certain time, when they open them, they find white lead produced from the lead masses. By the same method, by placing copper plates instead, they produce verdigris, which is called <term>eruca</term>. Truly, when white lead is baked in a furnace, its color changes under the heat of the fire and it becomes <term>sandarac</term> <note>original: "Sandaraca"; while often referring to red arsenic, Vitruvius here describes the production of "red lead" (minium) by roasting white lead</note>. Men learned this from an accidental fire; and this provides a much better use than the natural variety which is dug up from mines.

## How *ostrum*, the most excellent of all manufactured colors, is made. Chapter XIII.

I shall now begin to speak of <term>ostrum</term> <note>original: "ostrum"; a highly prized purple pigment derived from the murex sea snail</note>, which possesses a sweetness of appearance more expensive and excellent than any of these other colors. It is extracted from a marine shellfish <note>original: "conchilio marino"</note> from which purple dye is made. To those who consider the nature of things, its properties are as full of wonder as anything else, because it does not have the same kind of color in every place where it grows, but is naturally tempered by the path of the sun.

Therefore, the kind gathered in the Black Sea and Gaul—since these regions are closest to the north—is dark. As one moves between the north and the west, it is found to be a leaden blue. That which is gathered in the regions of the equinoctial east and west is found to be of a violet color. However, that which is extracted from southern regions possesses a red quality; for this reason, this "Red" is produced on the island of Rhodes and in other such regions that are closest to the sun’s path. 

When these shellfish have been collected, they are struck around the edges with iron tools. From these wounds, a purple fluid <note>original: "sanies"; literally "ichor" or "venom," referring to the snail's secretion</note> flows out like a falling tear, which is caught and ground in mortars. Because it is taken from the shells of these marine snails, it is called <term>ostrum</term>. Because of its saltiness, it quickly becomes dry <note>original: "siticulosum"; literally "thirsty" or "parched"</note> unless it has honey poured around it.

*...Attic ochre <note>original: "Atticum"; a highly prized yellow earth pigment from the region of Athens</note> is imitated by placing dried violets in a vessel with water and heating them over a fire until they boil. Then, when the mixture has cooled, they pour it onto a cloth and, squeezing it with their hands, they collect the water colored by the violets into a mortar. By pouring <term>creta</term> <note>original: "creta"; a general term for various white earths, clays, or chalks</note> into it and grinding it, they produce the color of Attic ochre. In the same way, by tempering <term>vacinium</term> <note>original: "vacinium"; likely the whortleberry or blueberry</note> and mixing it with milk, they create an elegant purple.*

*Likewise, those who cannot afford to use <term>chrysocolla</term> <note>original: "chrysocolla"; literally "gold-solder," here referring to a bright green copper mineral like malachite</note> because of its high price, dye a blue pigment <note>original: "ceruleum"</note> with the herb called weld <note>original: "luteum"; the herb Reseda luteola, used for yellow dye</note>, and they use this very green color. This is known as "dyed-color" <note>original: "infectiva"</note>. Furthermore, due to the scarcity of indigo <note>original: "indici"</note>, they create an imitation of it by dyeing Selinusian earth <note>original: "selinusiam"</note> or ring-clay <note>original: "anulariam"; a fine white clay used for making rings or cosmetics</note> with glass <note>original: "uitrum"</note>—which the Greeks call <term>hyalon</term> <note>original: "ΰαλον"</note>.*

*I have described in this book the methods and materials required for the proper arrangement and durability of paintings, as well as the inherent properties of all the colors, as far as I could recall them. Therefore, all the perfect details of building, and the appropriate arrangements they ought to have, have been completed in these seven volumes. In the following book, I shall explain the subject of water: how it may be found in places where it is lacking, the methods by which it is supplied, and by what means its healthfulness and suitability may be tested.*

## BOOK EIGHT.

Among the seven wise men, *Thales of Miletus* <note>original: "Thales milesius"; a pre-Socratic philosopher often cited as the first to investigate the basic principles of matter</note> declared that water is the first principle of all things. *Heraclitus* claimed it was fire. The *Priests of the Magi* <note>original: "Magorum Sacerdotes"; referring to Persian Zoroastrian priests who held fire and water as sacred</note> chose water and fire. *Euripides*—a student of *Anaxagoras*, whom the *Athenians* called the "philosopher of the stage" <note>original: "scenicum"; so named because his tragedies were deeply influenced by Anaxagoras’s natural philosophy</note>—suggested it was air and earth. He argued that the earth, having been inseminated by the conception of rains from the heavens, gave birth to the races of mankind and all the animals in the world; and when those things born of the earth are dissolved, forced by the necessity of time, they return to that same earth. Likewise, those things born of the air return to the regions of the sky and do not suffer total destruction, but rather, through a change in their dissolution, they fall back into the same essential property they held before.

However, *Pythagoras*, *Empedocles*, *Epicharmus*, and other *Naturalists* <note>original: "Physici"; those who studied "physis" or nature</note> and *Philosophers* proposed that these principles are four: air, fire, water, and earth. They argued that the cohesion of these elements, through a natural shaping based on the distinctions of their kinds, produces various qualities. We observe, indeed, that not only are living things generated from these elements, but also that no thing can be nourished, grow, or be sustained without their power. For bodies without breath <note>original: "spiritu"; also meaning air or vital spirit</note> cannot possess life, unless the air flowing in creates a continuous cycle of expansion and contraction. Furthermore, if there is not a balanced proportion of heat <note>original: "calor"</note> in the body, it will lack the breath of life... <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "ani" likely referring to "animus" (soul/mind) or "animalis" (pertaining to living things)</note>

...living animals, nor can there be a firm posture, and the strength of food will not be able to have the proper temperature for digestion <note>original: "concoctionis"; in ancient physiology, digestion was viewed as a "cooking" process driven by internal heat</note>. Likewise, if the limbs of the body are not nourished by earthly food, they will fail, and thus they will be abandoned by the mixture of the earthly principle. Indeed, if animals should be drained of blood and dried out from the liquid of the primary elements, lacking the power of moisture, they will wither away. 

Therefore, the divine mind did not make those things which are specifically necessary for peoples difficult or rare—such as pearls, gold, silver, and other things which neither the body nor nature truly craves—but instead, those things without which the life of mortals cannot be safe, it poured out ready at hand throughout the whole world. And so, if by chance any breath <note>original: "spiritus"</note> is lacking in the body, the air assigned for restoration provides it. Furthermore, the provision of the sun's heat and the discovery of fire make life safer; likewise, the fruit of the earth, providing an abundance of food, feeds and nourishes animals through continuous grazing even beyond their necessary desires. 

Water, however, provides not only drink but also countless useful benefits for our needs—and because it is free, these benefits are all the more welcome. For this reason, those who hold priesthoods according to Egyptian customs show that all things consist of the power of liquid; thus, when they cover the water jar <note>original: "hydriam"; a vessel used in the cult of Isis to represent the life-giving waters of the Nile</note>, which is carried back to the temple and sanctuary with pure devotion, they then fall prostrate on the ground and, lifting their hands to heaven, give thanks to the divine kindness for its discoveries.

...[the properties of the elements] have been explained; in this book, it is necessary to write about the discovery of water, what qualities it has based on the natural properties of different locations, by what methods it is channeled, and likewise how it may be tested. For water is most necessary for life, for pleasures, and for daily use. This discovery will be easier if the springs are open and flowing. But if they do not flow forth, the sources must be sought underground and collected. These are to be tested in this way: one should lie face down <note>original: "procumbatur in dentes"; literally "to fall upon the teeth," an idiom for lying prone</note> before the sun has risen in the places where the search is to be made, and with the chin placed and supported on the ground, the landscape should be observed. ...and the supply is meager and shallow, it will not have the best flavor. The signs by which water may be found in various types of earth, beyond what has been written above, are these: if there are found growing the <term>slender rush</term> <note>original: "tenuis iuncus"</note>, <term>wild willow</term> <note>original: "salix erratica"</note>, <term>alder</term> <note>original: "alnus"</note>, <term>chaste-tree</term> <note>original: "uitex"</note>, <term>reeds</term> <note>original: "harundo"</note>, <term>ivy</term> <note>original: "hedera"</note>, and others of this kind which cannot grow or be nourished by themselves without moisture. These spots are not to be trusted. But in regions and lands where these signs appear naturally—not in hollows, and not sown by hand but growing of their own accord—there one should seek water. In places where these signs do not appear, the search will be less certain...
