# BOOK EIGHT

These tests are to be conducted as follows. Let a place be dug out, no less than five feet wide in every direction. In this <term>pit</term> <note>original: "fossura"</note>, around sunset, place a <term>bronze basin</term> <note>original: "scaphium aereum"</note>, or one made of lead, or a bowl—whichever of these is available. Let it be smeared on the inside with oil and placed upside down, and let the top of the excavation be covered with reeds or green foliage, and buried over with earth. Then, on the following day, let it be opened; if there are droplets and "sweats" inside the vessel, that location will have water. Likewise, if a vessel made of unbaked clay is placed in that digging and covered in the same manner, if that place has water, the vessel will be damp and may even fall apart from the moisture when it is opened. Also, if a fleece of wool is placed in that excavation and water can be squeezed out of it on the following day, it will signify that the place has an abundance. Furthermore, if a prepared lamp, filled with oil and lit, is placed in that spot and covered, and if on the next day it has not burnt out but still has remains of oil and the <term>wick</term> <note>original: "ellychnij"</note>, and the lamp itself is found to be damp, it will indicate that the place has water, because all heat draws moisture toward itself. Also, if a fire is made in that place and the earth, being thoroughly heated and scorched, sends up a misty vapor from itself, that place will have water.

When these trials have been made and the signs written above have been found, then a <term>well</term> <note>original: "puteus"</note> must be sunk in that place. If a source of water is found, several more wells should be dug around it, and all of them should be led into one place through <term>underground channels</term> <note>original: "specus"</note>. These sources are to be sought especially in mountains and <term>northern regions</term> <note>original: "septentrionalibus"</note>, because in these places water is found to be sweeter, healthier, and more plentiful. For these areas are turned away from the path of the sun, and in these places trees are especially frequent and the lands are wooded;

->EIGHTH BOOK<-

The mountains themselves have their own obstructing shadows, so that the rays of the sun do not reach the earth directly and cannot suck up the moisture. Furthermore, the valleys between the mountains receive the greatest amount of rain, and because of the density of the forests, the snow is preserved there for a longer time by the shadows of the trees and the mountains. Then, having melted, it filters through the veins of the earth and thus reaches the lowest roots of the mountains, from which the flowing streams of springs burst forth. In level plains, however, an abundance of water cannot be maintained for the opposite reasons; even if it were present, it could not be healthy, because the violent force of the sun—due to the lack of obstructing shadows—snatches away the moisture by exhausting the heat from the flat surface of the fields. If there are any visible waters there, the air, calling away the lightest, thinnest, and most subtly healthy part, scatters it into the heights of the sky, while the heaviest, hardest, and most unpleasant parts are left behind in the springs of the plains.

### On Rainwater. Chapter II.

<margin>1</margin>Therefore, the water that is collected from rains has more healthful qualities, for the reason that it is selected from the lightest and most subtly thin parts of all springs; then, having been filtered through the agitation of the air and liquefied by storms, it reaches the earth. ...and creates the increasing waves of the winds. For wherever the winds blow, the gathered vapors <note>original: humores</note> from springs, rivers, marshes, and the sea are carried; when these are influenced by the sun, they are drawn out, and thus clouds are raised into the heights. These clouds then, floating upon the wave of the air, when they arrive at the mountains, are broken by the obstruction of the peaks and the storms. Because of their fullness and weight, they dissolve by liquefying and thus spread out over the lands. That vapor, mists, and moisture are born from the earth seems to be caused by this reason: that the earth contains within itself intense heat, immense spirits <note>likely referring to subterranean gases or air pressure</note>, cooling effects, and a great multitude of waters. Because of this, when it cools at night, blasts of wind arise through the darkness, and clouds emerge from humid places into the heights. When the rising sun touches the globe of the earth with its force, the air—warmed through by the sun—lifts the moisture from the earth along with the dews. 

One may also take an example from baths <note>original: balneis</note>. For no vaulted ceilings of the hot rooms <note>term: caldariorum (the hot, steamy rooms in a Roman bath complex)</note> can have springs located above them; rather, the "sky" <note>referring to the ceiling or the air within the room</note> that is there, being thoroughly heated by the vapor of the fire from the furnaces <note>term: praefurnia (the furnace rooms that heated the floors and walls of the baths)</note>, snatches up the water from the floors and carries it with it into the curvatures of the ceilings and holds it there. Because hot vapor always pushes itself upward, it is not at first released because of its lack of substance <note>original: breuitatem; literally "shortness" or "briefness"</note>; however, as soon as it has gathered a greater amount of moisture, it cannot be sustained due to its weight, but drips down upon the heads of the bathers. In the same way, the air of the heavens, when it receives heat from the sun, draws up moisture from all places, lifting and gathering it into clouds. For the earth, touched by heat, casts out moisture just as the human body emits sweat <note>original: sudores</note> because of heat. The evidence <note>original: indices</note> of this matter are the winds...

...it, from which those winds that come from the coldest regions—namely the North Wind <note>original: septentrio</note> and the North-Northeast wind <note>original: aquilo</note>—blow currents of air that have been thinned out by the dryness in the atmosphere. Circling out from these marshes through the rivers Astasoba and Astabora, and many others, it reaches the mountains at the cataract. From that precipice, it flings itself down and proceeds through the north between Elephantine and Syene <note>Modern Aswan</note> and the fields of Thebes into Egypt, and there it is finally called the Nile.

This is true unless they happen to run into a place rich in sulfur, alum, or bitumen; for then they are transformed, and the springs pour out either hot or cold waters with a foul odor and taste. For there is no inherent quality of "hot water" in its own right; rather, when cold water runs through a burning place, it boils up and, having been thoroughly heated, it emerges through the veins of the earth. For this reason, it cannot remain hot for long, but becomes cold in a short distance. If it were naturally hot <note>i.e., if heat were an essential property of the water itself</note>, its heat would not be cooled. However, its taste, odor, and color are not restored to their original state, because they have been infused and mixed in due to the porous nature of the earth.

# BOOK VIII

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the description of how water behaves under pressure.</note> ...with inflations in the open air, it settles back down to its own place. In the same manner, when the heads of springs are compressed by narrow spaces, the bubbles of the water's spirit rush to the top. However, as soon as they are opened more widely and emptied through the pores of their liquid power, they settle and are restored to the property of their own level.

Every hot water source is medicinal for this reason: because it has been strained through various substances and acquires a different virtue for use. For instance, **sulfurous springs** <note>original: "sulphurosi fontes"</note> refresh the labors of the nerves <note>In ancient medicine, "nerves" often referred to tendons and ligaments as well as neurological pathways.</note> by thoroughly warming them and sucking out the vicious humors from the body through heat. 

**Aluminous springs**, however, when they receive limbs weakened by paralysis or some other force of disease, revive them by warming the cooling parts through the open veins with a contrary force of heat; from this, they are continually restored to the former health of the limbs. 

**Bituminous springs** <note>Bitumen is a naturally occurring petroleum product; these waters were thought to act as internal cleansers.</note> are accustomed to heal the defects of the internal body by purging them through potions. 

There is also a nitrous type of cold water, such as at Pinna Vestina, Cutiliae, and other similar places, which purges through potions and, by passing through the bowels, even reduces the tumors of scrofula <note>original: "strumarum"; a swelling of the lymph nodes.</note>. 

However, where gold, silver, iron, copper, lead, and other similar things are mined, copious springs are found, but these are exceedingly defective. For they have defects contrary to the hot water emitted by sulfur, alum, and bitumen; when they enter the body through potions and, flowing through the veins, reach the nerves and joints, they harden them by causing swelling. Therefore, the nerves, swelling from the inflation, are contracted in length, and thus make men either "neuric" <note>suffering from nervous disorders or spasms</note> or "podagric" <note>suffering from gout, specifically in the feet</note>, because they have the pores of their veins saturated with the hardest, densest, and coldest substances. This species of water...

Likewise lead, which is most flexible and heavy, if it is placed in a vessel and vinegar is poured over it, and if it is then covered and sealed, it will result in the lead dissolving and becoming white lead <term>cerussa: a white pigment, also known as ceruse, used in ancient paints and cosmetics</term>. ### On the specific properties of certain places and springs.
### Chapter 4.

There are also, in some places, properties of springs that produce excellent voices for singing in those who are born there, such as at Tarsus, Magnesia, and other regions of that kind. There is also Zama, a city of the Africans, whose fortifications King Juba <note>Juba I, King of Numidia, who was a contemporary of Julius Caesar</note> enclosed with a double wall, and there he established a royal palace for himself. Twenty miles from there is the town of Ismuc, the territories of which are defined by an incredible boundary. For although Africa is the mother and nurse of wild beasts, especially serpents, none are born in the fields of this town; and if one is ever brought there and set down, it dies immediately. Not only that, but even the earth from these places, if transferred elsewhere, has the same effect. This type of earth is also said to exist in the Balearic Islands, but that land has another even more wonderful power, which I have learned as follows.

Gaius Julius, the son of Masinissa <note>Masinissa was the first King of Numidia and a famous Roman ally; his son here mentioned served with Julius Caesar</note>, who owned the estates of that entire town, served in the army with Caesar the father <note>Julius Caesar</note>. He enjoyed my hospitality, and thus in our daily life together, it was inevitable that we should discuss scholarly matters <note>Latin: *philologia*; here referring to the broad study of literature, science, and history</note>. During a conversation between us concerning the power of water and its properties, he explained that there were springs in that land of such a kind that those born there would have excellent voices for singing. For this reason, they always buy beautiful male slaves <note>Latin: *catastos*; specifically referring to the platforms on which slaves were displayed for sale</note> and mature girls from across the sea, and join them in marriage...

...manage <note>The Latin 'gerere' continues from the previous page, describing the influence of the environment on the population.</note>, so that those who were born from them possessed not only an excellent voice, but also a form that was not unattractive. Since nature has distributed such great variety among different things, and because the human body is composed in some part of earthy matter, there are within it many kinds of humors <term>humors: the primary fluids of the body—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient medicine believed regulated health and temperament</term>, such as blood, milk, sweat, urine, and tears. Therefore, if in so small a particle of earthy matter [the human body] such a discrepancy of flavors is found, it is not surprising if, in the vast magnitude of the earth, innumerable varieties of juices <term>juices: the Latin 'succus' refers to the mineral infusions or liquid essence of the soil</term> are found. The force of water, running through the veins of the earth, becomes infused by these juices until it reaches the outlets of springs. In this way, diverse and varied springs are formed in their specific types, according to the differences of the locations, the qualities of the regions, and the dissimilar properties of the soils.

Regarding these matters, there are some things I have observed for myself, while others I have found written in Greek books. The authors of these writings include Theophrastus, Timaeus, Posidonius, Hegesias, Herodotus, Aristides, and Metrodorus. These men, with great vigilance and infinite study, declared in their writings how the properties of locations, the powers of waters, and the qualities of regions are distributed according to the inclination of the heavens <note>original: "inclinatione coeli" — referring to latitude and the angle of the sun, which the ancients believed determined local climate and biology</note>. Following their lead, I have written in this book what I thought sufficient regarding the varieties of water. My goal is that, from these descriptions, people might more easily choose springs of water from which they can lead flowing supplies into cities and towns <note>original: "municipia" — self-governing towns under Roman law</note> for public use.

For among all things, none seem to have such great necessity for use as water. Indeed, the nature of all living creatures can sustain life if deprived of the fruit of grain, or of trees, or meat, or fish, or even any other such food. Without water, however, neither the bodies of animals nor any nutritional quality of food can be born, sustained, or prepared.

Therefore, sources must be sought and chosen with great diligence and industry for the health of human life.

## On the testing of waters. Chapter V.

The trials and tests of these waters should be managed as follows. If they are flowing and open, before they begin to be diverted <note>original: 'duci'—referring to the construction of an aqueduct to lead the water elsewhere</note>, they should be observed, and careful attention paid to the physical constitution of the people who live around those springs. If they have strong bodies, healthy complexions, sound legs, and eyes that are not bleary <note>The Latin 'lippis oculis' refers to chronic eye inflammation or discharge, which Vitruvius uses as a diagnostic for poor local water quality</note>, the waters will be highly approved.

Likewise, if a new spring has been dug, and if that water, when sprinkled into a Corinthian vessel <note>original: 'vas corinthium'—referring to a high-quality bronze alloy highly prized in antiquity</note> or another kind made of good bronze, leaves no stain, it will be of the best quality.

Similarly, if that water is boiled in a bronze pot <note>original: 'Aheno'—literally 'made of bronze,' used here to mean a kettle or cauldron</note>, and after being left to settle and poured off, no sand or mud is found at the bottom of the pot, that water will also be approved.

Likewise, if legumes <note>original: 'legumina'—beans, peas, or pulses</note> placed in a vessel with that water and set over a fire are cooked through quickly, they will indicate that the water is good and healthy.

Furthermore, the water in the spring itself, if it is clear and transparent, and wherever it reaches or flows, if neither moss nor reeds grow, nor is the place fouled by any contamination, but maintains a pure appearance, it is indicated by these signs to be light <term>light: ancient scientists believed 'lightness' (tenuitas) in water meant it was easier for the body to digest and free of heavy minerals</term> and of the highest healthfulness.

Now I shall explain how the conduits to habitations and city walls ought to be constructed; the first principle of which is **leveling** <term>perlibratio: the process of determining the relative heights of two points to ensure a proper slope</term>. This leveling is performed using **dioptrae** <note>original: 'dioptris'—an early surveying instrument using sights to measure angles</note>, **water-levels** <note>original: 'libris aquarijs'</note>, or the **chorobates**. However, it is done more accurately with the **chorobates**, because dioptrae and levels are prone to error. <margin>the chorobates</margin> The chorobates is a straightedge about twenty feet long. It has brackets at its extreme ends, crafted in an identical manner and joined to the ends of the straightedge at a right angle <note>original: 'ad normam'—literally 'to the square'</note>. Between the straightedge and the brackets, cross-pieces are joined by hinges, which have lines drawn exactly perpendicular <note>vertically straight</note>. Plumb-lines hang from the straightedge, <margin>water levels and dioptrae</margin> one over each cross-piece. When the straightedge is set in place and the lines touch the drawn markings equally and evenly, they indicate that the instrument is perfectly level.

If, however, the wind interferes and the movement of the plumb-lines prevents a certain reading, then the tool should have a channel on its upper part, five feet long, one finger wide, and one and a half fingers deep. Water is poured into this channel, and if the water touches the upper rims of the channel equally at both ends, it will be known to be level. Thus, once the leveling has been performed with this chorobates, the amount of the **slope** <term>fastigium: the gradient or incline required for water to flow</term> will be known.

Perhaps someone who has read the books of **Archimedes** <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) was a Greek mathematician who famously calculated the properties of spheres and fluids</note> will say that a true leveling cannot be done using water, because he holds that water is not level but has a **spherical** <note>original: 'spheroides'</note> shape, sharing the same center as the globe of the earth. However, whether the surface of water is flat or spherical, it is still necessary that the two extreme ends of the straightedge's channel hold the water at the same height. If the tool is tilted to one side, the higher end will not have water reaching the upper rims of the channel. For while it is necessary that water, when poured, has a swelling and curvature in the middle, its ends...

## Chapter 7: The Various Ways Water is Conveyed

Now, the conduction of water is carried out in three ways: by streams through **masonry channels** <note>original: 'canales structiles'—stone or brick-built conduits</note>, or by **lead pipes** <note>original: 'fistulis plumbeis'</note>, or by **earthenware tubes** <note>original: 'tubulis fictilibus'—ceramic pipes</note>. When the water reaches the city walls, a **distribution tower** <term>castellum: a header tank or reservoir used to regulate water pressure and organize distribution throughout a city</term> should be built, and joined to the tower there should be a **triple intake** <note>original: 'triplex immissarium'—a three-part chamber system for receiving water</note> to receive the water. Within the distribution tower, three **pipes** <note>original: 'fistulæ'—usually referring to lead pipes in this context</note> should be placed, divided equally among the joined reservoirs, so that when the water overflows, the excess from the two outer reservoirs spills into the middle one. 

In this way, the pipes in the middle reservoir will be arranged to supply all the public basins and **fountains** <note>original: 'salientes'—literally 'leaping' water features</note>. From the second reservoir, pipes lead to the **public baths** <note>original: 'balneas'</note> so that they may provide an annual tax to the people. From the third reservoir, water is directed to private houses, ensuring that there is never a shortage for public use. For users will not be able to divert the flow when they have...

If, however, the water is to be conducted by **lead pipes** <term>fistulis plumbeis: pipes made by rolling sheets of lead into a cylinder and soldering the seam</term>, a **reservoir** <term>castellum: a settling tank or header tank used to manage water pressure and distribution</term> should first be built at the source. Then, the thickness of the **lead sheets** <term>lamnae: flat sheets of lead before they are bent into pipes</term> for the pipes should be determined according to the volume of water, and these pipes should be laid from that reservoir to the reservoir situated within the city walls. The pipes should be cast in lengths of no less than ten feet. If they are of the "one-hundred" size, they should weigh 1,200 pounds each; if "eighty," 960 pounds; if "fifty," 600 pounds; "forty," 480 pounds; "thirty," 360 pounds; "twenty," 240 pounds; "fifteen," 180 pounds; "ten," 120 pounds; "eight," 96 pounds; and "five," 60 pounds.

The names of the pipe sizes are derived from the width of the sheets in **digits** <term>digitos: a Roman unit of measurement, approximately 0.73 inches or 1.85 cm</term> before they are bent into a circular shape. For instance, a sheet that is fifty digits wide when it is formed into a pipe will be called a "fifty-pipe," and the others are named similarly.

This method of conduction through lead pipes follows this procedure: if the source has a direct **level** <term>libramenta: the vertical alignment or gradient relative to the destination</term> toward the city walls and no intermediate mountains are high enough to interfere, it is necessary to build up the intervening spaces to the proper level using substructures, just as was described for open channels and masonry conduits. If, however, the distance is not too great, the pipes may follow a circuitous route. 

But if there are continuous valleys, the course of the pipes should be directed down the slope. When they reach the bottom, a low substructure is built so that the **level section** <note>original: 'libramentum'</note> is as long as possible. (This section is called the **belly** <term>uenter: the lowest part of an inverted siphon where water pressure is highest</term>, which the Greeks call the *koilia* <note>original: 'κοιλίαν' — Greek for 'stomach' or 'cavity'</note>). Then, when it reaches the opposite slope, because the water gently swells over the long distance of the "belly," it is forced up to the height of the top of the hill. However, if such a "belly" is not constructed in the valleys...

### BOOK EIGHT

...thickness should be no less than two fingers <note>approximately 1.5 inches or 3.7 cm</note> from the clay itself, but made so that these **clay pipes** <term>tubuli: small earthenware pipes used as an alternative to lead</term> are tongued at one end so that they can enter and fit into one another. Then, their joints must be coated with **quicklime** <term>calx uiua: lime that has not been slaked with water, which creates a chemical heat when mixed</term> kneaded with oil. In the downward slopes of the level of the **"belly"** <term>uenter: the lowest part of a siphon system where water pressure is highest</term>, a block of red stone must be placed right at the joint. 

This block must be bored through so that the last pipe from the descent is joined into the stone, and the first pipe of the level "belly" is similarly joined. In the same way, on the opposite rising slope, the last pipe of the level "belly" should be fixed into the cavity of the red stone, and the first pipe of the rising section <note>original: "expressionis," referring to the part where water is forced upward by pressure</note> should be joined in the same manner. By this method, the level alignment of the pipes, both in the descent and the rise, will not be forced out of place. 

For a **violent blast of air** <note>original: "uehemens spiritus"; this refers to compressed air or the "water hammer" effect that can shatter ancient conduits</note> is often generated in water conduction, so powerful that it can even burst through stone, unless the water is first let in slowly and sparingly from the source, and contained at the joints or turns by lashings or the weight of ballast. All other things are to be arranged just as they are for lead pipes. 

Likewise, when water is first let in from the source, **fine ash** <note>original: "fauilla"</note> should be sent in first, so that if any joints are not sufficiently sealed, they may be coated by the ash. These clay pipe conduits have the following advantages: First, in the work itself, if any defect occurs, anyone can repair it. Furthermore, water from clay pipes is much **healthier** than that through lead pipes; it appears to be damaged by lead because **white lead** <term>cerussa: lead carbonate, a toxic substance used as a pigment</term> is produced from it. This is said to be harmful to human bodies; thus, if what is produced from a substance is harmful, there is no doubt that the substance itself is not healthy. 

We can take an example of this from **lead-workers** <note>original: "artificibus plumbarys"</note>, whose complexions are affected by a sickly paleness. For when lead is melted and cast, the fumes from it settle upon the body...

### BOOK EIGHT

...weakening their limbs, and day by day, by burning them out, it robs the strength of the blood from their members. Therefore, it appears that water should by no means be conducted in **lead pipes** <term>fistulis plumbeis: pipes made from sheets of lead rolled into an oval or pear shape and soldered</term> if we wish to have it be healthful. That the flavor is also better from **clay pipes** <term>tubuli: earthenware pipes</term> can be proven by our daily diet; for although everyone has tables set with silver vessels, they nevertheless use earthenware for the sake of the purity of flavor. 

But if there are no springs from which we may conduct water, it is necessary to dig **wells** <term>puteos: shafts sunk vertically to reach an underground aquifer</term>. In the digging of wells, however, one must not neglect scientific reason, but the natural principles of things must be considered with great skill and sharp intelligence, because the earth contains many and various kinds of matter within itself. For, like all other things, it is composed of the four elements <note>the "four principles" or elements are earth, air, fire, and water</note>. First is the earthy part itself, which contains springs of moisture. 

There are also heats, from which **sulfur**, **alum**, and **bitumen** <note>original: "sulphur, alumen, bitumen"; these were associated with volcanic activity and mineral-rich soils</note> are produced, and massive drafts of air. When these gases, being heavy, reach the excavation of the wells through the porous passages of the earth and encounter the men digging there, they choke the **animal spirits** <term>spiritus animales: the ancient physiological concept of a life-force or "breath" that controlled movement and sensation</term> in their nostrils by their natural vapor. Thus, those who do not escape from there quickly are killed.

To guard against this, the following method should be used: Let a lighted lamp be lowered; if it remains burning, the descent may be made without danger. But if the light is extinguished by the force of the vapor, then **ventilation shafts** <term>aestuaria: secondary shafts or "breathing holes" designed to allow foul air to escape</term> shall be dug to the right and left of the well. In this way, just as through the nostrils, the vapors will be dissipated through the shafts. 

When these matters have been managed and the water is reached, then the well should be walled up with masonry in such a way that the veins of water are not blocked. If, however, the ground is too hard, or the veins of water are not found deep at the bottom, then one must resort to **cistern-work** <term>signinis operibus: *opus signinum*, a waterproof Roman building material made of lime, sand, and crushed pottery shards</term>...

### SEVENTH
<note>The header reads "SEPTIMVS" (Seventh), though the text continues from Book Eight of Vitruvius's *De Architectura*.</note>

...supplies of water are to be received in higher places. For **Signinum work** <term>opus signinum: a Roman waterproof building material made of lime, sand, and crushed stone or pottery, then rammed into place</term>, these steps must be followed: first, the purest and coarsest sand is to be prepared; **rubble** <term>cementum: rough pieces of broken stone or tile used in masonry</term> is to be broken from flint, with no piece weighing more than a **pound** <term>librarium: based on the *libra*, the Roman pound of approximately 327 grams</term>; and the strongest possible lime is to be mixed in a mortar, such that five parts of sand correspond to two parts of lime. 

The rubble is then added to the mortar. From this mixture, the walls are constructed in a trench dug down to the level of the intended depth and are to be rammed down with wooden pestles tipped with iron. Once the walls have been rammed, the earth remaining in the middle is to be cleared out down to the level of the bottom of the walls. After the ground is leveled, a floor is to be rammed down from the same mortar to the thickness that has been determined. 

If these reservoirs are made in double or triple sets, so that the water can be moved between them by means of **filtration** <term>percolationibus: the process of straining or filtering water to remove impurities</term>, they will make the use of the water much more healthful. For when the sediment has a place to settle, the water will become clearer and will keep its flavor without odors; if not, it will be necessary to add salt to thin it out <note>original: "salem addi... & extenuari"; Vitruvius suggests adding salt to clarify murky water or perhaps to mask poor taste when a settling tank is unavailable</note>.

## BOOK NINE.

The ancestors of the Greeks established such great honors for noble athletes who were victorious at the Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian, and Nemean games <note>These were the four great Panhellenic Games of ancient Greece, held in honor of the gods</note> that they not only receive praise while standing in the assembly holding the palm branch and wearing the crown, but even when they return to their own cities, they are carried into their walls and fatherlands in triumph with four-horse chariots <note>original: "quadrigis"</note>. Furthermore, they enjoy a lifetime of state-provided income from public revenues. When I observe this, I am amazed that the same—or even greater—honors have not been granted to writers <note>original: "scriptoribus," here referring to authors, scientists, and philosophers</note> who provide infinite benefits to all nations throughout all ages. Indeed, it would have been more worthy to establish such rewards for them, because while athletes only make their own bodies stronger through exercise, writers not only perfect their own perceptions but also prepare instructions in their books for everyone to learn from and to sharpen their minds.

What benefit does it bring to humanity that Milo of Croton <note>A famous wrestler of the 6th century BCE, legendary for his strength, such as allegedly carrying a bull on his shoulders</note> was never defeated? Or what of the others who were victors in that manner, except that they enjoyed fame among their own citizens only while they were alive? But the teachings of Pythagoras, Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and other wise men, cultivated through daily and constant industry, produce fresh and blooming fruits not only for their own citizens but for all peoples. Those who are filled from a young age with this abundance of learning gain the finest perceptions of wisdom and establish <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought on the following page</note>...

<summary>In the preface to Book Nine, Vitruvius argues that intellectual contributors like philosophers and writers deserve greater social honors than athletes, as their work provides universal and eternal benefits.</summary>
<keywords>Panhellenic Games, athletes, Milo of Croton, Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle, intellectual vs physical achievement, Vitruvius</keywords>

## Plato’s discovery concerning the measurement of a field.
### Chapter 1.

If there is a place or a field with equal sides in the shape of a square, and it becomes necessary to double it while keeping equal sides—because this cannot be found through the logic of numbers or multiplications—it is instead discovered by using corrected linear drawings. The demonstration of this matter is as follows: A square area that is ten feet long and ten feet wide produces a surface area of one hundred feet. If it is then necessary to double it and create an area of two hundred feet, likewise with equal sides, one must ask how large the side of that square must be so that the two hundred feet correspond to the doubling of the area. No one can find this by number <note>Vitruvius is highlighting the problem of irrational numbers; the square root of 200 is not a whole number</note>; for if fourteen is established as the side, the multiplication results in one hundred ninety-six feet. If fifteen feet are used, it results in two hundred twenty-five feet. Therefore, since it is not explained by number in that square of ten feet long and wide, a line should be drawn from corner to corner—the <term>diagonal</term> <note>original: "diagonios"; the line segment connecting opposite corners of a square</note>—through...

# BOOK IX #

When Pythagoras had discovered this, not doubting that he had been guided in that discovery by the Muses, it is said that he offered sacrifices to them with the greatest gratitude. Moreover, just as this ratio <note>The 3-4-5 ratio of the right-angled triangle</note> is useful in many things and measurements, it is also particularly effective in the construction of staircases in buildings, so that they might have balanced levels <note>term: levels <gloss>original: "librationes"; here referring to the balanced slope or pitch of the stairs</gloss></note> for the steps. 

For if the height of the floor <note>term: floor <gloss>original: "contignatio"; the timber framing of a floor</gloss></note>, from the highest planking <note>term: planking <gloss>original: "coassatio"; the wooden decking of the floor</gloss></note> to the level of the ground below, is divided into three parts, the length of the staircase stringers <note>term: stringers <gloss>original: "scapi"; the primary inclined beams that support the steps</gloss></note> will be five of those same parts for a correct inclination. For however large those three parts of the height between the floor and the lower level may be, let four parts recede from the vertical <note>term: vertical <gloss>original: "perpendiculum"; the plumb line dropping straight down from the top of the stairs</gloss></note>, and the lower ends <note>term: lower ends <gloss>original: "calces"; literally "heels," the base or foot of the staircase beams</gloss></note> of the stringers should be placed there. In this way, the arrangement of the steps and the placement of the stairs themselves will be well-proportioned. Likewise, a diagram of this matter is provided below.

# BOOK IX #

### How a portion of silver mixed with gold can be detected and distinguished in a finished work. Chapter III. ###

<margin>a</margin>Archimedes, indeed, though he had many wonderful and varied inventions, seems to have expressed an almost infinite ingenuity in this particular discovery which I shall now explain. For Hiero, having attained royal power in Syracuse <note>Hiero II (c. 308–215 BCE), a relative of Archimedes and King of Syracuse</note> and being successful in his affairs, vowed a golden crown to the immortal gods to be placed in a certain temple. He contracted its manufacture for a vast price and weighed out the gold <note>term: weighed out <gloss>original: "ad sacoma appendit"; to weigh against a counterpoise or standard weight</gloss></note> to the contractor. In due time, the contractor delivered the finely crafted work for the king's approval and appeared to have provided the crown at the correct weight.

Afterward, a report was made that, after some gold had been removed, an equal amount of silver had been mixed into the construction of that crown. Hiero, indignant at being deceived and finding no way to prove the theft, asked Archimedes to take the consideration of this matter upon himself. 

Then, while Archimedes was occupied with the care of this matter, he happened to go to the baths. There, as he stepped down into the tub <note>term: tub <gloss>original: "solium"; a deep stone or metal bathtub</gloss></note>, he noticed that as much of his body as sat within it, that same amount of water flowed out over the tub. Therefore, having stumbled upon the method for explaining the puzzle, he did not delay, but leapt out of the tub moved by joy. Running home naked, he declared with a loud voice that he had found what he was seeking. For as he ran, he repeatedly shouted in Greek: **"I have found it! I have found it!"** <note>original: "εὕρηκα εὕρηκα" (Eureka! Eureka!)</note>.

Then, following the lead of this discovery, he is said to have made two masses of the same weight as the crown—one of gold, the other of silver. When he had done this, he filled a large vessel to the very brim with water, and lowered the silver mass into it. Whatever its size <note>term: size <gloss>original: "magnitudo"; here referring to volume or displacement</gloss></note> submerged in the vessel, that much water flowed out. Thus, when the mass was removed, he found the water level had decreased by the same amount...

<summary>This page recounts the famous anecdote of Archimedes and King Hiero’s crown, detailing how the philosopher discovered the principle of displacement while bathing. It explains the beginning of his experimental method to detect if silver had been fraudulently mixed with the crown's gold.</summary>

<page-num>150</page-num>
<header>NINTH [BOOK]</header>

[...and as he ran home, he began his experiment.] He poured water and measured it with a **pint-sized measure** <note>original: "sextario"; a Roman unit of measure roughly equal to 0.5 liters</note>, so that it was leveled to the rim just as it had been before. In this way, he discovered how much a specific measure of water corresponded to a specific weight of silver. 

Once he had tested this, he then submerged a mass of gold in the same manner into the full vessel. Having removed it and refilled the water using the same method, he found that not as much water had overflowed. In fact, it was less by exactly as much as a mass of gold is smaller in **volume** <note>original: "corpore"; literally 'body' or physical bulk</note> than a mass of silver of the same weight. 

Finally, having refilled the vessel and submerged the crown itself into that same water, he found that more water overflowed for the crown than for the mass of pure gold of the same weight. Thus, reasoning from the fact that more water flowed out for the crown than for the gold mass, he detected the mixture of silver with the gold and the blatant **theft of the contractor** <note>original: "furtum redemptoris"</note>.

Let our attention now turn to the thoughts of Archytas of Tarentum and Eratosthenes of Cyrene. For these men discovered many useful and pleasing things for mankind through mathematical study. Thus, while they were appreciated for their various other inventions, they are most highly regarded <note>original: "suspecti"; literally "looked up to" or admired in this context</note> for their solutions to this specific challenge. For each of them strove to explain, in his own way, a command given by the oracles of Apollo at Delos: that the altar there, however many square feet it measured, should be doubled in size. By doing so, it was said that those living on the island would then be freed from their religious distress <note>original: "religione liberarentur"; according to legend, a plague had struck Delos, and the oracle required the doubling of the altar to end it</note>. Thus, Archytas explained the solution through the geometry of **cylinders** <note>original: "Cylindrorum descriptionibus"</note>, while Eratosthenes did so through the mechanical method of the **mesolabe** <term>mesolabe: an instrument consisting of sliding frames used to find two mean proportionals between two given lines, effectively solving the problem of doubling the cube</term>.

Therefore, the thoughts of such men are prepared for all time, intended not only to correct our conduct but to be of use to all people. Yet, even when honors are not bestowed upon the character or the works of outstanding writers, their very minds—gazing at things higher than the heavens and lifted to the sky by the steps of memory—ensure that not only their opinions but even their very likenesses <note>original: "figuras"; likely referring to their intellectual "forms" or portraits preserved in their books</note> are known to future generations through an immortal age. # BOOK NINE

Those who possess such minds cannot help but hold in their hearts a dedicated image of the poet Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BCE), often called the father of Roman poetry</note>, just as they do the images of the gods. Furthermore, those who take studious delight in the poems of Accius <note>Lucius Accius, a prolific Roman tragic poet</note> seem to carry with them not only the virtues of his words but his very likeness. Likewise, many born after our memory will seem to dispute "On the Nature of Things" with Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, author of the epic philosophical poem *De Rerum Natura*</note> as if face-to-face; regarding the art of Rhetoric, they will consult with Cicero; and many of posterity will hold discourse with Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific scholar and contemporary of Vitruvius</note> concerning the Latin language. No less will many, deliberating on many things with the wise men of the Greeks, seem to hold secret conversations with them. In short, the opinions of wise writers, flourishing through the ages even though their bodies are absent, carry greater authority when they are part of our counsels and discussions than the presence of any living person. Therefore, Caesar <note>Likely referring to Augustus Caesar, to whom Vitruvius dedicated his work</note>, relying on these authors and applying their perceptions and advice, I have written these volumes: the first seven on buildings, the eighth on water, and in this ninth volume I shall explain the principles of sundials <term>gnomonics: the art of measuring time using a gnomon or pointer</term>, how they were discovered in the universe by the rays of the sun through the shadow of a gnomon, and by what principles they are expanded or contracted.

### Chapter 4: On the principles of sundials discovered from the rays of the sun through shadows, and concerning the universe and the planets.

<margin>e</margin> These matters are arranged by the divine mind and provide great wonder to those who consider them: for the shadow of a gnomon at the equinox <note>The time of year when day and night are of equal length</note> is of one magnitude at Athens, another at Alexandria, another at Rome, and not the same at Piacenza <note>original: "Placentiae"</note> or other places across the globe. Therefore, the layouts of clocks <note>horologiorum: specifically sundials in this context</note> differ greatly according to the change of location. For the forms of the "analemmas" <term>analemma: a geometric construction used to describe the sun's path and design sundials</term> are marked out by the magnitudes of the equinoctial shadows, from which are perfected...

### BOOK NINE

...according to the nature of their locations, and the markings of the hours by the shadow of the gnomons <term>gnomon: the part of a sundial that casts a shadow</term>. The *Analemma* <term>Analemma: a geometric diagram used to calculate the sun's position and shadow lengths based on the time of year</term> is a method sought from the course of the sun and discovered by observing the increasing shadow at the winter solstice <note>original: "brumae"</note>. From this, through architectural principles and the descriptions made by compasses, the resulting effect in the universe is discovered.

The World <note>original: "Mundus," referring here to the totality of the universe or the "macrocosm"</note>, moreover, is the total sum of all things in nature, and the heavens shaped by the constellations. It revolves continuously around the earth and sea on the extreme pivots of its axis. For in these places, the power of nature has acted as an architect, positioning the pivots like centers: one above the earth and sea at the highest point of the world, behind the stars of the Great and Little Bears <note>original: "septentrionum," the seven stars of the North</note>. The other pivot is positioned opposite, beneath the earth in the southern regions. There, around the circular tracks of these pivots, as if around centers on a lathe, she perfected what are called the "poles" <note>Greek: πόλοι (poloi)</note> in Greek, through which the heavens fly in eternal revolution. Thus, the earth and sea are naturally placed in the center.

With things arranged this way by nature, the center in the northern part has a higher elevation above the earth, while in the southern part, it is placed in lower regions and hidden by the earth. Then, through the middle, crossing and slanted toward the south, there is a Belt <term>Zodiac: the circular "zone" or belt of the heavens containing the twelve constellations through which the sun travels</term> shaped by the twelve signs. These represent the forms depicted by nature through the stars, arranged in twelve equal parts. And so, these shining forms, along with the rest of the world and the adornment of the constellations, fly around the earth and sea, completing their courses following the roundness of the sky.

All things, both visible and invisible, are established by the necessity of the seasons. Of these, six signs in number travel across the sky above the earth, while the others, passing beneath the earth, are obscured by its shadow. Six of them, however, are always above the earth...

### BOOK NINE

...are supported. For as much of the final sign is hidden beneath the earth, forced down by the weight of the rotation, an equal portion of its opposite sign is driven by the necessity of that same rotation from hidden and dark places out into the light. Indeed, a single force and necessity completes both the rising and the setting simultaneously.

Since there are twelve of these signs, and each occupies a twelfth part of the world, and they revolve continuously from east to west, the Moon, the star of Mercury, Venus, the Sun itself, and likewise Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, travel through these signs in a contrary course. As they move through the ascending degrees, each wandering through the world with a different scale of orbit from west to east.

The Moon, running through the circuit of the heavens in twenty-eight days and about an hour more, completes the lunar month by returning to the sign from which it began its journey. The Sun, however, passes through the space of one sign—which is a twelfth part of the world—in the course of a turning month. Thus, by wandering through the intervals of the twelve signs in twelve months, when it returns to the sign where it began, it completes the span of the turning year. From this, it follows that the circle which the Moon runs through thirteen times in twelve months, the Sun measures out only once in those same months.

The stars of Mercury and Venus, however, crown the Sun itself as they circle its rays, making it the center of their paths; they perform backward movements <term>retrograde: when a planet appears to move backward in the sky from the perspective of Earth</term> and slowdowns. Furthermore, due to this circular motion, they linger in the spaces of the signs during their "stations" <term>station: the point where a planet appears to stand still before changing direction</term>.

This is most clearly recognized from the star of Venus, because when it follows the Sun and appears in the heavens after its setting, it shines most brilliantly and is called the Evening Star <note>original: "vesperugo"</note>; at other times, however, it runs ahead of the Sun, and...

T

...rising before dawn, it is called the Light-bringer <note>original: *Lucifer*, the Roman name for Venus when it appears as the morning star</note>. Because of this, the planets sometimes stay for more days in one sign, while at other times they enter the next sign more quickly. Therefore, because they do not complete the same number of days in every sign as they spent in the previous one, they make up for their delays by "leaping" forward on faster paths to complete their proper course. Thus, it happens that although they may linger in certain signs, they quickly catch up to their regular orbit once they free themselves from the necessity of that delay.

The star of Mercury flies through its path in the universe in such a way that, by the three hundred and sixtieth day, it runs through the spaces of the signs and returns to the sign from which it began its course in its previous revolution. Its journey is so balanced that it averages about thirty days in each sign.

Venus, however, once it is freed from the interference of the Sun's rays, runs through the space of a sign in thirty days. Although this means it spends less than forty days in individual signs <note>This refers to its average speed when not appearing to slow down</note>, when it has reached a station <term>station: a point where a planet appears to stand still in the sky before reversing direction</term>, it makes up the total sum of days by lingering in a single sign. Therefore, having measured out its entire orbit in the heavens in four hundred and eighty-five days, it returns again to the sign from which it first began its journey.

Mars, wandering through the spaces of the stars, reaches the point from which it first began its course on about the six hundred and eighty-third day; in those signs where it moved more quickly before, it completes its total count of days once it has reached a station.

Jupiter, however, ascending with more peaceful steps against the rotation of the world, measures out each individual sign in about three hundred and sixty-five days; it completes its full cycle in eleven years and three hundred and sixty-three days, returning to the sign in which it had been twelve years earlier.

Saturn, wandering for twenty-nine <gloss>literally "one from thirty"</gloss> months and a few additional days...

## NINTH

...passing through the space of a sign, in about twenty-nine years and one hundred and sixty days, it is restored to that sign in which it had been thirty years before <note>original: *restituitur*. This refers to Saturn's orbital period</note>. And because of this, the less it is distant from the edge of the universe <note>The outermost sphere of the fixed stars</note>, the larger the circuit of the wheel it must run through, and thus it seems to be slower.

However, those stars which complete their circuits above the path of the Sun <note>The outer planets: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, especially when they have entered a trine <term>trine (trigonum): an aspect where two celestial bodies are 120 degrees apart, or four zodiac signs away</term>, do not then move forward, but rather linger and perform a retreat <note>retrograde motion</note>, until that same Sun makes its transition from that trine into another sign.

Now, some people are satisfied with the explanation that this happens because they say that when the Sun is at a certain further distance, the wandering stars [planets] traveling through those constellations on paths that are not bright are hindered by obscured delays. To us, however, it does not seem that way. For the splendor of the Sun is visible and open without any obscurations through the entire universe, just as it appears to us when those stars perform their retreats and delays. 

Therefore, if our sight can perceive this at such great distances, why do we judge that darkness could be cast upon the divinity and splendor of the stars? Rather, this reasoning will hold firm for us: just as heat draws out all things and leads them to itself—just as we see crops rising from the earth to a height through heat, and no less do we see water vapors rising from springs to the clouds via the rainbow <note>The ancients believed the rainbow acted as a mechanism to "draw up" water from the earth to the clouds</note>—by that same reasoning, the Sun's powerful force, stretched out by rays in the form of a trine, draws the following stars toward itself. By checking and holding back those running ahead, as if with a bridle, it does not allow them to progress, but forces them to retreat toward it and remain in the sign of another trine. 

Perhaps it will be asked why the Sun causes these retentions through its heat in the fifth sign from itself <note>Counting the Sun's sign as the first, the fifth sign is a trine aspect of 120 degrees</note>, rather than in the second or third, which are closer. How I see this happening...

<summary>This page describes Saturn’s nearly thirty-year orbital cycle and proposes a theory for retrograde motion, arguing that the Sun’s heat and rays act as a physical force that "bridles" planets and pulls them backward when they reach a trine aspect.</summary>

...I will explain. Its rays <note>The Sun's rays</note> are extended throughout the universe in the form of an equilateral triangle <term>trine: an astrological aspect where celestial bodies are 120 degrees apart, forming a triangle within the circle of the zodiac</term>. This distance is neither more nor less than to the fifth sign from it <note>Ancient authors often used inclusive counting; the "fifth sign" from the first is 120 degrees away</note>. Therefore, if the rays, poured out through the entire universe, wandered in circular paths and were not stretched out in straight lines to the form of a triangle, closer things would be set ablaze. This even Euripides, the poet of the Greeks, seems to have noticed; for he says that those things which are further from the Sun burn more vehemently, while closer things are kept temperate. Thus he writes in the play *Phaethon*: "He burns what is far; what is near he keeps temperate" <note>original: *καίει τὰ πόῤῥω τὰ δ’ ἐγγὺς εὔκρατ’ ἔχει*</note>. If, therefore, the physical reality, the logic, and the testimony of the ancient poet demonstrate this, I do not think it ought to be judged otherwise than as we have written above regarding this matter.

Jupiter, however, running its circuit between those of Mars and Saturn, flies through a course larger than Mars but smaller than Saturn. Likewise, the remaining stars, as they are at a greater distance from the edge of heaven and have a circuit closer to the Earth, seem to run through it more quickly; because whichever of them performs a smaller circuit, by frequently passing underneath, it overtakes the one above.

Just as if seven ants were placed on a wheel which potters use, and seven channels were made in the wheel around the center at the bottom, increasing toward the edge, in which these ants were compelled to make their circuit; and if the wheel were turned in one direction, it would be necessary for them to complete their journeys against the turning of the wheel nonetheless. And the one which had the path closest to the center would wander through it more quickly, while the one performing its path on the outermost edge of the wheel, even if it walked just as fast, would complete its course much more slowly due to the magnitude of the circuit. In a similar way, the shining stars <note>original: *astra nitentia*</note> striving con—

...finish their circuit through the course of the world on their own paths, but by the rotation of the heavens they are carried back by the overflows of the daily revolution of time. Now, that some stars are temperate, others burning, and still others cold, seems to be for this reason: that all fire has a flame that climbs to higher places. Therefore, the Sun, burning the ether <term>ether: the "fifth element" or the substance of the upper atmosphere and heavens in ancient physics</term> which is above it with its rays, makes it glowing hot in the places where it has its course. The star of Mars, therefore, is made burning by the fire of the Sun. Saturn, however, because it is closest to the edge of the world and touches the frozen regions of heaven, is exceedingly cold. From this, Jupiter, since it has its course between the circuits of both, seems to have the most temperate effects, meeting in the middle of their cooling and heat. Concerning the Zone of the twelve signs <note>the Zodiac</note> and the seven stars <note>the Sun, Moon, and five known planets</note> and their contrary work and course—by what logic and numbers they pass from sign to sign and complete their circuit—I have explained as I received from my teachers. Now I shall speak of the waxing and waning light of the Moon, as it has been handed down to us by our ancestors.

Berosus, who traveled from the city or nation of the Chaldeans into Asia and revealed the Chaldean teachings <note>Berosus was a 3rd-century BC priest of Bel in Babylon who brought Mesopotamian astronomy to the Greeks</note>, declared this: that the Moon is a ball, of which one half is glowing white, while the rest has a dark blue color. When, in performing the course of her journey, she passes under the orb of the Sun, she is then caught by its rays and the force of its heat and is turned, becoming glowing white because of the affinity of light for light <note>original: "proprietatem luminis ad lumen"</note>. But when she is drawn toward the Sun's orb and looks toward the upper parts, then her lower part—because it is not glowing—appears dark due to its likeness to the air. When she stands perpendicular to his rays, all the light is retained on the upper surface; and she is then called "first" <note>the New Moon</note>. As she moves past and goes toward...

...the eastern parts of the sky, the Moon is released from the force of the Sun; its outermost glowing edge then sends its splendor to the earth in a very thin line, and for this reason, it is called the "second" <note>referring to the second day of the lunar month</note>. By the daily slackening of its rotation, the third and fourth days are counted as they pass. On the seventh day, when the Sun is in the west and the Moon occupies the middle regions of the sky between the east and the west—because it is separated from the Sun by a distance equal to half the span of the heavens—it likewise has half of its glowing surface turned toward the earth.

When, however, the entire expanse of the world lies between the Sun and the Moon, and the Sun—as it moves toward the west—looks back at the rising orb of the Moon, the Moon is released from the Sun's rays because it is at its furthest distance. On the fourteenth day, it sends forth the splendor of its whole orb as a full wheel <term>full wheel: a full moon</term>. Over the remaining days, decreasing daily as it completes the lunar month through its rotations and its course being drawn back toward the Sun, it passes beneath the solar wheel; its rays thus establish the monthly calculations of the days.

I shall now explain how the mathematician Aristarchus of Samos <note>a Greek astronomer who lived c. 310–230 BC and proposed the first known heliocentric model of the universe</note> left behind, with great intellectual vigor, explanations for this variety through various scientific disciplines. For it is no secret that the Moon does not possess its own light; instead, it is like a mirror, receiving its splendor from the power of the Sun. Indeed, of the seven stars <note>the Sun, Moon, and five planets known in antiquity</note>, the Moon wanders through the circle closest to the earth, which is the smallest of all the celestial paths.

Thus, every month, on the first day before it passes by, it is hidden and obscured beneath the wheel and rays of the Sun; while it is positioned with the Sun, it is called "new." On the following day, which is counted as the second, as it passes away from the Sun, it offers a thin glimpse of its outermost curvature. When it has moved away from the Sun for three days, it grows and becomes more illuminated. Departing further each day, when it reaches the seventh day, it is distant from the setting Sun and positioned roughly in the middle regions of the sky; there, half of it shines, and that part which...

...the remaining parts of Leo, it diminishes the length of the day and of its circuit, and returns to a path equal to that in Gemini. Then, passing from Leo into Virgo, and proceeding toward the fold of her garment, it contracts its circuit and matches the proportion of the path it has in Taurus. Moving from Virgo through the fold—which contains the first parts of Libra—at the eighth degree of Libra <note>Ancient astronomers typically marked the change of seasons at the 8th degree of a sign rather than the 1st</note> it completes the autumnal equinox. This path equals the circuit it had in the sign of Aries.

When the sun has entered Scorpio, as the Pleiades <note>original: "vergiliis"</note> are setting, it diminishes the length of the days as it proceeds toward the southern regions. When it runs out of Scorpio and enters Sagittarius at its thighs, it flies through a more contracted daily path. When it begins from the thighs of Sagittarius, at the part assigned to Capricorn at the eighth degree, it traverses the shortest space of the sky. From this daily shortness, the winter solstice <note>original: "bruma"</note> is named, and the days are called brumal days. 

Passing from Capricorn into Aquarius, it increases the day and matches the length of the day's space found in Sagittarius. From Aquarius, when it enters Pisces as the west wind <note>original: "fauonio"</note> blows, it provides a path equal to that of Scorpio. Thus, by traversing these signs at fixed times, the sun increases or decreases the duration of the days and hours. Now I shall speak of the other constellations positioned to the right and left of the belt of signs <note>the Zodiac</note>, arranged and figured with stars in the southern and northern parts of the world.

# BOOK NINE

Not far off is placed the head of the one called Nessus <note>original: Nessus; usually identifying the constellation Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer</note>. At their knees, however, the tops of their heads are quite easy to recognize, for they are formed from stars that are not dim. The foot of the Kneeler <note>term: Ingeniculatus; the constellation now known as Hercules, traditionally depicted in a kneeling posture</note> is supported near that temple of the Serpent’s head, in whose Bears—which are called the "Seven Stars" of the North <note>term: Septentriones; the seven bright stars of the Great Bear that the Romans used to define the North</note>—it is entangled; near them the Dolphin turns slightly, and opposite the beak of the Bird <note>the constellation Cygnus</note> the Lyre is placed. Between the shoulders of the Warden <note>the constellation Bootes</note> and the Kneeler, the Crown <note>Corona Borealis</note> is adorned.

In the northern circle, indeed, two Bears are placed with their backs arranged against each other’s shoulders and their chests turned away; of these, the smaller is called *Cynosura* <note>original: κυνόσουρα; "dog's tail," now known as Ursa Minor</note> and the larger is called *Helice* <note>original: ἑλίκη; "the twister," now known as Ursa Major</note> by the Greeks. Their heads are positioned so that they look away from each other, and their tails are figured as being opposite and set against their heads. For both are said to rise above and stand out at the highest point by their tails.

Likewise, the Serpent <note>the constellation Draco, the Dragon</note> is stretched out, from which the star called the Pole shines out most brightly around the head of the Greater North Bear. For that which is nearest the Dragon is wound around its head, while one part is cast in a winding stream around the head of *Cynosura* <note>the Little Bear</note> and stretched out very near its feet. This constellation, twisted and folded back, rising up, bends back from the head of the Lesser Bear toward the Greater, opposite the beak and the right temple of the head.

Likewise, above the tail of the Lesser Bear are the feet of Cepheus, and there, forming a peak at the very top, are stars making an equilateral triangle <note>the constellation Triangulum</note> above the sign of Aries the Ram. Between the Lesser North Bear and the figure of Cassiopeia, many stars are scattered in a cluster. I have now described the stars arranged in the heavens to the right of the east, between the Zodiac <note>term: Zona signorum; literally "the zone of signs," the belt of the heavens containing the twelve constellations through which the sun appears to move</note> and the northern constellations. Now I shall explain those which are distributed by nature to the left of the east and in the southern parts.

### Concerning the constellations which are from the Zodiac toward the south.
### Chapter VII.

<margin>p</margin>
First, situated beneath Capricorn, is the **Southern Fish** <note>original: piscis austrinus</note>, looking toward Cepheus with its tail. From there toward Sagittarius is an empty space. The **Censer** <term>Turibulum; the constellation now known as Ara</term> is under the sting of the **Scorpion**. The front parts of the **Centaur** are very close to the **Balance** <note>original: libra</note> and the **Scorpion**; they hold in their hands the figure that those skilled in the stars have named the **Beast** <term>Bestia; now known as the constellation Lupus, the Wolf</term>. Toward the **Virgin**, the **Lion**, and the **Crab**, the **Snake** <term>Anguis; the constellation Hydra</term> stretches out its line of stars; twisted, it encircles the region of the **Crab**, raising its snout toward the **Lion**, supporting the **Bowl** <term>Crater</term> with the middle of its body, and placing its tail—in which the **Raven** <term>Corvus</term> resides—near the hand of the **Virgin**. Those stars which are above the shoulders are equally bright toward the inner belly of the **Snake**, and the **Centaur** is situated beneath the tail.

Next to the **Bowl** and the **Lion** is the **Ship**, which is named **Argo**. Its prow is obscured, but the mast and the parts around the steering-oars appear prominent; the little ship itself and its stern are joined to the **Dog** <term>Canis Major</term> by the very tip of the Dog's tail. Following the **Twins** <note>original: Geminos</note> is the **Lesser Dog** <term>Canis Minor</term>, positioned opposite the head of the **Snake**; likewise, the **Greater Dog** follows the smaller one.

**Orion**, however, is placed crosswise, pressed by the hoof of the Centaur <note>The text reads "centauri," but astronomically Orion is located near the hoof of Taurus, the Bull</note>, holding a club in his left hand and raising the other toward the **Twins**; his head follows the base of the **Dog**, following the **Hare** at a small interval. Below **Aries** and the **Fishes** is the **Whale** <term>Cetus; often depicted as a sea monster</term>; from its crest, a thin flow of stars is arranged in order toward both **Fishes**, which is called the *ribbon* <note>original: ερμηδóνη (hermēdonē); the cord or "line" connecting the two fish of the constellation Pisces</note> in Greek. With a great gap, the knot of the snakes <note>the celestial bonds of the Fishes</note>, pressed inward, reaches the highest crest of the **Whale**. The **River** <term>Eridanus</term> flows through the appearance of stars, taking the beginning of its source from the left foot of **Orion**. Moreover, the water which is said to be poured from the **Water-Bearer** <note>original: aquario</note> flows between the head of the **Southern Fish** and the tail of the **Whale**.

### BOOK NINE. 159

I have now explained those images of the stars in the world which are figured and formed, as designated by nature and the divine mind, according to the views of the natural philosopher **Democritus**. <note>Democritus was a Greek philosopher often associated with the atomic theory, but here Vitruvius cites his work on cosmology.</note> But I have only described those whose rising and setting we are able to observe and perceive with our own eyes. For just as the northern stars <note>original: *septentriones*, referring to the Big and Little Dipper</note> revolving around the pivot of the axis do not set, nor go beneath the earth, so also around the southern pivot—which, because of the tilt of the world, is situated beneath the earth—there are stars revolving and remaining hidden that never rise or emerge above the ground.

Therefore, their configurations are not known to us because the earth stands in the way. The indicator of this fact is the star **Canopus**, <note>The second brightest star in the night sky, visible in the southern hemisphere.</note> which is unknown in these regions <note>Italy and Greece</note> according to the reports of merchants who have traveled to the furthest regions of **Egypt** and the boundaries closest to the ultimate ends of the earth.

I have thus taught concerning the revolution of the world around the earth, the twelve signs <note>the Zodiac</note>, and the arrangement of the stars in the northern and southern parts, so that they may be clearly understood. For from that rotation of the world, the contrary course of the sun through the signs, and the equinoctial shadows cast by gnomons <note>the vertical pins of sundials</note>, the descriptions of **analemmas** <note>original Greek: *ἀναλεμμάτων*; a geometrical method for projecting the celestial sphere to design sundials</note> are discovered. 

As for the rest of astrology—specifically what effects the twelve signs, the five planets, the Sun, and the Moon have upon the conduct of human life—this must be left to the calculations of the **Chaldeans**. <note>In antiquity, "Chaldean" was a term for Babylonian astronomers and astrologers famous for their predictive skills.</note> This is because the system of **casting nativities** <note>original: *genethlialogiae*, the branch of astrology dealing with birth charts</note> is their particular specialty, allowing them to explain past and future events through the calculations of the stars. 

The discoveries they have left in their writings show with what skill, sharpness of mind, and greatness those who sprang from the Chaldean nation were endowed. The first of these, **Berosus**, <note>A Babylonian priest and historian who brought Mesopotamian astronomical knowledge to the Greek world.</note> settled on the island and in the city of **Kos**, and there opened his school of discipline. Afterwards, his student Ant...

<summary>Vitruvius explains that while northern stars never set, southern stars like Canopus remain hidden from northern view, and he transitions from describing the heavens to the origins of astrology and sundial mathematics.</summary>
<keywords>Democritus, Canopus, Egypt, Chaldeans, analemma, astrology, genethlialogia, Berosus, Kos, astronomy</keywords>

# BOOK NINE

...Antipater, <note>Likely Antipater of Tarsus or a similar contemporary astronomer; the OCR reads "sipater."</note> as well as Archinapolus, who left behind explained theories of astrology <note>original: *genethliologiæ*, the practice of casting horoscopes based on the stars</note> based not only on the moment of birth but even on conception. Concerning natural philosophy, however, Thales of Miletus, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, Pythagoras of Samos, Xenophanes of Colophon, and Democritus of Abdera left behind theories they devised regarding the laws by which the nature of things is governed and how each effect is produced. Following their discoveries, Eudoxus, Eudemon, Callippus, Meton, Philippus, Hipparchus, Aratus, and others discovered the disciplines of astronomical calendars <note>original: *parapegmatorum*; these were stone tablets with movable pegs used to track the cycle of the stars and weather</note> and left them explained for posterity. Their knowledge is to be admired by all, for they were so diligent that they seem to predict upcoming weather patterns with a divine mind. For these reasons, credit must be given to their care and dedication.

### ->On the principles of sundials and the shadows of gnomons<-
### ->at the time of the equinox, in Rome, and several other places.<-

->Chapter VIII.<-

We must now separate from these matters the principles of sundials <note>original: *horologiorum*, referring here specifically to devices that tell time by the sun</note> and explain the monthly shortening of days, as well as the proportions of shadows. For when the Sun is passing through the signs of Aries and Libra at the time of the equinox, the shadow cast by the gnomon <note>The vertical rod or pin of a sundial.</note> in Rome is eight parts long to the gnomon’s nine parts. In Athens, the shadow is three parts to the gnomon’s four. At Rhodes, it is five parts to seven. At Tarentum, it is nine to eleven. At Alexandria, it is three to five. In all other places, the equinoctial shadows of gnomons are found by nature to be different from one another in various ways.

### BOOK NINE

->NINTH<-

Then, in those places where the parallel lines intersect the line called the **Horizon** <note>original: *Orizon*</note>, the letter **s** will be on the right side and **u** on the left. From the outer edge of the semicircle, where the letter **g** is, a line should be drawn parallel to the **Axis** <note>original: *Axoni*</note> toward the left semicircle, where the letter **h** is. This parallel line is called the **lacotomus** <term>lacotomus|A technical term meaning 'side-cutter,' referring to a chord that cuts through the circular paths in the diagram</term>. 

Then, the center of the compass must be placed at the spot where the equinoctial ray intersects that line, which will be marked with the letter **x**. The compass is then to be extended to the point where the summer ray intersects the circular line, marked with the letter **h**. With this equinoctial center and the distance to the summer ray, let the circle of the months be drawn, which is called the **manachus** <note>original: *manachus*; also known as the 'menacus,' this circle allows the designer to mark the sun's position for each month of the year.</note>. In this way, the construction of the **analemma** <note>The *analemma* is a complex geometric figure used by ancient architects to determine the lengths of shadows at different latitudes.</note> will be achieved.

### NINTH [BOOK]

->V ii<-

...will be taken from the description of the **analemma** <term>analemma|A geometric construction used to project the celestial sphere onto a plane, allowing for the calculation of solar positions and hours.</term>, and many varieties and types of **sundials** <note>original: *horologiorum*; though literally "hour-tellers," in this context they are solar timepieces.</note> will be based upon it, and they will be described according to these skillful methods. However, the purpose of all these figures and their descriptions is a single one: that the **equinoctial** day, the **winter** <note>original: *brumalis*; referring to the winter solstice, the shortest day of the year.</note> day, and likewise the **summer** <note>original: *solstitialis*</note> day may be equally divided into twelve parts.

I have not omitted these matters because I was deterred by laziness, but so that I do not cause offense by writing at too great a length. Instead, I shall set forth by whom the various types and descriptions of sundials were invented; for I cannot now invent new types, nor does it seem right to claim the work of others as my own. Therefore, I will recount what has been handed down to us and by whom they were discovered.
