# BOOK NINE

### Chapter IX. On the theory and use of clocks, their invention, and their inventors.

The **half-circle hollowed out from a square** <note>original: "Emicyclium excauatum ex quadrato"</note>, and cut according to the inclination of the earth's pole, is said to have been invented by **Berosus the Chaldean** <note>A Babylonian priest and astronomer, active in the 3rd century BCE</note>. The **bowl-shaped sundial** <note>original: "Scaphen"</note> or hemisphere was invented by **Aristarchus of Samos**. Likewise, the **flat disk** <note>original: "discum in planitia"</note> or the "Spider" <note>original: "Arachnem"; likely a complex network of lines on a dial</note> was invented by the astronomer **Eudoxus**, though some say it was **Apollonius**. The **Plinth** or **Coffered Ceiling** dial (one of which is placed in the Flaminian Circus) was invented by **Scopas of Syracuse**. The **universal dial** <note>original: "πρὸς τὰ ἱστορούμενα" (for historical/geographical inquiry) and "πρὸς πᾶν κλίμα" (for every latitude)</note> was developed by **Parmenion** and **Theodosius**, while **Andreas**, **Patrocles**, and **Dionysodorus** left behind inventions such as the **Axe-head** <note>original: "pelecinon"</note>, the **Cone**, and the **Quiver** <note>original: "pharetram"</note>. Many others, including those mentioned above, left behind various types such as the **Angle-joint**, the **Kneeling Man**, and the **Anti-Northern** dial.

Furthermore, many have left writings on how **portable hanging clocks** <note>early travel sundials</note> might be made from these types. Anyone who wishes to find the layouts for these from their books may do so, provided they understand the descriptions of the **analemma** <note>a mathematical method for projecting the sun's path</note>.

There are also methods for **water clocks** <note>clepsydrae</note> sought out by these same writers. The first of these was by **Ctesibius of Alexandria**, who also discovered the use of natural air pressure and **pneumatic principles** <note>original: "pneumaticasq; res"</note>. It is worthwhile for students to learn how these exquisite things were devised. Ctesibius was born in Alexandria, the son of a barber. Being of great talent and industry, excelling beyond all others, he was said to delight in ingenious things. For instance, when he wished to hang a mirror in his father's shop in such a way that when it was lowered and raised back up, a hidden cord would pull a weight, he arranged the mechanism thus: he fixed a wooden channel under a beam and placed pulleys there; he led the cord through the channel into a corner, and there he constructed small tubes, into which a ball...

He arranged for a lead weight to be lowered by a line; thus, as the weight, by running down into the narrow spaces of the small pipes, pressed the density of the air <note>original: "coeli crebritatem"; here referring to the air within the mechanism</note> with a forceful descent, it pushed out the crowded air—solidified by compression through the openings—into the open air. By this striking and contact, it expressed a clarity of sound.

Therefore, when Ctesibius had noticed that spirits <note>or "breaths of air"</note> and voices were born from the drawing in and expression of the air, using these principles, he was the first to establish <term>hydraulic machines</term> <note>water organs</note>. Likewise, he set forth expressions of water that were <term>automatic</term> <note>original Greek: "automata"; self-moving devices</note>, machines for raising water and for circular motion, and many kinds of delights, including even the arrangements of <term>clocks</term> <note>original: "horologiorum"</note> worked by water. And first, he established a hollow opening perfected from gold or from a bored-out gemstone. For these materials are neither worn down by the striking of the water, nor do they collect grime that might cause a blockage. For as the water flows equally through that hollow, it raises an inverted bowl (which is called a <term>float</term> <note>original: "phellos"</note> or a <term>drum</term> by craftsmen) in which...

# BOOK NINE

Once the rod is in place, a **revolving drum** <note>Latin: *versatile tympanum*; a gear or toothed wheel</note> is perfected with equal teeth. These teeth, by pushing one another, create measured rotations and movements. Likewise, other rods and other drums are toothed in the same manner; when forced into motion by a single impulse, they produce various effects and diverse movements through their turning. In these displays, small figures move, turning-posts <note>Latin: *metae*; often referring to the conical markers used in Roman circuses</note> revolve, pebbles or eggs are cast out, trumpets sound, and other **ornamental features** <note>original: "παρεργα" (parerga); secondary or decorative mechanical displays</note> are triggered. In these devices, the hours are marked either on a small column or a **pilaster** <note>Latin: *parastatica*; a square pillar or support</note>, which a figure—emerging from the bottom—points to with a wand throughout the entire day. The shortening or lengthening of these hours <note>Ancient Romans used "seasonal hours," where the length of an hour changed depending on the time of year</note> is managed by adding or removing wedges for each day and month.

The water regulators for tempering the flow are arranged as follows. Two "cones" are made—one solid and one hollow—finished on a lathe so that one can enter and fit into the other. By the same rule, their loosening or tightening produces either a forceful or a gentle flow of water into the vessels. Thus, by these principles and mechanical arrangements, water clocks are constructed for winter use. 

However, if the shortening or lengthening of the days is not favored by the addition and subtraction of wedges (because wedges very often cause errors), it should be explained as follows. On a small column, the hours should be drawn transversely according to the **analemma** <note>A diagram showing the sun's position; here used to calculate seasonal hour markings</note>, and the monthly lines should be marked on the column. This column is made to be rotatable so that, in relation to the figure and the wand (the wand of which points to the hours as it emerges), the column, by turning continuously, provides the shortening and lengthening of the hours for each respective month. There are also winter clocks made of another kind, which are called **anaphoric** <note>original: "anaporica"; a type of clock showing the rising of the stars and the sun's position in the zodiac</note>, and they are completed by these methods:

# BOOK

The hours are arranged by means of brass rods, positioned from the center on the face of the clock according to the design of the <term>analemma</term> <note>A geometrical diagram used to project the paths of the sun and stars onto a plane</note>. Within this, circles are inscribed which mark the boundaries of the monthly spaces. Behind these rods, a drum is to be placed, upon which the world and the <term>zodiac circle</term> <note>original: "signifer"; the circle of the zodiac signs</note> are described and depicted. This drawing is shaped from the twelve celestial signs, and from its center, the space for each sign is formed, one being larger and another smaller.

In the rear part, in the middle of the drum, a revolving axle is enclosed. Around this axle, a supple brass chain is wound, from which hangs a <term>cork</term> <note>original: "phellos"; a float</note> or drum on one side, which is lifted by the water, and on the other side, a counterweight of sand <note>original: "sacoma saburrale"</note> equal to the weight of the cork. Thus, as much as the cork is raised by the water, the weight of the sand, pulling down on the other side, turns the axle. The axle, in turn, rotates the drum.

The rotation of this drum causes either a larger or smaller portion of the zodiac circle to be displayed during its revolutions, thereby designating the specific properties of the hours according to the seasons. For within each individual sign, a number of holes are completed corresponding to the days of each month. A pin <note>original: "bulla"; a knob or stud</note>, which is seen to hold the image of the sun on clocks, signifies the spaces of the hours. As this pin is moved from hole to hole, it completes its course through the turning month.

Therefore, just as the sun, traveling through the spaces of the stars, expands and contracts the days and hours, so the pin in clocks—moving through the points against the rotation of the central drum—daily produces the representations of the hours and days. As it is moved at different times through wider or narrower spaces according to the monthly boundaries, it reflects the changing lengths of time. Regarding the management of the water, and how it may regulate itself according to this system, it must be done as follows: behind the face of the clock, a reservoir <note>original: "castellum"</note> is to be placed within...

...and into this, the water should leap through a pipe <term>fistula: a water pipe or tube</term>, and it should have a cavity at the bottom. Attached to this should be a drum <term>tympanum: a drum-shaped housing or wheel</term> made of bronze, having a hole through which the water may flow from the reservoir into it. Inside this, a smaller drum is to be enclosed, with its pivots turned on a lathe—male and female parts fitted together—so that the smaller drum, like a stopcock <term>epystomium: a valve or tap used to regulate flow</term>, may be turned closely and smoothly within the larger one. 

The rim of the larger drum should have 365 points marked at equal intervals. The smaller disk, however, should have a pointer <term>lingula: literally 'little tongue'; a small metal indicator</term> fixed on its outermost circumference, the tip of which points toward the regions of those marks. In this disk, a hole is bored through which the water flows into the drum and maintains the operation. 

When the figures of the celestial signs <note>The Zodiac constellations</note> have been depicted on the rim of the larger drum—which remains stationary—it should have the sign of Cancer depicted at the very top, with Capricorn at the perpendicular bottom, Libra to the right, and Aries to the left. The remaining signs should also be marked in the spaces between them, just as they appear in the heavens. 

Therefore, when the sun is in the circle of Capricorn, the pointer on the part of the larger drum corresponding to Capricorn touches individual points daily. Having the full weight of the running water at the perpendicular, it quickly thrusts the water through the hole of the disk into the receiving vessel. Then, because the vessel is filled in a short time, it seizes and contracts the shorter spaces of the days and hours <note>In antiquity, 'seasonal hours' varied in length; winter hours were shorter than summer hours</note>. 

However, when by the daily turning the pointer of the larger drum enters Aquarius, all the holes descend from the perpendicular, and the water is forced to emit its flow more slowly due to the change in the water's course. Thus, the less rapidly the vessel receives the water, the more it expands...

# BOOK NINE

...the spaces of the hours. Indeed, by climbing through the points of Aquarius and Pisces as if by steps, and by touching the opening of the small disk at the eighth part of Aries, the device provides equinoctial hours <note>Hours of equal length where day and night are balanced</note> by the flow of tempered water. From Aries, passing through the spaces of Taurus and Gemini to the highest points of Cancer—completing its revolutions through the opening or the drum at the eighth part—and returning to that height, the flow is weakened in its force. Thus, by flowing more slowly, it extends the duration by lingering, and produces the summer solstice hours in the sign of Cancer. 

When it inclines away from Cancer and passes through Leo and Virgo, returning to the points of the eighth part of Libra, it gradually shortens the intervals and contracts the hours; thus, reaching the points of Libra, it renders the equinoctial hours once again. However, through the spaces of Scorpio and Sagittarius, as the opening sinks lower on its downward slope and returns through its revolution to the eighth part of Capricorn, the speed of the water's flow is restored to the brevity of the winter hours <note>original: "brumales horarum breuitates"</note>. 

I have written down the principles and the construction of these timepieces as clearly as I could, so that they might be as convenient as possible for practical use. It remains now to reason about machines <term>machinationibus: the principles of mechanical devices and engines</term> and their starting principles. Therefore, so that the corrected body of architecture may be completed, I shall begin to write about these in the following volume.

<header>MARCUS VITRUVIUS ON MACHINES.</header>

# BOOK TEN.

In the noble and expansive Greek city of Ephesus, an ancient law is said to have been established by their ancestors under harsh conditions, yet by a right that is not unjust. For when an architect <note>The term 'architect' in antiquity encompassed civil engineering and machine building as well as design.</note> undertakes the care of a public work, he promises at what cost it will be completed. Once his estimate is handed over to the magistrate, his private property is held as collateral until the work is finished. When it is completed, if the expenditure matches the stated amount, he is honored with decrees and distinctions. Likewise, if no more than a fourth part <note>A 25% cost overrun.</note> is added to the estimate in the course of the work, it is furnished from the public treasury, and he is held liable for no penalty. However, when more than a fourth part is consumed in the work, the money required to finish it is exacted from his private property. 

Would that the immortal gods had seen to it that such a law were established for the Roman people as well, not only for public buildings but also for private ones! For then the unskilled would not run riot without punishment; instead, those who are truly wise through the highest refinement of learning would profess architecture without hesitation. Nor would heads of households <note>original: "patres familiarum"</note> be led into infinite outpourings of expense, even to the point of being cast out from their estates. The architects themselves, constrained by the fear of penalty, would more diligently set forth their calculations for the limit of expenses, so that heads of households might complete their buildings for what they had prepared, or by adding only a little more. For those who can prepare four hundred <note>The text cuts off here; likely referring to a specific denomination of currency like sesterces or talents.</note> for a work...

However, those who are burdened by an addition of half the cost, or by a more ample expense, having lost hope and thrown away their investment, with both their property and their spirits broken, are forced to desist. Nor is this vice found only in buildings, but also in the public gifts given by magistrates in the forum for gladiators and on the stages for games. In these matters, neither delay nor waiting is permitted, but necessity forces completion within a finished time—such as the seating for spectacles, the drawing of the awnings, and all those things which, according to theatrical custom, are prepared for the people's viewing through machinery. In these truly there is need for diligent prudence and the thought of a most learned mind, because none of them is completed without machinery and the varied and skillful vigor of study. Therefore, since these things are thus handed down and established, it does not seem out of place that, before works are begun, their accounts should be set forth with caution and the highest diligence. Therefore, since neither law nor the institution of customs can compel this, and every year both Praetors <note>High-ranking Roman magistrates</note> and Aediles <note>Officials in charge of public works and festivals</note> must prepare machinery for the sake of the games, it seemed to me, Emperor, not to be out of place—since I have explained buildings in the previous volumes—to explain in this one, which contains the final completion of the body of work, what the principles of machines are, ordered by precepts.

### Chapter I: What a machine is, its difference from a tool, its origin, and its necessity.

A machine is a continuous conjunction of material, having the greatest powers for the movement of weights. It is moved by art through the rotations of circles, which the Greeks call <term>circular motion</term> <note>original: "κυκλικήν κίνησιν" (kyklikēn kinēsin)</note>.

<summary>Vitruvius discusses the financial risks of public works and the necessity of machinery for theatrical spectacles before introducing his final book on the definition and principles of machines.</summary>
<keywords>machinery, Roman games, construction costs, Vitruvius, circular motion, engineering, public works</keywords>

--- Page 337 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of mechanics, likely from Vitruvius's "De Architectura," Book 10, focusing on the classification of machines and their origins in nature.</meta>

# BOOK TEN

There is, moreover, one type of machine for climbing which in Greek is called *acrobaticon* <note>original: "ἀκροβατικὸν"; referring to scaffolding or scaling machines</note>, a second powered by wind or air, which among them is called *pneumaticon* <note>original: "πνευματικὸν"; pneumatic or hydraulic devices</note>, and a third for hauling, which the Greeks call *banauson* <note>original: "βάναυσον"; literally 'mechanical' or 'laborious'</note>. The climbing type is used when machines are so arranged that, by setting up timbers to a great height and fastening crossbeams together, one may climb without danger to view the equipment. The pneumatic type is used when, by the pressure and strokes of air, sounds and musical notes are produced in an instrumental manner <note>original: "ὀργανικῶς"</note>. The hauling type, however, is used when loads are dragged along by machines or raised to a height and set in place.

The system of climbing relies not on art, but boasts of audacity; it is held together by chains, crossbeams, woven lashings, and the support of struts. However, that which achieves its movement through the power of air attains elegant results through subtle refinements. The hauling machines, meanwhile, offer greater opportunities full of magnificence for practical use, and possess the highest virtues of efficiency when operated with prudence.

Of these, some are moved mechanically <note>original: "μιχανικῶς"</note> and others instrumentally <note>original: "ὀργανικῶς"</note>. Between "machines" <term>machinae: complex devices requiring multiple operators or great force</term> and "engines" <term>organa: smaller instruments or tools operated by a single skilled person</term> there seems to be this difference: that machines are forced to produce their effects by more labor or greater power, such as catapults <note>original: "balistae"</note> and the presses of wine-cellars. Engines, however, accomplish their purpose by the skillful touch of a single worker, such as the turning of a "scorpion" <note>original: "scorpionis"; a smaller, more precise bolt-thrower</note> or "unequal circles" <note>original: "anisocyclorum"; likely a reference to a specific gear or pulley mechanism</note>.

Therefore, engines and the principles of machines are necessary for practical use, without which nothing can be free from impediment. All machinery, moreover, is derived from the nature of things, and was established by the rotation of the world—the teacher and mistress of all. For let us first observe and look upon the continuous revolution of the Sun, the Moon, and the five planets...

### Chapter IV

But if the loads in the works are of even greater size and weight, they must not be entrusted to a windlass; instead, just as the windlass is held by "tortoises" <note>original: "chelonijs," the sockets or brackets that hold the axle</note>, an axle should be installed having a large treadwheel in the middle, which some call a wheel, but the Greeks call an <term>amphireusin</term> <note>original: "ἀμφίρευσιν," meaning "flowing around"</note> or others a <term>peritrochion</term> <note>original: "περίτροχιον," a "revolving wheel"</note>. In these machines, the pulleys are prepared not in the same way, but in a different manner. For they have double rows of pulley-wheels both at the bottom and at the top. Thus, the hauling rope is passed through a hole in the lower pulley-block so that the two ends of the rope are equal when it is stretched out; there, at the lower pulley-block, the two parts of the rope are bound and fastened together with a small cord so that they cannot move to either the right or the left. Then the ends of the rope are passed up to the highest pulley-block from the outside, brought down around the lowest pulley-wheels, and return to the bottom. They are then passed from the inside to the wheels of the lowest pulley-block and are brought back on the right and left to the top of the highest pulley-block, around the uppermost wheels. ### Another type of hauling machine. Chapter V.

<margin>e</margin>
There is, moreover, another type of machine that is quite ingenious and ready for speedy use, but only those who are highly skilled <note>original: "periti"</note> can work with it. For it is...

<summary>This page describes the mechanics of a hoisting machine using a drum, axle, and capstan, while also suggesting that a human-powered treadmill drum is more efficient for heavy lifting. It introduces a more complex hauling machine intended for use by skilled operators.</summary>

<keywords>hoisting machinery, capstan, treadmill crane, mechanical engineering, construction tools, Vitruvian technology</keywords>

--- Page 343 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical description of hoisting machinery, specifically focusing on the assembly and operation of a single-beam crane system.</meta>

# BOOK TEN

A beam is erected and held upright by stay-ropes extending in four directions. Below these stay-ropes, two "cheeks" <term>chelonia; literally 'tortoises', these are brackets or sockets bolted to the timber</term> are fixed, and a pulley-block is bound with ropes above these brackets. Beneath the pulley-block, a long straight-edge—about two feet long, six digits wide, and four thick—is placed. The pulley-blocks are arranged with three rows of sheaves <term>orbiculorum; the small revolving wheels within a pulley</term> across their width. Thus, three hauling-ropes are fastened at the top of the machine. They are then brought down to the lowest pulley-block and passed through its uppermost sheaves from the inside. Next, they are carried back up to the upper pulley-block and passed from the right side toward the inside through the lowest sheaves. When they have descended to the bottom from the inside, they are passed through the second sheaves to the outside, and returned to the top to the second sheaves; having passed through, they return to the bottom. From the bottom they are returned to the head, and passing through the highest sheaves, they return to the base of the machine. At the foot of the machine, however, a third pulley-block is placed. The Greeks call this the *epagonta* <note>original: ἐπάγοντα; meaning 'the bringer-on' or 'lead-block'</note>, while our people call it the *artemon* <term>artemon; a lead-block or migger-block used to change the direction of the pull</term>. This pulley-block is bound to the base of the machine and has three sheaves through which the ropes are passed and handed over to men for pulling. In this way, three rows of men pulling without a capstan <term>ergata; a vertical winding drum</term> can quickly raise the load to the top. This type of machine is called a *polyspaston* <note>original: polyspaston; from the Greek for 'many-pulled' or 'hoist with many sheaves'</note> because its many rotations of sheaves provide both the greatest ease and speed. The use of a single upright beam has this advantage: that before it is fixed, it can lean to the right or left and deposit the load to either side.

The principles of all these machines described above are prepared not only for these purposes, but also for loading and unloading ships; some are set upright, others are laid flat on revolving pivots <note>original: "charchesijs," referring to the mast-head or a swivel joint</note>. ## The ingenious method of Ctesiphon for moving heavy loads.

### Chapter VI.

<margin>m</margin>
It is not out of place to explain the ingenious invention of Ctesiphon <note>An ancient Greek architect credited with starting the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus</note>. For when he wished to transport the shafts of columns <note>original: "scapos columnarum"</note> from the quarries to the Temple of Diana at Ephesus, he did not trust in wagons because of the greatness of the weights and the softness of the field roads, fearing that the wheels would be swallowed up <note>i.e., sink into the mud</note>. Instead, he attempted the following:

<summary>This page describes the versatile use of pulleys and cranes for maritime and construction work, introducing Ctesiphon's innovative solution for transporting massive column shafts across soft ground.</summary>

# BOOK TEN

From timber four inches thick <note>original: "materia trientali"</note>, he constructed a frame consisting of four beams: two long beams and two transverse beams placed between them, equal in length to the stone shafts. He then joined them together and fixed iron pivots <note>term: chodaces (pivots or axles used for rotation)</note> into the ends of the shafts, securing them with lead like tenons. He also fastened iron rings <note>term: armillas (circular sockets or collars)</note> into the timber to surround these pivots. Furthermore, he bound the ends with oaken rods. The pivots, being enclosed within the rings, had such free movement that when the oxen were yoked and pulled, the shafts rolled continuously, turning on the pivots and rings.

When they had transported all the column shafts in this manner and it was time for the transport of the architraves <note>term: epistyliorum (the horizontal beams that rest on top of columns)</note>, Metagenes, the son of Ctesiphon, adapted the method used for the shafts to the hauling of the architraves. He constructed wheels approximately twelve feet in diameter and inserted the ends of the architraves into the centers of these wheels.

In the same manner, he enclosed the pivots <note>original: "chodacibus," the metal pins acting as axles</note> within rings <note>original: "armillis," iron sockets or collars</note>. six feet high. Paconius, relying on his own glory, did not bring the stone in the same manner as Metagenes <note>Metagenes was an ancient Greek architect, son of Chersiphron, known for his work on the Temple of Artemis</note>, but instead decided to construct a machine of a different type using the same principle. Then, around the stone from wheel to wheel, he fastened small round rungs <term>fusi: cylindrical rods or rungs used in a treadmill-like mechanism</term> two inches thick, spaced no more than a foot apart. Next, he wound a rope around these rungs, and by hitching oxen to it, he pulled the rope. As the rope unwound, it turned the wheels. However, he could not keep the machine on a straight line along the road; it kept veering off to one side or the other. Thus, it was necessary to constantly pull it back. In this way, by pulling it forward and back, Paconius wasted so much money that he became insolvent <note>original: "ut ad soluendum non esset" — literally, he was unable to pay his debts</note>.

## On the discovery of the quarry from which the temple of Diana at Ephesus was constructed.
### Chapter VII.

<margin>Pixodarus</margin>
I shall step slightly outside my main subject to explain how these quarries were discovered. There was a shepherd named Pixodarus who lived in those parts. At the time when the citizens of Ephesus were planning to build the temple of Diana <note>The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note> out of marble, and were debating whether to bring the marble from Paros, Proconnesus, Heraclea, or Thasos, Pixodarus happened to be grazing his flock in that very location. Two rams ran at each other to fight, but they missed one another, and one, in its charge, struck a rock with its horn. A flake of the stone, which was of the most brilliant white color, was knocked off. It is said that Pixodarus left his sheep in the mountains and ran to Ephesus with the flake of stone, arriving just as the matter was being discussed.

<margin>Euangelus</margin>
Consequently, they immediately decreed honors for him and changed his name, so that instead of Pixodarus, he was called Euangelus <note>original: "Euangelus" — meaning "the bringer of good news" in Greek</note>. To this day, the magistrate travels to that location every month to perform a sacrifice to him; if he fails to do so, he is subject to a penalty.

### On the linear and circular motion of machines for lifting weights. Chapter VIII.

<margin>d</margin>
I have briefly set forth what I deemed necessary regarding the principles of <term>hoisting</term> <note>original: "tractoriis"</note>. The movements and powers of these machines are two different things, unlike one another, yet they work together to produce two types of effects: one is linear, which the Greeks call <term>straight-line</term> <note>original: "εὐθεῖαν" (eutheian)</note>, and the other is circular, which they call <term>rounded</term> <note>original: "κυκλωτήν" (kyklōtēn)</note>. However, in truth, neither linear motion without circularity, nor the rotations of circularity without linear motion, can achieve the lifting of weights. I shall explain this so it may be understood. Axles are inserted as centers into small wheels and placed within <term>pulleys</term> <note>original: "trocleis"</note>; a rope, passed around these wheels and pulled in a straight line, is then placed on a <term>windlass</term> <note>original: "sucula"</note> and turned by levers...

<summary>This page explains the fundamental mechanical relationship between linear and circular motion in lifting devices, using the lever and pulley as primary examples. It establishes that complex weight-lifting requires the integration of both types of movement.</summary>

<keywords>mechanics, lever, pulley, linear motion, circular motion, Vitruvian technology, engineering principles</keywords>

--- Page 350 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of mechanical principles from Book 3, specifically focusing on the application of the lever principle to maritime navigation and the transport of heavy loads.</meta>

# BOOK 3

<note>The author is explaining how small forces can move great weights by using the principle of the lever, or "center of motion."</note>

...leading it down from the bottom and drawing it upward without great force, it compels the weight to move. In the same way, the pilot of a massive merchant ship, holding the handle of the rudder—which is called the *oiax* <note>original: "οἴαξ" - the tiller or handle of a rudder</note> by the Greeks—moves it with one hand at the right moment. By applying the principles of art through the center of pressure, he turns the vessel even when it is burdened with the most ample and immense weights of merchandise and provisions.

Furthermore, when the sails are hanging at the middle height of the mast, the ship cannot have a swift course; but when the yards are hoisted to the very top, it then advances with a more powerful impetus. This is because the sails receive the wind not near the foot of the mast—which acts as the center—but further away at the summit. Just as a lever <term>vectis: a crowbar or mechanical lever</term> placed under a weight is harder to use if pressed in the middle and does not yield, but easily lifts the weight when its furthest end is pulled down, so it is with sails. When they are set at the middle, they have less power; but those placed at the very top of the mast, being further from the center, force the ship to advance more vehemently, not because the wind is stronger there, but because of the increased pressure from the summit.

Likewise, when oars are bound with leather straps <note>original: "strophis" - thongs used to pivot oars</note> around the thole-pins, and are pushed and pulled by hand at their ends, the blades—moving far from the center into the waves of the sea—push forward a foaming surge with a powerful impulse, while the prow cuts through the yielding water to propel the ship forward.

Moreover, when the heaviest weights are carried by porters <term>phalangarii: laborers who carry loads using poles (phalangae)</term> using six-man frames <note>original: "exaphoris"</note> or four-man frames <note>original: "tetraphoris"</note>, the weights are balanced through the very centers of the poles. This ensures that the solid weight of the undivided load is distributed by a certain method of division, so that each laborer carries an equal share on his shoulders. For the middle sections of the poles, where the straps of the four-man frames are attached, are fixed with pins so they do not slide to one side or the other. If the load moves beyond the center point, it weighs more heavily upon the neck of the person it has approached, just as in a balance scale <term>statera: a steelyard or balance scale</term>...

<summary>This page explains the physics of levers as applied to rudders, sails, oars, and the coordinated carrying of heavy loads by groups of porters. It demonstrates how distance from a center point (the fulcrum) increases mechanical advantage.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, naval architecture, lever principle, maritime technology, weight distribution, phalangarii, ancient engineering</keywords>

--- Page 351 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of mechanical principles, specifically the physics of levers and centers of gravity, before transitioning into a practical guide for water-raising machines.</meta>

weight with the balance-scale proceeds to the limits of weighing; by the same reasoning, when the yokes of draft animals are balanced by straps through the middle of the crossbar, they pull their loads equally. But when their strengths are unequal, and one by being stronger overcomes the other, the strap is shifted to make one part of the yoke longer, which assists the weaker animal. Thus, in carrying-poles <note>original: "phalangis"; these were poles used by several men to carry heavy loads</note> as in yokes, when the straps are not placed in the middle, it makes the part where the strap is moved from the center shorter, and the other part longer. By that reasoning, if both ends are rotated around that center point where the strap was moved, the longer part will describe a larger circle and the shorter part a smaller one. And just as smaller wheels have harder and more difficult movements, so carrying-poles and yokes press harshly upon the necks in those parts where they have shorter distances from the center to the ends; however, those which have longer spaces from that same center lighten the loads for those pulling and carrying. Since these objects receive their motion through extensions from the center and circular revolutions, then indeed wagons, carriages, drums, wheels, screws, scorpions <note>a type of engine for throwing bolts or arrows</note>, ballistae <note>large siege engines for throwing stones</note>, presses, and other machines work toward their intended effects by these same principles of the extended center and the rotation of the compass.

## Concerning wheels and drums for grinding flour.
### Chapter 10.

There are also wheels placed in rivers, designed according to the same principles as those described above. Around their outer faces, paddles <note>original: "pennae," literally feathers or wings</note> are attached; when these are struck by the force of the river, they compel the wheel to move forward and rotate. ### Concerning the screw which raises a great abundance of water, but not as high. Chapter XI.

There is also the design of the screw <note>original: "coclea" - literally "snail shell," referring here to the Archimedean screw used for irrigation</note>, which draws up a great force of water but does not lift it as high as a wheel. Its design is explained as follows. A beam is taken, and however many feet in length that beam may be, its thickness is prepared to be that many inches. It is then rounded with a compass. At the ends, the circumferences are divided with the compass into four parts by quadrants, or into eight parts by octants, with lines drawn; and these lines should be so placed that, when the beam is laid on a flat surface and leveled, the lines of each end correspond to one another perpendicularly. From these, lines are then drawn from one end to the other, matching—

In this way, the spaces will be equal in both the rounding and the length. Thus, where the longitudinal lines are drawn, intersections <note>original: "decussationes"</note> must be made, and at these intersections, specific points are marked. Once these have been accurately laid out, a thin lath of willow or cut from a chaste-tree <note>original: "vitice"</note> is taken. This lath, smeared with liquid pitch, is fixed at the first point of intersection; then it is passed obliquely to the subsequent longitudinal and circumferential intersections. Proceeding in order, passing through each point and winding around, it is positioned at every intersection. It continues until it reaches and is fixed to the same longitudinal line from which it started, moving from the first to the eighth point. In this manner, as much as it progresses obliquely through the space and through the eight points, it advances an equal distance in length to the eighth point.

Following this same logic through the entire length and circumference, the laths fixed obliquely at each intersection create channels wound through the eight divisions of the thickness, forming a correct and natural imitation of a snail shell <note>original: "cocleæ naturalemq; imitationem"</note>. Along this track, other laths are fixed one over the other, smeared with liquid pitch, and are built up until the total thickness becomes one-eighth of the length. Over these, boards are wrapped and fixed to cover the winding; then these boards are saturated with pitch and bound together with iron plates so that they are not forced apart by the pressure of the water. The ends of the beam are secured with iron nails and plates, and into these, iron pivots <note>original: "stili ferrei"</note> are driven. To the right and left of the screw, supporting beams are placed, having cross-pieces <note>original: "transuersaria"</note> fixed at both ends. In these, iron-lined sockets are enclosed, and into them...

## On the Ctesibian machine, which raises water to a great height.
### Chapter 12.

It follows now to describe the machine of Ctesibius <note>Ctesibius of Alexandria (3rd century BCE) was a Greek inventor and mathematician, often called the "father of pneumatics."</note> which raises water to a high elevation. It is made of bronze. At its base are two twin cylinders <term>modioli: small buckets or cylinders used as pump chambers</term> placed a short distance apart, having pipes—shaped like a fork—joined together in a similar fashion and meeting at a central basin <term>catinum: a collection chamber or pressure vessel</term>. In this basin, valves <note>original: "axes"</note> are placed at the upper openings of the pipes, fitted with precise joinery. These valves, by plugging the openings, do not allow what has been forced into the basin by the air pressure to escape. 

Above the basin, a cover <term>penula: literally a "cloak," here referring to a cowl or airtight lid</term> is fitted, like an inverted funnel; it is held down and joined to the basin by a pin <note>original: "fibulam"</note> with a wedge driven through it, so that the force of the water pressure does not force the cover to rise. Above this, a pipe called a "trumpet" <note>the rising main pipe</note> is joined and stands upright. Furthermore, the cylinders have valves placed over the openings in their bottoms, below the lower mouths of the pipes. 

Thus, from above, male pistons <term>emboli: plungers or pistons</term>, polished on a lathe and treated with oil, are enclosed in the cylinders and moved by rods and levers. As these pistons move back and forth with frequent strokes, they compress the air mixed with water; the valves then plug the openings, and the pressure forces the water through the mouths of the pipes into the basin. The cover receives this pressure and pushes the water out through the upright pipe. In this way, water is supplied from a lower level to a reservoir <term>castello: a distribution tank or "castellum"</term> for the use of fountains.

However, this is not the only refined method attributed to Ctesibius <note>An inventor from 3rd-century BCE Alexandria, known as the "father of pneumatics."</note>; there are many others of various kinds which, driven by the compression of liquids and air, are shown to produce effects borrowed from nature. ### On Hydraulic Engines by which Organs are Constructed.
### Chapter XIII.

<margin>
I could have shown more regarding the internal and external workings of these things, but I believe I have done enough by opening the doors for the studious and showing the paths by which this author <note>Referring to Vitruvius, the Roman authority on architecture and mechanics</note> might be understood.
</margin>

I shall not omit to describe, as briefly and accurately as I can in writing, the principles governing water organs <note>original: "De Hydraulicis," referring to the hydraulis, an ancient pipe organ powered by water pressure</note>. Upon a base constructed of solid timber, a chest made of bronze is placed. Above the base, upright frames are erected on the right and left, joined in the manner of a ladder. Within these are enclosed bronze cylinders <term>modioli: the pump cylinders of the engine</term> with movable pistons finely polished on a lathe. These pistons have iron rods fixed in their centers and are connected by pins to levers, and they are wrapped in skins with the wool still on them.

Likewise, in the top surface of the cylinders are holes about three fingers wide. Near these holes, bronze dolphins are placed on pivots, holding cymbal-valves hanging by chains from their mouths below the holes of the cylinders. These are lowered into the chest where the water is held. Inside this chest is a vessel like an inverted funnel, beneath which small blocks about three fingers high are placed to level the space at the bottom between the lips of the funnel <note>original: "phigæos," likely referring to the base or rim of the air-chamber</note> and the floor of the chest.

Above the neck of this funnel, a small box is joined which supports the head of the machine, which in Greek is called the *musical rule* <note>original: "κανών μουσικός" (kanon mousikos)</note>. Along its length are channels; if it is a four-stringed type <note>tetrachord</note> there are four; if six-stringed <note>hexachord</note>, six; if eight-stringed <note>octachord</note>, eight. For each channel, there are individual stop-cocks <term>epistomia: valves or taps used to control the flow of air</term> fitted with iron handles. When these handles are turned, they open the openings from the chest into the channels. Furthermore, the "rule" has holes arranged crosswise, corresponding to the openings in the top board, which in Greek is called the *tablet* <note>original: "πίναξ" (pinax)</note>. Between the tablet and the "rule," sliding strips are interposed, perforated in the same manner and treated with oil.

...carefully finished, so that they may be easily pushed forward and drawn back again; these components close the openings and are called **sliders** <note>original: "pleuritides"</note>. The back-and-forth movement of these sliders alternately closes and opens the bored holes. These rules <note>the sliding bars</note> have iron **linkages** <note>original: "choragia"</note> fixed and joined to the **keys** <note>original: "pinnis," literally 'feathers' or 'fins,' here referring to the manual keys</note>, and the touching of these keys produces the movement of the sliders. From the small cylinders, however, pipes are continuously joined to wooden **necks** <note>connectors</note>, extending to the openings in the wind-chest; in these, there are valves <note>original: "axes"</note> finished on a lathe and placed there, which, when the chest receives the air, do not allow the wind to escape back, effectively blocking the holes.

Thus, when the levers are raised, the connecting rods pull the pistons of the cylinders to the bottom; and the **dolphins** <note>ornamental counterweights or pivoting arms</note>, which are enclosed in the swivels, dropping the **valves** <note>original: "cymbala," literally 'cymbals,' here disk-shaped valves</note> into the openings, fill the spaces of the cylinders with air. Then the connecting rods, lifting the pistons within the cylinders with a rapid and forceful stroke, and closing the upper holes with the valve-disks, force the air that is trapped there by the pressure into the pipes. Through these, the air rushes into the wooden reservoir and through its necks into the wind-chest. By the more vigorous motion of the levers, the air is frequently compressed and flows through the openings of the **stop-cocks** <note>original: "epistomiorum"</note>, filling the channels with wind. Therefore, when the keys, touched by the hands, continually push and pull the sliders, they alternately close some holes and open others; by these musical arts, they produce sounding voices in a manifold variety of melodies.

# BOOK X

The wheels of the carriage <note>Latin: *rhedæ*</note> should be four feet and one-sixth in diameter, so that when a wheel has a fixed starting point and begins its forward rotation on the surface of the road, it will have completed a precise distance of twelve and a half feet <note>The math here relies on the approximation of Pi as 3 (3 x 4.166 = 12.5)</note> by the time it returns to that same starting point. Once these wheels are prepared, a drum <note>Latin: *tympanum*, a circular gear or wheel</note> is to be firmly fixed to the inner side of the wheel's hub, having a single small tooth <note>Latin: *denticulum*</note> projecting beyond its circular face.

Furthermore, a housing is to be securely fastened to the body of the carriage, containing a revolving drum placed on its edge and enclosed on a small axle. On the face of this drum, four hundred teeth are to be crafted, spaced equally apart, which will engage with the single tooth of the lower drum attached to the wheel.

Additionally, a second small tooth is to be fixed to the side of this upper drum, projecting beyond its teeth. Above this, a third drum—this one lying flat and toothed in the same manner—is placed in another housing, with its teeth matching the single tooth fixed to the side of the second drum. In this third drum, holes are to be made, the number of which corresponds to the number of miles <note>Latin: *miliariorum*</note> a carriage might travel in a day's journey; whether there are more or fewer holes does not hinder the mechanism.

In all these holes, small round stones <note>Latin: *calculi*</note> are to be placed. In the case (or housing) of this drum, a single hole is made with a small channel, through which the stones placed in the drum can fall one by one into the body of the carriage and into a bronze vessel placed beneath it, whenever they reach that specific point.

Thus, as the carriage wheel moves forward, it carries the lowest drum with it; its single tooth, at every revolution, strikes a tooth of the upper drum and forces it to move forward. This ensures that when the lowest drum has turned four hundred times, the upper drum has itself...

# BOOK X

Likewise, the middle axis <note>The main drive shaft</note> in the center of the ship has a drum <term>tympanum: a drum-shaped gear or wheel</term> with a single small tooth protruding beyond its circumference. At that point, a housing is positioned containing a drum within it, which has four hundred teeth of equal size that align with the single tooth of the drum fixed to the axis. Furthermore, attached to the side of this second drum is another tooth that projects beyond its circumference.

Above this, in another housing, there is a flat drum fixed and enclosed in the same manner, likewise toothed. The single tooth fixed to the side of the vertical drum <note>original: "in cultro" - positioned like a knife-edge or vertically</note> strikes the teeth of this flat drum with every full rotation, pushing them forward one by one and causing the flat drum to turn in a circle.

In this flat drum, holes are to be made, and in these holes, round pebbles <term>calculi: small stones used for counting or calculation</term> shall be placed. In the cover of this drum (or its housing), a single hole is excavated with a small channel, so that when a pebble is freed from its restraint and falls into a bronze vessel, it signifies the distance with a sound.

Thus, when the ship gains momentum, either by the force of oars or the blowing of the winds, the paddles on the wheels, touching the water as they move against it, are forced backward with a violent impulse and turn the wheels. These wheels, in their turning, drive the axis; the axis, in turn, drives the drum. The tooth of this drum, as it revolves, strikes the individual teeth of the second drum with each rotation, causing it to make small movements.

Therefore, when the wheels have been turned four hundred times by the paddles, the single tooth fixed to the side of the vertical drum will have driven the flat drum around exactly once. Consequently, every time the revolution of the flat drum brings a hole to the opening, it will release the pebbles through the small channel. In this way, by both the sound and the count, it will indicate the miles <note>original: "miliaria spatia" - literally 'thousand-pace spaces'</note> traveled in the voyage.

<margin>h</margin> This description of a ship was not made according to the exact method handed down by the original author, but by another no less skillful way. For he <note>referring to the original authority, likely Vitruvius</note> instructs that wheels <term>rotas</term> <note>paddle wheels used for propulsion</note> ought to be placed outside the sides of the ship. However, whenever the ship is tilted to one side or the other—as the force of the winds and sails <term>velorum</term> requires—the wheel on that side, being tilted and lying face down, is submerged too deeply in the water. Thus, it hinders navigation and cannot complete a proper rotation. Meanwhile, the other wheel is lifted higher up and, similarly tilted, touches the water only slightly or not at all. Because of this imbalance, one wheel cannot help the other, nor be helped by it, so that they cannot move in any way.

### *On the proportions of catapults and scorpions. Chapter XV.*

<margin>n</margin>
Now, however, I shall explain the principles of the scorpions, catapults, and ballistae <note>These are types of ancient torsion-powered siege engines; the scorpion was a smaller, more precise version of the catapult</note> which were invented for protection against danger and the necessity of safety, and the symmetries by which they may be constructed. First, concerning catapults and scorpions: all their proportions are calculated based on the proposed length of the arrow which the engine must shoot. One-ninth of that length determines the size of the holes in the frames <note>original: "capitulis"</note>, through which the twisted sinews are stretched to hold the arms of the catapults. The height and width of the frame for these holes are shaped as follows: the boards at the top and bottom of the frame, called "parallels," should be one hole-diameter thick and one and three-quarters wide; at the ends, they should be one and a half hole-diameters. The side-posts <term>parastatae: the vertical supports of the engine's frame</term> on the right and left, excluding the tenons, are four holes high and five-sixths of a hole thick; the tenons are nine-sixteenths of a hole. From the hole to the middle post is also nine-sixteenths of a hole. The width of the middle post is one and one-eighth holes, and its thickness is one hole. The space where the arrow is placed in the middle post is one-quarter of a hole. The four corners around the sides and fronts should be fastened with iron plates or bronze pins and nails. The length of the trough (which is called a *spix* <note>original: "σπῖξ"</note> in Greek) is nineteen holes. Of the rails, which some call "cheek-pieces" <note>original: "bucculas"</note>...

The length of the joint is 1/4 of an opening; the length of the head of the column is 1 and 1/2. The width of the front attachment is 1 and 1/2 openings, and the thickness is 1. The smaller rear column, which in Greek is called the *antibasis* <note>original: "ἀντίβασις," meaning a counter-base or back-stay</note>, is eight openings; the width of the opening is 1 and 1/2, and the thickness is 1. The underlying piece <note>the sleeper or base-frame</note> is 12 openings, with the same width and thickness as that smaller column. Above the smaller column is the "little claw" or "cushion" <note>original: "cheloniū siue puluinus"</note> of 2 and 1/2 openings in height, and 1 and 1/2 in width. The windlass-sockets <note>original: "carchebi sucularum"</note> are 2 and 1/2 openings; the thickness of the opening is 1/2 and 1/12, and the width is 1 and 1/2. With the cross-beams and their joints, the length is 10 openings, the width is 1 and 1/2, and the thickness is the same. The length of the arm is 7 openings, and the thickness at the base is 5/12 of an opening.

at the top of the opening. <note>The "opening" or "hole" refers to the *peritreton*, the socket in the catapult frame through which the twisted hair-springs were threaded.</note> The curvature of the openings is eight parts. These components are adjusted through specific proportions, either by adding or subtracting from their dimensions. For if the capitals <note>The upper part of the catapult frame</note> are made taller than their width—which are called *anatora* <note>original: "anatora"; a Greek-derived term for "extended upward"</note>—then length must be taken away from the arms, so that while the tension is softened by the height of the capital, the shortness of the arm makes the strike more powerful. 

If the capital is less tall—which is called *catatonum* <note>original: "catatonum"; Greek-derived for "lowered" or "under-stretched"</note>—then because of the resulting stiffness, the arms should be made a little longer so they may be drawn back easily. For just as a lever four feet long requires five men to lift a weight, but if it is eight feet long it can be raised by only two, in the same way, the longer the arms are, the more easily they are pulled, and the shorter they are, the more difficult they are to draw.

# On the principles of ballistae. Chapter XVI.

I have already described the principles of catapults and the components and proportions from which they are constructed. The principles of **ballistae**, however, are varied and different, though all are designed to achieve a single effect. For some are turned by levers and windlasses <note>original: "suculis"</note>, some by systems of multiple pulleys <note>original: "polyspastis"</note>, others by capstans <note>original: "ergatis"</note>, and some even by the mechanics of drums. Nevertheless, no ballista can be completed unless it is proportioned to the intended weight of the stone that the engine is meant to throw. Therefore, the logic of these machines is not easily understood by everyone, but only by those who are familiar with numerical calculations and multiplications through arithmetic.

For holes are made in the frames <note>original: "capitibus," literally 'heads' or 'spring-frames'</note> through which the ropes—made primarily of woman's hair or animal sinew—are stretched. These ropes are selected based on the weight of the stone the ballista is to throw, calculated by a ratio of gravity and proportion, just as the proportions for catapults are derived from the lengths of the arrows. Therefore, so that even those who do not know the principles of geometry and arithmetic may be prepared, and not be delayed by calculations in the midst of the dangers of war, I shall set forth what I have learned for certain through my own practice, and what I have received as defined rules from my teachers. I will explain how the Greek measurements <note>original: "pentiones," likely referring to the Greek 'tonos' or tension-units</note> relate to the modules, and I will provide these explained so that they correspond to our own weights.

---

## On the proportion of the stones to be thrown to the hole of the ballista. Chapter XVII.

For a ballista that is to throw a stone of two pounds, the hole in its frame shall be five digits <note>term: digitus; a Roman unit of measurement, approximately 0.73 inches</note>. If it is to throw four pounds, the hole shall be six digits; for six pounds, seven and one-eighth digits <note>note: the symbol ⸭ indicates a fractional part</note>. For ten pounds, nine and one-eighth digits. For twenty pounds, ten and five-eighths digits. For forty pounds, twelve and a half digits plus a small fraction. For sixty pounds, fourteen digits and one-eighth of a digit.

### On the Tensioning and Tuning of Catapults and Ballistae. Chapter XVIII.

Very large beams are taken, and upon them are fixed "tortoises" <note>original: *cheloniæ*; these are bracket-like supports</note> in which windlasses are enclosed. ### *On matters of siege and defense, and first on the invention of the ram and its construction. Chapter XIX.*

I have said what I could on these matters; it remains for me to speak of siege warfare—how commanders may be victorious and cities defended by means of machines. First, regarding sieges, the ram is said to have been invented in this way: the Carthaginians set up camp to besiege Cadiz <note>original: "Gades"</note>. When they had previously taken a fort, they attempted to demolish it. Since they did not have iron tools for the demolition, they took a timber, and supporting it with their hands and repeatedly striking the top of the wall with its head, they knocked down the upper rows of stones, and so step by step they dismantled the entire fortification in order. 

Afterward, a certain Tyrian craftsman named Pephasmenos, led by this method and invention, set up a mast and suspended another cross-beam from it like a weighing scale; by drawing it back and driving it forward with violent blows, he threw down the wall of the people of Cadiz. Later, Cetras the Chalcedonian first made a base of timber with wheels underneath, and upon it he joined uprights and cross-beams, and from these he suspended the ram, covering it with ox-hides so that those who were stationed in the machine to strike the wall might be safer. This, however...

Once these first steps in this type of machinery had been established, later, when Philip, son of Amyntas, was besieging Byzantium, Polyidus the Thessalian developed many easier and more varied types. Therefore, Diades showed in his writings that he had invented **walking towers**, which he used to carry around with the army in a disassembled state; furthermore, he invented the **borer** <note>original: "terebram"</note>, and the **climbing machine**, by which one could cross over to a wall on level footing, and also the **demolishing crow**, which some people call the **crane**. He likewise made use of the **ram on wheels**, the principles of which he left in writing.

He states that the smallest tower ought to be built no less than sixty cubits high <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> and seventeen cubits wide. The **tapering** <term>contractura: the narrowing of a structure toward the top</term> at the very top should be one-fifth of the base. The upright beams at the bottom of the tower should be nine inches thick, and at the top, six inches. He says this tower should have ten stories, with windows in every part of it.

The larger tower, however, was 120 cubits high and 23.5 cubits wide; its tapering at the top was likewise one-fifth. The upright beams were one foot thick at the bottom and six inches at the top. He made this massive tower with twenty stories, with each story having a gallery three cubits wide; he covered it with raw hides so that it would be safe from every blow.

The construction of the **ram-tortoise** was carried out on the same principle. It had a width of thirty cubits and a height of sixteen, excluding the roof-ridge. The height of the ridge itself, from the floor to the peak, was seven cubits. Above the middle of the roof, there also rose a small turret at least twelve cubits wide, which was raised to a height of four stories...

### On the preparation of the "tortoise" shed for filling ditches.
#### Chapter XX.

The "tortoise" <note>term: *testudo* (tortoise); a heavy, wheeled protective shed used to shield soldiers while they worked</note> which is prepared for the filling of ditches, and which can also provide access to the wall, shall be made in this manner. Let these be held together by two other beams, one and a half feet thick and one foot wide. Let the transverse beams be spaced about one and a half feet apart, and under each of their intervals, let there be placed "little trees" <note>term: *arbusculae*; here referring to the heavy timber housings for the wheels</note>, which are called *hamaxopodes* in Greek <note>original: "ἁμαξόποδες"; literally "wagon-feet"</note>, in which the axles of the wheels turn, enclosed in iron plates. And let those housings be so tempered that they have pivots and holes, through which levers may be passed to facilitate their turning, so that they may move forward or backward, to the right or left side, or diagonally at an angle as needed, by means of the turning housings. Furthermore, let two beams be placed upon the base, projecting six feet on each side, around which projections let there be fixed...

Another design projects two beams in front of the face, seven feet thick and wide, as described in the base. Above this framework, composite posts are to be erected, nine feet high excluding the tenons <note>tenons: the projecting part of a joint (cardines) that fits into a mortise</note>, and a foot and a quarter thick in every direction, with intervals of a foot and a half between them. Above the rafters, a square beam is placed by which the rafters are joined together. These rafters are held in place by side-pieces fixed around them and are covered with boards, preferably of palm wood; if not, from other material that has the greatest strength, excluding pine or alder. For these are brittle and easily catch fire. Around the boarding, hurdles <note>original: "crates"</note> made of thin, very closely woven twigs are placed, and the whole machine is covered around with fresh, raw double-hides sewn together and stuffed with seaweed or straw soaked in vinegar. In this way, the blows of the ballistae <note>ballistae: large ancient missile launchers that threw heavy stones or bolts</note> and the force of fires will be repelled by them.

# BOOK TEN

## On other types of tortoises. Chapter XXI.

<margin>e</margin>There is also another type of tortoise <note>The 'testudo' or tortoise was a mobile shed used to protect soldiers as they approached enemy walls</note> which possesses all the same features as those described above, except for the "rams-heads" <note>original: "capreolos," referring here to the bracing timbers or perhaps the battering mechanism</note>. Instead, it features boards around the parapet and the battlements, with eaves sloping forward above them; these are held together by boards and hides firmly fixed in place. Furthermore, clay kneaded with hair should be spread over it to such a thickness that fire cannot damage the machine at all. These machines can, if necessary, be mounted on eight wheels, should the nature of the terrain require such an adjustment.

Those tortoises, however, which are prepared for the purpose of digging are called *oryges* in Greek <note>original: "ὄρυγες," meaning "diggers" or "trench-makers"</note>. They have all other features as described previously. Their fronts, however, are shaped like the angles of triangles, so that when missiles are launched from the wall against them, the machine does not receive the blows on a flat face; instead, the missiles slide off the sides, protecting those digging inside from danger.

It does not seem to me out of place to explain the principles by which the tortoise made by Agetor of Byzantium <note>A famous ancient engineer; Byzantium is modern-day Istanbul</note> was constructed. Its base had a length of 60 feet and a width of 18 feet. The uprights, which were placed above the frame, were four in number, joined together from pairs of beams; each reached a height of 36 feet, with a thickness of one foot <note>original: "palmopedali," literally a foot and a palm</note> and a width of one and a half feet. Its base had eight wheels on which it was moved. The height of these wheels was six and a half feet, and their thickness was three feet, constructed of triple layers of material fastened together with alternating dovetail joints and bound with cold-forged iron plates. These wheels were mounted in "little trees" <note>original: "arbusculis," a technical term for the housings or axle-blocks</note>—or what might be called "carriage-feet" <note>original: "amaxopodes"</note>—which allowed them to pivot. Thus, above the level of the crossbeams which were on the base...

The ropes were bound with transverse girdles, leaving spaces of one foot <note>original: "palmipedalia" - a measurement of roughly 12 to 13 inches</note> between them. This machine could be moved in six ways: forward, backward, to the right and left, and it could also be raised upward or lowered by tilting. The machine could be raised to a height of about 100 feet to demolish a wall. Likewise, by extending to the right and left, it could cover a distance of no less than 100 feet. ## Conclusion of the Entire Work. Chapter 22.

<margin>a</margin>
I have explained the subjects of scorpions, catapults, and ballistae <note>various types of ancient artillery for throwing bolts or stones</note>, as well as tortoises <term>testudo: a wheeled shed used to protect soldiers</term> and towers—those which seemed to me most suitable, who invented them, and how they ought to be made. However, I did not find it necessary to write about ladders, pulleys <note>original: "carchesiorum"</note>, and those things whose principles are simpler. The soldiers themselves are accustomed to making these; furthermore, such devices are not useful in all places or by the same methods, because fortifications differ from one another, as do the courageous spirits of different nations. For machines should be prepared in one way for the bold and reckless, in another for the diligent, and in another for the fearful.

Therefore, if anyone wishes to pay attention to these prescriptions, by selecting from their variety and bringing them together into a single comparison, he will not lack for resources. Instead, he will be able to explain without hesitation whatever matters are necessary, whether by reasoning or by topographical locations. However, regarding defensive measures <note>original: "repugnatorijs"</note>, these should not be explained solely through writings. For enemies do not prepare their siege works according to our writings; rather, their machinations are more often overturned through the clever speed of timely counsel, without the need for machines.

This is remembered to have happened to the Rhodians. There was a Rhodian architect named Diognetus, and he was granted a certain fixed annual salary from the public treasury in honor of his skill. At that time, a certain architect from Aradus named Callias came to Rhodes and gave a public lecture <note>original: "acroasin"</note>. He produced a model of a wall, and above it, he placed a machine on a rotating crane <note>original: "carchesio uersatili"</note> with which he seized a "Helepolis" <note>term: Helepolis; a massive, "city-taker" mobile siege tower</note> as it approached the walls and transported it inside the fortifications. When the Rhodians saw this model, they were filled with admiration and took away from Diognetus the annual sum that had been established for him, transferring that honor to Callias.

In the meantime, King Demetrius—who, on account of his stubbornness of spirit, was called *Poliorcetes* <note>term: Poliorcetes; Greek for "The Besieger"</note>—prepared for war against Rhodes and brought with him Epimachus of Athens, a noble architect. This man prepared a Helepolis of immense cost and the greatest industry and labor. Its height was 125 feet and its width was 60 feet. He reinforced it with goat-hair cloth and raw hides so that it could withstand the blow of a stone weighing 360 pounds thrown by a ballista <note>term: ballista; a large ancient missile launcher</note>. The machine itself weighed 360,000 pounds. However, when Callias was asked by the Rhodians to prepare a machine against this Helepolis and to bring it inside the wall as he had promised, he said he was unable to do so. For not all things [can be scaled in the same way].

# BOOK TEN. 191

Some things can be managed by theoretical calculations, but there are others which, when modeled on a small scale, produce the same effects when made large; others, however, cannot have models, but are established on their own merits. Indeed, there are some things that seem plausible in models, but when they begin to increase in size, they fall apart, as we can observe from this example. A hole is bored with an auger <note>a tool for boring holes in wood</note> of half a finger's width, a finger's width, or a finger and a half; if we wished to make one a palm wide <note>about 3 inches</note> by the same method, it is not feasible, and one of half a foot or larger seems altogether unthinkable. Likewise, just as it appears possible in some small models, it seems it can be done in those that are not very large, yet it cannot be achieved in the same way in larger versions.

When the Rhodians <note>the inhabitants of the island of Rhodes</note> noticed this, having been deceived by the same reasoning—they who had treated Diognetus <note>a famous Rhodian architect</note> with injustice and insult—and after they saw the enemy persistently hostile and a machine <term>machinatio</term> prepared for the capture of the city, fearing the danger of slavery and expecting nothing but the devastation of the state, they prostrated themselves before Diognetus, begging him to aid his fatherland. At first, he refused to do so, but after noble virgins and youths <term>ephebi</term> <note>young men of military age</note> came with the priests to plead with him, he then promised to help on these terms: that if he captured that machine, it would be his own. 

These things having been so established, in the area where the machine was to approach, he broke through the wall and ordered everyone, publicly and privately, to pour whatever water, filth, and mud they had through that opening via channels in front of the wall. When a great quantity of water, mud, and filth had been poured out there during the night, on the following day, the *Helepolis* <note>original: "helepolis"; a massive "City-Taker" siege tower used by Demetrius Poliorcetes</note> approaching, before it could reach the wall, it sank and became stuck in the wet quagmire, and could neither move forward nor retreat afterward.

They filled this from wells and from the harbor. And so, when the tunnels were suddenly opened at their ends, a violent force of water was let in and undermined the supports; those who were inside were all overwhelmed, both by the mass of water and by the collapse of the tunnel. I have now completed in this volume the accounts I could provide regarding the logic of machines in times of both peace and war, which I deemed most useful. In the previous nine books, I have arranged individual types and components so that the entire body of work might have all the members of architecture explained across ten volumes.

# THE WRITINGS OF SEXTUS JULIUS FRONTINUS,
## OF CONSULAR RANK, ON THE WATER
## SUPPLY OF THE CITY
## OF ROME.

### THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS

<margin>c</margin> *Since every task assigned by the Emperor* <note>The Emperor Nerva, who reigned 96–98 AD.</note> *demands the most focused attention, and since I am driven—whether by my own natural concern or by a devoted sense of loyalty—not only to diligence but even to an affection for the work entrusted to me; and since I have now been appointed by Nerva Augustus (an Emperor of whom I cannot say whether he is more diligent or more devoted to the Commonwealth) to the office of Water Commissioner* <note>original: "aquarum officium"</note>, *a post pertaining both to the utility and the health, and even the security of the City, and one which has always been administered by the leading men of our state; I consider it my first and most vital priority, as I have established in my other duties, to understand thoroughly what I have undertaken. For I believe there is no firmer foundation for any action than the ability to distinguish what is to be done and what is to be avoided. Indeed, what is so unseemly or intolerable for a man as to carry out an assigned duty according to the instructions of assistants? Yet this must happen whenever the one in charge is preceded by his own ignorance. While the experience of such assistants is a necessary component, they ought to serve merely as the hands and tools of the director. Therefore, following the custom I have observed across many offices, I have gathered what information I could find pertaining to the whole matter, arranged it in order, and brought it together into this manual* <note>original: "commentarium"</note> *as a unified body of work.*

# On Aqueducts

...which I might look to as a manual for my administration. In other books, which I composed after gaining experience and practice, I dealt with the deeds of my predecessors; in this one, however, and in those that follow, the utility will perhaps pertain to my successor. But since it was written at the beginning of my administration, it will primarily serve for my own instruction and as a rule of conduct, so that I do not seem to have overlooked anything pertaining to the knowledge of the whole matter. 

First, I shall set down the names of the waters that flow into the city of Rome; then by whom each of them was brought in, under which consuls, and in what year after the founding of the city <note>original: "ab urbe condita"</note>; then from what places and at what milestone they began to be led; how much by underground channel, how much by masonry substructure, and how much by arched work. Afterward, I will describe the elevation of each, the system of their measurements, and the distributions from them—how much outside the city and how much within; how much each region is served by each water according to its capacity; how many public and private delivery tanks <term>castella: distribution basins where water was collected before being piped to consumers</term> there are; and from these, how much is given to public works, how much to "gifts" <note>original: "muneribus"</note>—for so the more ornamental fountains are called—how much to the public basins, how much in the name of Caesar, and how much is granted for the use of private individuals by the favor of the Emperor. Finally, I will discuss the law for maintaining them and the penalties imposed on the defiant by law, decrees of the Senate, and the mandates of the Emperors.

During the consulship of Marcus Valerius Maximus and Publius Decius Mus <note>original: "M. Valerio Maximo. P. Decio murena. COSS." - 312 BCE</note>, in the thirtieth year after the beginning of the Samnite War, the **Appian water** was brought into the city by **Appius Claudius Crassus** the Censor (who was later surnamed "the Blind"). He was the same man who took charge of paving the **Appian Way** from the Capena Gate all the way to the city of Capua. He had Gaius Plautius as his colleague, who was given the surname **Venox** <note>meaning "The Searcher of Veins"</note> because he discovered the veins of this water source. 

However, because Plautius resigned from the censorship within eighteen months—having been deceived by his colleague into believing Appius would do the same—the name of the aqueduct remained solely to the honor of Appius. It is recorded that Appius extended his censorship through many shifts and delays until he could complete both the road and this water channel. 

The Appian water is collected in the Lucullan fields along the Praenestine Way, between the seventh and eighth milestones, by a side-path to the left of seven hundred and eighty paces. Its channel has a length from the source to the Salt Works <note>original: "Salinas"</note>—a place near the Trigeminia Gate—of eleven thousand one hundred and ninety paces. Of this, eleven thousand one hundred and thirty paces are in an underground channel, while sixty paces are on substructures and arches above ground near the Capena Gate. 

A branch of the **Augustan Alsietina** joins it near the Old Anio at the border of the Torquatian Gardens. <insert>A branch was added to supplement it at the [blank] milestone</insert>, which was given the name **The Ten Twins** <note>original: "decem gemellorum"</note>. Here, at the sixth milestone of the Praenestine Way, by a side-path to the left of nine hundred and eighty paces near the Collatian Way, it receives a spring. The channel of this branch reaches the "Twins" via an underground pipe of six thousand three hundred and eighty paces. 

The distribution of the **Old Anio** <note>original: "Vetus anio"</note> begins at the Publician Slope by the Trigeminia Gate, at the place called the Salt Works. This occurred forty years after the Appian water was brought in, in the 481st year from the founding of the city <note>272 BCE</note>. **Marcus Curius Dentatus**, who held the censorship with Lucius Papirius Cursor...
