# On Aqueducts

The <term>Anio Vetus</term><note>The "Old Anio," the second oldest aqueduct in Rome, drawing water from the Anio River.</note>, as it is now called, was brought into the City using the spoils captured from <term>Pyrrhus</term><note>King of Epirus, whose defeat in 275 BCE provided the wealth for this project.</note> during the consulship of Spurius Carvilius and Lucius Papirius. Two years later, the Senate discussed the completion of this water project. After nine years, the praetor Minutius published the findings. Then, by decree of the Senate, <term>duumviri</term><note>A commission of two men appointed for a specific task.</note> were created to oversee the leading in of the water; Curius and Fulvius Flaccus had contracted the work. Curius died within five days of being appointed to the commission. The glory of completing the project belonged to Fulvius. The Old Anio begins above <term>Tibur</term><note>Modern-day Tivoli.</note> at the twentieth milestone outside the Rarana Gate, where a portion of it is diverted for the use of the Tiburtines. Its channel has a length of 43,000 paces <note>Approximately 43 miles or 64 kilometers.</note>, as required by the <term>leveling</term><note>The precise engineering of the slope to ensure water flow.</note>. Of this, the underground channel accounts for 42,297 paces. The substructure above ground covers 702 paces.

Twenty-one years later—that is, 127 years after the first project, in the year 608 from the founding of the city <note>144 BCE</note>—during the consulship of Servius Sulpicius Galba and Lucius Aurelius Cotta, the channels of the <term>Appia</term> and the <term>Anio</term> had been shattered by age. They were also being intercepted by the <term>frauds of private individuals</term><note>Illegal tapping of the public water supply by private citizens.</note>. The Senate gave the task of repairing and reclaiming these channels to Marcus Titius, who was then the <term>praetor</term><note>A high-ranking magistrate.</note> presiding over cases between citizens and foreigners. And since the growth of the city seemed to demand a more ample supply of water, he was also mandated by the Senate to see to it that he lead other waters into the city as far as possible. For the sake of the Republic, he led more extensive channels from the third milestone of the <term>Way of the Smiths</term><note>original: "fabrorum"</note>, which is named the <term>Marcia</term> after its author. We read in the works of <term>Fenestella</term><note>A Roman historian and encyclopedist.</note> regarding these works: a sum of 180 million <term>sesterces</term><note>A massive sum of Roman currency.</note> was decreed to Marcus; but because this was not sufficient to complete the business, the Senate decided that his praetorship should be extended for another year.

# Julius Frontinus
->A iii<-

At that same time, while the <term>Decemviri</term> <note>A board of ten officials responsible for religious and legal duties</note> were consulting the **Sibylline Books** <note>A collection of oracular prophecies consulted by the Roman state during emergencies</note> for other reasons, they are said to have discovered that it was not the **Marcia** water, but rather the **Anio**, that should be brought to the **Capitol**. <note>original: "non esse aquam Martiam sed anienem... in Capitolium perducendam"</note> Regarding this matter, it is recorded that a debate took place in the Senate, with **Lepidus** speaking on behalf of his colleague. This occurred during the consulship of **Appius Claudius** and **Quintus Caecilius**. Three years later, the matter was reopened by **Lucius Lentulus** during the consulship of **Gaius Laelius** and **Quintus Servilius**. However, on both occasions, the influence of **Marcus Titius** prevailed, and thus the water was successfully brought to the Capitol.

The **Marcia** has its source on the **Valerian Way** at the thirty-fourth milestone, on a side road three miles to the right for those traveling from the city of Rome. It is near the **Sublacensian villa**, which was first paved under the Emperor **Nero**. At the thirty-eighth milestone, two hundred paces to the left, the water is collected in stone-walled basins, appearing almost immediately with a deep green, pond-like color. The length of its channel from the source to the city is 61,710 and a half paces. <note>A Roman pace was roughly five feet; this total is approximately 57 miles</note> This consists of 54,267 and a half paces of underground channel, and 7,443 paces of work above ground. Further from the city, in several places across private and public lands, there are 463 paces of arched structures across valleys. Nearer the city, starting from the seventh milestone, there are 188 paces of substructure and 6,470 paces of arched work.

**Gnaeus Servilius Caepio** and **Lucius Cassius Longinus** (who was nicknamed **Ravilla**), acting as <term>Censors</term> <note>High-ranking officials in charge of the census and public morality</note> in the 627th year after the founding of the city <note>125 BCE</note>, during the consulship of **Marcus Plautius Hypsaeus** and **Fulvius Flaccus**, arranged for the water called **Tepula** to be brought to Rome and the Capitol from the **Lucullan** estate (which some believe to be the **Tusculan** estate). The **Tepula** is collected on the **Latin Way** at the eleventh milestone, on a side road two miles to the right for those traveling from Rome.

# On Aqueducts

From there, it was conducted into the city in its own channel, later to be joined with the Julia. For Agrippa, acting as <term>aedile</term> <note>An elected official responsible for public maintenance and infrastructure</note> after his first consulship, during the reign of Emperor Caesar Augustus and the consulship of Marcus Lelius Volcatius <note>original: "M. Lelio uolcatio COSS." referring to 33 BCE</note> in the 719th year after the founding of the city, collected additional water sources at the twelfth milestone from the city. This was located twelve miles to the right for those traveling from Rome along the Latin Way. He also intercepted the flow of the Tepula; this newly acquired water was given the name "Julia" after its discoverer <note>Agrippa named it in honor of the Julian family of Augustus</note>. However, the distribution was divided in such a way that the name of the Tepula remained distinct. The conduit of the Julia reaches a length of 15,426 <term>paces</term> <note>A Roman pace or 'passus' was roughly five feet</note>. Of this, 7,000 paces consist of work above ground; specifically, in the areas nearest the city starting from the seventh milestone, 528 paces are on substructures and 6,472 paces are on arched structures.

Past the source of the Julia flows a stream called the Crabra. Agrippa bypassed this, either because he disapproved of its quality or because he believed it should be left to the landowners of Tusculum. For that is the water which all the villas of that district receive, distributed in turn on fixed days and in certain measures. However, our <term>water-men</term> <note>original: "aquarij" - the laborers and technicians of the water department</note> did not maintain the same restraint; they always claimed a portion of it to supplement the Julia—not to actually increase the Julia's flow, but to exhaust it by granting favors for their own profit. Therefore, the Crabra was excluded and, by order of the Emperor, entirely restored to the people of Tusculum, who now perhaps take it with some wonder, unaware of why they have such an unusual abundance. The Julia, meanwhile, having had the diversions through which it was being pilfered revoked, maintained its proper measure even during notable droughts.

In that same year, Agrippa restored the conduits of the Appia, the Anio, and the Marcia, which had nearly fallen into ruin, and with singular care, he furnished the city with numerous <term>fountains</term> <note>original: "salientibus aquis" - literally 'leaping waters'</note>. This occurred when he had already been consul for the third time, during the consulship of Gaius Sentius and Spurius Lucretius.

Thirteen years after he had brought in the Julia, he also collected and led to Rome the "Virgin Water" <note>Latin: Aqua Virgo</note> from the Lucullan estate. The day on which it first answered <note>i.e., arrived or flowed</note> in the city is found to be the 9th of June <note>original: "v. iduum iunij"</note>. It was named the "Virgin" because, when soldiers were searching for water, a young girl pointed out certain veins of it; those who followed and dug there found a vast quantity of water. A small shrine placed by the spring displays this young girl in a painting.

The source is taken at the eighth milestone on the Collatian Way in marshy places, surrounded by a wall of Signine work <note>a durable Roman concrete made of lime, sand, and broken pottery</note> for the purpose of containing the gushing springs. I do not quite perceive what reason moved Augustus, that most provident prince, to bring in the Alsietinian water—which is called the "Augusta"—since it has no pleasing quality; indeed, it is not very healthy and nowhere flows for the use of the people. ...three hundred and fifty-eight paces <note>A Roman pace, or *passus*, is approximately five feet.</note> of arched work. After these, Gaius Caesar <note>The Emperor Caligula, who succeeded Tiberius.</note>—since the seven existing aqueducts seemed insufficient for both public needs and private pleasures—began two more conduits in the second year of his reign, during the consulship of Marcus Aquilius Julianus and Publius Nonius Asprenas, in the 790th year from the founding of the city <note>38 AD</note>. Claudius completed this work with great magnificence and dedicated it during the consulship of Sulla and Titianus, in the 800th year from the founding of the city <note>52 AD</note>, on the first of August.

To one of these, which was brought from the Cerulean and Curtian springs, the name Claudia was given; this water is closest in quality to the Marcia. The other was named the New Anio, so that the two waters from the Anio River flowing into the city could be more easily distinguished by their names; because the one that had preceded them was the first Anio, the nickname "Old" was added to it.

The Claudia begins at the thirty-eighth mile-marker on the Sublacensian Way, on a side road to the left within three hundred paces. It draws from two very large and beautiful springs, the Cerulean <note>original: *cerulo*, named for its sky-blue color</note> and the Curtian. It also receives the spring called the Albudinus, which is of such high quality that whenever the Marcia needs assistance, it suffices so well that its addition does not change the Marcia's quality at all. The Augusta spring, because it was apparent that the Marcia was self-sufficient, was diverted into the Claudia, though it remains as a reserve for the Marcia, so that the Augusta would only assist the Claudia if the Marcia's conduit [could not carry it].

The **Anio Novus** <note>The "New Anio," so named to distinguish it from the earlier Anio Vetus.</note> is diverted from the river at the sixty-second mile-marker on the Sublacensian Way. Because the river flows through rich, cultivated lands with loose soil, its banks are easily eroded, and thus it flows muddy and turbid even without the damage caused by rains. For this reason, a settling tank <term>piscina limaria: a basin designed to slow the water flow so that sediment and grit can settle to the bottom</term> was placed at the intake of the aqueduct, so that between the river and the conduit, the water might come to a rest and be clarified. Even so, whenever heavy rains occur, the water reaches the city in a turbid state. It is joined by the **Herculanean stream**, which rises on the same road at the forty-second mile-marker, across from the springs of the Claudia on the other side of the river and the road. This stream is naturally very pure, but once mixed, it loses the charm of its clarity.

The channel of the Anio Novus totals 58,700 paces. Of this, 49,300 paces are in a subterranean channel and 9,400 paces in work above ground. Within that, there are 12,800 paces of substructures or arched work in various places in the upper section; and nearer the city, from the seventh mile-marker, there are 609 paces of masonry substructure and 6,491 paces of arched work. These are the highest arches, raised in certain places to a height of 109 feet.

**With such an array of indispensable structures carrying so many waters, compare, if you will, the idle Pyramids or the other useless—though famous—works of the Greeks!**

# On Aqueducts

Since a portion of the maintenance falls under their protection, it is necessary to understand which areas require the greatest expenditures. For our part, it was not enough to simply inspect each detail with our own eyes; we also took care to create maps <note>original: "formas"; these were likely architectural plans or topographical diagrams</note> of the aqueducts. From these, it is apparent where the valleys are and how large they are, where rivers are crossed, and where tunnels are attached to the sides of mountains. These maps show how much greater and more constant care is required for maintaining and reinforcing them. From this, we gain the advantage of being able to have the matter immediately before our eyes, as it were, and to deliberate as if we were standing right there.

All the waters arrive in the city at different levels <note>original: "libra"; referring to the water pressure and elevation relative to sea level</note>. Consequently, some serve the higher locations, while others cannot manage to reach the more elevated spots; for even the hills have grown higher due to the accumulation of rubble from frequent fires.

There are five heights of the aqueduct channels, two of which are raised high enough to reach every part of the city, but of the remaining ones, some are forced with greater pressure and others with lighter pressure. The highest is the **New Anio**; the next is the **Claudia**; the third place is held by the **Julia**; the fourth by the **Tepula**; and then the **Marcia**, which at its source even equals the level of the Claudia. However, the ancients constructed the older lines at a lower elevation, either because the subtle art of leveling <note>term: "librandi" — the Roman engineering practice of measuring gradients using tools like the chorobates or dioptra</note> had not yet been fully explored, or because they deliberately buried the waters underground so they could not be easily intercepted by enemies, since frequent wars were still being waged against Italian tribes. Now, however, in certain places where a channel has collapsed due to age, the underground circuit is abandoned, and for the sake of brevity, the paths are carried across valleys on substructures <note>term: "substructionibus" — massive masonry foundations used to support the weight of the water channel</note> and arches <note>term: "arcuationibus" — the iconic arched bridges that allowed aqueducts to maintain a steady gradient over low ground</note>.

The **Old Anio** holds the sixth place in level, which is likewise capable of supplying higher places; wherever the condition of valleys and low-lying regions requires it, the old sections are raised on substructures and arches. The **Virgo** follows the level of this one, and then the **Appia**.

...either established by the measure of fingers or by the measure of inches. Fingers are the standard in Campania and in most places in Italy. Inches are observed in <note>original: "pupula" - likely referring to the area around Rome or a specific local district</note>. Now, a finger, as is agreed, is the sixteenth part of a foot, and an inch is the twelfth part. Just as there is a difference between an inch and a finger, so too the observation of the finger itself is not simple; for one is called "square" and the other "round." The square finger is larger than the round by three-fourteenths of its own area; the round is smaller than the square by three-elevenths of its own area, specifically because the corners are worn away <note>Frontinus is explaining the geometric difference between a square area and a circle inscribed within it</note>. Later, a standard measure was introduced that took its origin neither from the inch nor from either of the two types of fingers. This was brought into use for the city, displacing the earlier measures, and was called by the name "quinaria" <term>quinaria: a standard Roman pipe size, roughly 2.3 cm in diameter</term>. Some think this was introduced by Agrippa <note>Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, the statesman who overhauled Rome's water system</note>, others by lead-workers through the influence of the architect Vitruvius. Those who make Agrippa the author say that five ancient, slender measures—which were like mere points used to divide water when it was scarce—were combined into a single pipe. Those who credit Vitruvius and the lead-workers say it is because a flat sheet of lead five fingers in width, when curved into a circle, creates this standard pipe size. But this is uncertain, because when it is curved, the inner part is compressed while the outer part is stretched. It is most probable that the quinaria was named from its diameter of five quarter-fingers. This ratio continues in the subsequent measures up to the "twenty-pipe," with the diameter increasing by the addition of one quarter-finger for each step; for example, the "six-pipe" has six quarters in its diameter, the "seven-pipe" has seven, and so on by similar increase up to the "twenty-pipe." Every standard measure is determined either by the diameter, the perimeter, or the area of the opening, from which...

and the capacity is apparent. In order to more easily distinguish the difference between the <term>uncia</term><note>A twelfth part of a foot; an inch</note>, the **square digit**, the **round digit**, and the <term>quinaria</term><note>The standard Roman unit for water flow, based on a pipe with a diameter of five-quarters of a digit</note> itself, we must use the value of the quinaria, which is the most certain and widely accepted standard. The <term>uncia</term> measure, therefore, has a diameter of one digit and one-third of a digit; it carries more than the quinaria by one-eighth—that is, a <term>sescuncia</term><note>An ounce and a half</note>—plus three <term>scripuli</term><note>Small units of weight or measure; scruples</note> and two-thirds of a scripulus. The **square digit**, when reduced to a round shape, has a diameter of one digit and one-eighth plus one-seventy-second of a digit; it carries ten-twelfths of a quinaria. The **round digit** has a diameter of one digit; it carries seven-twelfths, one-twenty-fourth, and one-seventy-second of a quinaria.

Furthermore, because the standard measures originate from the quinaria, they increase in two ways. One way is when the quinaria itself is multiplied—that is, multiple quinariae are included within the same opening. In these cases, the size of the opening grows according to the addition of quinariae. It is now almost common practice, when multiple quinariae have been granted, to use a single <term>fistula</term><note>A lead water pipe</note> so that the streets are not frequently torn up; these pipes are received into a <term>castellum</term><note>A distribution tank or water tower</note>, from which individuals receive their own allotted measure.

The second way is when the pipe increases not by a multiple of the quinaria, but according to the measure of its own diameter, from which it also receives its name and increases its capacity. For example, when a quarter-digit is added to the diameter of a quinaria, it makes a **senaria** <note>A "sixer" pipe</note>. This does not increase the capacity in a simple whole number; it carries one quinaria, five-twelfths, and a <term>sicilicus</term><note>A quarter-ounce or 1/48th of a unit</note>. And so on, by the same reasoning, as quarter-digits are added to the diameter, the measures grow—the **septenaria** <note>seven-pipe</note>, the **octonaria** <note>eight-pipe</note>, up to the **vicenaria** <note>twenty-pipe</note>. Following this is the system based on the number of square digits contained in the area—that is, the opening—of each measure; from which also...

# Julius Frontinus

->The pipes receive their names<- from the area of their circular opening, measured in square digits. For instance, a pipe that has twenty-five square digits is called a "twenty-five-pipe." Similarly, there is the "thirty-pipe," and so on, increasing by digits up to the "one-hundred-and-twenty-pipe." In the case of the "twenty-pipe" <note>Latin: *uicenaria*</note>, which sits at the boundary of both methods of calculation, it nearly matches both systems. According to the calculation used for the intervening modules, it has a diameter of twenty quarters of a digit, while the diameter itself is five digits. According to the ratio of the modules that follow it, it contains twenty square digits based on the mathematical tables <note>Latin: *gnomonijs*; referring here to geometric or mathematical scales used for calculation</note>. The ratio of the pipes, from the five-pipe <note>the *quinaria*, the standard unit</note> up to the one-hundred-and-twenty-pipe, holds true through all modules as we have shown, and remains consistent within its own kind. 

This also agrees with the modules established and confirmed in the records <note>Latin: *commentarijs*</note> of our most invincible and pious Emperor <note>likely referring to Trajan or Nerva, under whom Frontinus served</note>. Therefore, whether we follow mathematical reasoning or official authority, the modules in the records prevail. However, the water-men <term>aquarij: the technicians and laborers who managed the Roman water system</term>, though they agree with manifest reasoning in most cases, have deviated in four specific modules: the "twelve-pipe," the "twenty-pipe," the "hundred-pipe," and the "one-hundred-and-twenty-pipe." 

Regarding the twelve-pipe, because the error is not great and it is not in frequent use, they added to its diameter a half-ounce and a *sicilicus* <note>a *sicilicus* is 1/48th of a Roman digit or foot; a small fractional unit</note>, and to its capacity a five-pipe plus eight-twelfths <note>Latin: *bessem*; representing 2/3 or 8/12 of a unit</note>. In the remaining three modules, however, more significant discrepancies are found. They make the twenty-pipe smaller in diameter by a half-digit, and in capacity by three five-pipes and a half-ounce—this being the module most frequently used for distribution. Conversely, the hundred-pipe and the one-hundred-and-twenty-pipe, through which they regularly receive water, are not diminished but increased. To the diameter of the hundred-pipe, they added a third, two-thirds, and a half-ounce. To its capacity, they added ten five-pipes, a half, a half-ounce, and a *sicilicus*. To the one-hundred-and-twenty-pipe's diameter...

For in this way the account of the whole will be established; and just as, for example, the ratio of a sextarius <note>roughly a pint</note> corresponds to cyathi <note>small cups</note>, and the ratio of a modius <note>a peck</note> corresponds to both sextarii and cyathi, so also the multiplication of quinariae in the larger modules ought to preserve the rule of its own sequence. Otherwise, when less is found in the distribution module and more appears in the receiving module, it is clear that this is not an error, but a fraud.*

If it is placed facing the flow of water and tilted downward, it seizes more; if it is turned to the side of the passing water and tilted back, not being inclined toward the intake, it takes in water sluggishly and in small amounts. # THE WATER
# SUPPLY OF THE CITY OF ROME
# BY JULIUS FRONTINUS.
## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS.

Having followed through those matters which were necessary to say regarding the modules <note>The *quinaria* and other standard units of pipe measurement discussed in Book One.</note>, I shall now set down how much water each aqueduct was recorded to have had from its beginning up until the start of my administration, according to the records <note>original: "commentariis"; these were the official imperial ledgers or notebooks of the water office.</note>, and how much each one delivered. Then, I will describe what I myself discovered through a scrupulous investigation, guided by the foresight of the best and most diligent Emperor Nerva. In the records, there were a total of 12,755 *quinariae* <note>The *quinaria* was the standard Roman unit for measuring water flow, based on a pipe with a diameter of five-quarters of a digit.</note>; in the actual distribution, 14,018 were recorded. Thus, 1,263 more *quinariae* were being distributed than were accounted for in the supply. Since I believed the primary duty of my office was to investigate the honesty and the actual abundance of the waters, the wonder of this discrepancy turned me in no small measure toward examining how more could be delivered than was, so to speak, in the estate. Therefore, before all else, I set out to measure the intakes of the aqueducts; but I found a much greater measure—specifically about 10,000 *quinariae* more—than was in the records, as I shall demonstrate for each individual line.

To the **Appian Way Aqueduct** <note>The *Aqua Appia*, Rome's oldest aqueduct, built in 312 BCE.</note> was assigned in the records a measure of 841 *quinariae*. A measurement could not be taken at the intake of each branch because it consists of two channels. However, at the "Twins" <note>original: "Gemellas"; a location where two branches of the aqueduct met.</note>, which is a place within the Old Hope <note>original: "Spem Veterem"; a temple and district on the eastern side of Rome where several aqueducts entered the city.</note> where it joins with the Augustan branch, I found the depth of the water to be five feet and the width of the water to be one foot...

The **Anio Novus** <note>The "New Anio," an aqueduct commissioned by Caligula and completed by Claudius, drawing water from the Anio River.</note> was recorded in the official registers <note>original: "commentariis"</note> as having 3,262 *quinariae* <term>quinaria: a standard Roman unit of water flow based on a pipe's diameter</term>. However, upon measuring it at the source, I found 4,738 *quinariae*—which is 1,476 *quinariae* more than what is listed in the records. I do not claim this surplus greedily; indeed, there is no clearer way to prove my point than by looking at the distribution records themselves, where the greater part of this water is accounted for. For while the recorded intake is listed as no more than 3,262 *quinariae*, the distribution is recorded as 4,211 *quinariae*. Furthermore, I discovered that not only are the 527 *quinariae*—the difference between our measurements and the distribution—being intercepted, but the discrepancy is actually much larger. From this, it is apparent that the volume we measured even exceeds the actual capacity, the reason being that the force of the water is more "rapacious" <note>meaning the water flows with high velocity</note>; as it is taken from a large and swift river, its very speed increases the measured volume.

I do not doubt that some will remark that a far greater supply was found by actual measurement than was in the Imperial records. The cause of this is the error of those who, from the beginning, performed the estimation of each flow with too little diligence. And lest I believe they strayed so far from the truth out of fear of summer droughts, I verified these measurements in the month of July, and I continuously monitored the total supply of each throughout the remainder of the summer. Whatever the cause may be, one thing is certainly uncovered: 10,000 *quinariae* have been "lost" while the Emperor regulates his grants according to the limited amounts recorded in the registers. The next discrepancy is that one volume is measured at the intake, another (and not a small amount less) at the settling tanks <note>original: "piscinis"</note>, and finally the smallest amount is recorded during distribution. The cause of this is...

# On Aqueducts

The fraud of the water-men <note>Latin: *aquarii*; these were public slaves or officials responsible for the maintenance of the pipes</note> whom we have caught diverting water from the public conduits for private use is significant. Furthermore, many landowners, through whose fields the water lines pass, fraudulently pierce the sides of the channels. Consequently, the public conduits are made to serve private individuals, either for the irrigation of their gardens or to provide water for their private pathways. Regarding vices of this kind, nothing more or better can be said than what was stated by Caelius Rufus <note>Marcus Caelius Rufus (82–48 BCE), a famous orator and politician</note> in that speech titled *On Waters*. We wish that we were not now proving all these same things—usurped with similar boldness—through our own painful experiences. We have found irrigated fields, shops, upper-story apartments, and finally all manner of illicit establishments equipped with constant flowing taps. This is not to mention that some waters were being distributed under false titles in place of others, though that is among the lighter of the various offenses.

Meanwhile, among the matters that seemed to require correction, it is a wonder what occurred especially around the Caelian and Aventine hills. Before the Claudian water <note>The *Aqua Claudia*, completed by Emperor Claudius</note> was brought there, these hills used the Marcian and Julian waters. But after the Emperor Nero took the Claudian water at the Arches <note>The *Arcus Neroniani*, an extension of the Aqua Claudia</note> and brought it as far as the Temple of the Divine Claudius to be distributed from there, the earlier waters were not increased but were actually lost. For he added no new distribution tanks <note>Latin: *castella*; these were header tanks used to regulate pressure and distribute water to local pipes</note>, but used the existing ones; although the water source was changed, the old names remained.

Enough has now been said regarding the volume of each source, the "new acquisition" of water (so to speak), and the frauds and vices surrounding them. It remains for us to arrange the distribution—which we found, if I may say so, lumped together in a mass and recorded under false names—according to the specific names of the waters and the regions of the city. I know that this detailed list may seem not only dry but also complex; nevertheless, we shall set it down as briefly as possible, so that nothing is missing from the rules of our office.

# On Aqueducts

Furthermore, in every part of the city, most basins—both new and old—have received two pipes from different aqueducts, so that if an accident should impede one, the supply would not fail while the other remained sufficient. 

The Queen and Mistress of the world <note>Rome</note>, who stands as a goddess of the earth and to whom nothing is equal and nothing is second, feels this care of the most pious Emperor Nerva, her prince, daily. And she will feel it even more as the healthfulness of the same Eternal City increases through the enlarged number of distribution tanks <term>castellorum: small towers or reservoirs used to distribute water to different neighborhoods</term>, works, public fountains, and basins. No less is the benefit to private individuals spread through the increase of his favors. Even those who, out of fear, used to draw water illegally, now enjoy it securely through his grants. 

Nor is the water that runs to waste left idle; for the appearance of filth is removed, the air is purer, and the causes of that heavy atmosphere, for which the air of the city was infamous among the ancients, have been cleared away. It does not escape me that a new plan of distribution is owed to this work, but it must be understood that this should not be set down until the work is completed. What of the fact that even this does not suffice for the diligence of the Prince, which he provides most exactly to his citizens? He believes he has contributed too little protection and pleasure to our people by merely adding such a great quantity, unless he also makes it purer and more pleasant. # Julius Frontinus

<column-break/>

...had turbulent and muddy waters. This is not because such is the nature of all waters from their origin, nor because those which are taken from springs ought to suffer this defect—especially the **Marcia** and **Claudia**, and the others whose brilliance is pristine at the source and which are not at all, or only minimally, defiled by rain, provided that covered settling tanks <note>original: "putei extructi"; these were structural shafts or basins used to filter sediment</note> have been constructed. The waters of the **Anio** <note>The Anio River, which fed two of Rome's major aqueducts</note> are less consistently clear. For it is drawn from a river and is often clouded even in fair weather, because the Anio—although flowing from a very pure lake—nevertheless carries away material from its shifting, crumbling banks, by which it is muddied before it enters the conduits. It suffers this disadvantage not only from winter and spring rains, but even from summer showers, at which time a more pleasing purity of water is expected.

Of these, therefore, one—that is, the **Old Anio**—keeps its defect within itself, as it is generally at a lower level <note>original: "libra"; referring to the elevation or water-level of the channel</note>. The **New Anio**, however, used to contaminate the others; for since it arrives at the highest elevation and is especially abundant, it sometimes supplements the failures of the other lines. Yet, through the lack of skill of the water-men <note>term: "aquarii" (subordinate technicians responsible for the physical management of the pipes and channels)</note> who diverted it into the channels of others, it frequently defiled even those waters that were sufficient in themselves, more than was necessary for replenishment. This was especially true of the **Claudia**, which, after being carried for many miles in its own channel, was finally mixed with the **Anio** at **Rome**, and until this time lost its own qualities. Thus, it did not truly help the waters it met; rather, many waters were summoned through imprudence, not being used as was worthy of the waters of the **Marcia**. Consequently, we discovered that even the **Marcia**, most pleasing in its brilliance and coldness, was serving baths, fulling mills <note>term: "fullonicis" (laundries where cloth was cleaned and thickened, often using harsh substances like urine)</note>, and other services too foul to mention.

It was therefore decided that all should be separated, and then each so regulated that, first of all, the **Marcia** should serve entirely for drinking water, and thereafter the others should be assigned to suitable uses according to their respective qualities.

For he ordered that the river source be abandoned and the water instead be drawn from the lake located above the Neronian Villa at Subiaco, where the water is clearest. For although the Anio rises above Treba Augusta, it arrives at that point extremely cold and brilliant, either because it runs through rocky mountains with few cultivated fields around the town itself, or because it is purified, as it were, by the depth of the lake in which it is received, being further shaded by the density of the overhanging forests. This fortunate quality of the water equals the *Marcia* <note>The Aqua Marcia was traditionally considered the best drinking water in Rome</note> in all its virtues, and even surpasses it in quantity; this will now take the place of that formerly unseemly and turbid water. The inscription shall bear the name of the **New Emperor Caesar Nerva Trajan Augustus**.

It follows that we should indicate what the law is for leading water, and what care must be taken for the conduits. One of these concerns restraining private individuals within the limits of the grants they have obtained; the other pertains to the protection of the conduits themselves. In researching the laws on each of these matters—which I found were widely observed among the ancients—I decided that their equity and wisdom should not be kept silent. Among the ancients, all water was distributed for public use, and it was provided by law that no private person should lead any water other than that which falls from the basin to the ground. These are the very words of that law. That is, the water which has overflowed from the basin, which we call "lapsed" water <term>caduca: overflow water that was not part of the official piped supply</term>. Even this was granted for no use other than for baths or for the fullers <note>Fullers were laundry workers who used large amounts of water and chemicals to clean cloth</note>, and a fixed tax was established to be paid into the public treasury. # Julius Frontinus

...was granted by the leaders with the consent of the rest. However, regarding which magistrate the right of granting or selling water belonged to, the laws themselves vary. For I find that it was sometimes permitted by the **aediles** <note>magistrates in charge of public buildings and festivals</note> and sometimes by the **censors** <note>high-ranking officials responsible for public morality and state finances</note>; but it appears that whenever censors were in office, the request was primarily made to them. When they were not in office, that power belonged to the aediles. From this, it is manifest how much greater the care of our ancestors was for common utilities than for private pleasures, since even that water which private individuals diverted pertained to public use.

Furthermore, I find that the maintenance of individual aqueducts was usually put out to contract. This imposed a necessity upon the contractors to maintain a fixed number of slave workmen for the conduits outside the city and a fixed number within the city; and indeed, they had to enter the names of those they intended to have in service for each district into the public records. The responsibility for approving these works fell sometimes to the censors and sometimes to the aediles. Occasionally, that duty fell to the censors as a specific province, as is apparent from what was done during the censorship of **Gaius Licinius** and **Marcus Fabius**.

How much care was taken so that no one would dare to damage the conduits or divert water that had not been granted can be seen from many things, but especially from this: that the **Circus Maximus** <note>Rome's largest chariot-racing stadium</note> was not irrigated even on the days of the Circensian games except by permission of the aediles or censors. We read in the works of **Atteius Capito** <note>a famous Roman jurist under Augustus</note> that this practice continued even after the administration passed to the **Water Commissioners** <term>Curatores Aquarum: a permanent board established by Augustus to manage the water supply</term> under **Augustus**. Indeed, lands that had been irrigated with public water against the law were confiscated to the state. Slaves, likewise, were seized as a fine if they were said to have acted against the law. In these same laws, it was added: "Neither shall anyone foul the water with malicious intent where it leaps forth publicly; if anyone fouls it..." <note>original: "ita neque aquam oletato dolo malo, ubi publice salit siquis oletarit"</note>

There shall be a fine of ten thousand sesterces <note>A sesterce was a standard Roman silver or bronze coin; 10,000 was a substantial penalty for the time.</note> if anyone is seen to have polluted the water. For this purpose, the Curule Aediles <note>High-ranking Roman magistrates responsible for public buildings and festivals.</note> were ordered to appoint two men from each district—chosen from those who lived or owned property in that district—under whose judgment the water would flow for public use. Marcus Agrippa was the first, who, after his term as Aedile and during his consulship, acted as a permanent overseer of his own works and gifts. Now that the supply allowed it, he determined how much water should be allocated to public works, how much to basins, and how much to private individuals. He also maintained his own personal staff of slaves for the water system, who looked after the conduits, the distribution tanks, and the basins.

Augustus made this staff—which had been left to him as an inheritance by Agrippa—public property. After him, during the consulship of Quintus Aelius Tubero and Paullus Fabius Maximus for the second time, matters which until then had been managed by personal power rather than specific law were regulated by a Decree of the Senate, and a law was promulgated. Augustus also issued an edict defining the rights of those who received water according to the records of Agrippa, bringing the entire matter under his own patronage. He established the standard pipe sizes <note>original: "modulos"</note> of which we have spoken, and appointed Messala Corvinus as the overseer for maintaining and managing the system. Messala was given assistants: Postumius Sulpicius, a former Praetor, and Lucius Cominius, a junior senator <note>original: "pedarius," referring to a senator of lower rank who usually voted by walking to a side of the chamber rather than speaking.</note>. They were granted official regalia as if they were magistrates, and a Decree of the Senate was passed regarding their duties, which is transcribed below:

**The Decree of the Senate:** Whereas the Consuls Quintus Aelius Tubero and Paullus Fabius Maximus have made a report <note>original: "V. # Julius Frontinus 18

...and to have as many secretaries, clerks, assistants, and heralds as those officials have through whom grain is distributed to the common people. Furthermore, whenever they are conducting business related to this matter within the city, they may use the same attendants as the others, with the exception of the lictors <note>Lictors were bodyguards who carried the fasces, symbolizing a magistrate's power to punish.</note>. According to this Decree of the Senate <note>original: "S. C." or "Senatus Consultum"</note>, it is permitted for the Water Commissioners to use these attendants within ten days of the Decree being filed at the Treasury <note>original: "ærarium"</note>. For those attendants who have been so reported, the Praetors of the Treasury shall grant and assign the same annual food allowance as is usually given and assigned to the officials in charge of grain distribution. These attendants are permitted to accept such funds without penalty. Additionally, the tablets, paper, and other supplies necessary for the purpose of this administration shall be provided to the Commissioners. Quintus Aelius and Publius Fabius, the Consuls, or either one of them if they see fit, shall, in consultation with the Praetors presiding over the Treasury, arrange for these supplies to be provided.

Likewise, since the commissioners of roads and grain—who performed public service for a quarter of the year—are exempt from serving on private or public juries, so too are the Water Commissioners. Although the Treasury continues to pay for their attendants and services to this day, these roles seem to have ceased to exist due to the laziness and inactivity of Commissioners who do not perform their duties. 

However, the Senate had ordered that lictors should be present for us when we leave the city specifically for the purpose of conducting business. As we go about inspecting the water channels <note>original: "rivos"</note>, our own integrity and the authority granted to us by the Emperor <note>original: "principe"</note> shall serve in place of lictors. Since we have traced this matter back to the beginning of the office of Commissioner, it is not out of place to list those who presided over this office from Messala down to our own time. 

Messala was succeeded, in the consulship of Silius and Plancius, by Atteius Capito. Capito was succeeded, in the consulship of Lucius Martius and Gaius Antistius Vetus, by Satrius Rufus. Satrius was succeeded, in the consulship of Sergius Cornelius Cethegus and Lucius Visellius Varro, by...

# On Aqueducts

Marcus Cocceius Nerva, the grandfather of the Divine Nerva <note>Emperor Nerva, who reigned 96–98 AD</note>, was a man illustrious for his knowledge of the law. He was succeeded, during the consulship <note>original: "COSS." - an abbreviation for Consuls, the two chief magistrates of Rome who gave their names to the year</note> of Fabius Persicus and Lucius Vitellius <note>34 AD</note>, by Gaius Octavius Laenas. In both cases, however, great care must be applied to counter manifold frauds. The conduits outside the city must be inspected frequently and with concern to verify the grants. # Julius Frontinus. 19

The water should flow without interruption both day and night, which the Water Commissioner <note>Latin: *curator*</note> is also ordered to ensure by a Decree of the Senate, the words of which are as follows: "Aelius Tubero and Paullus Fabius Maximus, being Consuls <note>7 BCE</note>, spoke regarding the number of public fountains <note>Latin: *salientes*, literally 'leapers' or 'jets'</note> that were within the city and within the buildings joined to the city, which Marcus Agrippa had constructed. Regarding this matter, the Senate has decreed that the number of public fountains—which those commissioned by the Senate to inspect the public waters and count the fountains have reported—shall neither be increased nor diminished. Likewise, it is decreed that the Water Commissioners, whom Caesar Augustus named by the authority of the Senate, shall see to it that the public fountains pour out water for the use of the people as continuously as possible, by day and by night."

In this Decree of the Senate, I believe it should be noted that the Senate forbade the number of public fountains to be either increased or decreased. I think this was done because the volume of water coming into the city at that time—before the *Aqua Claudia* and the *Anio Novus* were brought in—did not seem able to support a larger distribution.

Whoever wishes to draw water for private use must obtain a grant for it and bring a letter from the Emperor to the Water Commissioner. The Commissioner must then promptly act upon Caesar's favor and write to the Emperor's Deputy <note>Latin: *procurator*, a high-ranking official, often a freedman</note> of that same office. It appears that Tiberius Claudius was the first to appoint such a Deputy after he introduced the *Anio Novus* and the *Claudia* aqueducts. The Commissioner must also be aware of what the letter contains and what orders have been given, so that he may never defend his own negligence or fraud under the pretense of ignorance. The Deputy must ensure that a delivery pipe <note>Latin: *calicem*, literally a 'chalice' or 'cup', referring to the bronze nozzle used to regulate flow</note> of the specific size that was granted is stamped in the presence of the levelers <note>Latin: *liberatoribus*, officials who surveyed and verified water levels</note>, and he must carefully attend to the measurements which I have described above.

...so that he may have the measure and knowledge of these things, lest it be left to the discretion of the **levelers** <note>original: "libratorum" — officials responsible for measuring water flow and levels</note> to approve a delivery pipe <note>original: "calicem" — literally a 'cup,' referring to the bronze nozzle used to regulate flow</note> of *sometimes a larger aperture, sometimes a smaller one* based on personal favor; nor should he immediately allow the free discretion of attaching any lead pipe whatsoever. Rather, he should ensure that for fifty feet, the pipe remains the same diameter as the aperture for which the nozzle was stamped, just as is provided for in the **decree of the Senate** <term>senatusconsulto: a formal resolution of the Roman Senate</term> which is to be added below.

Regarding the matter brought forward by the Consuls Quintus Aelius Tubero and Quintus Fabius Maximus: that certain private individuals were drawing water from the public channels. Concerning this matter, the Senate has decreed: that no private individual shall be permitted to draw water from the public channels, but all those to whom the right of drawing water has been granted shall draw it from the distribution tanks <note>original: "castellis" — small towers or reservoirs used to distribute water to specific neighborhoods</note>; and the **water commissioners** <term>curatores aquarum: the high-ranking officials in charge of the Roman water supply</term> shall determine in which places, inside and outside the city, private individuals may suitably construct distribution tanks from which they may draw the water they have received as a common share from the commissioners. Furthermore, none of those to whom the right to public water is given shall be permitted, within fifty feet of the distribution tank from which they draw water, to attach a pipe wider than a **five-pipe** <term>quinariam: the standard Roman unit of water measurement, roughly 2.3 cm in diameter</term>.

In this Decree of the Senate, it is worthy of admiration that it permits water to be drawn only from a distribution tank, so that neither the channels nor the public pipes are frequently damaged. The right to granted water follows neither the heir, nor the buyer, nor any new owner of the lands. For baths that serve the public, a privilege was granted in ancient times so that water, once given, should remain in perpetuity, as we learn from the old Decrees of the Senate, one of which I have added below. Now, every benefit of water is renewed with the new owner. # Julius Frontinus

->**Julius Frontinus**<-

<note>Sextus Julius Frontinus was a Roman civil servant and author who served as the water commissioner (Curator Aquarum) of Rome in the late 1st century AD.</note>

...and that those to whom the waters had been assigned should lead them into the city. **Regarding the matter at hand, the Senate has decreed** <note>original: "Q.D.E.R.F.P.D. E.I.C." - an abbreviation for "Quid De Ea Re Fieri Placeret De Ea Ita Censuerunt," a standard legal formula</note> that the assignment of waters should remain with them, with the exception of those given for the use of public baths, or those granted in the name of Augustus, for as long as the owners themselves possess the land for which they received the water. When any waters begin to be vacant <note>unallocated or available due to a change in ownership</note>, it is announced and entered into the records, which are consulted so that they may be granted to petitioners from the vacant supply. Formerly, they used to cut off these waters immediately, so that in the meantime they might sell them either to the owners of the estates or to others. It seemed more humane to our Prince <note>likely referring to Emperor Nerva or Trajan</note> that, lest the estates be suddenly deprived, a period of thirty days should be granted, within which those whom the matter concerns might irrigate. Regarding water granted to the estates of partners, I find nothing established; however, it is observed just as if it were provided by law, that as long as any of those who jointly obtained the grant survives, the entire measure of water assigned to the estates should flow, and only then should the benefit be renewed when each of those to whom it was given has ceased to possess it. It is clearly not permitted by a **Decree of the Senate** <note>original: "S. consul." for Senatus consultum</note> to lead water obtained for any purpose other than for the estates to which it was given, or from any reservoir <term>castellum: a distribution tank or water tower where the aqueduct water was divided into smaller pipes</term> other than that specified in the Emperor's letter. But this is also prohibited by mandates. Furthermore, those waters which are called "fallen" <term>caducae: literally 'falling' or 'lapsed' water; this refers to overflow or leakage from the system</term> are also obtained—that is, water which either flows out of the reservoirs or from leaks in the pipes. This benefit was usually granted very sparingly by the Emperors, but it is subject to the frauds of the water-men <note>aquarii: the slaves or laborers who maintained the pipes and were known for taking bribes to divert water illegally</note>. How much care must be taken to prevent these frauds will be manifest from the chapter of the mandates which I have subjoined: "I wish no one to lead 'fallen' water, except those who have it by my benefit or that of previous Emperors; for it is necessary that some part of the water from the reservoirs..."

<meta>This page continues the technical and administrative discourse on the Roman water system, likely from Frontinus's "De aquaeductu." It focuses on the prevention of fraud and the proper installation of water gauges.</meta>

# On Aqueducts

...to flow out, as this pertains not only to the health of our city, but also to the usefulness of flushing the sewers <note>original: "cloacarum"</note>. Having explained those matters which pertained to the regulation of water for private use, it is not out of place to touch upon certain instances by which we have detected the most wholesome regulations being bypassed in the very act of administration. For example, I found larger nozzles <note>term: "calices" (bronze thumb-pieces or gauges used to regulate the flow of water into private pipes)</note> than had been granted placed in many of the distribution tanks <note>term: "castellis" (castella), the reservoirs where water was divided for local distribution</note>, and some of these were not even stamped with an official seal. Whenever a stamped nozzle exceeds the legal measure, it reveals the favoritism of the deputy <note>term: "procurator," the high-ranking official in charge</note> who stamped it; but when it is not even stamped, the fault is clearly shared by all, especially the recipient, and then the overseer <note>term: "uillicus," the slave or freedman managing the local works</note>. In some cases, although nozzles of the legal measure were stamped, pipes of a larger diameter were immediately attached to them. As a result, the water was not constrained for the legal distance, but being forced through a short, narrow space, it easily filled the wider pipe placed next to it. Therefore, whenever a nozzle is stamped, this additional precaution must be taken: that the next pipes also be stamped for a distance which we have said was determined by decree <note>note: likely 50 feet, as specified in Roman water law</note>. For only then, when the overseer knows that pipes must not be installed unless they are stamped, will he be without any excuse. Regarding the placement of nozzles, it must also be observed that they are arranged in a line, and that one person's nozzle is not placed lower while another's is placed higher. The lower nozzle draws more, while the higher one leads less, because the flow of water is pulled down by the lower one. In the pipes of some individuals, no nozzles were placed at all; these are called "loose" pipes, and they are widened or narrowed at the whim of the water-man <note>term: "aquarius," the technician or laborer maintaining the pipes</note>. Furthermore, there is that intolerable fraud of the water-men: when water is transferred to a new owner, they punch a new hole in the distribution tank and leave the old one behind, from which they draw water to sell.

<summary>Frontinus describes various fraudulent methods used to steal water in Rome, such as using oversized or unstamped bronze nozzles and manipulating pipe placement. He proposes stricter stamping regulations for both the gauges and the connecting pipes to ensure administrative accountability.</summary>
